# DECISIONS — locked, with reasons

Every line here is a decision Dan made or approved, dated. Do not re-litigate these
without him. Where a decision was measured rather than chosen, the measurement is named.

## The charter (6 Sept 2026)

- **D-1** Cheap on the expensive parts, **perfect on the cheap parts**. Worldgen and
  (maybe) rendering may deviate; *everything else is absolute full parity*.
  Dan: "literally everything except worldgen and maybe rendering should be absolutely
  full parity, i really mean that."
- **D-2** Version target **1.18**, chosen because MC-Lite is doing big caves.
- **D-3** Audience is Dan and a few friends. Non-commercial, no redistribution.

## Scope, settled 6 Sept 2026

- **D-4** Block roster: **all of 1.18's block states**, not a survival-relevant subset.
- **D-5** The registry is **generated from Mojang's own blockstate and model JSON**,
  extracted from Dan's installed jar — not hand-written. **Measured against the real
  target jar, `1.18.2.jar`, 6 Sept 2026: 900 blockstates, 1,725 block models, 1,235 item
  models, 861 block textures.** (An earlier draft of this line quoted 1,062/2,137/1,012
  from `1.21.1.jar`, before the version was settled on 1.18.2 — those numbers were never
  about the version this project targets.) Extraction result: **900 blocks, 6,200 states,
  12,864 placements, 1,563 unique models, 809 referenced textures, 60 multipart blocks,
  0 missing models, 0 dangling textures, 0 empty states.** A generated registry cannot
  silently disagree with the real game; a typed one will.
- **D-6** Textures: **pre-1.14** ("the old ones"), from **his own game files**, built into
  a local atlas. Blocks that did not exist before 1.14 use modern textures, recorded as
  such. Programmer Art is **not** bundled in 1.21.1 *or in 1.18.2* — both checked, zero
  entries — so `1.13.2.jar` is the only old-texture source, and it is in hand.
  **Measured 6 Sept 2026:** 809 textures referenced by the roster, **527 (65%) come from
  1.13.2**, 282 fall back to 1.18.2, 0 missing, 41 animated (frame 0 taken and recorded).
  Every fallback is named in `assets/atlas-report.json`.
- **D-7** Texture compression must be **lossless** — "exact quality". Dedupe tiles ->
  shared indexed palette -> lossless WebP -> base64. Measure and report the real number.
- **D-8** **Full parity** for: gamemodes (creative/survival/spectator), the survival loop
  (health, hunger, damage, death, respawn, XP), inventories and crafting (real recipes,
  furnace fuel values, stacking, drag-splitting), the player hand and swing, block/item
  behaviour. These are tables and 2D drawing: exactly right costs time, not frames.
- **D-9** **Mobs come after everything else.** Full parity when they come. The one parity
  item with a real runtime cost — measure it on the 2200G.
- **D-10** **Structures come after blocks, textures, lighting and the parity items.**
  Dan chose "none yet" deliberately: structures on ugly terrain still look ugly.
  The plan is `docs/STRUCTURES.md`.
- **D-11** **Sounds: real, from his game files**, same local-only handling as textures.
- **D-12** File size ceiling **15 MB**. Parity beats portability. Still one file.

## Rendering and threading, settled 6 Sept 2026

- **D-13** Rendering stays **recognisably Minecraft-shaped**. Sodium/Starlight-style
  optimisation of the normal pipeline. **No** Distant-Horizons-style far-terrain LOD, no
  techniques that would make a screenshot look obviously un-Minecraft. Dan chose the
  conservative option here even though the charter would have permitted more.
- **D-14** **Full C2ME-style parallelism**: worldgen, meshing *and* lighting off the main
  thread, worker count scaled to the machine, a real job graph, and cancellation for work
  the player has walked away from. Chosen now because it is far cheaper to design in than
  to retrofit. Dan asked specifically that the **async** behaviour be researched against
  the real mods, and pointed at MineHTML's notes as prior art.
- **D-15** **WebGL2 is the default backend.** Measured 6 Sept 2026: the WebGPU path
  renders a **black world with a working GUI** on Dan's RX 6800XT. F9 swaps at runtime and
  fixes it. WebGPU had never executed anywhere before that — the cloud container has no
  GPU and always fell back. WebGPU stays opt-in until it is proven on hardware.
- **D-16** A **title menu** before the world. The game currently launches straight in,
  which is wrong, and the menu is also the right home for the backend picker, the seed
  and the quality preset.

## Inherited constraints (unchanged)

- **D-17** One self-contained `.html`, opened by double-clicking, therefore `file://`:
  no ES modules, workers from Blob URLs only, no `SharedArrayBuffer`, no runtime `fetch`.
- **D-18** Pure JS, no WASM.
- **D-19** World range −64 to 256, deep dark preserved.
- **D-20** Hardware ladder 7600 → 3600 → 2200G → Celeron. **The 2200G is the target.**
- **D-21** Worldgen is the "middle path": three cheap 2D fbm fields through splines, not a
  3D density stack. Terracing for plateaus and cliffs. Caves are cheese + worms + ravines.
- **D-22** A **full latitude-driven climate model** is the point of this project's
  worldgen — Hadley-cell precipitation bands, lapse rate, rain shadow, Whittaker biome
  lookup. World scale is a **configurable world-creation setting** with a sane default
  (research recommends 12,000 blocks equator-to-pole; Dan's mod reference is 35,000-50,000).
  See the climate research document.

## Process

- **D-23** MineHTML may be **copied from** for GUI, damage, hunger and inventory work —
  Dan chose "copy wholesale and adapt", with the words "but be careful". Careful means:
  a MineHTML session may be running concurrently, so **read, never write**, and adapt to
  MC-Lite's own architecture rather than importing MineHTML's assumptions.
- **D-24** Usage: **stop at ~97% of the session window, never touch usage credits.**
  Credits are real money ($50 limit, $1.19 used).

## Added 6 September 2026, session 1 (measured, not chosen)

- **D-25** ⚠ **`data/minecraft/worldgen/` is EMPTY in the 1.18.2 client jar.** Every biome,
  noise, density function, noise setting, feature, carver, structure set, template pool and
  processor list is a built-in registry defined in Java; 1.16.2–1.17.1 shipped them as JSON,
  1.18 moved them into code. **Any plan that says "port the worldgen JSON out of the jar" is
  wrong for this version.**
- **D-26** The worldgen data is therefore fetched from `misode/mcmeta` branch `1.18.2-data`
  — the mirror of Mojang's own `--reports` generator output — with the file list taken from
  that mirror's registry index so the fetch is **exhaustive by construction, not by
  crawling**. `tools/fetch-vanilla-data.mjs`, **766/766 files, 0 failures**. Mojang's own
  server-jar route is closed here: `piston-data.mojang.com` is refused by the egress proxy
  from both machines, and the device VM has Java 11 where 1.18.2 needs 17.
- **D-27** Quality settings are **one profile object resolved at boot**, never scattered
  `if (lowEnd)` branches. Done before the block roster grows, while the code is small.
- **D-28** ⚠ Multipart `when` clauses **enumerate only the value that TRIGGERS a part** —
  `oak_fence.json` names `"north": "true"` four times and never mentions `"false"`. A naive
  reader gets 1 state instead of 16. Property domains must be unioned across the whole file
  and seeded with `{true,false}` for any boolean-valued property.
- **D-29** ⚠ Blockstates files describe only what is **VISUAL**. `waterlogged` on slabs,
  `powered` on doors are absent because they change no model. The state space from
  blockstates JSON is a **lower bound**; the truth comes from `blocks.json`.
- **D-30** Every suite must contain at least one deliberately broken variant it is asserted
  to catch. Dan: *"make sure every test does something."* A test that cannot fail is not
  evidence. `modelcheck.mjs` already works this way; the rest follow it.
- **D-31** ⚠ Real per-state collision shapes (**898 blocks, 4,105 shapes**) and the ≈880
  hardness/resistance/light constants come from `PrismarineJS/minecraft-data`, cross-checked
  against the jar's own tags and loot tables. The plan's earlier assumption that ~60
  collision exceptions would need hand-tabulating is **obsolete** — do not do that work.
- **D-32** The full schedule is `docs/PLAN.md` (F / W / G / X tracks). It supersedes the
  ordering in `NEXT.md`. It does not supersede this file or `CHARTER.md`.

## D-33 … D-93 — backfilled 6 September 2026 (session 2)

⚠ **These sixty-one numbers were cited throughout `src/` and `tools/` and documented
nowhere.** This file stopped at D-32 while the code went on referring to D-41, D-57, D-85 and
D-93 as if they were written down. A decision number that points at nothing is worse than no
number at all: it reads as a citation, so nobody checks it.

Each entry below is the decision **as the code states it**, with the file that states it. Where
a number is not cited anywhere in the current source it is recorded as unused rather than
invented — `tools/doccheck.mjs` enforces both directions from now on, so this cannot drift again.

- **D-33** Stone ores and deepslate ores are **separate block ids**, kept in step by a pair
  table, so the surface pass never has to ask "which rock am I in?" twice. `04_worldgen.js`.
- **D-34** Aquifers are **faked** with one 2D noise per column rather than a real fluid-level
  density field. Revisited and kept. `04_worldgen.js`.
- **D-35** The world keeps a **deep dark** region below y=0. ⚠ Amended in session 2: sculk is a
  1.19 block with no 1.18.2 equivalent, so the region keeps its shape and its darkness and is
  filled with deepslate. See D-101.
- **D-36** The worker pool size is the quality **preset's** number, clamped by
  `navigator.hardwareConcurrency`. `09_jobs.js`.
- **D-37** *(unused — no citation in the current source.)*
- **D-38** The worker bundle runs **the same source files** the main thread does, not a copy, so
  an inline-mode fallback and a worker produce byte-identical worlds. `09_jobs.js`, `build.mjs`.
- **D-39** The **main thread is the sole owner of world data**. Workers receive copies and
  return buffers; nothing is shared. `07_world.js`.
- **D-40** A mesh job is sent as **packed section copies**, not an unpacked padded volume — the
  worker does the unpack, so the message is small and the copy is cheap. `07_world.js`.
- **D-41** A missing neighbour section meshes as an **opaque sentinel**, so the loaded area does
  not grow a shell of faces facing the void. `05_mesher.js`.
- **D-42** The worker message protocol is `init` / `gen` / `mesh` / `opt` / `cancel`, and
  cancellation is **advisory** — the result is dropped by the main thread. `09_jobs.js`.
- **D-43** Streaming budgets (chunks per frame, mesh milliseconds per frame) are **constants in
  one place**, not scattered. They are what decide whether a 2200G keeps 60 fps. `07_world.js`.
- **D-44** Device pixel ratio is **capped by hardware tier**: a 2200G iGPU at DPR 2 loses ~4x
  fill rate for nothing. `17_main.js`.
- **D-45** Section culling is a **6-plane frustum test against the section AABB**. `10_gfx.js`.
- **D-46** The render distance ring is **reallocated only when it grows**, not every time the
  camera moves a section. `10_gfx.js`.
- **D-47** `build.mjs` output is **idempotent** — no timestamps, no build ids — so an unchanged
  source produces a byte-identical file and a diff means something.
- **D-48** The build's minifier is **whitespace-only** by default. Renaming identifiers would
  make every stack trace in a bug report useless.
- **D-49** The build **syntax-checks** every module before writing the output.
- **D-50** The atlas ships as a **2D texture ARRAY, one tile per layer**, so layers cannot bleed
  into each other and REPEAT wrapping makes the greedy mesher's tile repeats exact — no UV
  inset, no `textureGrad` tricks. `06_atlas.js`, `12_gfx_webgl2.js`.
- **D-51** Animated textures are a **vertex flag the shader scrolls**, not an animated texture
  upload. Fluids only. `02c_states.js`, the shaders.
- **D-52** Every shading constant lives in `MCL.Gfx.SHADE` and both backends read it, so "the
  two backends render identically" is a testable claim rather than a hope. `12_gfx_webgl2.js`.
- **D-53** The depth prepass is **one program used twice**, not a second program variant —
  no toggling bugs. `12_gfx_webgl2.js`.
- **D-54, D-55** *(unused — no citation in the current source.)*
- **D-56** A cross model's four corners are all integers, so it costs the cube vertex path
  nothing. ⚠ Superseded in session 2: plants draw their real 1.18.2 models out of the model
  stream and the fake cross path is deleted. See D-104.
- **D-57** Atlas layers **0..56 are pinned** to exactly the tiles `Blocks.T` names, in that
  order, so the mesher's tile numbers mean the same thing on the main thread and in every
  worker without shipping the atlas to the workers. `06_atlas.js`, `build-atlas.mjs`.
- **D-58** Terrain is a **column function**, not a 3D density stack: one height per column plus
  carvers. This is the "middle path" the charter licenses. `04_worldgen.js`.
- **D-59** **Terracing** is what produces plateaus and hard cliff faces without a density stack.
  `04_worldgen.js`.
- **D-60** Surface rules apply only in a **band near the preliminary surface height**, so a cave
  floor eighty blocks down stays stone. ⚠ **SUPERSEDED IN PLACE by W6**: the rule is unchanged
  and the code moved — `src/04h_surface.js` interprets vanilla's own surface rules, and
  `G.surfacePass` is gone from `04_worldgen.js`. The band survives as `params.surfaceBand`.
- **D-61** A column's decoration reads its **neighbouring columns'** heights, which is why
  generation is a two-phase pass. ⚠ **SUPERSEDED by W8 (D-136)**: decoration is no longer a
  neighbour-reading pass over columns but a source/target split over CHUNKS, and the tree pass
  this decision was written for is deleted (D-139). The invariant it protected — a canopy is the
  same canopy from either side of a chunk border — is the one W8 inherited and proves.
- **D-62** Ores are **blobs from a per-chunk RNG**, vanilla-shaped by depth. ⚠ **SUPERSEDED by
  W8**: `src/04j_features.js` runs vanilla's own 29 configured ore features through vanilla's own
  placement modifiers, so the depth shape is the DATA's. `G.ORES`, `G.orePass` and `placeBlob`
  are deleted (D-126).
- **D-63** Worldgen is **deterministic from (seed, cx, cz)** alone — no order dependence, no
  global mutable state between columns. `04_worldgen.js`, asserted by `gencheck`.
- **D-64** The NOISE caves are **cheese + worms**, the two cheapest shapes that read as modern
  Minecraft. `04b_caves.js`. ⚠ This entry read "cheese + worms + ravines" until W7: ravines are
  now the CANYON CARVER out of vanilla's own data (D-126), and `04b_caves.js` no longer makes
  them.
- **D-65** The carver has a **per-cell early-out** before the expensive test. `04b_caves.js`.
- **D-66** A carver **never opens a cave into water above it** — draining the ocean through a
  cave roof is the classic bug. `04b_caves.js`.
- **D-67** ⚠ **SUPERSEDED by D-126.** It read: *"Ravines are carved as ellipse sweeps, not as a
  noise threshold. `04b_caves.js`."* Session 1's ravine was in fact a noise corridor, and it is
  gone; ravines are `04i_carvers.js`'s canyon carver, configured by
  `worldgen/configured_carver/canyon.json`.
- **D-68** The mesher is **greedy per face plane**, merging along one axis then the other.
  `05_mesher.js`.
- **D-69** Merge decisions are keyed on a **single packed integer** (tile, AO, light, tint,
  flags), so two quads merge iff every one of those is identical. `05_mesher.js`.
- **D-70** Light is seeded **in the worker, per column**, with cross-chunk spill fixed up on the
  main thread; the error at a chunk seam is at most one level. `04_worldgen.js`, `08_lighting.js`.
- **D-71** Streaming is **budgeted in milliseconds per frame**, not in chunks per frame, so a
  slow machine degrades by loading later rather than by stuttering. `07_world.js`.
- **D-72** Break times were hand-written in seconds. ⚠ Superseded in session 2: they are derived
  from vanilla hardness and the harvest bracket. See D-102.
- **D-73** An **ungenerated column reads as SOLID**, not as air, so the player cannot fall
  through the world while it streams in. `14b_physics.js`.
- **D-74** Saving is **localStorage and only localStorage**. `16b_save.js`.
- **D-75** The selection box and the break particles are **drawn in 2D** on the HUD canvas — no
  geometry, no upload, no extra draw call. `15_hud.js`.
- **D-76** Break particles are **twelve cubes of dust coloured by sampling the broken block's
  own texels**. `14_player.js`.
- **D-77** Player physics quotes **vanilla's own numbers**: gravity 0.08, jump impulse 0.42,
  drag 0.98. `14b_physics.js`.
- **D-78** Step height is vanilla's **0.6**. `14b_physics.js`.
- **D-79** The player is simulated at **20 Hz and interpolated** to the frame rate; rendering
  reads `ex/ey/ez`, never `x/y/z`. `14_player.js`.
- **D-80** The build keeps entry points that are **only reachable from tests** (`Gfx.selfTest`)
  rather than dead-code-eliminating them. `build.mjs`.
- **D-81, D-82, D-83** *(unused — no citation in the current source.)*
- **D-84** The pool size is the preset's, **clamped by the machine**. `09_jobs.js`.
- **D-85** Sections carry a **15-bit visibility mask** (which pairs of faces a single connected
  air component touches) and the renderer floods the section grid through it — a section of
  solid stone connects nothing and stops the flood dead. `05_mesher.js`, `10_gfx.js`.
- **D-86** WebGL2 uses **vertex arenas**: one buffer and one VAO per arena, a section is a slot.
  `12_gfx_webgl2.js`.
- **D-87** The streaming budget **scales with measured frame load**, so a struggling machine
  streams less rather than dropping frames. `07_world.js`.
- **D-88** A mesh snapshot is **returned to World's pool** the moment the worker no longer needs
  it. `09_jobs.js`.
- **D-89** There is a **hard resident chunk cap**; past it the furthest columns are evicted.
  `07_world.js`.
- **D-90** The sky is drawn **without a fullscreen clear pass** where fog already covers it —
  drawing it would cost fill rate to produce the clear colour. `10_gfx.js`.
- **D-91** Settings are **one profile object resolved at boot** and stored whole. `16_settings.js`.
- **D-92** The in-game benchmark is part of the shipped file, not a separate harness.
  `18_bench.js`.
- **D-93** **Fast leaves**: leaves become opaque and occluding, a canopy collapses to its
  silhouette and the cutout pass empties. Light attenuation is deliberately unchanged so the two
  modes cannot produce different lighting. `02c_states.js`. ⚠ **The MECHANISM stated here was
  partly wrong and D-178 is current:** leaves are not in the self-cull set at all — fast leaves
  cull because the state becomes solid-render, so this win applies only at the setting that asks
  for it. Fancy leaves had been paying it too.

## Session 2 — 6 September 2026

- **D-100** ⚠ **ONE ID SPACE.** The world stores a **registry REAL STATE id**, and the legacy
  49-entry block table no longer supplies a single block id. The alternative — keeping the 49
  and converting at the edges — was rejected by Dan directly: two id spaces means a conversion
  function in nineteen places and a bug living in whichever one somebody forgot.
  `02c_states.js` holds the per-state tables every hot loop indexes.
- **D-101** ⚠ **`sculk` is dropped.** It is a 1.19 block with no 1.18.2 equivalent and the
  version target is 1.18.2 (D-2). Dan's call: drop it rather than pin it to a stand-in. The deep
  dark keeps its shape and is filled with deepslate, which is what 1.18.2 puts down there.
- **D-102** ⚠ Break time is **derived**, not written down:
  `seconds = hardness * (requiresCorrectToolForDrops ? 100 : 30) / 20`. The harvest bracket is
  minecraft-data's `harvestTools` (present ⇔ true) — not `needsTier`, which is null for stone,
  and not `mineable/pickaxe`, which wrongly contains rails and ice. With it the derivation
  reproduces the hand-written table exactly on all twelve blocks that used to disagree.
- **D-103** ⚠ **AIR IS PINNED TO BLOCK 0** by `extract-blocks.mjs`. Section palettes, the
  mesher's 18³ scratch volume and all neighbour padding are zero-filled typed arrays that read
  zero as "nothing here". Alphabetically air is block 16, which would make state 0 a stone
  button and grow a wall of them at every chunk edge.
- **D-104** The mesher has **two paths and only two**: a greedy path for full cubes (1,683 real
  states, and almost all of the world by volume) and the baked model stream for everything else
  (17,356). The fake cross path is deleted — a plant draws the model vanilla draws.
- **D-105** The **render layer is derived from the texture's alpha**, measured per atlas tile at
  build time (opaque / cutout / blend), plus a short explicit list of blocks vanilla puts in the
  translucent pass with opaque textures (stained glass, ice, honey, slime). Vanilla keeps this
  in Java and it is in no data file; hand-writing it per block does not scale to 900.
- **D-106** **Fluids get a fabricated full-cube part.** Vanilla has no block model for water or
  lava — they are drawn by a dedicated renderer that varies surface height per corner — so
  without this a lake draws nothing. Two synthetic parts are appended past the registry's own.
- **D-107** Save format **v3** stores a palette of `(name, local state index)` and resolves
  `realFirst[block] + local` on load. The LOCAL index is what survives: a global state id moves
  the moment any earlier block gains a property. v1 and v2 saves are refused, not reinterpreted.
- **D-108** ⚠ **1.18's `blocks.json` reports hardness 0 for the 122 blocks added in 1.17.**
  Patched from `pc/1.19`, licensed by the two datasets agreeing on 658 of 658 blocks where 1.18
  has any value. Recomputed and asserted every run by `constcheck`.
- **D-109** The browser checks drive **headless Chromium over the DevTools protocol**
  (`tools/cdp.mjs`), with no npm dependency. `titlecheck` used to import playwright and was
  therefore un-runnable on any machine without a matching browser build.
- **D-110** **Every decision number cited in the source must exist in this file, and every
  number in this file must be cited or explicitly marked unused.** `tools/doccheck.mjs`.

## Session 3 — 6 September 2026 — Track W4, the climate

- **D-111** ⚠ **The climate mode and the world scale are WORLD-CREATION settings.** They sit on
  the title screen beside the seed, are written into the save envelope beside the seed, and are
  read exactly once by `Gen.init`. They are disabled on the title screen once a saved world
  exists, because changing either would move every biome out from under everything already built
  in that world. A save that predates them is a vanilla-climate world by definition, so they are
  **optional** in the envelope and default rather than forcing a save-format bump: the block-edit
  encoding did not change, and bumping it would have thrown away every existing save's buildings
  to record a field whose absence already carries the answer. ⚠ **D-182 flipped which mode a NEW
  world starts in to earth**; the load-side ternary described here is unchanged and still reads a
  save with no `climate` key as vanilla.
- **D-112** ⚠ **The compiled multi-noise climate table comes from `dimension/overworld.json`.**
  PLAN W4 carried this as an open item for two sessions and the risk register carried it as
  risk #2, with three named routes: the data generator (blocked — `piston-data.mojang.com` is
  refused by the egress proxy and the device VM has Java 11), a scrape of misode.github.io, or
  deriving it from the 61 biome files' own `climate` blocks. The third would have produced a
  **wrong** table quietly: those blocks carry 1.17's `temperature`/`downfall`/`precipitation`,
  which are the *rendering* climate, not the six noise axes. The route that works is a twelfth
  registry on the mirror already in use: a dimension carries its `biome_source` fully expanded,
  which is `MultiNoiseBiomeSource.Preset.OVERWORLD` already compiled — **7,578 entries over 50
  biomes**, verbatim from Mojang's own generator. Fetched, packed and asserted field-by-field
  against its source by `climcheck` section 1.
- **D-113** **Vanilla's `Climate.RTree` is BAKED at build time, not built at boot.** Measured:
  searching it costs 1.1 µs against 131 µs for a linear scan of all 7,578 entries, but BUILDING
  it costs 85 ms — on the main thread and in every worker, every launch, for a structure that is
  a pure function of data that never changes. `tools/pack-biomeparams.mjs` builds it once and
  ships it flat (843 internal nodes, 8,420 child slots, 48.7 KB deflated).
  Vanilla's `lastResult` ThreadLocal search seed is **not** ported: it changes nothing except
  which of two exactly equidistant entries wins, and it makes that depend on which query came
  before, which the determinism rule forbids.
- **D-114** ⚠ **The depth axis is `(surfaceY − y) / 128`, not `1 − y/128 + offset`.** The two are
  the same function in vanilla — `climcheck` section 4 asserts the identity across 3,000 points —
  because vanilla's surface is at `y = 128 · (1 + offset)`. MC-Lite's is not: deviation #1
  dropped `base_3d_noise`, so W3 anchors the surface on `HEIGHT_CURVE` instead. Taking vanilla's
  literal formula anyway gave a world whose surface columns selected **lush caves and dripstone
  caves as their top two biomes** — 642 of 2,000 sampled columns. The second form is vanilla's
  axis written in terms of the surface rather than in terms of an offset that no longer predicts
  the surface, and it is the only formulation that survives deviation #1.
- **D-115** ⚠ **Earth mode changes WHERE a biome goes, never WHICH biomes exist.** The physical
  model computes temperature, precipitation and aridity and then hands back vanilla's own
  `temperature` and `humidity` axes; the other four axes — continentalness, erosion, weirdness,
  depth — are terrain SHAPE and pass through untouched, so Earth mode does not move a single
  ocean, river or mountain. The dispatch is vanilla's 7,578-entry table in both modes. `climcheck`
  asserts that all 50 biomes remain reachable in both, because a mode that deletes a biome
  deletes its features, mobs and loot with it.
- **D-117** ⚠ **`Column.height` clamps to the world that EXISTS, not to the one the data file
  describes.** Vanilla's noise settings declare `-64..320`; MC-Lite's world is 20 sections,
  `-64..256` (D-19). W3 clamped to the declared 320. Measured on seed 1337: **2 of 160,801
  columns come out at y=256**, one block above a world that cannot hold them — a rate at which
  the failure reaches a player as "one mountain had its top sliced off" and never reaches a test
  that samples a neighbourhood. `Column.worldTop` is now the engine's top, `colcheck` walks
  58,081 columns for a height at or above it, and the wrong clamp is one of its anti-vacuity
  cases.
- **D-116** ⚠ **Vanilla's temperature axis is not ordered by temperature, and the Whittaker
  lookup is therefore 2D.** Read out of the shipped table: band T3 holds jungle and band T4 is
  desert at *every* humidity, so the hottest wettest place in the game sits one band BELOW the
  band that means "hot". A separable temperature→axis map cannot work, and the first version of
  `04f_earth.js` proved it by putting a desert on the equator. Aridity (P/PET), not
  precipitation, is the second axis — 400 mm is a desert at 30 °C and a forest at 0 °C.

## Session 3, continued — Track W5, the biomes

- **D-118** ⚠ **A SECOND, OLDER NOISE STACK ships alongside the Xoroshiro one.** 1.18 moved
  worldgen to Xoroshiro128++, but three `Biome` statics never migrated: `BIOME_INFO_NOISE`
  (seed 2345, the swamp grass mottle), `TEMPERATURE_NOISE` (1234, the wobble in the
  height-adjusted temperature above y = 80) and `FROZEN_TEMPERATURE_NOISE` (3456, three
  octaves, the frozen-ocean patchwork). All three are `PerlinSimplexNoise` over
  `LegacyRandomSource` — `java.util.Random` and Mojang's `SimplexNoise`, neither of which the
  Xoroshiro stack can produce. `src/03b_noise.js` carries both. The legacy random is verified
  against the JDK's own published outputs (`new Random(0)`: −1155484576, −723955400,
  0.730967787376657) rather than against itself.
  ⚠ All three seeds are **constants**, not the world seed: every world's swamps are mottled in
  the same places relative to the origin. That is vanilla, and it looks like a bug.
- **D-119** **The four data lists a biome carries — `spawners`, `spawn_costs`, `carvers`,
  `features` — are passed through BY REFERENCE, never copied or normalised.** Which mobs spawn
  where is not worldgen; it is "everything else" under D-1 and gets absolute parity, and a build
  tool that paraphrased those lists into its own shape would be deciding a parity question in a
  place no test would look. `biomecheck` asserts identity (`===` against the registry's own
  object) and then deep-walks 7,499 values against the JSON on disk.
- **D-120** ⚠ **`features` is not always eleven entries long.** Mojang's generator truncates
  trailing empty decoration steps: `end_barrens` has 0, `the_end` 5, `basalt_deltas` 8, the
  Nether biomes 10, and every overworld biome 11. The fix is `Biomes.featureStep(i, step)`
  returning an empty list past the end, **not** padding the array — padding would edit data
  D-119 requires to survive untouched.
- **D-121** **The biome TINT SEAM is a TEXTURE keyed on world position, not a per-vertex
  colour.** DELIVERED in W6 (`src/06b_tintmap.js`, both backends, `tools/tintcheck.mjs`); it was
  deliberately deferred out of W5, because until the surface rules landed the world still
  generated its biomes from session 1's twelve-value enum and tinting by the 1.18.2 map would
  have painted a desert's yellow onto a forest's floor. Why a texture: a per-vertex RGB needs a
  third 32-bit word on the greedy path (measured: `data0` has three spare bits and `data1` two),
  which is +50% on the vertex memory of the format carrying almost all of the world by volume,
  for a colour that changes once every few hundred blocks. The texture costs nothing per vertex
  because the shader already reconstructs world position, and bilinear filtering across its
  4-block grid IS the border blend. Three RGBA8 layers of 256×256 — 768 KB, covering 1,024
  blocks, re-anchored about once every 256 blocks of walking.
  ⚠ **One texel is four blocks and that is vanilla's own resolution**, not an approximation:
  biomes are stored and sampled at quart resolution, so a finer map would interpolate between
  duplicated values.
- **D-122** ⚠ **The tint sampling expression has NO half-texel offset, and the `+ 0.5` an earlier
  draft carried shifted every colour in the world two blocks north-west** — the exact failure the
  note above it claimed the offset was there to prevent. `wpExpr` is a VERTEX position, so it is
  a block CORNER: quart cell k spans the continuous range `[origin + 4k, origin + 4k + 4)` and
  has its centre at `origin + 4k + 2`, while texel k's centre in texture space is `(k + 0.5)/N`.
  The one requirement is `uv(origin + 4k + 2) = (k + 0.5)/N`, giving
  `uv(p) = (p − origin) · 0.25 / N`, and then a vertex at a cell boundary lands exactly halfway
  between two texels so the crossfade is centred on the border. `tintcheck` §7 asserts both
  halves at 601 cell centres and 601 boundaries and, in its anti-vacuity section, puts the
  `+ 0.5` back and requires the miss to be exactly two blocks. The code was wrong, the comment
  argued for the wrong thing in detail, and the screenshot looked fine: only the arithmetic
  caught it.

- **D-123** **A source chunk's carver walk is generated ONCE and bucketed by target chunk, not
  regenerated per target.** Vanilla carves chunk T by re-running the entire random walk of every
  chunk within range of T — with a range of 8 that is 289 generations of each chunk's carvers,
  288 of them thrown away. `src/04i_carvers.js` generates each source chunk's ellipsoids once,
  files them under the target chunks they touch, and caches that; a cache hit and a cache miss
  produce identical numbers, and `cavecheck` empties the cache in the middle of a run and
  requires the chunks to come out byte-identical. ⚠ **That is the whole of deviation #3's
  cheapening.** The range is vanilla's 8, the tunnel count is vanilla's, the radii are vanilla's:
  none of the licensed shortcuts was needed once the 288 wasted generations were gone. Measured
  cost of the carvers, steady state: **0.3–0.9 ms per chunk** of a 7.5 ms chunk.
- **D-124** ⚠ **The carvers do NOT reproduce vanilla's random SEQUENCE, and do not claim to.**
  Every other ported stage in track W is checkable against a file — the noise stack against
  published JDK outputs, the climate table against `dimension/overworld.json`, the surface rules
  against the rule tree itself. The carver algorithm is compiled Java and nothing in the jar
  states the order in which it draws. So MC-Lite honours the CONFIGURATION exactly (all four
  `configured_carver` files, field by field, both vertical-anchor forms, all three float-provider
  shapes) and reproduces the SHAPE (rooms, tunnels that branch once, decaying wandering pitch, a
  canyon with a 1,024-entry width table), and draws from its own PRNG — sfc32, seeded per SOURCE
  chunk from (seed, cx, cz, carver index). What W7's invariant needs is that the sequence be a
  deterministic function of the source chunk, and it is; `cavecheck` proves it from five
  approach directions and three chunk orders.
- **D-125** ⚠ **A ravine is a stack of discs cut to the ELLIPSOID'S OWN PROFILE, not a stack of
  full-width discs.** The width table is indexed by y, so a canyon cannot be one node — a node
  has one horizontal radius for its whole height. The first draft emitted a disc per block at the
  full radius, which is a CYLINDER: with `yScale` 3 that turned a 20-block ravine into a
  45-block-tall, 50-block-wide cathedral with a flat roof. Each disc's radius is now
  `hr · widthFactor · sqrt(1 − ry²)`, which reconstructs the ellipsoid and leaves the table doing
  only what it is for — scalloping the walls. It was obvious in an ASCII cross-section and
  invisible in every number being measured at the time, which is why `gencheck`'s pictures and
  `--print` exist.
- **D-126** **Session 1's noise ravines are GONE, superseded by the canyon carver.** `04b_caves.js`
  cut them as a 2D corridor along the zero-contour of a slow noise with a region gate — a decent
  fake of a thing MC-Lite now has for real, out of `configured_carver/canyon.json`. Two systems
  making ravines would have made twice as many, and a `params.ravines` flag that defaulted to
  false would have been dead code with a name that lied.
- **D-127** ⚠ **A carver removes vanilla's whole `CARVABLE_BLOCKS` set — 38 states, not two — and
  that is what a cave ENTRANCE is.** Session 1's noise caves removed `stone` and `deepslate`
  only, so no cave in MC-Lite had ever reached daylight: every one was a sealed pocket, and the
  ceiling of dirt and grass over it was the reason. The set now includes dirt, coarse dirt,
  rooted dirt, podzol, grass block, mycelium, sand, red sand, gravel, both sandstones, snow,
  packed ice, calcite, tuff, dripstone and all seventeen terracottas, exactly as vanilla's does —
  and pointedly NOT ores, so a tunnel through a vein leaves the vein hanging in the air, which is
  vanilla and is how you find one. `cavecheck` measures the openings: **3.8% of land columns** in
  its sample are open within three blocks of the surface. ⚠ The ocean guard (D-66) still holds
  above it: nothing is carved within six blocks of the floor of an underwater column, or the
  first tunnel to clip an ocean drains it.
- **D-128** **Sub-agent rules are MineHTML's, transposed rather than re-derived** — `docs/AGENTS.md`,
  on Dan's instruction (*"read mchtmls rules on agents and transpose them to this project, max 2 at
  a time"*, 6 Sept 2026). The four that carry: **two agents at a time** (Dan's number for this
  project, lower than MineHTML's four); **a weaker model only where a MACHINE grades its output**,
  never for interpretation or a decision; **the cost driver is what the agent READS on the way in**,
  so every worker prompt carries an explicit cheap-orientation clause; and **every dispatch is
  recorded from the agent's own testimony**, because a tier alias like `sonnet` is a request and not
  a record. ⚠ The first two dispatches under this rule both omitted their `DISPATCH-RECORD` line and
  are in the ledger labelled as non-compliant — and one of them returned a wrong count inside an
  otherwise exact report, which is the bright line earning its keep on its first outing.
- **D-129** ⚠ **`WorldCarver.getRange()` is FOUR and the chunk loop is EIGHT, and they are not the
  same number.** `ChunkGenerator.applyCarvers` iterates −8..+8 chunks around the one being
  carved; the carver's own step count is `(getRange() * 2 − 1) * 16` = **112 blocks**, not 240.
  W7's first draft used 8 for both. A tunnel's pitch decays toward level, so it holds its height
  for its whole length — at 240 steps a tunnel that clipped a flat desert stripped a 200-block
  open TRENCH through it instead of leaving an entrance, and cave volume roughly doubled.
  Measured: surface columns cut by more than three blocks went from **6.93% to 0.90%** of a
  128-block square when the two numbers were separated. Dan found it by playing — *"their are
  wrid walls in the deserts"* — and the walls were the sides of the trench.
- **D-130** ⚠ **The "cross models" setting drops DECOR — geometry that occludes nothing and is
  opaque to nothing — and not the whole model pass.** D-56 gave the setting its name when the
  model stream carried tufts and flowers. Session 2 made every block in the game a real registry
  state, which put **4,573 OCCLUDING states** on that stream — every slab, stair, carpet, cactus,
  and `grass_block` itself, whose side overlay is a second element — and from that moment the
  Celeron preset deleted the ground and the player could see through the world.
  `States.decor` is derived, not named: model geometry, covering no face of its own cell, not
  opaque by material. `facecheck` asserts that no decor state occludes anything and that
  grass_block, slabs, stairs, carpets, cactus and snow are not decor.
- **D-131** ⚠ **A section belongs in a render layer's draw list when EITHER stream has geometry
  in that layer.** The rule was the GREEDY count alone, which was the same thing while nothing
  but torches was on the model stream and stopped being the same thing the moment the world held
  real states: a forest section under `fancyLeaves: false` carries its cube quads in the OPAQUE
  layer and hundreds of model quads in the CUTOUT layer, so `quads[1]` is zero, the section never
  entered the cutout list, and none of it was drawn. Measured on ordinary terrain: **8 model-only
  layers over 68 sections, 2,854 quads** that the old rule discarded. `facecheck` §4 measures
  that reachability so the assertion cannot go vacuous.
- **D-132** ⚠ **A model quad is lit by the cell its cullface looks INTO, not by the cell it
  stands in.** The greedy path always did this; the model path took `light[own cell]`, which is
  15 for a plant standing in air — so plants looked right — and **0 for a grass block**, which is
  opaque and has no light inside it. Every grass block in the game rendered black. The mesher now
  carries seven packed light bytes per model block (its own, then the six neighbours in mesher
  face order) and each quad selects by its own cullface; a quad with no cullface — the two
  crossed planes of a tuft — takes the cell's own, which is where it stands.
- **D-133** ⚠⚠ **MODEL QUADS ARE EMITTED WITH THEIR CORNERS REVERSED, because Mojang's element
  order winds the opposite way from the shared index ramp.** The index buffer is one linear ramp
  and the pipeline culls back faces with `frontFace(CCW)`; the greedy stream's corner table is
  wound to suit it and the baked model corners are not. **Every single-sided model face in this
  game has been drawn inside out since the model stream landed** — grass block tops, slabs,
  stairs, carpets, cactus — and therefore invisible. Cross-shaped plants survived because a cross
  is two planes emitted twice, once each way, so one of the two always faced the camera: which is
  precisely why the world looked like flowers and grass tufts standing on nothing at all.
  ⚠ **`emitcheck` compared every emitted corner against the baked source and passed throughout**,
  because an inside-out quad has exactly the same four corners as a correct one. It now derives
  each quad's normal from the winding the GPU will see and requires it to point the way the
  quad's own face says — 119,989 assertions — and asserts in the same loop that the bakery's own
  order comes out inverted, so the reversal cannot be silently undoing something that was right.
- **D-134** **A placement's `heightmap` modifier is evaluated against `Column.height`, not against
  the chunk's live heightmap.** Vanilla recomputes its heightmaps as each feature is placed, so a
  flower placed after a tree sees the tree. MC-Lite evaluates every heightmap query against W3's
  pure column function plus the sea level — the terrain BEFORE any feature ran. ⚠ That is what
  makes the whole architecture possible: a SOURCE chunk's placements can be computed without
  generating that chunk's blocks at all, which is what lets a chunk be decorated from its
  neighbours without ever loading them. The cost is that two features in the same step cannot see
  each other, which shows up as a flower occasionally sitting where a tree now stands.
- **D-135** **A `below_top` vertical anchor resolves against THIS world's top, not vanilla's.**
  Vanilla's noise settings declare −64..320 and MC-Lite's world is −64..256 (D-19), so an ore
  that runs "from y=136 to the top of the world" runs to 255 here rather than 319. Resolving it
  against 320 and discarding what lands above 255 would keep the SHAPE of the distribution and
  throw away a third of the ore; resolving against our own top keeps the DENSITY, which is what a
  player notices. `above_bottom` and `absolute` need no such choice — both worlds have the same
  floor, which is why `ore_diamond`'s trapezoid still peaks at exactly y=−59.
- **D-136** ⚠ **W8's feature pipeline inherits W7's invariant and its shape, with one addition:
  the SOURCE chunk decides WHERE and the TARGET chunk decides WHETHER.** Placements are a pure
  function of (seed, source chunk) and are cached; the GENERATOR is re-run per target, because
  what a feature writes depends on what is already there — an ore blob replaces stone and leaves
  a diamond standing. The application order across the 3×3 is defined here rather than inherited:
  (decoration step, source chunk in a fixed spiral, index within the step). Vanilla's own order
  says nothing about a neighbour's spill, so MC-Lite states one and `featcheck` proves it from
  four approach directions.
- **D-137** ⚠ **CAVE BIOMES DO NOT DECORATE, and the reason is a measurement rather than an
  oversight.** (**Fixed in D-180**; this entry is the diagnosis and the rejected fix.) A chunk's
  feature list is taken from the biome at its origin's SURFACE, so `dripstone_caves` and
  `lush_caves` — real biomes with real feature lists — never get a chance: their dripstone clusters
  and moss patches compile, work when driven directly, and never appear in a generated world. The
  obvious fix, offering the union of every biome in the column and letting the per-position `biome`
  modifier sort it out, was **built and measured: 86 ms a chunk, up from 15**, because every
  placement then needs a 3D biome lookup and `Climate.biomeAt` is **38 microseconds**. Vanilla does
  not pay that: it computes the chunk's biome VOLUME once, at quart resolution, at the biomes stage,
  and every later question is an array read. So the fix is a cached per-chunk biome volume, written
  down as a W11/W12 job rather than half-done at five times the cost — and D-180 shows the estimate
  was a claim about the DATA as much as the algorithm.
- **D-138** **W8's feature generators live in five files, one per family, each registering itself
  through `Features.register`.** `04k` trees, `04m` water, `04n` terrain, `04p` cold and cave,
  `04q` coral — **32 registered generator types over 2,969 lines**, on top of the eight the
  pipeline itself handles inline (`ore`, `disk`, `simple_block`, `patch`, `column` and the three
  selectors). They are separate files for two reasons: a
  three-thousand-line generator switch is a file nobody reads, and they were written in parallel
  by five sub-agents against the published `Features.api` contract (see `docs/AGENTS.md`; all
  five recorded themselves as `claude-opus-5`, which is full strength, because writing a
  generator from vanilla's data is interpretation and the bright line forbids delegating that to
  a weaker model). ⚠ The contract's load-bearing clause is that a generator's `run` is called
  once per TARGET chunk its placement can reach, with the same position and an identically seeded
  rng — so it must be a pure function of its arguments, drawing every random it needs BEFORE any
  block read, or the two halves of a feature that straddles a chunk border disagree.
- **D-139** ⚠ **A STAGE IS NOT DONE UNTIL ITS PREDECESSOR IS DELETED, and W8 proved it by
  failing.** W8 replaced session 1's ore, plant and tree passes. Ore and plant were deleted with a
  ⚠ note in their place; **the tree pass was not**, and `if (P.trees) G.treePass(cx, cz)` kept
  running every chunk for the whole of W8 while three documents said it was gone. Measured over 200
  chunks: **29.8 logs and 101.9 leaves per chunk with the legacy pass against 25.5 and 76.6
  without** — one log in seven was a tree chosen by a twelve-value biome enum, standing next to
  vanilla's. The same file's ore note says why: *"two ore systems would have made twice as much ore,
  and a flag that defaults to false is dead code with a name that lies."*
  The close-out sweep found the rest of the class, all live and read by nothing: the twelve-value
  enum itself (`G.BIO`, `LEGACY_MAP`, `LEGACY_OF`, `G.legacyOf`, `cBiome`), whose own comment
  promised it would go when W8 landed; the `F_TREEMIX` noise field and the `cMix` array — **256
  `noise2` calls in every chunk generated for two stages**; sixteen frequency and offset constants;
  `clamp1`, `fold` (D-58) and `terrace` (D-59) left behind by W6; and `candidates()`, the
  union-of-biomes fix D-137 rejected. All deleted.
  **The generic rule: a replacement stage's acceptance test must compare against a world with the
  old system OFF, not merely count what the new one produced** — every check in the suite counted
  trees, and a count cannot tell you a quarter of them came from the wrong source. The preset flag
  goes with the pass: `params.trees` and `params.ores` are gone from `defaults()`, replaced by
  `params.features`, with an explicit `false` under either old name still honoured in `G.init` so a
  caller that means "off" gets off.
- **D-140** ⚠ **NOTHING STANDS ON NOTHING: the write-time support rule.** Dan played the session 3
  build and reported *"tons of floating grass, and a floating mob spawner"* while the suite was
  green at 675,213 assertions. Measured over 169 chunks at seed 1337: **2,864 dead bushes, 1,934
  grass, 427 glow lichen and 47 mushrooms in mid-air**. The cause is a JOIN: a placement's y comes
  from `Column.height`, the terrain BEFORE the carvers (D-134, and that purity is what makes W8's
  3x3 architecture affordable), W7's carvers then take the ground out (D-127), and the plant is
  written into a cell whose floor no longer exists. Vanilla avoids it via
  `SimpleBlockFeature.place` → `state.canSurvive`, per-block rules in compiled Java that cannot be
  ported.
  **What CAN be derived is the CLASS of rule**, from `material` in the pc dataset: `plant` → needs
  a floor (54 blocks), `vine_or_glow_lichen` → needs one solid face anywhere (2), plus a NAMED list
  of the six that hang the other way up (`cave_vines`, `cave_vines_plant`, `hanging_roots`,
  `spore_blossom`, `weeping_vines`, `weeping_vines_plant`), because `material` calls a cave vine a
  plant exactly like grass. Two blocks are deliberately left with no rule: `pointed_dripstone`
  grows from either a floor or a ceiling, and `lily_pad` stands on water, which is not solid.
  The class is packed into the runtime blob's spare flag bits (16|32, no size change), reaches the
  engine as `States.support[state]`, and is enforced in `Features.setBlock`, the one chokepoint
  every generator writes through. A plant counts as support for a plant (keeping two-tall grass and
  sugar cane), and **a neighbour outside the target chunk reads as support**, because a rule whose
  answer depends on which chunk is being filled is a seam (D-136). The acceptance test is
  `tools/floatcheck.mjs`, and its point is that it walks the FINISHED world: every existing feature
  check counts what a feature produced, and a dead bush in mid-air is a perfectly correct dead bush
  by that measure.
- **D-141** ⚠ **A DUNGEON NEEDS A ROOM AROUND IT, AND ITS GATE MAY NOT READ BLOCKS.** The same
  session found **158 spawners in open air over 169 chunks** and **5.5 monster rooms per chunk**,
  where vanilla makes a dungeon every several chunks. `MonsterRoomFeature` walks its whole footprint
  first: solid floor and ceiling everywhere, and between one and five open cells around the walls —
  none and it is a sealed box nobody finds, more than five and it hangs in a cave. W8's own note
  (04n's header) had dropped that abort as unaskable, because the footprint spans up to four chunks
  and `run` is entered once per chunk with the same arguments (D-136): a gate that reads blocks
  answers differently in each pass and tears the room in half.
  **The fix is a gate made only of PURE functions of position**, which every pass agrees on by
  construction: `Column.height` for "is it underground" and `Gen.isCave` — W7's cheese field, pure
  noise — for "does a wall open onto something", accepted at one to three openings. It is vanilla's
  rule with a smaller mouth: worms and ravines are random walks and cannot be asked pointwise, so a
  room vanilla would have opened onto a tunnel is lost — that is the cheapening. The cage is a
  single cell, so exactly one chunk ever writes it and it MAY read: no floor under it and no ceiling
  over the room, no spawner. Measured after: **121 rooms over the same 169 chunks (0.72 a chunk) and
  4 unhoused cages**, all four rooms whose floor a later overlapping feature took back out — an
  interaction vanilla has too, which is why `floatcheck` §3 holds the bound at 5% rather than 0 and
  says so.
- **D-142** ⚠ **W9'S SCHEDULE IS STAGED: the incremental light pass runs on the MAIN THREAD, in
  bounded slices, and W11 is where it moves off it.** PLAN W9 asks for "Starlight-style: light
  propagates on the worker, not the main thread, with no main-thread stalls"; W9 delivers the second
  half of that sentence. The bulk pass — sky-down-the-column plus a column-local BFS — stays on the
  worker inside `Gen.lightPass`; the two things it CANNOT do, chunk seams and player edits, run in
  `src/08_lighting.js` on the main thread with a per-frame microsecond budget
  (`Settings.lightBudgetUs`, 800 low / 2,000 default). `step()` returns mid-BFS when the budget is
  spent and resumes next frame, so the work is bounded by construction and cannot stall a frame
  however large the edit — which is the property "no main-thread stalls" actually asks for.
  It is not on a worker YET for transport, not principle: a border seed needs the column and its
  eight neighbours, and shipping nine columns of blocks and light per seed is exactly the job-graph
  problem **W11** exists to solve for worldgen, meshing and lighting at once (D-14). The engine is
  written against an ADAPTER (`Light.setAdapter`) rather than against `World`, so moving it is a new
  adapter, not a rewrite — and that is also what lets `tools/lightcheck.mjs` run the real engine
  over a hand-built room.
  ⚠ **Two rules were WRONG before this and are fixed with it**, in both the worker pass and the
  engine: vanilla's propagation cost is `max(1, opacity)`, not `1 + opacity` — a water block costs
  one level exactly like air, and the old formula made every cell under water a level too dark,
  compounding with depth — and full sky light falls straight down through a zero-opacity cell
  WITHOUT losing a level, while the old column seed kept a once-attenuated value all the way to
  bedrock. The removal pass carries the matching exception: a 15 under a 15 is derived light and
  must be cleared, which the plain `n === level - 1` test walks past, leaving a lit shaft under a
  block the player just placed.
- **D-143** ⚠ **A HARDWARE BENCHMARK CANNOT BE A STAGE'S ONLY ACCEPTANCE.** PLAN W10 named
  `bench.mjs` on the 2200G profile as its acceptance, and that number cannot be produced by the
  suite: the machine the suite runs on has no GPU — GL is SwiftShader — and the bench there
  reports 15 fps for reasons that have nothing to do with the mesher. A stage whose only test
  cannot run is a stage nobody can regress, which is how the spiral, the eviction cap, the
  snapshot pool, the cancellation accounting and the visibility mask all reached session 4 built
  but unasserted. The split, and the rule for every later stage that names a frame rate:
  **everything CPU-side gets a machine-independent check** (`tools/streamcheck.mjs`), with its
  throughput numbers stated as a REGRESSION FENCE — wide enough that a slow CI box passes,
  narrow enough that a mesher three times slower fails — and **the hardware question goes on the
  human list in NEXT.md**, where the person with the hardware answers it. A fence is not a
  performance claim and the check says so out loud, so nobody later reads 0.45 ms a section as a
  promise about the 2200G.
- **D-144** ⚠ **W11'S LIGHT TRANSPORT IS DEFERRED ON A MEASUREMENT, NOT ON A SHRUG.** With D-142
  the seam and edit passes run on the main thread. Before deciding whether that is a problem it
  was measured, on the suite's machine, over 81 real columns: **border settling costs 1.64 ms per
  column (5,916 seeds, 10,077 spreads) and 200 block edits cost 2.0 ms end to end.** Streaming
  admits a handful of columns a frame, and `Settings.lightBudgetUs` (800 low / 2,000 default)
  slices whatever is left over into later frames — so the worst case is a few milliseconds spread
  across several frames, and `budgetHits` counts it when it happens. Moving it to a worker means
  shipping a column and its eight neighbours per seed, which is the same transport worldgen and
  meshing already have and which W11's job graph should design once for all three. Deferred with
  the numbers written down, and the engine written against an ADAPTER so the move is a new
  adapter rather than a rewrite. ⚠ The two bugs `parcheck` §5 found on its first run are the
  reason the order-independence test is in the suite permanently: **a light pass that is correct
  for one arrival order and wrong for another cannot be seen in a screenshot, because both
  screenshots look plausible.**
- **D-145** ⚠ **THE FRUSTUM TEST BELONGS AT DRAW TIME, NOT INSIDE THE VISIBILITY FLOOD** — and the
  artifact it caused was invisible to every check in the suite until one took two screenshots.
  `Gfx.floodVisible` refused to ENTER a section outside the frustum, which the file's own comment
  called "Minecraft's own artifact — a section reachable only through sections that are off-screen
  is dropped" (D-8). `tools/cullcheck.mjs` measured the price by taking the same frame twice, flood
  on and off: **3,160 pixels of a 435,000-pixel frame differed underground, every one of them
  BRIGHTER with culling on** — a hole through a wall, exactly where a player standing in a cave
  would be looking. The frustum is a property of the ENDPOINT, not of the sight line, so the gate
  moved out of the graph search into `buildLists`, where vanilla and Sodium both have it. Measured
  after: **pixel-identical to the frustum-only picture on the surface AND underground, 18 sections
  drawn where the frustum alone draws 22 and the old flood drew 27, 6,950 triangles against 7,518**,
  for about 1,100 extra flood steps. Fewer draws, fewer triangles, no hole.
  ⚠ **The measurement that nearly sent this the other way, and a trap any later session can fall
  into: the adaptive render distance (D-46).** Turning the flood off makes frames slower, the
  adaptive system answers by pulling the render distance in, and the screenshot is then missing
  83,000 pixels of distant terrain that culling had nothing to do with. The first run read that as
  "the fix makes it worse" and it was ninety minutes before `Settings.adaptive = false` went into the
  check. **Any A/B screenshot of this game freezes the adaptive render distance first**, and
  `cullcheck` says so at the line that does it.
- **D-146** ⚠ **THE ATLAS BLEEDS COLOUR UNDER ITS TRANSPARENT TEXELS, and the bug it fixes is the
  one Dan could see.** A cutout texture stores a colour under every texel including the invisible
  ones, and in the 1.13.2 jar that colour is **black**: `acacia_leaves` is 101 black texels out of
  256. Nothing reads them while the texel is discarded — but two things do. `fastLeaves` (D-93),
  the DEFAULT on the low presets, moves leaves into the OPAQUE layer where nothing is discarded; and
  every mipmap and bilinear tap averages a texel with its neighbours, so a black texel one step
  outside a leaf darkens the leaf at any distance. Session 4 photographed a savanna and every tree
  in it was mottled with black holes. **No assertion in the suite could see it** — the atlas, the
  mesher and the shader were all correct and the picture was wrong (§23's lesson for the fourth
  time). `tools/build-atlas.mjs` now floods the opaque colour outward into the transparent texels,
  alpha untouched: **42,020 texels in 289 tiles**. Cutout rendering is unchanged by construction;
  fast leaves and every filtered tap get the leaf's own colour instead of black.
  ⚠ The fill COPIES a neighbour's colour rather than averaging: the first version averaged, invented
  colours the textures never had, and cost 140 KB in the shipped file because the atlas PNG is
  stored indexed — for texels that are either discarded or filtered anyway. `tilecheck` §5 asserts
  the pass ran AND walks the real pixels of seven named cutout textures, requiring that no
  transparent texel beside an opaque one is still black.
- **D-147** ⚠ **GENERATE ONE RING FURTHER THAN YOU MESH, or the outermost ring of the world is
  invisible for ever.** `World.stream` requested generation and meshing over the SAME `spiral(rd)`.
  A section is only meshed once all eight neighbouring COLUMNS exist (`neighbourhoodReady` — the
  mesher needs a 3x3 to resolve faces at a border), so the outermost ring could never satisfy that:
  the world was a disc of radius rd−1 with a ring of generated-but-never-meshed geometry around it,
  and **256 sections sat permanently dirty**. Found by flying underground and photographing the
  frontier — at rd 4 that is a wall of sky-coloured nothing 16 blocks closer than it should be, and
  on the surface the fog hides it, which is why it survived three sessions. Generation now walks
  `spiral(rd + 1)` while meshing walks `spiral(rd)`; eviction's margin was already 2. Vanilla loads
  renderDistance + 1 for exactly this reason. Measured at rd 4: **368 section meshes against 174
  before, everything within d=3 fully meshed and nothing stuck dirty inside the render distance.**
  `streamcheck` §2c drives the real `W.stream` against a recording stub and asserts the two radii
  differ by exactly one ring.
  ⚠⚠ **And the first version of this fix was still wrong, which `soakcheck` caught by flying two
  thousand blocks and then stopping.** `spiral(rd + 1)` is a DISC, and the eight neighbours a rim
  column needs include the diagonals — the furthest at **d² = (rd+1)² + 1**, one unit outside that
  disc. So the four columns on the compass points still had no north-east neighbour and stayed
  unmeshable: nine or ten sections each, dirty for ever, invisible unless you looked due east.
  `W.spiral` now takes a slack in SQUARED units and generation asks for `spiral(rd + 1, 1)`;
  measured over a 2,000-block flight, **zero stuck sections inside the render distance**, where the
  first fix left 29. That is why `soakcheck` exists: a bug that needs TIME and MOTION cannot be
  found by a check that photographs one moment, and the first fix for one of those is itself worth
  re-testing over time.
  ⚠ One thing the same investigation found and did NOT fix, because it is a G-phase job: with the
  camera INSIDE a solid block the screen shows the clear colour, because the mesher correctly emits
  no interior faces. Vanilla draws a full-screen quad of the block you are standing in. It is in
  NEXT.md's gap table.
- **D-148** ⚠ **THE LIGHT QUEUE HAD A 2,048-BLOCK WORLD IN IT.** `Light`'s ring packed a voxel into
  ONE int32 — x:11, y:10, z:11, biased — which is exactly ±1,024 blocks in x and z. Session 4's
  audit did the arithmetic on a coordinate from its own soak flight: **x = 1441 packs and unpacks to
  x = −607**. So every block edit and every chunk seam more than a thousand blocks from spawn was
  applied to a completely different place, or — more often, because that place is usually not loaded
  — dropped by the adapter and never applied at all. Nothing crashed, and no check could see it:
  every light test in the suite ran within a few dozen blocks of the origin, and `lightcheck`'s own
  pack/unpack assertion tested the four corners of the range it was asserting rather than the range
  a player reaches. The ring now stores **three** words per entry — x and z whole, and one packed
  word holding y, the level and the channel — so there is no coordinate limit at all, and
  `L.seed(x,y,z,level,ch)` replaces the callers that were packing by hand. `lightcheck` §2b is the
  test that would have caught it: the same room, the same assertions, built at **(5000, −7000)**,
  plus an assertion that nothing was written back at the origin. ⚠ **The general lesson, worth more
  than the bug: a test that runs at the origin tests the origin.** Anything that packs coordinates
  gets tested at a coordinate a player actually reaches.
- **D-149** ⚠ **THE WORLD STOPS DRAWING AT ABOUT THREE MILLION BLOCKS, and the fix is
  camera-relative rendering — deferred here, DONE in D-179.** Session 4's far-coordinate audit flew
  to x = 29,000,000: **402 section meshes resident, 89 columns loaded, light correct at the player's
  own cell — and 0 triangles drawn.** Not the culling heuristics: a frustum plane's constant is a
  distance from the WORLD ORIGIN and the camera's matrices are `Float32Array` because that is what a
  GL uniform takes. At three million blocks the gap between representable float32 values is about a
  quarter of a block, the plane equations stop meaning anything, and every section tests as outside
  the frustum. The same limit applies to the vertex path (`uOrigin` is a float32 world position), so
  the first visible wobble starts around a hundred thousand blocks — the same place vanilla's does
  and for the same reason.
  **It was scoped and NOT done here on purpose:** it touches both backends and the HUD, the only GPU
  available to test it was a software rasteriser, and the session's instruction was to stop at the W
  gate and test rather than rebuild. `streamcheck` §3b fenced what was true then — correct to
  ±2,000,000 blocks, wrong past four million. ⚠ **That fence was itself wrong** (it sampled one
  heading per distance and the failure is chaotic); see **D-179** for the fix, the correct
  measurements, and the lesson about fences that record limits.
- **D-150** ⚠ **A PLAYER-PLACED GLOWSTONE LIT NOTHING, because `queueEdit` skipped emission for
  opaque blocks.** Most emitters in Minecraft ARE solid: glowstone, lava, jack o'lanterns,
  shroomlight, sea lanterns, magma. `Light.queueEdit` computed the new block-light level inside
  `if (!opaque)`, so placing any of them stored nothing and seeded nothing — while the SAME block
  placed by worldgen lit correctly, because `Gen.lightPass` seeds every emitter without asking
  about opacity. A split like that survives a green suite easily: the world looks right, and only
  building lights up by hand shows the bug. It was found by an audit probe that put a glowstone
  underground, not by any check — because ⚠ **every light test in the suite used a TORCH**, which
  is one of the few emitters that is not a solid block. Vanilla stores an emitter's own level in
  its own cell whatever its opacity; only the SKY channel is zero inside a solid. `lightcheck`
  §4b now places glowstone, lava and a jack o'lantern, asserts the falloff at four distances,
  breaks each one and asserts the light goes away, and asserts that the sky channel inside the
  solid emitter is still zero. **The general form: when a test picks an example, check whether it
  picked the easy member of the family.**
- **D-151** ⚠ **`docs/ARCH.md` EXISTS.** Twenty-two `src/` headers had been citing sections of it
  since session 1 — §1 through §17: the constants, the section codec, the face numbering, the
  vertex layout, the chunk state machine, the frame order — and the document was never written.
  `doccheck` §6 had it exempted BY NAME, with an assertion that it was still missing, so that
  writing it would fail the check and force the exemption to be deleted rather than let the map
  quietly appear half-done. That is what happened in session 4's closing pass: the file is
  written, the exemption list is empty, and `doccheck` now asserts the opposite — that ARCH.md
  exists and that at least fifteen files cite it. It is a REFERENCE and it says so in its first
  line: look up the section the code names, do not read it end to end. It is deliberately NOT in
  `doccheck` §7's reading budget for the same reason.
- **D-152** ⚠⚠ **THE WHOLE GAME COLLIDED AS FULL CUBES — `Physics.shapesFor` was a stub, and two
  checks were shaped so that neither could see it.** `shapeAt` — the function every sweep calls —
  went through `Ph.shapesFor(id)`, which returned `Ph.FULL_CUBE` for every id and ignored its
  argument. Its own comment said what to do: *"it is the single line that changes when the world
  starts storing registry real-state ids: it becomes `Ph.shapesForState(state)` … and slabs become
  step-onto-able with no other edit."* **The world started storing real states in session 2** and
  the line never changed, so for two sessions you could not step onto a slab, a fence was a wall a
  block wide, a carpet was a full block, and F7's 4,105 measured collision shapes were loaded,
  packed, shipped and never consulted.
  ⚠ **Why nothing caught it.** `physcheck` tested `shapesForState` — the real function, which was
  correct — and its FIRST SECTION asserted that `shapesFor` returns `FULL_CUBE` for every block,
  enshrining the stub as expected behaviour. `gamecheck`'s collision tests all walked into a wall
  of STONE, which is a full cube, so every one passed either way. It took a test that walks into a
  SLAB. That is D-139's lesson for the third time (a replacement is not done until the thing it
  replaces is gone) and the session's other for the second (when a test picks an example, check
  whether it picked the easy member of the family).
  **Three things changed.** `shapesFor` is now `shapesForState`. `physcheck` §1 asserts the two are
  the same function across a seventh of the state space, that stone still comes back as `FULL_CUBE`
  BY IDENTITY (so `clip` keeps its fast path) and that an oak slab does not, with an anti-vacuity
  break that fails on the stub. And `shapesForState` now CACHES by shape index (4,105 shapes shared
  across 20,344 states): it used to build a fresh array of fresh arrays on every call, which is
  garbage in the hottest loop in the game and is also what made the shapes impossible to compare by
  identity.
  ⚠ **A second bug fell out of the first**, and it needed the fence to find it: `clip` tested only
  the cells the player's box overlaps, but **a shape can stick out of its own cell** — a fence is
  1.5 blocks tall — so a player who had jumped to y+1.2 overlapped only the cell ABOVE the fence and
  sailed over it. The cell rectangle swept ACROSS is now one wider on every side, with the full-cube
  fast path skipped for those extra cells: a full cube cannot reach out of its own cell, and letting
  the fast path answer for them makes the FLOOR collide with every horizontal step (measured: every
  speed in `gamecheck` went to zero). Widening the SWEPT axis was tried too and is wrong for the
  same reason in the other direction.
- **D-153** ⚠ **BREAKING A BLOCK LEFT THE HOLE DARK.** `Light.queueEdit` computed the changed
  cell's own new level — an emitter's emission, or full daylight falling in from directly above —
  and seeded the removal pass. It never seeded the cell's NEIGHBOURS, so a cell opened by a break
  had to be lit BY them and nothing asked them to try: dig sideways into a hill with a torch
  behind you and the new cell stayed at zero until some unrelated edit happened to re-run the
  flood through it. `fuzzcheck` measured it as **181 light discontinuities over 2,000 random
  edits**, the worst a fully lit cell against a black one. The fix is six queue entries: after an
  edit, push the six face neighbours at their current levels and let the ordinary propagation
  pass flow in. ⚠ Note what did NOT catch this: `lightcheck` §4 breaks a torch and asserts the
  light goes away (removal, which was correct), and `smoke` breaks a block and asserts the BLOCK
  is gone. Nobody had asserted that a hole gets lit.
- **D-154** ⚠ **NO LIGHT SPREAD SIDEWAYS INSIDE A TREE.** `Gen.lightPass` bounds its horizontal BFS
  at `topL = maxH + 2`, and `maxH` is the column height from `Column.heightAndClimate` — **computed
  before the features run**. A tree is six to thirty blocks taller than the ground it stands on, so
  every cell in and above a canopy kept whatever the straight-down pass gave it and was never lit
  from the side. Measured in four freshly generated columns: **553 lateral sky discontinuities — air
  at 12 next to air at 15.** In play that is hard black patches inside and under every canopy, on
  the ONE part of the world a player is always looking at. The fix is one variable: the sky pass
  already walks each column from the top down to find the heightmap, so it records the highest
  non-air cell it actually passed and the spread ceiling is that. Measured after: **zero.**
  ⚠ **PARTLY WRONG, corrected by D-193:** the code fed that ceiling from `hi`, the highest OPAQUE
  cell — the heightmap's question — not from the highest non-air cell this entry describes, so
  canopies above the tallest stone in their chunk still went unlit. D-193 adds `hiAny` and is
  current.
  ⚠ Both this and D-153 were found by `tools/fuzzcheck.mjs` on its first run, which is the argument
  for having written it: hand-written cases test what someone thought of, and both of these are
  joins between two stages that were each correct on their own.
- **D-155** ⚠ **FLOATING GRASS, THE OTHER HALF.** D-140 put a `canSurvive` gate on the worldgen
  side, and Dan still reported "tons of floating grass", because worldgen was never the only way to
  get it. `World.setBlock`, the one runtime edit path, did neither of the two things vanilla does:
  it did not REFUSE a placement the block could not survive (a tuft placed in mid-air stayed there),
  and it sent no block update to the six neighbours, so **mining the dirt under a plant left the
  plant hanging** — which is what a player does hundreds of times an hour. Both halves now live in
  `World.setBlock`: a support-ruled state that fails `World.canSurvive` is refused before the write,
  and after the write a queue drains the six neighbours, breaking anything that can no longer
  survive. It is a QUEUE and not recursion, so a stacked sugar cane, a two-tall grass and a column of
  vines fall in one pass at constant stack depth; nested `setBlock` calls enqueue rather than
  starting a second drain. `World.canSurvive` is the live twin of `Features.supported` and must
  answer the same three rules, including treating an UNLOADED neighbour as support — the alternative
  makes a vine at the load frontier vanish as you walk away from it. The save replay writes through
  `Section.set`, not here, so a rebuilt column is not re-judged and a build cannot be eaten by a
  replay ordering.
  ⚠ What let this live: `fuzzcheck` §3 already counted floating plants and asserted
  `unsupported <= ruled * 0.5` — "at most half of them may float" — a fence written around the gap
  instead of a statement of the rule. It read **55 of 167** and passed. The assertion is now `=== 0`,
  plus the two halves stated directly at a hand-picked site. **A fence that accommodates a known gap
  will accommodate an unknown one.**
- **D-156** ⚠ **EVERY SLAB, STAIR, WALL, FENCE, CARPET AND SNOW LAYER WAS A FULL LIGHT BLOCKER.**
  `States.opaque` is opaque BY MATERIAL (the pc dataset's `transparent` flag) and is the right
  answer for FACE CULLING — a bottom slab's down face really does hide the top of the block
  beneath it. The light engine and `Gen.lightPass` were asking it a different question. Vanilla's is
  `getLightBlock`: `isSolidRender ? 15 : (propagatesSkylightDown ? 0 : 1)`, and `isSolidRender` is
  false for anything whose collision shape is not a full cube. **196 blocks** are opaque by material
  and not full cubes, and every one held no light at all and cast a full shadow: a snow layer under
  open sky read **sky 4 with the air above it at 14**, so every snow-capped mountain — the
  silhouette 1.18 is famous for — rendered near-black on top, as did dirt paths, farmland, and every
  slab, stair and carpet a player places.
  The fix needed no new data: the pc dataset already ships vanilla's own number as `filterLight`,
  loaded all along as `States.atten` (stone 15, leaves 1, water 1, glass 0, **slab 0, snow 0,
  carpet 0**). So `States.lightSolid[s] = atten[s] >= 15`, and the two light consumers —
  `Light.worldAdapter().opaque` and `Gen.lightPass`'s two propagation tests — ask that instead.
  `opaque` is untouched and still owns culling and the heightmap. `Settings.fastLeaves` flips
  `opaque` for leaves and deliberately does NOT flip `lightSolid`: a graphics setting must not
  change the light in the world.
  ⚠ `facecheck` §3 asserted `dark * 20 < tops` — "at most five per cent of upward faces may be
  black". At the shipped seed it read 0 of 483 and passed; at seed 4242 it reads **45 of 1024**,
  still under the fence. The assertion is now exact and local — a face may be dark only when the
  cell it looks INTO is dark — which is a statement of the rule instead of a tolerance around it.
  Second time this session (see D-155) that a percentage fence was the only thing between a live
  bug and the suite.
- **D-157** ⚠ **PLACEMENT NEVER CHOSE A STATE.** A block id here is a REAL STATE (D-100), so every
  placement is a CHOICE — which way a stair faces, which half of the cell a slab fills, which axis a
  log lies on, which wall a torch hangs on. `Player.placeBlock` wrote the hotbar's default state
  verbatim, so every stair faced north, every log stood upright, and **a torch clicked onto a wall
  stayed the standing `torch`** — Dan's *"torches don't properly attach to walls"*. Once D-155 began
  enforcing support, that click was refused outright and nothing appeared at all, so the two
  decisions had to land together.
  The blocker was that the runtime carries no property NAMES — deliberately: 900 blocks of them is
  40 KB nobody needs. What it now carries is the SUBSET placement resolves, as numbers: a
  **placement table** (`MCLP`, trailing section of `block-runtime.bin`, +1.6 KB deflated) giving,
  per block and per property, the stride to multiply a value index by and which of a shared 15-value
  vocabulary that property offers. Vanilla's local-state numbering is positional — properties in
  declaration order, the last varying fastest — so a local state is a mixed-radix number and ONE
  DIGIT can be rewritten in place. That is `States.withProp(state, prop, value)`, the whole
  primitive: 389 property entries over the roster, with every block's properties multiplying out to
  its own state count, so the arithmetic is exact rather than assumed (the packer throws if it ever
  stops being).
  On top of it, `Player.placementState` states the four rules once instead of per block — `axis`
  from the clicked face, `half`/`type` from which part of the cell was clicked, `facing` from the
  player (`getHorizontalDirection().getOpposite()`) or from the wall for a wall-mounted block — plus
  vanilla's `StandingAndWallBlockItem`: 43 standing/wall pairs, derived by name so a block added to
  the data is picked up without editing the packer. It is PURE, so `gamecheck` drives it directly
  rather than through a click.
  ⚠ Still G2's, and stated rather than hidden: a slab placed against a slab does not MERGE into a
  double (that needs the target cell's own state), and a stair's `shape` is left `straight` rather
  than auto-connecting to its neighbours.
- **D-158** ⚠ **A WALL TORCH DID NOT FALL WHEN ITS WALL DID.** D-155 gave `setBlock` a support
  cascade, but the support CLASSES (D-140) could not describe a wall-mounted block: floor,
  ceiling and any-face were the three, and a torch on a wall needs a fourth — **BEHIND**, the
  neighbour opposite its own `facing`. So D-157's freshly correct wall torches hung in the air
  after the wall was mined, which is the same floating-block class Dan reported, one block later.
  Class 4 is derived, not listed: it is exactly the wall half of D-157's standing/wall pairs plus
  the two blocks whose facing follows the clicked face — 45 blocks. Both twins implement it,
  `World.canSurvive` and `Features.supported`, and both read the facing through
  `States.propValue`, so no new packed data was needed beyond the class itself.
  ⚠ The support class had to widen from TWO bits to THREE in the registry flag byte. A stale
  `& 3` reads a wall-mounted block as class 0 — no rule at all — and says nothing about it, so
  `R.support`'s comment names the trap.
- **D-159** ⚠ **LEAVES WERE GREY ON EVERY PRESET BELOW MEDIUM.** `setFastLeaves` moves leaves
  into the OPAQUE layer, which is what vanilla's fast graphics does too. The fragment shader,
  both backends, then computed the biome tint as `mix(white, tint, t.a)` — the tint weighted by
  the texel's ALPHA. That was harmless while only genuinely opaque blocks reached mode 0, where
  `a` is 1 everywhere. A cutout texture in the opaque pass is not discarded, so the leaf
  texture's holes arrive with `a = 0`, `mix(white, tint, 0)` is WHITE, and every hole rendered
  UNTINTED. Vanilla leaf textures are greyscale and carry no colour of their own, so the result
  was grey leaves — which is exactly what Dan reported, on exactly the presets that turn fast
  leaves on. The tint is now weighted by alpha only in the CUTOUT pass, where every surviving
  texel is opaque anyway and the weight does nothing; opaque and translucent tint in full.
