  ⚠ Both shaders were changed in the same edit: WebGL2 and WebGPU must render identically
  (CLAUDE.md constraint 3), and a fix applied to one of them is half a bug.
  ⚠ How it was found: by LOOKING. `facecheck` meshes leaves under every preset and asserts the
  quads — same tile, same tint index, same everything — because the mesh was never wrong. The
  bug was three instructions downstream in the shader, and no check in the suite reads a pixel
  of a leaf. A screenshot at the `low` preset shows it instantly.
- **D-160** ⚠ **THE RENDER DISTANCE SLIDER DID NOTHING ON A FAST MACHINE.** `Settings.adapt`
  (D-46) walks the render distance one chunk at a time inside a band of `base-3 .. base+2`, and
  `base` was read from `PRESETS[S.preset]`. Moving the slider calls `markCustom`, which sets
  `S.preset = 'custom'`; there is no `PRESETS.custom`, so the fallback took the band from
  whatever preset the machine was DETECTED as. A player on a machine detected `high` who pulled
  the distance down to 4 got a band of 13..18, and the first fast frames walked their setting
  back up to 18 — slowly enough to read as the world loading in rather than as the settings
  fighting them, which is why it survived. Dan reported it as "set the render distance lower and
  the chunks render in anyway".
  The band is now centred on `S.rdBase`, which is what the PLAYER asked for: `applyPreset` sets
  it, and `S.setRenderDistance` — the one place the slider writes, and it clamps — moves it with
  every manual change. It persists with the rest of the settings. Adaptation still works in both
  directions: at a manual 4 the band is 2..6, and slow frames still pull it down.
  ⚠ The class, worth naming: a value with TWO writers, one of them a UI and one of them a control
  loop, and no agreed record of which one the player meant. The fix is a chokepoint, the same
  answer as D-140's `Features.setBlock` and D-155's `World.setBlock`.
- **D-161** ⚠ **THE WHOLE WORLD WAS TERRACED IN 3-BLOCK STEPS.** D-59's terracing pulls heights
  toward multiples of eight by `terraceStrength(erosion)`, which was `0.75 * smoothstep((1-e)/2)`.
  Erosion is a Gaussian centred on ZERO, and at erosion 0 that expression is `0.75 * 0.5 = 0.375` —
  so the terrace jump was `8 * 0.375 = 3` blocks for **95% of the world**: every terrace boundary
  everywhere was the same 3-block ledge at the same 8-block vertical spacing, a corduroy landscape.
  Dan reported it as "3 block high steps in terrain that really don't happen in vanilla", twice.
  ⚠ **The measurement is what made it obvious, and it is worth keeping as a technique: histogram the
  height step between ADJACENT COLUMNS.** A terrain field's step distribution decays monotonically —
  85.7% flat, 10.5% one block, 0.64% two — and this one **spiked back up to 1.61% at exactly three**.
  A distribution that stops decaying at one value is a quantum, and a quantum in terrain is a bug
  however pretty the code that makes it.
  The plan asked for blocky UNERODED land and smooth eroded land; ordinary land is neither and was
  getting half strength. The curve now ramps from erosion −0.25 to −0.80 instead of from +1.0, so
  85.6% of the world is not terraced at all and the rest spreads its cliffs over 1..6 blocks. After:
  the step histogram decays monotonically again (81.4 / 15.4 / 1.72 / 0.79 / 0.39).
  ⚠ This is a WORLDGEN SILHOUETTE change and therefore Dan's call, not mine; it is recorded with the
  numbers so it can be reversed by moving two constants.
- **D-162** ⚠ **A SETTINGS CHANGE FLASHED THE WHOLE SCREEN.** The clear colour is the FOG colour,
  which is the SKY — `[0.62, 0.76, 0.98]`. So a frame that draws nothing is not a black frame, it
  is a full screen of pale blue, and against a dark landscape that reads as a white flash. Two
  things made the world draw nothing: `Settings.push` called `Gfx.dropAll()` — which destroys
  every section mesh on the GPU — immediately before `World.remeshAll()`, and `remeshAll` then
  cleared every chunk's `meshed` mask, which is what the draw list is built from. Measured: a
  preset change took the draw list to **0 sections for 15+ consecutive frames**.
  Neither was necessary. The buffers are not INVALID after a settings change, only STALE, and a
  stale mesh is worth drawing for the third of a second it takes to replace it — which is exactly
  what vanilla does when you change a graphics setting. `dropAll` is gone from that path and
  `remeshAll(dropGpu)` only clears `meshed` when the buffers really are gone: the backend swap
  (F9) and loading a different world. Measured after: **0 blank frames**, worst draw-list depth
  during the change 16 against a baseline of 14.
  ⚠ Dan reports the flashes as random and not obviously tied to changing a setting, so this is
  one cause and not provably the only one. What is now asserted, in `soakcheck` §5c, is the
  CLASS: the draw list must never collapse. Anything else that empties it will fail there.
  ⚠ **It was not the only one, and this entry's "0 blank frames" is about THIS cause only:** see
  D-171/D-175 for the second and **D-194** for the third, which supersedes any reading of this
  entry as closing the white-flash class.
- **D-163** ⚠ **THE SUITE COULD NOT SEE A COLOUR.** Thirty-four checks, 676,000 assertions, and
  D-159 — grey leaves on every preset below medium — sailed through all of them, because every check
  that touches leaves asks the MESHER what it emitted and the mesh was correct.
  `tools/palettecheck.mjs` is the answer: it photographs the world at each preset with the render
  distance held constant, so fog is not what is being compared, and asserts that a quality preset
  changes the frame rate and not the palette.
  ⚠ **Its first design did not work, and the failure is the useful part.** A whole-frame comparison
  — mean saturation, per-channel mean, hue histogram — was written first and validated by putting
  D-159 BACK into the shader. It passed: the worst preset moved mean saturation 5.8% against a 15%
  bound. A frame is mostly ground and sky, and a bug that touches only leaves is a bug in a few per
  cent of the pixels; averaging over the frame averages it away. What works is a DIFFERENCE: toggle
  nothing but `fancyLeaves`, diff the two frames, and measure only the pixels that moved — which
  are, by construction, the leaves, whether or not the camera was aimed at them. On the shipped
  build those pixels keep their saturation; with D-159 reintroduced they lose **41.1%** of it. The
  broad comparison is kept as §1 because it catches the other shape of the same class, with its
  blindness written into the header.
  ⚠ **The general lesson: validate a new check by reintroducing the bug it was written for.**
  Anti-vacuity breaks are synthetic — they prove the arithmetic can fail, not that the check can see
  the thing. Both designs passed their anti-vacuity section; only one saw the bug.
- **D-164** ⚠ **EVERY FIX THIS SESSION WAS VALIDATED BY PUTTING ITS BUG BACK, AND ONE CHECK
  FAILED THAT TEST.** D-163 learned the technique on `palettecheck`; this applied it to all ten
  of the session's post-gate fixes mechanically — revert the fix, rebuild, run the check that is
  supposed to hold it, and require the check to FAIL.

  | fix | check | what it said with the bug back |
  |---|---|---|
  | D-153 | `fuzzcheck` | 63 light discontinuities, worst a lit cell against a black one |
  | D-154 | `fuzzcheck` | 101 discontinuities, sky 15 against sky 13 |
  | D-155 | `fuzzcheck` | 31 of 111 floor-supported blocks floating |
  | D-156 | `lightcheck` | ⚠ **PASSED** — see below |
  | D-157 | `gamecheck` | 20 failures |
  | D-158 | `gamecheck` | 3 failures |
  | D-159 | `palettecheck` | 41.1% of the changed pixels' saturation lost (D-163) |
  | D-160 | `gamecheck` | 2 failures |
  | D-161 | `colcheck` §3b | "a preferred cliff height at step 3: 0.96% against 0.31% at 2" |
  | D-162 | `soakcheck` | 15+ consecutive frames drawing nothing |

  ⚠ **`lightcheck` did not catch D-156**, and the reason is worth more than the fix. Its §4c
  asserted the TABLES — `States.lightSolid[slab] === 0`, `States.opaque[slab] === 1` — and then
  exercised the light engine through the adapter THAT FILE builds. Both were still correct when
  the bug was reintroduced, because the bug was one line inside `Light.worldAdapter()`, which
  nothing in the check ever calls. **A check that never calls the function the game calls cannot
  see a bug inside it.** §4c now asks the shipped adapter directly, and with the bug back it says
  "the SHIPPED light adapter calls oak_slab opaque — it is reading the culling table".
  D-161 had no check at all until this sweep; `colcheck` §3b is now that check, and it is the
  measurement that found the bug in the first place — the adjacent-column step histogram, whose
  monotone decay a quantum breaks.
- **D-165** ⚠ **PLANTS GREW OUT OF TREE CANOPIES AND STOOD ON EACH OTHER.** D-140's floor rule
  read "a solid block under it, OR any block that itself has a floor rule", and both halves were
  too wide. **Leaves are SOLID** — they have a collision box — so grass and dead bushes grew out
  of canopies; and "anything with a floor rule" let a plant stand on a plant stand on a plant.
  Measured over 36 chunks: **19 plants on leaves and 7 on plants**, `dead_bush on dead_bush`
  among them. Dan saw the towers from inside the game: *"multiple small grasses stacked on top of
  each other, some even stacked on top of flowers, some 3 high, some on tree leaves"*.
  A plant stands on OPAQUE GROUND — dirt, sand, stone, terracotta, farmland — and the comment
  that justified the old exception said what the exception was for: the upper half of a two-tall
  grass and the segments of a sugar cane. That is `States.stacksOnSelf`, and it is narrow: a
  block may stand on ITSELF, and only if it has an upper/lower `half` (which the D-157 placement
  table can be asked directly) or is one of the fourteen segmented plants vanilla implements a
  block at a time. `dead_bush` is in neither, so it can no longer tower. After: 0 and 0.
- **D-166** ⚠ **NO PRESET DROPS GRASS AND FLOWERS ANY MORE.** The `celeron` preset set
  `crossModels: false`, which drops all decor geometry (D-56, D-130) — the cheapest frame in the
  game. Dan, on seeing it: *"celeron shouldn't drop it. that's just a cheap solution and may hurt
  gameplay."* That is the governing principle applied exactly: the expensive things are terrain,
  meshing and lighting, and those are where MC-Lite is allowed to be clever; a tuft of grass is
  a table and a quad, and removing it changes what is IN the world rather than how it looks. The
  weakest tier takes its budget from render distance, DPR, AO and fancy leaves instead. The
  setting still exists for a player who wants it; no preset turns it off, and `gamecheck` asserts
  that of every preset so one cannot quietly acquire it again.
- **D-167** ⚠ **A TORCH STUCK TO THE UNDERSIDE OF BLOCKS.** D-158 gave the WALL half of every
  standing/wall pair the "behind" support class, and stopped there. The STANDING half had no rule
  at all: the class comes from the pc dataset's `material`, and a torch is not a plant, so
  `support[torch]` was 0 and it could be placed on a ceiling, in mid-air, anywhere. Dan found it
  by trying it. The standing half of every pair — 43 of them, torches, signs, banners, heads,
  coral fans — now carries the FLOOR class, which is what vanilla gives it, and it is derived
  from the same pair table rather than listed. Floor-ruled blocks went from 54 to 97.
- **D-168** ⚠ **UNDERWATER PLANTS CARVED AIR HOLES IN THE OCEAN.** Vanilla asks a block for its
  `getFluidState`, and for seagrass, kelp, tall seagrass and any waterlogged block that answer is
  WATER: the plant and the water occupy the same cell, so there is no surface between them.
  MC-Lite stored only the plant, and the mesher's `selfCull` matches an identical id and nothing
  else — so the water around a seagrass emitted **six translucent faces into it** and every
  underwater plant sat in a bubble of air. Dan recognised it immediately: MineHTML had the same
  bug. `States.waterIn` is the answer, filled two ways — a named list of the blocks vanilla
  implements as water-filled with no property to say so, and generically from the `waterlogged`
  property for the other **6,895** states, which meant adding `waterlogged` (and `upper`/`lower`,
  which double plants use where stairs use `top`/`bottom`) to D-157's placement vocabulary. The
  mesher culls a water face against any neighbour that also holds water. Measured: 6 faces → 0,
  with water-against-stone still 6 as the control.
- **D-169** ⚠ **THE SUPPORT RULE HAD THREE IMPLEMENTATIONS AND `floatcheck` HELD THE STALE ONE.**
  `Features.supported`, `World.canSurvive` and `tools/floatcheck.mjs` each restated the rules.
  D-165 tightened two of them; the third — the CHECK — kept the old version, so it would have
  walked the world Dan was complaining about and passed it. This is D-164's finding a second time
  in a single session, and the second time is what makes it a rule: **a check that reimplements
  the rule tests the copy.** `States.floorOk`, `States.ceilingOk` and `States.anyFaceOk` are now
  the one implementation, taking the NEIGHBOUR'S STATE rather than coordinates so that a worldgen
  scratch buffer, the live world and a generated column can all call the same function.
- **D-170** ⚠ **EVERY SCREENSHOT COMPARISON IN THE SUITE WAS READING THE WRONG BYTES.** Headless
  Chromium's `Page.captureScreenshot` returns a **3-channel RGB** PNG. `cullcheck`'s `compare` and
  `palettecheck`'s `stats`/`diffStats` indexed it as `(y * w + x) * 4`. Two consequences, the second
  serious: every "pixel" after the first was a MISALIGNED triple — pixel n's red read from byte 4n
  instead of 3n, so the red it compared was an earlier pixel's green — and past three quarters of
  the way down the image the index ran off the end of the array, where `undefined - undefined` is
  NaN, `NaN > 0` is false, and **every difference in the bottom quarter of the frame counted as
  zero**. `cullcheck` had been printing `mean NaN%` in its own failure message for a whole session.
  `pngdec.mjs` now exports `toRgba`, the screenshot helpers call it, and `compare` and `stats` THROW
  on a non-RGBA image rather than quietly producing numbers. `pixelAt` and everything built on it
  were always channel-aware; it was only the two files that indexed the raw buffer.
  ⚠ What this cost: with the comparison fixed, `cullcheck` immediately failed on a real bug it had
  been unable to see (D-171). **The check was green for a session because it was blind, which is
  worse than a check that fails.**
- **D-171** ⚠ **A SECTION OUTSIDE THE FLOOD'S GRID WAS REPORTED AS OCCLUDED.** `Gfx.floodHas`
  returned **false** for any section outside the visibility flood's scratch grid, and false means
  "definitely hidden". Meshes routinely outlive the flood's radius: a column is evicted at
  `rd + evictMargin`, and the adaptive render distance (D-46) pulls `rd` in while meshes built at
  the old distance are still resident — so on a normal frame there are dozens of sections past `r`
  holding real geometry. They were culled as "occluded" while the frustum alone would have drawn
  them: a band of missing terrain at the horizon, measured at up to **2,975 pixels** of distant tree
  canopy appearing and disappearing with the flood.
  Outside the grid is UNKNOWN, not hidden, and the honest answer to unknown is `true` — let the
  frustum decide. `World.visOf` already states exactly this rule for an unloaded column. **A culling
  test may only ever say NO when it is certain.**
  ⚠ The check needed forcing. `cullcheck` §2 caught this only two runs in three, because whether
  out-of-grid meshes exist depends on what the adaptive system happened to be doing. §2c now MAKES
  the condition — load at rd 10, pull to rd 4 with eviction frozen — and asks `floodHas` directly
  about those sections rather than diffing the whole frame. With the bug reintroduced it says "69 of
  69 meshes outside the flood grid are reported OCCLUDED"; the whole-frame version said nothing at
  all on the same run. It also asserts that inside the grid the flood still answers BOTH ways, so the
  fix cannot degenerate into `return true`.
- **D-172** ⚠ **VANILLA'S OWN HEIGHT MAP IS IN THE REPO, AND WE ARE 37 BLOCKS OFF AT THE PEAKS.**
  `density_function/overworld/depth.json` — a file this project ships — is
  `y_clamped_gradient(-64..320, 1.5..-1.5) + terrain_shaper_spline("offset")`, and the mean surface
  is where depth crosses zero. So vanilla's offset-to-height map is arithmetic, not a guess:
  **y = -64 + 384 (1.5 + offset) / 3**, i.e. `128 + 128·offset`. Applying it to our offsets puts the
  whole world at y 100-130 — exactly the observation `04d_column.js`'s header records as the reason
  W3 replaced the map with a hand-fitted eight-anchor `HEIGHT_CURVE`.
  ⚠ **That observation was made with a term missing.** Vanilla's `TerrainShaper.offset(p)` is
  `spline(p) - 0.50375F`, and **that subtraction lives in Java, not in the JSON**, so a port that
  reads the spline tree out of the data and stops does not have it. Ours does not. With the constant
  restored, vanilla's linear map lands on the real game's heights at every landform: ocean floor 35,
  deep ocean 46, plains 66, plateau 108, mountains 177, peaks 182 — the evidence that the constant is
  a TRUE OMISSION and not part of deviation #1 (Dan's question, asked before any of this was changed).
  ⚠ **AND IT IS STILL NOT A STRAIGHT FIX, WHICH IS WHY NOTHING WAS CHANGED.** Deviation #1 drops
  `base_3d_noise`, and that term carries vertical VARIANCE as well as position. `HEIGHT_CURVE` does
  two jobs at once: it absorbs the missing 0.50375 (an accident) and it STRETCHES the range to stand
  in for the variance deviation #1 removed (deliberate, the "lite" trade the charter licenses).
  Adopting vanilla's map alone would put the means right and leave the world flatter than vanilla.
  How much stretch to keep is a decision about how the game LOOKS, it has a free parameter, and it is
  Dan's — so this session measured it and left it alone. Today: ocean 40 vs 35, deep ocean 48 vs 46,
  plains 69 vs 66, plateau 127 vs 108, **mountains 214 vs 177**. `colcheck` §3c derives vanilla's map
  from the shipped file, asserts the file still says what this decision claims, and **PINS the
  disagreement at under 45 blocks** — not a tolerance around a bug but a statement of a deliberate
  deviation's size, so a change to the world's vertical scale fails a check instead of arriving
  unannounced.
- **D-173** ⚠ **THE VISIBILITY FLOOD'S OWN LIMIT, SEPARATED FROM ITS BUGS.** Once D-170 let
  `cullcheck` read its screenshots correctly, the flood-on/flood-off diff was ~3,000 pixels of
  435,000. Two of the causes were real bugs and are fixed (D-171: outside the grid reported as
  occluded, and the corner wedges of the square grid the flood's CIRCLE is inscribed in — the
  flood refuses any step past `ddx² + ddz² > r²`, so a quarter of the grid is never visited and
  was being reported hidden). What is left is the algorithm itself: a section-granular visibility
  graph cannot express a diagonal sight line that clips the CORNER of a section it never enters,
  so at the horizon a one-to-two-pixel band along the top of a distant canopy is drawn without
  the flood and not with it. Vanilla and Sodium have the same shape of gap.
  ⚠ The check was restructured rather than have its number widened, which is the move this
  session has condemned four times. §2 PINS the far-field residue with the mechanism named — a
  regression that widens it fails — and **§2d makes the sharp claim instead**: pull the render
  distance to 4, so every section on screen is near and large, and the two pictures must be
  PIXEL-IDENTICAL with no fence at all. Measured: **199 sections drawn, 0 pixels differ, noise
  floor 0.** A culling bug that hides something a player can walk up to fails there, which is the
  failure that matters; the residue is a horizon artifact with an owner in NEXT.
- **D-174** ⚠ **A BOUND MUST BE DERIVED FROM A MEASUREMENT, NOT CHOSEN.** `palettecheck` §1 broke
  when D-166 kept decor at every preset: celeron moved the frame's mean saturation 16.4% against
  a flat 15% bound. Widening 15 to 20 would have been the same mistake as D-155's "at most half
  of them may float" and D-156's "at most 5% may be black". Instead the bound is now MEASURED in
  the same run, one flag at a time: a preset may move the picture as much as its own flags do,
  plus a small margin. Fast leaves are worth 13.6% of the frame's saturation, so celeron's
  allowance is 19.6% and its 16% passes for a stated reason.
  ⚠ Doing that turned up a second thing: **ambient occlusion cannot move saturation at all.** It
  is a per-vertex BRIGHTNESS multiplier and saturation is `(max − min) / max`, which a uniform
  scale leaves exactly alone — measured at 0.1%. An assertion that AO must move saturation would
  have been a check that can only ever fail, and it was written and then removed. What is
  asserted now is only what the allowance rests on: that AO leaves saturation alone, and that the
  leaf mode moves it, so the budget has something real behind it.
- **D-175** ⚠ **THE WHITE FLASH, MEASURED — two of its three causes.** Dan reported random
  full-screen white flashes, *"MOSTLY when new chunks and stuff are loading"*. The clear colour is
  the fog colour, which is the SKY (`[0.62, 0.76, 0.98]`), so a frame that draws little is mostly
  pale blue and against dark terrain reads as a white flash. **D-162** was the first cause: a
  settings change dropped every GPU mesh, taking the draw list to 0 for 15+ consecutive frames.
  **D-171** is the second: `floodHas` reported every section outside the flood's grid as OCCLUDED,
  and the grid's radius IS the render distance — which D-46's adaptive system moves by one chunk
  every couple of seconds, most often while chunks are arriving, culling every mesh beyond the new
  radius on the very next frame.
  Measured with the same probe on both builds, sweeping the render distance 10 → 4 → 10: **before,
  the draw list fell by up to 60% in a single frame, three times past 50%; after, 44% worst and none
  past 50%** — and 44% is the honest consequence of drawing a smaller world. `cullcheck` §2e is that
  probe, kept: it forbids the draw list falling further than the world it is drawing. With D-171
  reintroduced it says "280 of 280 meshes outside the flood grid are reported OCCLUDED".
  ⚠ **This entry did not claim these were the only causes, and it was right not to: there is a
  third. See D-194** — evictions sharing the upload budget — which supersedes the sense in which
  this entry and D-162 read as closing the class.
- **D-176** ⚠ **STAIRS WERE PLACED BACKWARDS.** D-157 gave placement one rule for `facing` —
  the player's horizontal direction, OPPOSITE — because that is what a furnace and a chest do:
  furniture faces the player. A STAIR does not. Its raised step is on the side the block faces,
  which is measurable from the collision shape rather than remembered: `oak_stairs[facing=east]`
  puts its upper box at x 0.50..1.00, the east half. So a stair placed by a player walking east
  must face EAST, or the step lands on the player's own side and they walk into a wall instead of
  up it. Vanilla spells this as `StairBlock.getStateForPlacement` calling
  `getHorizontalDirection()` where `HorizontalDirectionalBlock` calls `.getOpposite()`; doors and
  beds take the same rule, and the three are derivable by suffix rather than listed.
  ⚠ `gamecheck` asserted the WRONG convention — it was written from the same wrong assumption as
  the code, so it agreed with it. It now asserts the GEOMETRY: the raised half of a placed stair
  must be on the side away from the player, read out of `Physics.shapesForState`. And it asserts
  the other convention on the same axis, so a change that "fixes" stairs by breaking furnaces
  cannot pass. A check written from the same belief as the code tests the belief.
- **D-177** ⚠ **GLAZED TERRACOTTA DOES NOT ROTATE.** (**Fixed in D-181**; this entry is the
  diagnosis and the measurement of the limit, not the current state.) Found by sweeping the roster
  and asking, for every block with a `facing` or `axis` property, whether its values actually
  produce different geometry. Sixteen do not: all four facings of every glazed terracotta render
  identically, and a directional pattern that tiles into designs is the entire point of the block.
  The bake is correct — the four states bake to four different parts. The loss is in the GREEDY
  vertex format: `data1` packs `(tile, uRep, vRep, corner, tint)` into 32 bits with nothing spare,
  so the mesher regenerates canonical UVs from the corner index and a per-face UV ROTATION cannot be
  expressed. `classifyPart` accepts the part as a full cube because its positions, cullfaces and
  tiles are all cube-shaped; it never looks at the UVs. It was not fixed here because `classifyPart`
  is on the path EVERY block in the world takes and the target is a 2200G.
  ⚠ **The real size of the limit is 176 of 688 full-cube parts, across 40 blocks** — command blocks,
  jigsaw, observers, pistons, logs and glazed terracotta all have at least one face whose baked UV is
  not the canonical layout. For all but the terracotta the TILE also differs per face, so the right
  texture is still on the right face and only its rotation is lost: invisible on a log's underside,
  near enough on a piston. Glazed terracotta is the case where the rotation is the ENTIRE difference
  between the four states. `statecheck` §4b pins both numbers. (D-181 splits the 176 into 154
  rotations, now fixed, and 22 mirrors, still a limit.)
  ⚠ **Three things the sweep got wrong first.** Comparing TILES alone called every `*_wood` and
  `*_hyphae` block a bug — a bark cube is the same texture on all six faces, so its three axes bake
  to genuinely identical parts and vanilla looks the same either way; checked against the geometry
  and CLOSED, not left open. Comparing the part's UVs in STORAGE ORDER found nothing, because a
  rotation does not change the SET of UV layouts in a part, it changes which FACE carries which one
  — the signature has to be keyed by face. And the first home for the section was `meshcheck`, which
  reads the JSON and never loads the engine, so it could not ask `States` anything.
- **D-178** ⚠ **LEAVES SELF-CULLED IN BOTH GRAPHICS MODES — 65-67% OF EVERY LEAF FACE IN THE WORLD
  WAS NEVER EMITTED.** Dan, playing: *"i am seeing trees with half their leaves cut off."* He was
  looking through a canopy at the sky. `SELFCULL_SUFFIX` in `02c_states.js` §3 carried `'_leaves'`
  and `setFastLeaves` wrote `SR.selfCull[st] = 1` on BOTH branches, so turning fancy leaves back on
  never cleared it; the mesher then dropped every face between two leaf blocks — vanilla's
  FAST-graphics behaviour, applied while the FANCY default was on.
  ⚠ **A misreading of `skipRendering`, and it revises part of D-93's leaf reasoning.** In vanilla,
  `HalfTransparentBlock` and `IronBarsBlock` override it; `LeavesBlock` does not. Fast leaves cull
  in vanilla because they become SOLID-RENDER, and MC-Lite already models that:
  `setFastLeaves(true)` gives a leaf state a full `SR.cull` mask and the ordinary opaque-neighbour
  rule removes the same faces. So leaves leave the self-cull set entirely and **D-93's win survives
  untouched at the setting that asked for it.**
  **Measured before the fix**, real terrain at seed 1337, four regions of 25 chunks: **65.0-67.5% of
  all leaf faces missing, 143 of 143 leafy sections affected, worst section 72.4%**; a synthetic
  5x5x5 leaf blob emitted 150 faces where vanilla emits 750. After: 61,448 of 61,448 in a real
  forest, and fast leaves still collapses the blob to 150. The engine's own tables had contradicted
  the setting all along — `SR.cull[oak_leaves]` is 0 (a leaf occludes nothing) while `SR.selfCull`
  said it fully occludes its own kind.
  ⚠ **The alpha is not what changed.** Leaves stay on the CUTOUT layer with the same 39.5%
  see-through texels; the bug was that there was no second layer of leaves behind the holes to see.
  ⚠ **`gencheck` had ENSHRINED it** — *"fancy leaves are 6 cutout quads (self-culling already merges
  the inside)"* is the empty shell the bug produces, written down as the specification. It now
  asserts 48, derived from the geometry rather than the table under test: 512 leaf blocks each emit
  6 faces, the greedy pass merges each uniform 8x8 plane to one quad, 8 planes x 6 directions.
  `statecheck` kept an independent copy of the self-cull list and agreed with the bug for the same
  reason. **The lesson is D-152's and D-139's again:** a check whose expectation is derived FROM the
  table it is testing agrees with any value that table holds. Five sites had to move together —
  `02c_states.js` §3 and `setFastLeaves`, `02_blocks.js`'s three leaf `def`s and its own
  `setFastLeaves`, and `statecheck`'s copy of the list.
- **D-179** ⚠ **THE RENDERER NOW DRAWS AT TWENTY-NINE MILLION BLOCKS — camera-relative, and no
  shader changed.** D-149 scoped this and left it: at x = 29,000,000, **402 section meshes resident,
  89 columns loaded, light correct at the player's own cell — and 0 triangles drawn.** Never the
  culling heuristics: a frustum plane's constant is a distance from the space's ORIGIN, that space
  was the WORLD, and `cam.viewProj` is `Float32Array` because that is what a GL uniform takes. Out
  there a float32 step is two blocks, so each plane constant was a 3e7 number quantised to two
  blocks and the dot product against a 3e7 box coordinate was pure cancellation. Same limit on the
  vertex path: `uOrigin` was a float32 WORLD position, and modelled the way the shader computes it —
  `f32(f32(origin) + lp)` — a vertex at 2.9e7 landed **one full block** away.
  ⚠ **What found it.** Not a check: an audit that flew somewhere no test had been — D-148's lesson
  for the third time, *a test that runs at the origin tests the origin*. And the failure is CHAOTIC,
  not monotone: over sixty camera positions at 29,000,000, **twenty-nine culled the entire world**
  and the rest drew about half, so one sample point out there proves nothing. The old `streamcheck`
  §3b sampled one heading per distance and honestly reported "correct to ±2,000,000, wrong past four
  million" — a fence built on a lucky yaw.
  **The fix is what vanilla does.** `Cam.update` builds the view matrix with the eye at `(0,0,0)`,
  so `view`, `viewProj` and the extracted planes are eye-relative; `extractPlanes` records the eye
  in `cam.px/py/pz`, and `aabbVisible`/`sphereVisible` move the caller's world box into that space
  **in doubles** before the dot product. `Gfx.drawList` hands the backends `sectionOrigin − camera`,
  also in doubles, so `uOrigin` stays under a few hundred at any world coordinate; the camera
  becomes `(0,0,0)`, the fog term degenerates to `length(wp)`, and the tint map's world origin moves
  into the same space in both backends because the shader reads `wp.xz − uTint.xy` and only the
  difference is meaningful. The selection outline and the particles subtract the eye in `toClip`.
  ⚠ **Not one line of shader source changed, in either language** — `wp = uOrigin.xyz + lp` simply
  means something else now, which is why WebGPU could be brought along correct by inspection on a
  machine where it does not run. ⚠ Three places quietly recompute a matrix and had to move together:
  F7's frozen frustum (which rebuilds `viewProj` outside `Cam.update` — and must NOT touch
  `px/py/pz`, since leaving the plane origin behind is what freezes the frustum),
  `Gfx.testCameraState`, and `selfTest`, whose test section sits at world zero and now draws at
  `−eye`.
  **Measured over 84 camera positions from spawn to 1e8 blocks:** 0 frames blank, 0 disagreeing with
  the same maths in `Float64`, emptiest frame passing 116 of ~394 sections against ~130 at spawn. At
  29,000,000 the four side-plane constants are now 0 rather than 3e7 and the vertex error is 0
  blocks instead of 1. Reverting the two lines in `Cam.update` puts 16 of 84 frames back to blank
  and 31 back to disagreeing. `streamcheck` §3b now asserts the opposite of what it used to,
  sampling twelve headings per distance, and carries an anti-vacuity block that rebuilds the
  pre-D-179 camera (world-space `fpsView`, plane origin at zero) and proves each of the four
  assertions rejects it.
  ⚠ **THE LESSON: precision is a property of the FRAME OF REFERENCE, not of the type.** Widening
  `cam.planes` to `Float64Array` had already been tried (D-149) and bought nothing, because the

  world coordinate itself; once the origin follows the camera, float32 is exact to a thousandth of a
  block at any distance the world can reach. Corollary: **a fence that records a limit is a
  liability once the limit is a bug.**

  `tools/pack-geometry.mjs` writes it as a trailing `UVRT` section of `block-geometry.bin`

  `src/02b_registry.js` decodes it to `R.partUvRot`; and `src/02c_states.js` reads it in exactly one

- **D-180** ⚠ **CAVE BIOMES DECORATE, AND WHAT MADE THEM AFFORDABLE WAS ONE PROPERTY OF THE TABLE
  NOBODY HAD LOOKED AT.** D-137's bug: a chunk took its whole feature list from the biome at its
  origin's SURFACE, and `dripstone_caves`/`lush_caves` are nobody's surface. The union-of-biomes fix
  measured **86 ms a chunk against 15** and was rejected — it asked `Climate.biomeAt` (**38 µs**: a
  whole column climate plus an R-tree search) per candidate placement. Accepted instead: **a cached
  per-chunk biome VOLUME at quart resolution**, vanilla's granularity, one sample per 4x4x4 cell.
  MC-Lite's world is 320 tall, not 384, so **4 x 80 x 4 = 1,280 cells a chunk**, not 1,536.
  ⚠ **NAIVE 49 ms, SHIPPED 0.89 — the difference is a fact about the data.** Folding the six climate
  axes that do not move with y once per quart COLUMN, and sweeping only depth through the R-tree,
  got 4.3 ms: still over budget. What collapsed it: **the 7,578-entry table uses exactly THREE
  distinct depth intervals** — `[0,0]` on 3,788 entries, `[1.0,1.0]` on 3,788, `[0.2,0.9]` on the
  two cave biomes. Every other axis is fixed once the column is, so the nearest entry at any depth
  is one of three — the closest of each depth group on the other six axes. One linear fold over the
  table (**34 µs**; linear because an R-tree cannot help when the query is a LINE, not a point)
  yields those three, and each of the 80 cells is three adds and a compare. **Nobody measured that
  distribution for four stages of worldgen.** It was three lines of probe.
  ⚠ **Same answer, ties included, proved not hoped.** The distance is a sum of squares of integer
  differences, exact in float64, so the split changes no bit. Ties are where vanilla's own
  optimisation goes wrong — Mojang seeds each search from the previous result's distance, changing
  which of two exactly equidistant entries wins (D-113 refused it for that). Safe here because
  `searchEntry` returns the FIRST entry in the tree's leaf order attaining the minimum (a node is
  pruned only on `nodeDist >= best`, so a prune that hides a minimal entry proves an equally close
  one was found earlier in that order), and the sweep records that leaf order once and breaks its
  ties on it. `climcheck` §2b: **32,000 queries through both functions, same entry every time**;
  `featcheck` §5b: the volume against `Climate.biomeAt` **cell for cell, 5,120, all agreeing**.
  ⚠ **Pipeline.** Every biome in the chunk's volume offers its feature lists, deduplicated per step;
  the `biome` placement modifier asks (x, y, z) instead of the surface biome at (x, z) — vanilla's
  `applyBiomeDecoration` plus `BiomeFilter`. **The deviation, stated:** vanilla iterates a GLOBAL
  per-step feature list and salts each feature's rng with its index in THAT list; MC-Lite does not
  build it, and adopting it would reseed every feature in the world. So the origin biome's lists run
  first in their existing order and salt, and other biomes follow in the volume's scan order,
  contributing only what has not run. `order` is a running counter per step — 0..n-1 for the origin
  biome as before, unique for anything appended.
  ⚠ **MEASURED, gencheck's 49-chunk window at seed 1337, before/after interleaved.** Chunk
  generation **12.2 → 13.5 ms** (0.89 the volume, the rest every biome in it decorating).
  `dripstone_caves` at chunk 16,8: **0 → 1,751 pointed_dripstone, 1,941 dripstone_block** over 16
  chunks from 528 placements. `lush_caves` at 156,-104: **0 → 13,582 moss, 1,830 cave vines, 2,485
  rooted dirt, 252 azalea leaves** from 3,708 placements. Surface unmoved: 25 plains chunks at 24,37
  are **identical placement for placement** — `trees_plains` 4, `patch_grass_plain` 250,
  `flower_plains` 2, `patch_tall_grass_2` 7, `patch_sugar_cane` 4, `glow_lichen` 1,246 — pinned by
  `featcheck` §5b. Two surface things DID change, both the same bug: a chunk with a plains origin
  corner and a `sparse_jungle` half now gets jungle decoration (jungle grass 202 → 294), and
  `dripstone_caves` lists `ore_copper_large` where others list `ore_copper`, so `ore_copper` goes
  784 → 729 against 57 new `ore_copper_large`. Vanilla arriving late, not regressions — and
  invisible without the before/after census.
  ⚠ **The volume is a facility.** `Gen.biomeAt3(x, y, z)` reads `Gen.biomeVolume(cx, cz)`, cached
  512 chunks deep, dropped on `Gen.init`. **W13-W18 structure placement asks the same question** and
  must get its answer from the same array, or a structure lands in a biome whose own features say it
  cannot. W8's `biomeAtMemo` and its two 4,096-slot tables are DELETED, not left beside it (D-139).
  **Lesson: when a cost estimate kills a feature, the estimate is a claim about the DATA as much as
  the algorithm — probe the data before deferring a stage.**

  rate every run — PLAN §9's risk 5 as a number instead of a worry.
  ⚠ **A maker may decline.** `igloo` and `ruined_portal` are NBT templates; with no template blob
  decoded they have no pieces, and the honest answer is *"this structure has no grammar in this

  discovered the blob it had forgotten to send.
- **D-189** ⚠ **A VILLAGE OF FIFTY STREET TILES AND NOT ONE HOUSE, THREE SEEDS RUNNING, AND THE
  PIECE COUNT LOOKED FINE.** The matcher assembled 50, 48 and 23 pieces and every one was a street or
  a terminator. The rejection histogram — which exists because a count cannot tell you this — said
  **4,347 of 4,398 candidates rejected on bounding-box overlap**.

  `building_entrance` jigsaw sits at local (8, 1, 6) — the MIDDLE of the tile — so the block in front
  of it is inside the street's own bounding box and a house attached there necessarily overlaps the

  `pieceBox.isInside(frontPos)`. Ported: when the front position is inside the parent, the parent's

  house connector is exactly the case where only one fits.
  ⚠ **`terrain_matching` IS A VERTICAL FIT AT ASSEMBLY TIME, NOT A PER-COLUMN DRAPE.** Vanilla's
  `JigsawPlacement` gives a terrain-matching child its Y from the heightmap AT ITS CONNECTOR instead

  street tile is a `legacy_single_pool_element`, so it WRITES ITS AIR — and draping put that air

  ⚠ **PLAN §9's risk 5 — *"terraced terrain rejects too many village sites"* — did not

- **D-190** ⚠ **`final_state` IS `structure_void` ON 1,124 OF THE 2,605 JIGSAW BLOCKS IN THE JAR,

- **D-191** ⚠ **THE STRONGHOLD IS FOURTEEN PIECES OF CODE AND PLAN SAID SO TWICE** — W14 flags it

- **D-192** ⚠ **FOUR STAGES OF STRUCTURES COST 0.51 ms A CHUNK, AND THE THREE THINGS THAT GOT IT

  version was **17.28**.
  ⚠ **The block cache's size had to become PER SET.** D-184 keyed the start cache by a 4x4 BLOCK of

- **D-193** ⚠ **A TREE TOP IS NOT A HEIGHTMAP, AND `Gen.lightPass` HAD BEEN BOUNDING ITS SEED SCAN
  WITH THE WRONG ONE SINCE D-154.** `lightcheck` §5b — *no two adjacent open cells in a 5x5 region
  differ by more than one sky level* — went from 0 seams to **33, worst sky 15 beside sky 12 at
  (−16, 146, 14)**. Nothing in `src/08_lighting.js` had changed: D-182 made earth mode the default
  world type, §5b named no climate mode, and it started lighting a different world. **This corrects
  D-154.**
  ⚠ **A latent bug newly reached, not a regression, and never mode-specific.** The same scan finds
  **5 bad cells in VANILLA mode at seed 3** and 0 at seed 31337 — the historical §5b world happens
  to have a canopy count of **zero** above its chunks' stone. Pinning the check back to vanilla mode
  would have hidden a real bug.
  ⚠ **One variable answering two questions.** `lightPass` seeds sky straight down, then runs a
  lateral BFS whose SEED SCAN stops at `topL`. D-154 raised that ceiling to `topSeen + 2` and its
  comment says `topSeen` is *"the highest non-air cell the sky pass actually walked past"* — but the
  code fed it from `hi`, the highest **OPAQUE** cell, the HEIGHTMAP's question. Leaves, snow layers,
  plants and glass are not opaque, so a canopy above the tallest stone in its chunk sat above `topL`
  and the open sky beside it was never queued: cells under the leaves were lit only the long way
  round, arriving at 12 next to a 15 that could never spread sideways. Earth mode's peaks in the
  240s and its much larger stone-to-tree spread made it ordinary rather than rare.
  ⚠ **The fix is a second top, not a higher ceiling.** `hiAny` — the highest non-air cell — is
  tracked alongside `hi` in the same downward walk and feeds `topSeen`; `hi` still feeds `hmap`, so
  no heightmap and no save moves. It is free (the walk was already reading `SB[i]`), and the walk
  always sees `hiAny` before it can break, because `sky` only starts falling at the first attenuating
  block and the `sky === 0` break is always below it.
  ⚠ **The check is strengthened, because finding this was luck.** §5b's region scan is a function now
  and runs over a MATRIX — every mode in `Gen.CLIMATES` at the origin, each naming its mode
  explicitly — plus a new §5c over **deliberately tall terrain**: earth mode at chunk (0, 12),
  topping out at **y=232** with **325 cells of canopy above its chunks' stone**, scanning to y=256
  instead of 200. Both numbers chose that origin: a bare 247-block summit at (6, 12) does not reach
  this bug, and the trees over a mountain's shoulder do. Measured: **1.71 M adjacent pairs at
  (0, 192), 1.63 M earth and 1.62 M vanilla at the origin, 0 seams in all three**; against the
  pre-fix `lightPass` the new matrix fails in TWO places (33 cells and 50). Two anti-vacuity entries
  join §6: the matrix must contain a canopy above the stone at all, and its two climate rows must
  generate different terrain.
  ⚠ **THE LESSON, D-126's in another coat: a check that does not name its world is asserting
  whatever the defaults say today.** This one was rescued by a default changing under it; the next
  will be silently weakened by one. Any check that generates a world names the mode, and the ones
  that care about terrain shape pick their region on a measured property of it.
  ⚠ This entry was first assigned D-190, already taken by the structures work in the same session;
  `doccheck` §3 rejects duplicates, so it is D-193.
- **D-194** ⚠ **THE THIRD WHITE FLASH IS A QUEUE, NOT A CULL: freeing a mesh was charged the same
  per-frame budget as uploading one.** An eviction (`Gfx.setSectionMesh(…, null)`) rides the upload
  fifo and `flushUploads` took `uploadsPerFrame` jobs a frame regardless of kind. One frame after a
  teleport: **399 jobs queued, 386 of them removals**, at `uploadsPerFrame = 2` — **193 frames, six
  seconds at 30 fps, spent only freeing memory** while 336 real uploads waited. `Gfx.drawn` drained
  to 0 and the clear colour is the sky. This is Dan's *"mostly when new chunks and stuff are
  loading"*: every eviction burst — preset change, teleport, D-46's adaptive render distance pulling
  `rd` in — stalls the uploads that would refill the screen. **Fix: removals get their own
  `removalsPerFrame` (512) and touch neither the upload count nor the byte budget; the queue still
  drains strictly in order, so a drop and a re-upload of one section cannot swap places.** D-43's
  budget exists because an upload is bytes across the bus; a `deleteBuffer` is not. After: that
  teleport drains in **one frame**.
  ⚠ **Supersedes the "white flashes are closed" claims in D-162 and D-175** — each closed one real
  cause and then called the class closed. This entry is the current state of the class.
  ⚠ **`Gfx.drawn` was the LENGTH OF THE DRAW LIST (D-170's mistake again)** —
  `listOpaque.length + listCutout.length + listTrans.length` stays healthy through a blank screen,
  because it describes what the cull loop asked for; `tris` was `m.quads[layer] * 2` over the list,
  doubled when D-53's prepass was on. Both backends' `drawSection`/`drawSectionModels` now RETURN
  the triangles actually submitted — 0 for a lost context, dead handle, empty layer, or a full
  WebGPU dynamic-offset ring, which had been dropping sections silently — and `drawList` counts
  those in the picture passes only. The old number survives as `drawnListed` so the two can
  disagree; identical in a healthy frame, so `cullcheck` does not move.
  ⚠ **Neither backend could recover from a lost context and neither said so.** WebGL2 called
  `preventDefault()` on `webglcontextlost` — which is what makes the browser promise a restore —
  with no `webglcontextrestored` listener; WebGPU set a private flag on `device.lost` and returned
  early for the rest of the session. Both now count the loss, tell the player, re-run `init` (WebGPU
  unless the reason is `'destroyed'`, which means the backend swap asked for it), and
  `Gfx.onBackendRestored` forgets every handle without freeing it into a dead context before
  `World.remeshAll()`. `Gfx.stats()` reports `contextLost`, `contextLosses`, `contextRestores`.
  ⚠ **`flashcheck` scored the PREVIOUS FRAME, which is not the question.** `1 - drawn / prevDrawn`
  cannot tell *the world vanished* from *the player teleported 400 blocks*, and the second is most
  of the probe's runtime by design. A frame is scored against `eligible` — resident AND inside the
  render distance — over a 12-frame WINDOW, because a drain of 100 → 60 → 36 → 21 → 12 is five
  frames of "only 40% down" plus one empty screen that a frame-pair fence never sees. The blankness
  floor self-calibrates to **half the fullest world the run has seen at that render distance**
  (~380 sections at `rd` 4, thousands at 11).
  ⚠ **Its anti-vacuity section was the part actually broken, in D-164's way:** the scoring lived as
  text in a `Runtime.evaluate` string and §4 re-implemented a paraphrase in Node, so the mutants
  proved nothing about the code that runs — one asserted a 40 → 0 collapse was invisible to a rule
  that plainly saw it. `scoreFrame` is one function now, shipped in by `.toString()` and called
  directly over synthetic frames: a one-frame collapse and a four-frame drain must be flagged, a
  legitimate shrink and a blank screen with a tenth of a world must not, half a world must. An
  un-injected helper (`floorFor`) then threw out of `Gfx.render`, stopping the world at frame 1
  while the check reported a flash — so the scorer is self-contained and the hook REPORTS throws.
  ⚠ **Two of the six phases proved nothing:** `chunk-border-flight` (160 blocks a second) and
  `combo` (370-block teleports) never had one loaded section inside the render distance for a whole
  phase. They keep their provocations and gain a recovery beat that waits for the streamer to
  PLATEAU (radius-independent); §1 fails on a phase whose p90 eligible never reached half a world.
  ⚠ **F7 is exempt, and exempt is not untested.** Frozen frustum plus flying empties the picture by
  design (43 sections against an unchanged 378 resident), so frozen frames and any window containing
  one are unscored. The phase-average comparison that first accused F7 was measuring the probe
  outrunning its streamer; it is replaced by a round trip at ONE position — freeze, fly 40 blocks,
  unfreeze, fly back — asserting the plane origin stayed behind while frozen, is exactly the live
  eye afterwards in all three doubles, and the picture is the one it started with. D-179's freeze
  path passes.
  ⚠ **THE LESSON: a check that compares a number to itself one frame ago has no idea what the number
  means.**

- **D-200** ⚠ **THE TAG CORPUS IS 270 FILES AND FIFTY-TWO OF THEM WERE ALREADY PACKED.** PLAN G1
  asks for "the 270 tag files", and W13 had quietly taken 52 of them a session earlier: a
  structure's `biomes` field is a `worldgen/biome` tag reference and nothing else, so D-183 read
  and flattened those into `worldgen.bin` before a general substrate existed. Packing all 270 here
  would have shipped 6 KB twice and given two answers to one question. `tools/pack-tags.mjs`
  therefore takes the five REGISTRY directories — blocks 133, items 71, fluids 2, entity_types 10,
  game_events 2 — and `tagcheck` §1 asserts that this payload plus the worldgen one account for
  every file in the jar, so the split cannot silently lose one. The 99 nested `#tag` references are
  flattened at BUILD time, which is exact and means no runtime code walks a tag graph and nothing
  downstream ever sees a `#`. ⚠ **THE CYCLE DETECTOR IS PROVED INSIDE THE BUILD**, on two synthetic
  tags pointing at each other, because vanilla's own tags have no cycle and a build would exit 0
  whether the detector worked or not. Measured: 70.2 KB of JSON → 23.6 KB binary → **9.8 KB
  deflated**, 13.0 KB of base64, decoded in 1.6 ms, plus a 15.3 KB membership bitset (133 tags ×
  900 blocks) that turns "is this block in that tag" from a 368-entry scan into a shift and an AND.
  The lesson: before packing a corpus, ask what already packed part of it.

- **D-201** ⚠ **THE COMPILED-JAVA GAP PLAN G3 EXPECTED DOES NOT EXIST.** `Item.getDestroySpeed` and
  `Item.isCorrectToolForDrops` are Java overrides across six classes, and PLAN reasonably assumed
  both would have to be hand-tabled. They are both already EVALUATED, pair by pair, in the `pc`
  dataset the project has used since F7. `materials.json` is `getDestroySpeed` as a table: 16
  material classes, each a map from item id to the speed that item returns, and every block in
  `blocks.json` carries its class — 121 (material, item) speeds, including shears-on-wool 5,
  shears-on-leaves 15, sword-on-cobweb 15 and sword-on-plants 1.5, which are four separate Java
  overrides. `harvestTools` is `isCorrectToolForDrops` as a table, present exactly when
  `requiresCorrectToolForDrops` is set (the same fact D-102 leaned on) and listing the item ids that
  answer true — **including cobweb's swords-and-shears set, which no tier comparison produces**. So
  the six tier speeds PLAN quotes (wood 2, stone 4, iron 6, diamond 8, netherite 9, gold 12) are
  REPRODUCED from data rather than typed, and `minecheck` §2 asserts that they are. What is
  genuinely absent is `Tiers.java`'s LEVEL integers, and they are neither ported nor guessed: a
  level exists only to be compared against the `needs_*_tool` tags, and `harvestTools` is that
  comparison's answer. The lesson: name the gap, then look for it in the data one more time.

- **D-202** **THE LOOT PACKER REFUSES TO BUILD ON A VERB THE INTERPRETER DOES NOT KNOW.** The 835
  block loot tables use a closed vocabulary — 3 entry types, 9 conditions, 8 functions — and
  `tools/pack-loot.mjs` surveys every file and checks that vocabulary against a list it shares with
  `src/07e_loot.js`. A table using an unimplemented function would otherwise drop the wrong thing
  at runtime and nothing would say so; now it is a build failure with the verb named. The tables
  ship WHOLE (497 KB of JSON → 139.8 KB interned → **12.7 KB deflated**) rather than flattened to a
  drop list, because Fortune and Silk Touch are `apply_bonus` and `match_tool` nodes INSIDE them:
  flatten and you throw the game away and then need four hand-written special cases to put a worse
  version back.

- **D-203** ⚠ **PLAN'S OWN BREAK-TIME FORMULA IS WRONG IN THREE PLACES, AND THE CODE FOLLOWS THE
  GAME.** PLAN §5's G3 block writes Efficiency as a MULTIPLIER `(level² + 1)`, Haste as `1.2^level`
  and Mining Fatigue as `0.3^min(level,4)`. Vanilla's `Player.getDestroySpeed` **adds** `level² + 1`
  and only when the base speed already exceeds 1; multiplies by the linear `1 + 0.2·level` for
  Haste; and switches on `0.3 / 0.09 / 0.0027 / 0.00081` for Fatigue, whose third step is a tenth of
  a power of 0.3. Concretely: Efficiency V on a diamond pickaxe is 8 + 26 = **34, not 208**, and
  Efficiency V on a pickaxe mining DIRT is **1, not 26**, because a pickaxe is not the right tool
  and the bonus never applies. CLAUDE.md's governing rule decides it — *"does real Minecraft do it?
  If yes, and it is not worldgen or rendering, do it exactly"* — and PLAN's block is a summary
  written from memory. `minecheck` §7's first break re-implements PLAN's paraphrase and asserts the
  suite can tell the two apart. The lesson: a specification written from memory is evidence about
  the author, not about the game.

- **D-204** ⚠ **THE PLACEMENT TABLE CARRIED SIX PROPERTIES AND THE GAME LAYER NEEDS ALL SIXTY-NINE.**
  D-157 built `block-runtime.bin`'s `MCLP` section for placement alone and hard-coded its two name
  lists to `facing`, `axis`, `half`, `type`, `face`, `waterlogged` and their 19 values. That was
  right for what it was for, and it made `States.propValue(state, PROP.age)` return −1 for every
  crop in the game. G2 cannot advance a crop it cannot read; G3 drops one slab where vanilla drops
  two, because `type=double` is unreadable; and **180 of the 835 loot tables carry a
  `block_state_property` condition** naming `age`, `part`, `candles`, `moisture`, `honey_level` or
  `type`. The name lists are now DERIVED from `block-constants.json` — 69 properties, 120 values,
  1,306 entries — with the original six and nineteen kept first and in order so a cached numeric id
  cannot be surprised, and both counts checked against the u8 the format writes them as. Cost:
  **+2.6 KB deflated**, 31.8 → 34.4 KB. The lesson: a table built for one caller acquires a second
  caller, and the second one is the one that finds the limit.

- **D-205** **BLOCK BEHAVIOUR HANGS OFF `World.setBlock`, THE ONE PLACE A BLOCK CAN CHANGE.** The
  same argument the save journal (ARCH §13) and the support cascade (D-155) already make: a
  neighbour-shape update called at each call site is an update some future caller forgets. So
  `setBlock` calls `Behave.changed`, which re-runs `updateShape` on the six neighbours, schedules
  any fluid that now has somewhere to go, and creates or destroys the block entity. It is
  re-entrant by construction — updating a neighbour is itself a `setBlock` — and capped at depth 8,
  which every connection family in the game clears and a rule that oscillates does not.
  ⚠ **`faceSturdy` IS A REAL COVERAGE TEST OVER THE COLLISION BOXES, NOT "IS IT OPAQUE".** A bottom
  slab is opaque by material and has no sturdy east face; a fence that connected to it would look
  right in a screenshot and be wrong in the game. `behavcheck` §11's first break makes exactly that
  substitution and the check sees it.

- **D-206** ⚠ **THE WALL TEST IS AGAINST THE BLOCK ABOVE'S *DOWN FACE*, NOT ITS VOLUME.** `WallBlock`
  decides LOW vs TALL by asking whether the above block's shape contains a thin test column, and
  the shape it asks is `getCollisionShape(...).getFaceShape(Direction.DOWN)` — the 2D slice at that
  plane, extruded. A bottom slab's VOLUME contains no full-height column, so a volume test reads
  `low`; its DOWN FACE is a full 16×16 square, so vanilla reads `tall`. Every wall under a slab in
  every village in the game is the difference, and the first implementation here had it wrong until
  `behavcheck` §4 asked. **A NAMED GAP RIDES WITH IT:** the five test rectangles are
  `private static final VoxelShape` constants in `WallBlock.java`, in no data file, not in the jar's
  data and not in the pc dataset. They are stated as a hand-sourced table and the check asserts the
  OBSERVABLE consequences instead — full block above is tall, air above is low, bottom slab above is
  tall, a straight line has no post.

- **D-207** **`isRandomlyTicking` IS COMPILED JAVA, AND IT IS UNOBSERVABLE WHERE IT DIFFERS.** No
  data file says which blocks receive a random tick. What a player can observe is only whether a
  block DOES something when one arrives, so the set of blocks with a rule IS the honest set: crops,
  leaves, saplings, grass/mycelium/podzol, farmland, sugar cane, cactus, ice, snow and nether wart.
  The difference between "never picked" and "picked and does nothing" is the tick budget and
  nothing else. Written down rather than papered over, because the next session should not have to
  re-derive that it is safe.

- **D-208** **WHICH BLOCKS HAVE A BLOCK ENTITY IS `BlockEntityType.java`, SO THE 34 TYPES ARE A
  HAND-SOURCED LIST.** There is no tag, no `blocks.json` field and nothing in the jar's data that
  names them. Five of the lists ARE tags and are read as tags — `signs`, `beds`, `banners`,
  `shulker_boxes`, `campfires` — which is 60 hand-typed names avoided and the reason G1 came first.
  The rest are named, `behavcheck` §9 asserts every named block exists in the registry so a rename
  cannot rot the list into silence, and the count is asserted against 1.18.2's 34. What is NOT here
  is most of their behaviour: a furnace's recipes are G9 and a hopper's slots are G8, so this stage
  owns the STORE — creation, destruction and the tick loop — and each type carries the fields its
  owner stage will fill. The furnace's burn and cook counters are the exception and run now,
  including vanilla's detail that the tick a furnace LIGHTS on does not spend any of its fuel.

- **D-209** ⚠ **THREE BREAK TIMES ARE ONE TICK LONGER THAN THE WIKI, AND FLOAT32 IS WHY.** Vanilla
  computes `progress = float(float(speed/hardness)/bracket)`, and for cobblestone broken bare-handed
  that is 0.0049999998882 rather than 0.005 — reciprocal 200.0000045, so the block comes apart on
  tick **201** and the wiki's "10 seconds" is 10.05. The same lands on obsidian by hand (5001, not
  5000) and cobweb by hand (401, not 400); every other block in `minecheck`'s 44-row table rounds
  the other way and the rational and float answers are identical. Vanilla's client ACCUMULATES the
  float a tick at a time and its server multiplies by the elapsed ticks; all three forms agree to
  within this same one tick, so `Mining.ticks` uses the closed form, because obsidian with the wrong
  tool under Mining Fatigue IV is 6.2 million ticks and must not be a 6.2-million-iteration loop on
  the frame the player looks at it. The lesson: "to the tick" means deciding which arithmetic the
  tick is counted in.

- **D-210** **FIRE'S FLAMMABILITY INTEGERS ARE A NAMED GAP; ITS BURN-OUT IS NOT.**
  `FireBlock.bootStrap()` is about thirty `setFlammable(block, encouragement, flammability)` calls
  in compiled Java, in no data file and in no tag. Those two integers set the spread PROBABILITY
  only. What decides whether a fire SURVIVES is which neighbours burn at all, and that is a family
  question the tags answer — `logs`, `planks`, `leaves`, `wool`, `wool_carpets`, the six wooden
  furniture tags — plus a short named list for the singletons. So this build's fire goes out exactly
  when vanilla's does (PLAN G2's own acceptance: on stone with nothing to burn, once its age passes
  3) and spreads at a rate this stage does not claim to have ported. Stating which half is exact and
  which half is unknown is the whole point of writing it down.

- **D-211** **THE SUITE PRINTS EACH STAGE AS IT FINISHES, NOT ONLY IN THE TABLE AT THE END.** With
  Track G's three new checks the `--fast` run is about 190 s on this machine, and the development
  shell it is driven from caps a single command at 180 s. Every buffered byte was then lost when
  the run was cut off, so **forty-five green stages and one catastrophic failure printed exactly
  the same thing: nothing**. `suite.mjs` now emits each row the moment that stage returns and
  repeats the whole table at the end, so a truncated run is still evidence and the completed one
  still reads as one block. It costs nothing and it is the same principle the file's own closing
  note argues for: a green line that does not say what it did NOT do is a lie, and so is a silent
  one that does not say what it DID.
- **D-195** ⚠ **THE BUILD REPORTED CHARACTERS AND CALLED THEM BYTES, AND NOTHING CHECKED D-12's
  CEILING AT ALL.** `build.mjs` printed `html.length` — UTF-16 code units — as the output size.
  This project's source is dense with `—`, `⚠` and `°` in its comments, so the file on disk was
  **3,381,625 bytes against a reported 3,319,830**: 61,795 bytes, 1.9%, growing with every
  comment anyone writes. Found by `ls` disagreeing with the build in the same terminal.
  ⚠ **The second half is the real finding.** D-12's 15 MB ceiling is one of the project's five
  hard constraints, and NOTHING asserted it. The number lived in `CHARTER.md` and in a comment in
  `bake-geometry.mjs`, and the only thing between the shipped file and the limit was somebody
  noticing — while the build's own estimate of the size was low and getting lower. `build.mjs`
  now prints headroom on every run and EXITS 1 over the ceiling, telling the reader to compress a
  payload rather than raise the line. Today: 3,302 KB, 21.5% used, 12,058 KB free.
  **The lesson is D-30's in a new place:** a constraint no check can fail is a preference. This
  one had survived fourteen stages of Track W, including W15 adding 866 structure templates.
- **D-196** ⚠ **EVERY BROWSER CHECK THIS PROJECT HAS EVER RUN HAS RUN AT THE *CELERON* PRESET,
  AND THAT IS WHY FOUR SESSIONS OF WHITE-FLASH HUNTING KEPT MISSING.** `Settings.detect()` scores
  the machine and then lets cores and memory pull the answer DOWN: `cores <= 2` clamps the index to
  0. The headless container that runs `smoke`, `titlecheck`, `cullcheck`, `palettecheck`,
  `soakcheck` and `flashcheck` has **two cores**, so all six have always run at render distance 4,
  `uploadBytesPerFrame` 96 KB, `maxChunks` 160, one worker — and **`fancyLeaves: false`**. Dan plays
  at medium and high. Asked when he sees the flashes he answered *"when medium or above, randomly"*,
  which is the first time anyone had a preset to test against.
  ⚠ **The consequence for D-178.** `fancyLeaves` is false on celeron and low and true on medium and
  high, so the FANCY leaf path — D-178's entire subject — had never once been drawn by a check.
  A fix declared and fenced in session 5 was fenced only on the branch it was not about.
  **The hook.** `S.detect` honours `window.__MCLITE_FORCE_PRESET` when it names a real preset, and
  `tools/cdp.mjs` sets it through `Page.addScriptToEvaluateOnNewDocument` — before the page's own
  scripts run — whenever `MCLITE_PRESET` is in the environment, then re-navigates, because the tab
  is opened at the target URL before the debugger socket exists. Nothing in the game writes that
  property and no player can reach it. `MCLITE_PRESET=medium node tools/soakcheck.mjs dist/mclite.html`
  is now a sentence anybody can type.
  **What it found within the hour**, on a build the suite called green at 792,255 assertions:
  `soakcheck` at medium — **14 of 3,147 frames collapsed from a drawing world to nothing, a
  full-screen sky flash** (first at f2240, 656 meshes resident, 656 culled, 0 drawn), and the world
  never caught up after the flight stopped (2,255 sections still dirty after 40 s); `titlecheck` at
  medium and high — **the tint map is one and two versions ahead of the GPU's copy**, so the world
  is drawn with the colours of where the player used to be. Both pass at celeron.
  ⚠ **The general lesson, and it is the third time this project has learned a version of it**
  (D-148 *a test that runs at the origin tests the origin*; D-179 *one sample point out there proves
  nothing*): **a check that runs at one configuration tests that configuration.** A preset is not a
  label, it is twenty numbers, and six of them change the streaming behaviour by a factor of eight.
- **D-197** ⚠ **"OPAQUE" IS NOT A PLACEMENT RULE, IT IS A CLASS OF THEM — AND A GRAPHICS SETTING
  WAS GENERATING THE WORLD.** `States.floorOk` asked one question of every floor-class block:
  *is the block below opaque?* Vanilla asks the BLOCK. `BushBlock.mayPlaceOn` is `#minecraft:dirt`
  or farmland and nothing else; `DeadBushBlock`'s is sand, terracotta or dirt; `SugarCaneBlock`'s
  is sand or dirt. Measured over 81 chunks at seed 1337: **891 `grass` on SAND, 216 on GRAVEL, 2
  on stone, 21 `tall_grass` on sand**, plus poppies, dandelions and lilies of the valley on both.
  Vanilla generates none of them. Every one passed `floatcheck` §2 and §2c, because sand is opaque.
  ⚠ **The second half is worse than the first.** `SR.setFastLeaves(true)` writes
  `SR.opaque[leafState] = 1` so the mesher can cull through a canopy (D-93), and `floorOk` read
  `SR.opaque`. So **the same seed grew 2,050 plants at one quality preset and 1,993 at the other**
  — 59 cells different in 81 chunks, `43 grass ON oak_leaves`, `4 red_mushroom ON oak_leaves`,
  `1 poppy ON oak_leaves` among them. A RENDERING TABLE MUST NEVER BE AN INPUT TO WORLDGEN. The
  fix is not to remember to snapshot at the right moment: `SR.opaqueBase` is the opacity table as
  built, the renderer cannot reach it, and the support predicates read that one.
  **The mechanism.** Eleven named PLACEMENT SETS — `bush`, `wither_rose`, `dead_bush`, `mushroom`,
  `sugar_cane`, `cactus`, `bamboo`, `azalea`, `big_dripleaf`, `small_dripleaf`, `nether_wart` —
  are built from vanilla's own block tags (`#dirt`, `#sand`, `#terracotta`, `#mushroom_grow_block`,
  `#bamboo_plantable_on`, `#azalea_grows_on`, `#big_dripleaf_placeable`, `#small_dripleaf_placeable`)
  and ride **`worldgen.bin`**, not `tags.bin`: worldgen asks this question on the CHUNK WORKERS and
  `src/02f_tags.js` is main-thread only. D-183 put the 42 biome tags there for the same reason.
  119 floor members, 41 blocks governed, 153 real states. The SETS are data; WHICH BLOCK OBEYS
  WHICH is compiled Java, so that half is an explicitly named table in `tools/pack-worldgen.mjs`,
  in the style of `NO_RULE_BLOCKS` — a wrong list should be a visible wrong list.
  ⚠ **Blocks with no set were NOT narrowed**: torches, signs, banners, skulls, coral fans, the
  standing halves of D-167, the crops, the two nether fungi and `moss_carpet` keep the opaque test
  they have always had. Narrowing a block whose rule the table does not state would delete it from
  the world, and that mistake already has two numbers (D-152, D-178). `mushroom` keeps an
  `anyOpaque` fallback because vanilla's rule is the tag OR any solid-render face AND light ≤ 12,
  and worldgen cannot ask about light before the light pass — looser than vanilla, and named.
  Still exactly ONE implementation (D-169): `Features.supported`, `World.canSurvive` and
  `floatcheck` all route through `States.floorOk`. The flattener is `tools/taglib.mjs` now, shared
  with `pack-tags.mjs` rather than copied — `tags.bin` is byte-for-byte unchanged by the move.
  ⚠ **Two checks had ENSHRINED the old rule, and both are the D-152 shape.** `floatcheck` §5's
  anti-vacuity case asserted a plant is accepted on STONE, which vanilla refuses; the example is
  now `grass_block`. And `featcheck` §4b asserted ">40 grass tufts per plains chunk" while **971
  of its 1,121 tufts stood on sand** — it was passing ON the bug. It now counts per chunk-
  equivalent of grass_block SURFACE (43.9, and 41 before the fix too: the feature was never
  wrong), and it asserts its own sample is really plains, which nothing had ever checked.
  ⚠ **And that rewrite found a third bug, unfixed and named here rather than absorbed into a
  threshold: 58% of that sample's top surface is SAND while all 49 chunks are `minecraft:plains`.**
  Vanilla's plains above sea level is grass_block. A surface rule is laying beach across an inland
  biome, nothing in Track W compares the top block against the biome, and that is why nothing has
  caught it. It is the reason the raw per-chunk tuft count fell to 15.1 once the sand tufts stopped
  being generated.
  **New fences** (`floatcheck` §2d and §2e): zero plants on a floor their own block refuses, judged
  against the PACKER's sets by name rather than against `floorOk` itself (D-164); and the world
  generated with fast leaves is compared cell-for-cell against the world generated with fancy
  leaves and must be IDENTICAL — 2,048,000 cells, 25 chunks. §5's deliberate break puts the
  pre-D-197 `floorOk` back and requires that comparison to differ, or the fence proves nothing.

- **D-198** ⚠ **THE FOURTH WHITE FLASH IS NOT A CULL AT ALL — THE STREAMER WAS BUILDING THE
  WORLD IN THE WRONG ORDER AND THE WORKERS WERE IDLE WHILE IT DID.** D-196 gave the project a
  preset hook and `MCLITE_PRESET=medium node tools/soakcheck.mjs` reproduced Dan's flash for the
  first time: **14 of 3,147 frames collapsed from a drawing world to nothing**, first at
  (1001200, −599500) with 656 meshes resident, 656 culled and 0 drawn. The obvious reading of that
  frame is that the culler ate the world. **It did not, and the measurement says so.** Re-running
  `Cam.aabbVisible` and `Gfx.floodHas` independently over every resident mesh on the collapsed
  frames: **31 of 471 rejected by the occlusion flood, 440 by the frustum's LEFT plane alone**, the
  nearest mesh 27 blocks away and behind the camera. The frustum was correct — its normals match
  the yaw, pitch, fov and aspect of that frame to four places. **There was genuinely nothing meshed
  in front of the camera**, and the meshes that did exist were the trail the flight had left behind.
  ⚠ **Three faults, each ruled in by a number, and two of them only exist above celeron.**

  **1. Meshing was ordered in two dimensions and the world is three.** `W.spiral` orders COLUMNS
  nearest-first — that part was right since session 1 — and the inner loop then walked `sy` from 0
  to 19, from bedrock upwards. A section at (dx 0, dz 0, sy 0) is 336 blocks from a camera at
  sy 17; a section eight columns away at eye level is 128 blocks from it and on screen. The first
  was meshed first. Measured at medium at the flash site: **the visible world was complete at 4,720
  of the disc's 7,345 section meshes** once the order was fixed, i.e. a third of the work is
  basement nobody can see and it was being interleaved with the picture. `sy` now walks outward
  from the camera's own section, and a first pass takes only `d² + Δsy² ≤ rd²` — the disc the
  spiral already walks, made a hemisphere — before a second pass takes everything else. Nothing is
  skipped, only ordered. Vanilla and Sodium sort their rebuild queue by camera distance for exactly
  this reason.

  **2. `maxMeshPerFrame` was scaled by the frame-time load, and it is the only thing that refills
  `maxMeshInflight`.** D-87's scaler exists so one slow frame does not become a run of them, and
  `07_world.js` said in its own comment that "generation and meshing IN FLIGHT are not scaled —
  those cost worker time, not frame time". The code contradicted the comment: the pool is refilled
  only by the loop the scaler was throttling, so a slow frame throttled the WORKERS. Frames are slow
  exactly when the render distance is large, so this bit at medium and above and never at celeron,
  where `load` sits near 1. Measured at medium, parked a million blocks out with 3,000 sections
  dirty: **`load` 0.27–0.49, `meshPerFrame` 2–4, the mesh pool at 3.3 of its 10 slots and the
  workers idle**. The main-thread cost the cap exists to bound is `snapshotFor`, measured at
  **0.05 ms a job** — topping a 10-slot pool up costs half a millisecond against the 60 ms frames it
  was protecting. One line: `meshPerFrame` is never fewer than the free slots. Pool occupancy
  3.3/10 → 10/10, throughput **56 → 95 sections a second**.

  **3. The occlusion flood's queue was three per cent from a silent cliff.** `qcap = cap * 3` was
  never a measured ceiling. At high (r = 16, cap 21,780, qcap 65,340), flying a million blocks out
  and looking off a mountain top: **63,227 flood steps — 97% of the queue**. At medium, 34,156 of
  37,500 — 91%. An overflow is silent and it is the D-171 failure arriving through the middle
  instead of the edge: the step is dropped, every section behind it is never visited, and
  `floodHas` reported "not visited" as *occluded*. **A culling test may only ever say NO when it is
  certain**, so the frame that overflows now says nothing at all — `_flood.overflow` makes
  `floodHas` return true for the whole frame and the frustum decides alone. The queue is 4× as
  well, which is 40% headroom over the worst frame ever measured here, and
  `Gfx.stats().floodQueue`/`.floodOverflows` exist so a check can see the cliff at all (D-194's
  rule: a check cannot see a flag it is never shown).

  ⚠ **What was ruled OUT, and how**, because the brief's other four candidates all sounded better
  than the answer: the **upload budget** (D-194's frees-versus-uploads at 8× the bytes) —
  `uploadQueue.length` was 0–12 for the whole flight and 0 on every collapsed frame, and `removed`
  was 0; **an eviction burst** — same numbers, and the resident set never came within a third of
  `maxChunks`; **the resident set outrunning the flood's extent** — measured above, 31 of 471; **the
  frustum itself** — its planes were recomputed by hand against yaw/pitch/fov/aspect on the
  collapsed frames and are right.

  **The result at medium**, same box, same flight: blank frames **14 → 0**, sections meshed over the
  flight 10,935 → 15,169, `drawn` through the flight roughly 1.7× higher, and **the backlog now
  drains to zero — "2,255 still dirty after 40 s" became "0 dirty, caught up in 49.6 s"**. At high
  the flash is gone too and the flood sits at 72% of its queue instead of 97%.

  **The fence**, and it is the point: `soakcheck` now **forces the medium preset by default**
  (`MCLITE_PRESET` still wins, so `high` and `celeron` are one word away). Against a build with
  these three lines reverted it reports **3 failures** — the flash, the backlog, and the flood at
  92% of its cap; against the fixed build, **44 assertions and 0 failures**. New sections: §5a the
  mesh pool is not left idle while 500+ sections are dirty, §5d the flood never overflows and never
  passes 90% of its queue, and §5's near-disc floor — **nothing unmeshed within four chunks of the
  player**, which is the celeron render distance and therefore means the same thing at every preset;
  no machine is too slow for the fifty columns it is standing in.

  ⚠ **What is NOT fixed, with the arithmetic rather than an excuse.** `soakcheck` at **high** still
  fails §5 on this box: render distance 16 holds 957 columns, which is about 16,000 section meshes, and at the
  measured 95 sections a second that is 168 s against a 70 s window. Two cores, four workers and a
  software rasteriser competing for the same two cores is **21 ms of CPU per section mesh**; the
  same flight at medium needs 7,900 and finishes in 49.6 s. High is not a preset this container can
  hold, which is D-196's point restated — and the near-disc floor still passes there, so what fails
  is the horizon, not the ground.

  ⚠ **And one check bug found on the way**: `soakcheck` §5c waited 900 ms and then took element 10
  of the last twenty frames as its baseline. At medium, drawing 3,000 sections on a software
  rasteriser, 900 ms is six frames — `slice(-20).sort()[10]` is `undefined`, `|| 0` makes the
  baseline zero, and both of the section's guard assertions fail while the thing they guard is
  perfectly healthy. It waits for FRAMES now. **A check may not be calibrated in frames per second.**

  ⚠ **And a second one, in `flashcheck`, of exactly the shape D-131 is named for.** Its "drew a
  list and no geometry" rule compared `Gfx.drawn` — which counts a section drawn by EITHER of its
  two streams — against `Gfx.tris`, which is the greedy stream alone. A frame whose only drawn
  section is a grass tuft or a torch has `drawn` 1, `tris` 0 and `modelTris` 240, and is perfectly
  healthy: measured over a 120 s run, 8 such frames on the pre-D-198 build and 4 on the fixed one,
  none of them a defect. The rule now sums both streams, and §5 gained the two synthetic frames
  that prove it fires on one and not the other. **A rule that exists to catch a check trusting one
  of two streams was trusting one of two streams.**
- **D-199** ⚠ **THE REFEREE IS NOW THE REAL GAME, AND THE ORE NUMBER THIS PROJECT HAS BEEN

  headless at `level-seed=1337`, `level-type=minecraft:normal`, force-loading **6,626 chunks in

  chunks present in the region headers and then, after the JVM has exited, by an NBT census of

  The driver is `_scratch/mclite/vg_pregen.js` in MineHTML's jobs lane, which is the only machine

  is the check, and it SKIPS CLEANLY with the paths it looked in when the golden data is absent,

  **WHAT MATCHED, and each of these is a claim no file could have made:**
  · **Biome, at vanilla's own 4x4x4 quart cells: 99.994% — 19 of 332,477 non-cave cells.** W4's

  · **Ore, per chunk, over a named 10x10 box (chunks x -20..-11, z -20..-11): every ore between
  0.91x and 1.15x of vanilla.** Coal 76.98 vanilla / 88.22 MC-Lite, iron 74.65/73.34, copper
  73.31/75.13, redstone 37.39/34.06, gold 35.39/36.48, lapis 24.52/22.51, **diamond 16.64/15.28**.
  ⚠⚠ **`docs/NEXT.md`'s standing gap — "we over-generate rare ores 3-4x (diamond 12.5/chunk)" —
  IS WRONG, and it was wrong because there was no referee.** Vanilla 1.18.2 makes ~16 diamond ore

  uniform**: §4's own histogram window (40..47, -20..-13) is mountainous and reads 297 coal a

  · **Carved void below the terrain, y −59..40: 1.006x** (2,805 cells a chunk vanilla, 2,821
  MC-Lite). ⚠ Counted as *not-solid* — air, cave_air, water and lava — because counting only air

  · **Sea-level terrain, y 63..99: median residual 0-1 blocks, 94.6% of columns within 8.**

  · ⚠ **Bamboo: 1.11 a chunk against vanilla's 12.18 — 0.09x**, the only decoration family outside

  cave_vines_plant 4.1x, moss_carpet 3.9x — while the aquatic chain is at 1.0x. Recorded as a
  ledger with a ratchet, not asserted away, and not previously measured at all.
  · ⚠ **Rivers are 96% water at the surface where vanilla's are 75%** — MC-Lite's river channel
  is wider or deeper than vanilla's. Not fixed here; the number is in §3's table.

  above y=140, which run **+21 blocks** above vanilla (**D-172**, Dan: "Keep today's 214");

  so before this check does: the grid is vanilla's data, the offset inside it is MC-Lite's PRNG);
  which cells a carver hollowed (**D-123**); individual feature positions (**D-134**); the

  **WHAT IS STILL OWED.** The pregen is overworld only and its two boxes contain no plains, no

  And the ratchets in §3 and §6 are ratchets: when the jungle surface rules and bamboo are fixed,
  tighten them to zero rather than leaving a fence around ground nobody stands on any more.

- **D-212** ⚠ **THREE WRITERS DRAINED THE OCEAN, AND ONE SHIPPED MOJANG'S DEBUG MARKERS INTO THE
  WORLD.** Dan, on the structures: *"i was mostly commenting on a glitched underwater dungeon i
  found. dont go duckhunting glitches just build general tools."* `tools/structaudit.mjs` is that
  tool — it generates every sampled chunk TWICE, with `params.structures` on and off, and the
