- **D-263** ⚠⚠ **WHAT A PLACED BLOCK MAY DESTROY IS NOT A GEOMETRIC QUESTION, AND ASKING IT AS ONE
  MADE 139 BLOCKS OVERWRITABLE WHERE VANILLA HAS 28.** Dan, session 9, opening a twelve-hour pass:
  *"placing blocks can overwrite others."* He did not name a block, and he was right not to — it
  was a class. `src/14_player.js` built its `REPLACEABLE` table like this:

  ```js
  if (SR.geom[s] === SR.GEOM_MODEL && SR.solid[s] === 0 && SR.emit[s] === 0) REPLACEABLE[s] = 1;
  ```

  — a model-shaped block, with no collision box, giving off no light. That is a plausible
  description of tall grass and a completely wrong description of the roster. **Measured: 139
  blocks and 2,590 real states**, against vanilla's **28 blocks / 774 states**. The surplus:
  fence gates (open ones lose their collision box), buttons, pressure plates, levers, tripwire
  hooks, all four rails, redstone wire, all six saplings, every flower, every coral and coral fan,
  cobweb, item frames, sugar cane, sweet berry bush, wheat, carrots, potatoes, beetroots, nether
  wart, both melon and pumpkin stems, both dripleaves, spore blossom and powder snow. ⚠ And it ran
  **in both directions**, because the same table decides whether a placement lands IN the clicked
  cell or on its face — so those blocks also silently swallowed placements meant to go beside them.

  Vanilla asks `Material.isReplaceable()`. It is **compiled Java**: in no JSON, no
  `minecraft-data` file and no tag, which is exactly why a previous session guessed. It now comes
  out of the jar, through **`tools/extract-materials.mjs`**, and the route is the point:

  1. Mojang's mapping host is outside this container's egress allowlist, so the **obfuscated jar
     is read structurally** and nothing in the tool trusts a name.
  2. `Blocks` is the class with 898 static finals of one type. `Material` is **picked by USE** —
     the 47-constant final class `Blocks` reads 684 times. ⚠ The first cut picked it by SHAPE
     (a final class with 40–60 self-typed constants) and **chose the wrong class**; several match
     that description. The mistake is in the tool's header.
  3. **Which builder call is `replaceable()` is DERIVED.** `AIR` and `STRUCTURAL_AIR` are the
     first two constants and are byte-identical; `PORTAL` is the third and differs by exactly one
     call. That call is `notPushable()`; the one `AIR` has and `PORTAL` lacks is `replaceable()`.
  4. Helper-built blocks (logs, leaves, beds, ores) resolve by method **descriptor**;
     `Properties.copy` blocks inherit to a fixed point. **898 of 898 resolve, 0 unresolved** —
     that is the assertion, not a convenience.
  5. The tool then asserts the answer's SHAPE in both directions: 20 blocks that must be
     replaceable, 24 that must not. A wrong builder call would still have produced a set.

  The flag rides in the runtime blob as **flags bit 128** (16|32|64 are the support class),
  decodes as `Reg.replaceable(block)`, and is copied per real state to `States.replaceable`.
  `Player.REPLACEABLE` is now **that table itself**, not a second derivation of it — `placecheck`
  §4 asserts the identity, because a second derivation beside the real one is the whole bug.

  ⚠ **The seven Java OVERRIDES are the half that makes this not a lookup.** `States.canBeReplacedBy
  (state, held, face, hitY, replacingClicked)` implements them, and each has a partner in
  `Player.stackOnto` which says what replacing it actually PRODUCES:

  | block | rule | produces |
  |---|---|---|
  | `snow` | the same item and `layers < 8`; otherwise **only a single layer** | `layers + 1` |
  | `*_slab` | the same slab, not `double`: UP onto a bottom, DOWN onto a top, or a horizontal face on the half the click landed in | `type = double` |
  | `sea_pickle`, `turtle_egg`, `candle`/`*_candle` | the same item, count `< 4` | count + 1 |
  | `scaffolding` | the same item, always | — |
  | `vine`, `glow_lichen` | ⚠ the same item **REFUSES** — less replaceable than its material | — |

  The snow row is a second real bug found by writing this down: **every one of snow's eight states
  was replaceable before**, so a block placed against deep snow deleted all of it at once. And the
  slab row is why splitting `canBeReplaced` from `getStateForPlacement` is how a clone ends up
  with a slab that deletes the slab under it.

  Held by **`tools/placecheck.mjs`** — 142 assertions, 7 breaks. Its §2 is the section that would
  have caught this: it **re-runs the old geometric predicate** and asserts every block that
  predicate admits beyond vanilla's 28 is refused today, written against the rule rather than a
  list of names, so any future geometric shortcut fails there even if it is spelled differently.
  Its book-keeping is itself an assertion — the 21 blocks the old rule and vanilla agree on plus
  the 7 vanilla has that the rule never admitted (`fire`, `soul_fire`, `cave_air`, `void_air`,
  `light`, `structure_void`, `bubble_column`) must add to exactly 28.

  ⚠ **The same golden table carries every block's MATERIAL**, so **G9's furnace burn times** and
  **G13's per-block `SoundType`** — both written down in PLAN as "hand-table it and mark it
  hand-sourced" — now have a route out of the bytecode instead.

- **D-264** ⚠ **THE RAYCAST TREATS A BLOCK WITH NO COLLISION BOX AS A FULL CUBE, AND THAT IS
  DECLARED, NOT FIXED.** Found while auditing D-263's class. `14c_raycast.js` asks
  `Physics.shapeOf`, which is the **collision** shape, and its `if (!shape || shape === FULL_CUBE)`
  branch reports a hit on the whole cell. Vanilla has a separate **interaction/outline** shape:
  a flower's selection box is a small cross, a button's is a button, and the face you click is
  that shape's face, not the cell's.

  So today the outline around a flower, a torch, a rail, a button or a lever is a **full block**,
  and the entry face a placement is offset by is the cell's. With D-263 in place this no longer
  destroys anything — the cell is refused and the block goes on the clicked face — but it is a
  real parity gap in what the picture shows and in which face a placement uses at grazing angles.

  Closing it needs outline shapes baked at build time beside the 4,105 collision shapes, which is
  an F7-shaped job and belongs with **G10** (the block-breaking overlay wants the same data).
  Until then `placecheck` §5 **measures and pins it**: the count of blocks with no collision box
  is asserted inside a declared band, and a flower is asserted in the set with stone out, so the
  gap cannot grow in silence and the number is a fact rather than an estimate when the stage
  arrives. ⚠ This is the D-196 lesson applied early: a gap that is written down but not measured
  is a gap nobody can tell has changed.

  clone, throw, pickup-all and the quick-craft DRAG — branch for branch off the 1.18.2 bytecode,
  with the dump's offsets cited in the comments so the next reader can check a rule without
  re-deriving which method it is.

  ⚠ **The method is identified by SHAPE, because the dump is obfuscated.** `AbstractContainerMenu`
  is class `bqp`; `doClick` is `private void b(int, int, bqy, boj)` — the only private method
  taking (int, int, a seven-constant enum, Player) — and `bqy` is `ClickType`, whose seven
  constants are in declaration order PICKUP, QUICK_MOVE, SWAP, CLONE, THROW, QUICK_CRAFT,
  PICKUP_ALL. Same discipline as D-263: nothing here trusts a name.

  ⚠⚠ **THE BUG THIS SESSION MADE AND THE BYTECODE CAUGHT.** The quick-craft button packs two
  fields, and the pair reads backwards from what the mask builder suggests:

  ```
  public static int c(int)     ->  iload_0; iconst_2; ishr; iconst_3; iand   ==  i >> 2 & 3
  public static int d(int)     ->  iload_0; iconst_3; iand                   ==  i & 3
  public static int b(int,int) ->  header & 3 | (type & 3) << 2
  ```

  `doClick` stores `d(button)` into the STATUS field (offset 20) and `c(button)` into the TYPE
  field (offset 82) — so the **header is the low two bits and the type the next two**, even though
  `getQuickcraftMask(header, type)` reads as though it were the reverse. Written the obvious way
  round, all eleven drag assertions failed at once; written the other way they all pass. A clone
  that guesses here has drags that silently do nothing, and no count anywhere can see it.

  The rules that are in this file because they were READ rather than remembered:

  | rule | why it matters |
  |---|---|
  | right-click takes `(n + 1) / 2` | the LARGER half — five gives three in hand and two in the slot |
  | a **one-slot drag is a CLICK** | re-entered as PICKUP with the drag's TYPE as the button, so a one-slot right drag places exactly one rather than splitting |
  | `Slot.index` is the MENU index | `addSlot` overwrites it with `slots.size()`; using the container index re-clicks a different slot |
  | the split uses the stack **as it was when the drag began** | and `getQuickCraftSlotCount`'s `+ slotStackSize` is what makes a drag over a part-full slot TOP IT UP |
  | the status machine resets on any out-of-order message **except `1 -> 2`** | `if ((i != 1 || status != 2) && i != status) reset` — the obvious "prev or prev+1" leaves a menu stuck mid-drag after a dropped packet |
  | `moveItemStackTo` is **two passes** | stackables merge across the whole range first; one pass scatters a stack past a half stack of the same thing |
  | the backpack sends to the HOTBAR and the hotbar to the BACKPACK | they are not one range, and treating them as one makes shift-click a no-op half the time |
  | double-click's **first pass skips full stacks** | otherwise it empties the first full stack it meets and leaves every partial one |
  | every cap is the ITEM's, never the container's | the same trap D-261 recorded: ender pearls stop at 16 |

  Held by `invcheck`, now **153 assertions, 0 failures** (was 42), in six new sections of scripted
  CLICK SEQUENCES rather than calls to one function — the bugs in a slot machine live between
  clicks. ⚠ Its §13b is anti-vacuity of a different shape from §13's: these sections cannot be made
  vacuous by breaking a data file, so each break **re-runs a real sequence against the wrong rule**
  and asserts the expectation would have failed — including the header/type swap above, a
  merge-less `moveItemStackTo`, and a cancelled drag finished by a later END.

- **D-266** ✅ **CLOSED THE SAME SESSION — SHIFT-CLICKED ARMOUR EQUIPS, AND THE TABLE CAME OUT OF
  THE BYTECODE.** It was opened as a declared deviation and shut an hour later, so both halves are
  here: what was deviated from, and what closed it.

  ⚠ **The closing tool is `tools/extract-equipment.mjs`**, D-263's technique reused, and it needed
  one refinement that is worth keeping: **two six-constant enums are read exactly thirty times
  each by `Items.<clinit>`**, so "pick the class by USE" — D-263's own correction — TIED. The
  tiebreak is not a tiebreak but more evidence: the enum that is `EquipmentSlot` is the one whose
  constants land on the four iron armour pieces as **four distinct constants**. 25 armour items
  (six sets plus `turtle_helmet`), and vanilla's own four literal special cases quoted from
  `Mob.getEquipmentSlotForItem` — `carved_pumpkin`, the six skull blocks, `elytra`, `shield`.
  ⚠ Those seven skull-and-pumpkin rows are BLOCK items: `Items.<clinit>` registers them from
  `Blocks.X` with no string literal, so iterating the scan alone silently dropped exactly the
  cases this file exists for. The writer takes the UNION, and the names are checked against the
  built item registry so a stale quote fails rather than doing nothing.

  The slot rides in the item flags byte as **bits 32|64|128** (0 mainhand · 1 offhand · 2 feet ·
  3 legs · 4 chest · 5 head) and reads back as `Items.equipSlot`. The armour band is reversed
  against it — head is slot 5 and menu slot 5, feet is 2 and menu slot 8 — hence `10 - slot`,
  which is vanilla's `8 - equipmentslot.getIndex()` written the other way.
  `invcheck` holds nine equip cases **and both negatives**: an occupied head slot is left alone,
  and stone is not equipment. Without those two, a rule that sent everything to slot 5 would pass.

  ⚠ **AND THE SUITE CAUGHT TWO REGRESSIONS THIS WORK CAUSED**, neither of which a reading of the
  diff would have found:
  1. `merge-constants` wrote the new material name into `out[name].**material**` — a key
     **minecraft-data already owns**, and the one `pack-runtime`'s support class (D-140) reads to
     decide that a block containing "plant" is FLOOR-supported. One build later `floatcheck` had
     **25 floating plants** and `fuzzcheck` three refused placements that wrote anyway. A new fact
     gets a new key: it is `vanillaMaterial` now.
  2. `14g_menu.js` asked `player.creative`. **That boolean does not exist** — G6 (D-253) replaced
     it with vanilla's Abilities, and `modecheck` scans the source for reads of it precisely so
     this cannot creep back. The ability is `instabuild`.

  ⚠ Both are the same shape and worth naming: **a new field or a new read is a place where the
  old world's vocabulary can leak back in**, and the only reason either was caught in minutes is
  that a check already existed whose whole job was to notice.

  ### What it was, before it was closed

  `InventoryMenu.quickMoveStack` checks two branches before the backpack/hotbar ones: a piece of

  The branches were **absent rather than approximated**. A name-suffix rule ("ends in `_helmet`")

  ### The original entry

  ⚠ **(superseded above — kept for the record.)**

- **D-267** ⚠⚠ **G9 — EVERY RECIPE IN THE GAME, AND THE NBT LAYER THIRTEEN OF THEM NEEDED.**
  1,058 recipes: **1,045 are DATA** in the jar and are read, never written (`tools/pack-recipes.mjs`
  → 120.4 KB of JSON → **15.8 KB deflated**, 378 distinct ingredients), and **13 are
  `crafting_special_*`** — files carrying a type and nothing else, whose entire content is a
  hard-coded Java class.

  ⚠ **THIRTEEN, NOT TWELVE.** PLAN's G9 says twelve, and a census read by eye says twelve, because
  `tippedarrow` is easy to miss in a list of thirteen near-identical lines. The packer carries an
  **expected set that fails the build** when it changes, and that is the only reason it was caught
  rather than shipping one recipe nobody had implemented.

  **The NBT layer (`14f_inventory.js`).** A stack was `(item, count, damage)`; the specials need
  `display.color` on dyed leather, `Explosion` on a firework, `generation` on a written book,
  `Potion` on a tipped arrow, `BlockEntityTag.Items` on a shulker box. So a stack now carries an
  optional `t`, a plain JSON-able object, and:
  - it is a **VALUE, not a reference** — `copy` and `split` each deep-copy it, because two stacks
    sharing one tag object are a single edit away from silently changing each other, which is the
    classic NBT bug in every clone;
  - `isSameItemSameTags` now compares it, **order-insensitively over object keys** (two stacks
    built by different code paths will not agree about key order) but **order-SENSITIVELY over
    arrays** (a banner's pattern list is a sequence, not a set). Without this, two dyed leather
    caps of different colours stack into one.

  **The two matchers, and why neither is the obvious loop:**
  - **shaped** tries every offset the recipe fits, **mirrored and not**, and requires every cell
    OUTSIDE the recipe's box to be empty. Dropping the mirror breaks half the player base's muscle
    memory; dropping the outside test lets a pickaxe craft with a stray plank in the corner.
    ⚠ Patterns are padded to a rectangle by the packer with the width taken from the LONGEST row —
    and **MEASURED: 0 of 543** patterns in 1.18.2 are ragged, so that padding currently changes
    nothing. It is reported as 0 rather than asserted as necessary, because a defence whose
    necessity is assumed is one nobody notices has stopped being exercised.
  - **shapeless** is a **maximum bipartite matching** by augmenting paths, not a greedy walk.
    ⚠ And here the measurement changed what the test is: **0 of 183** shapeless recipes in 1.18.2
    mix a tag ingredient with a literal one the tag also contains, which is the shape greedy fails
    on. So the algorithm is INSURANCE, `craftcheck` says so, and it is proved against a SYNTHETIC
    recipe (`[#planks, oak_planks]` over `[oak_planks, birch_planks]`) built from the real
    ingredient table. A test that had quietly found no such recipe and passed would have proved
    nothing about the matcher at all.

  ⚠ **INGREDIENTS ARE NOT FLATTENED.** `#minecraft:planks` stays a tag reference and is resolved
  through `Tags.items()` at match time. Flattening would have put the same eleven names in the
  blob sixty times AND frozen a set the tag payload is supposed to be the single source of truth
  for. 198 of the ingredient references are tags.

  **`craftcheck` — 1,250 assertions, 0 failures, 8 breaks.** PLAN's acceptance was "every one of
  the 1,058 recipes is exercised once"; §2 is not a sample — **726 crafting · 112 cooking · 198
  stonecutting · 9 smithing** recipes each get a grid built out of their OWN ingredients and are
  crafted. ⚠ **0 collisions**: not one grid built from a recipe's ingredients matched a different
  recipe first. The count is fenced rather than assumed, because vanilla has the same ambiguity and
  what must not happen is the matcher becoming less discriminating and the number climbing.

  Eight specials are implemented — `repairitem`, `bookcloning`, `mapcloning`, `mapextending`,
  `bannerduplicate`, `shielddecoration`, `shulkerboxcoloring`, `tippedarrow` — each with the trap
  its clones fall into asserted: a copy of a copy cannot be copied again, a scale-4 map cannot be
  extended, a banner of a different colour is not a blank, and **dyeing a full shulker box keeps
  its contents** (a clone that rebuilds the item from its name eats a chest of diamonds).

- **D-268** ✅ **CLOSED THE SAME SESSION — ALL THIRTEEN SPECIALS ARE LIVE, AND THE COLOUR TABLES
  CAME OUT OF THE BYTECODE.** Opened as a declared deviation and shut an hour later, like D-266.

  `tools/extract-colours.mjs` writes two golden tables: **16 dye colours** (id, textureDiffuse,
  firework, text, plus the MaterialColor the constructor references) and **13 flower effects**.

  ⚠ **DyeColor was picked by USE, and the margin was five to one.** FIVE classes in the jar are
  enums with exactly sixteen constants of their own type, so "an enum with 16 constants" would
  have chosen wrong four times out of five. `Items` reads exactly ONE of them, and reads it
  exactly sixteen times — once per dye item. The tool asserts both the narrowing and the count.

  ⚠ **The columns were labelled by ANCHOR, and every search asserts exactly one hit.** The
  constructor takes four ints; the tool finds the slot equal to the ordinal (id), the slot
  carrying white=16383998 AND black=1908001 AND red=11546150 (textureDiffuse), the slot carrying
  white=15790320 (firework), and names the one left over (text). ⚠⚠ **THE FIREWORK COLOUR IS NOT
  THE DIFFUSE COLOUR** — white is 0xF0F0F0 against 0xF9FFFE — and that single fact is why
  `armordye` and `firework_star` cannot share a column. A table with one "colour" per dye would
  have looked complete and been wrong in one of the two recipes.

  ⚠ **THIRTEEN flowers, not eleven** — the brief said eleven because it collapsed "the four
  tulips" into one line, and the four tulips are four separate `Blocks` entries. The extractor
  asserts 13 and says so in the header, so a future reader cannot mistake it for a parse slip.
  `WitherRoseBlock` is a subclass and its 8 seconds is read from the `bipush 8` before its own
  `super(...)` call, not assumed. The bytecode holds **SECONDS**; `SuspiciousStewItem` multiplies
  by 20 at eat time, so the engine's tag carries ticks and the conversion happens once.

  ⚠ **The extractor's anti-vacuity was PROVEN, not claimed**: the agent perturbed two anchors
  against the real jar (white's diffuse by one, lily_of_the_valley's duration by a second) and
  confirmed each produced `1 failures — NEITHER file written` and exit 1.

  What the five now do, with the traps their clones fall into asserted in `craftcheck`:
  - **`armordye`** implements vanilla's `dyeArmor` blend — ⚠ NOT an average. The components AND
    the per-colour maxima are summed and divided by the count, then the mean is rescaled so its
    own largest component equals the mean maximum. `craftcheck` asserts a two-dye mix differs
    from the plain average and is BRIGHTER than it, which is the whole point of the rescale.
  - **`firework_star`** — all five shape types from their own items, flicker from glowstone,
    trail from a diamond, colours from the FIREWORK column.
  - **`firework_star_fade`** — gains `FadeColors` and keeps its own shape and colours.
  - **`firework_rocket`** — ⚠ makes **three** rockets, the one special whose output is a stack.
  - **`suspiciousstew`** — the flower decides the effect, and a sunflower is refused because it is
    a two-block plant and not a `FlowerBlock`.

  `craftcheck` is **1,299 assertions, 0 failures**, and the "unavailable" set is now empty in both
  the file and the check — which is still asserted in both directions, because an empty list that
  had stopped being compared would be the same picture as a working one.

  ### What it was, before it was closed

- **D-268 (original entry)** ⚠ **FIVE SPECIALS NEED A COLOUR TABLE THAT IS COMPILED JAVA, AND THEY WERE DECLARED
  UNAVAILABLE RATHER THAN APPROXIMATED.** `armordye`, `firework_star`, `firework_star_fade` and
  `firework_rocket` need `DyeColor`'s RGB values; `suspiciousstew` needs `FlowerBlock`'s
  flower-to-effect map. Both are hard-coded Java, in no JSON and no tag.

  Inventing sixteen RGB values that look about right is exactly the D-263 mistake wearing a new
  hat, so the five are registered with `unavailable: true` and `craftcheck` **asserts the
  unavailable set matches the file's own declaration** — in both directions. That is the part that
  matters: a special which quietly stopped working would otherwise be indistinguishable from one
  that was always on this list.

  ⚠ The route is the one D-263 and D-266 already opened: `DyeColor` is an enum whose constants
  carry their colours as constructor arguments, and `FlowerBlock`'s map is built in a `<clinit>`
  pairing block fields with `MobEffect` fields. Both are the same technique again — pick the class
  by use, derive the meaning of the constants from cases that cannot be in doubt, assert the
  answer's shape in both directions before writing.

- **D-269** ⚠ **THE FURNACE BURN TIMES CAME OUT OF THE BYTECODE TOO, AND ONE NUMBER PROVES IT.**
  `AbstractFurnaceBlockEntity.getFuel()` is a hard-coded Java map: no JSON, no `minecraft-data`
  file, no tag. PLAN's G9 says *"hand-table them and mark the table as hand-sourced"*. It is now
  `tools/extract-fuel.mjs` instead — **48 fuel items and 14 fuel tags**, generated, with the same
  standing as `block-materials-1.18.2.tsv` and `item-equipment-1.18.2.tsv`.

  ⚠ **The class is found by SIGNATURE, not by its contents.** `AbstractFurnaceBlockEntity` is the
  one class in all 6,399 that declares a no-argument `public static Map<Item, Integer>` method;
  `ItemTags` is picked by its GENERIC parameter (the only tag holder parameterised by the Item
  type) rather than by how many constants it has. The distinctive integer literals only *confirm*
  the find — they are the guard, not the search. That is the D-263 technique two refinements on.

  ⚠⚠ **`dried_kelp_block` burns for 4,001 ticks.** Not 4,000. Nobody writing this table from
  memory produces that number, and nobody reviewing a hand-written 4,000 would query it — which is
  the entire argument for generating it. `carpets` at 67 is the same shape.

  The map rides in the recipe blob (a furnace is a recipe machine, and a second 1 KB payload would
  cost more in plumbing than in bytes), and `pack-recipes` asserts its coverage in both directions
  before writing — lava bucket 20000, coal block 16000, blaze rod 2400, coal and charcoal 1600,
  stick 100, the planks and logs tags present; and stone, dirt, iron ingot, diamond and water
  bucket absent. A fuel map that had silently emptied would make every furnace in the world refuse
  to light and nothing else in the build would notice.

  ⚠ **The ITEM is asked before the TAGS**, which is vanilla's order and is load-bearing:
  `dried_kelp_block` would otherwise never be reached past a tag that contains it.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE FINDING THAT MADE GENERATING IT WORTH MORE THAN THE NUMBERS: AN EXCLUSION TAG.**
  `getFuel`'s tag helper calls a private guard, and that guard reads exactly one `ItemTags` field —
  **`#minecraft:non_flammable_wood`**. So crimson and warped **planks, stems, doors, slabs, stairs,
  fences, signs, buttons, pressure plates and trapdoors** are members of `#planks`, `#logs`,
  `#wooden_doors` and the rest **and are not fuel**. The first cut of the engine's lookup checked
  the item rows and then the tags, which would have made the entire nether wood family burn —
  ⚠ and **no count of recipes, items or tags could have seen it**, because every table involved
  would have been correct. The lookup order is now item row → exclusion → tag, and `craftcheck`
  asserts twelve nether-wood items at 0 against oak planks at 300, which is the pair that
  separates "the exclusion works" from "the tag is missing".
  ⚠ The extractor DERIVED the tag name from the guard predicate rather than being told it.

  Two smaller findings from the same work, both of which silently corrupted names before they were
  caught by an assertion rather than by reading: `Blocks.SCAFFOLDING`'s item registers through a
  one-argument overload, so "a block item must have its own name literal" was wrong and became
  "any register call whose first parameter is not a String takes the block's name"; and
  `HorseArmorItem`'s constructor takes a SECOND string literal after the registry name, so a
  last-literal-wins walk renamed `diamond_horse_armor` to `diamond`. The fix — take the FIRST
  literal per registration, and assert no two fields resolve to the same name — is the general
  lesson: **a name walk over a `<clinit>` needs a uniqueness assertion, or it corrupts quietly.**

  This entry exists because the same table also closes a claim in two other places: PLAN's **G13**
  says the per-block `SoundType` must be hand-tabled, and **D-263**'s material table already
  carries it. Neither stage now begins with a hand-written constant.

- **D-270** **G10's HAND IS A TICK MACHINE, AND FOUR OF ITS CONSTANTS ARE NOT THE OBVIOUS ONES.**
  `src/14i_hand.js` is the swing, the attack cooldown and the ten crack stages — arithmetic over
  ticks, so `handcheck` runs a whole mining session without a browser (63 assertions, 6 breaks).

  | rule | the obvious wrong answer |
  |---|---|
  | a swing is **6 ticks**; haste subtracts `1 + amplifier`, fatigue **adds `(1 + amplifier) * 2`** | `6 / (1 + haste)` — symmetric, and wrong in both directions |
  | `swing()` restarts the animation **only past the halfway point** | restarting unconditionally, which makes the hand stutter under fast clicking |
  | `swingTime` starts at **-1**, not 0 | starting at 0, which drops the first frame of every swing — one in six |
  | the crack stage **clamps at 9**, not 10 | `(progress * 10) \| 0`, which indexes past the last texture for one frame at the end of every block |

  ⚠ **The ten `destroy_stage` textures are reachable from NO MODEL.** They are named in Java, not
  in any blockstate or model file, so `extract-blocks.mjs`'s model walk cannot find them and the
  atlas shipped without them. They are forced in by name, and `handcheck` asserts all ten are in
  the atlas index — a breaking overlay with a missing stage is a block that stops cracking half
  way, which looks like a rendering bug and is a build one.

  The hand is ticked from `Player.tick`, not from the frame: a swing is six TICKS, and driving it
  from `dt` is how a clone ends up swinging faster on a better computer.

- **D-271** ⚠ **THE PER-ITEM ATTACK SPEED IS NOT BOUND, AND `handcheck` SAYS SO.**
  `Player.getCurrentItemAttackStrengthDelay()` is `1 / attackSpeed * 20`, and the per-item speed is
  a compiled-Java attribute modifier — a sword is -2.4, an axe between -3.2 and -3.0 — in
  `items.json` nowhere and in no tag. Every item currently swings at the base 4.0 (a five-tick
  cooldown), and the check asserts *that*, in the else-branch of an `if (bound)`, so the day the
  table lands the test changes deliberately rather than silently passing either way.
  ⚠ The route is open and cheap: the modifiers are literal floats in `Items.<clinit>`'s
  `new SwordItem(tier, damage, speed, props)` calls — the same walk `extract-fuel.mjs` already does.

- **D-272** ⚠ **THE HIT-PARTICLE CADENCE IS A DECLARED APPROXIMATION: four ticks.**
  The little chips that fly off a block while you mine it come from the client's attack loop and
  the exact interval is not something this project has measured. It is rendering, which the
  charter permits to deviate — but a deviation is a ruling with a number, not a shrug. Four ticks
  is the interval, `handcheck` pins it, and when somebody measures the real one the change is one
  constant and a failing assertion rather than an archaeology exercise.

- **D-273** ⚠⚠ **THE BREAKING OVERLAY AND THE HAND ARE DRAWN ON THE HUD CANVAS, NOT IN A THIRD
  GEOMETRY PASS — AND THE CHECK THAT PROVES IT WORKS IS THE INTERESTING PART.**
  Vanilla draws the crumbling texture as a third pass over the block's own shape with a multiply
  blend and a depth offset: two backends, a shader variant and a dynamic mesh. MC-Lite draws it on
  the 2D HUD that already projects the selection box, as two clipped affine `drawImage` calls per
  camera-facing face. The charter allows rendering to be clever instead of faithful; the declared
  cost is that the texture is affine WITHIN each triangle rather than perspective-correct, which
  is sub-pixel over one block.
  ⚠ The alternative — three fills of increasing darkness — was rejected: a block that *darkens*
  instead of cracking is precisely what Dan's "cannot easily tell it is not Minecraft" bar is for.
  The hand is `drawIcon`, the same call the hotbar uses, moved along **vanilla's own swing curve**
  (`f = sqrt(progress)`, then `-0.4 sin(f π)`, `0.2 sin(2 f π)`, `-0.2 sin(progress π)`) — the
  cheap half of getting it right, which a single sine does not.

  **`tools/g10check.mjs` is the first browser stage that reads the HUD's own 2D canvas** rather
  than a screenshot — exact, cheap, and immune to the compositor, which is D-247's whole lesson.
  16 assertions, 4 breaks: the overlay appears only while breaking, every one of the ten stages
  draws something, **stage 9 is crackier than stage 0** (13,271 → 114,734 px, so a tile lookup
  returning one texture for all ten fails), the hand appears only when something is held, the hand
  MOVES through the swing, and a spectator has none.

  ⚠⚠ **AND TWO OF ITS OWN ASSERTIONS WERE WRONG BEFORE THE ENGINE WAS.** It reported "151 pixels
  of overlay above the block" twice, and both times the fault was the test:
  1. the first version measured the band above the block's projected bounding box — which
     collapses to row 0 when the block's box starts at y = -87 because the block fills the top of
     the screen. The "band" was the block.
  2. the guard added for it (all eight corners in front of the near plane) was the wrong guard and
     did not fire.
  The fix is to measure whichever side of the block has at least 60 px of room and to **say which
  side and how much room** on every run — and to print a row profile on failure, because a picture
  test that fails with only a number costs the next session an hour. ⚠ The per-triangle transform
  was written while chasing that phantom; it is kept because a triangle's affine map is exact for
  its three points and a parallelogram's fourth corner is not, so it is right for a reason that
  survives the fact that it fixed nothing. **Writing that down is the point:** the number in a
  picture test is a claim about the test first and the engine second.

---
- **D-274** **the GUI is vanilla's own pixels, and the font's widths are measured, not tabled**

  **PLAN G11.** The charter puts the GUI inside "absolute full parity", so `tools/build-gui.mjs`
  lifts seven PNGs out of the **1.13.2** jar (D-5, the same game the block atlas comes from — 1.14
  redrew the hotbar, the hearts and the buttons, and a 1.14 heart beside a 1.13 block is a tell) and
  ships them as one deflated RGBA blob: `widgets`, `icons`, `container/inventory`,
  `container/crafting_table`, `container/furnace`, `container/generic_54`, `font/ascii`.
  **1,600.9 KB raw → 38.2 KB deflated**, against D-12's 15 MB ceiling. Everything else in the jar's
  GUI folder — the recipe book, advancements, the trade screen — belongs to stages that do not
  exist, and a sheet nothing draws is a quarter-megabyte of nothing.

  ⚠ **The per-glyph widths are NOT in any file.** Vanilla's `FontTexture` scans each 8×8 cell of
  `ascii.png` from the right for the first column with a non-transparent pixel; that scan is done
  here, at build time, and 256 bytes ship instead. So the text is spaced like the game's — the
  one-pixel `i`, the four-pixel space (blank, so vanilla hard-codes it) — rather than like a table
  somebody typed. Eleven anchors are asserted before anything is written, and `guicheck`
  **re-measures all 94 printable glyphs from the shipped pixels** and requires every one to agree.

  ⚠ **The sheet rectangles are the one thing here that is not derived**, so `guicheck` asserts each
  of them against the artwork rather than against itself: the full heart is red, the empty container
  is dark and unsaturated and *larger* than the fill it frames, the blinking container differs from
  the plain one, hunger is brown and is not red, the XP bar's two 182-wide rows differ by 60 in
  green, the selector's centre is transparent and the hotbar's is not. **A property of the artwork,
  not of the coordinates** — so a rectangle that drifted onto the blinking heart, which is also a
  heart, fails.

  Three of those assertions were wrong on the first run, and all three were wrong *about the
  artwork* rather than about the code:
  - the full heart is **34 opaque texels of 81**, not most of the rectangle — the fill is drawn
    *over* the container, which supplies the outline. Same for hunger: 20.
  - the half heart keeps its **left** (columns 5–8 completely clear, centroid 4.00 → 2.75); the half
    hunger icon keeps its **right** (centroid 3.45 → 4.14) and is *not* a clean split, because the
    drumstick's bone runs into the bottom-right corner of both. They empty in **opposite**
    directions, which is why vanilla mirrors the hunger row — and the check now measures centroids
    instead of asserting a split that the pixels do not have.
  - the 176×166 panel is opaque but for **18 texels**, the four rounded corners.
- **D-275** **the player has a real inventory and a real menu, and the placeholders are deleted**

  **PLAN G8/G9/G11.** `P.inventory` is a real 41-slot `Inventory`, `P.menu` is a real
  `InventoryMenu`, and `src/14g_menu.js` is the whole of vanilla's `AbstractContainerMenu.doClick` —
  all six click types, the quick-craft drag with its header/type mask, `moveItemStackTo`'s two
  passes, the equipment branches. `P.heldItem()` returns the held **stack**; the hotbar's block
  states remain only as what the creative picker writes into slot items.

  ⚠ **D-139 applies to both halves and it was enforced late.** See D-276.
- **D-276** **a later assignment silently wins, and `tools/dupcheck.mjs` is why that is now visible**

  G11 wrote a new `H.drawSurvival` out of `icons.png`, and **the whole 404-line region it sat in was
  pasted into `src/15_hud.js` twice**. The stale copy came second, so it won: `drawSurvival`,
  `hotbarRect`, `drawCrumbling`, `drawHand`, `drawParticles` and `drawSelection` all ran from the
  old block, every screenshot of the "new" HUD was the old placeholder's coloured rectangles, and
  the build was green throughout — a duplicate definition is perfectly legal JavaScript.

  The same scan found a **worse** one. G3's placeholder `P.heldItem = ''` and G11's
  `P.heldItem = function ()` are 280 lines apart in `src/14_player.js`. The function won, so
  `miningContext().item` — which `Mining.itemSpeed` and `Mining.canHarvest` both read as a **name**
  — was a function object. Both take a miss quietly. **Every pickaxe mined at bare-hand speed and
  harvested nothing**, and no check saw it, because `minecheck` calls `Mining.itemSpeed` directly
  with its own fixtures and never goes through `miningContext`. The fix is `P.heldItemName()`,
  derived from the stack, and the placeholder is deleted.

  So the class is: **a later top-level assignment silently replacing an earlier one in the same
  file.** It is invisible in review (the two are never on screen together), invisible to the build,
  and invisible to every behavioural check that happens not to exercise the shadowed path. It is
  visible to a forty-millisecond parse, which is `tools/dupcheck.mjs`: one definition per `X.y` per
  module, across **1,083 top-level names in 64 modules**, plus a repeated-run scan that catches the
  pasted block by its shape. The indent rule is the whole trick — exactly two spaces is the module
  body's own level, so `P.slot = i` inside a function is not a redefinition.

  ⚠ The lesson that generalises past this one: **a check that passes proves only what it touches.**
  `minecheck` was green for three sessions across a bug that turned every tool into a bare hand,
  because it tested the formula and not the call site. Where a value crosses from one stage's code
  into another's, the crossing itself needs an assertion.
- **D-277** **the held item's name is anchored to the screen, not to the hotbar, and it fades**

  Vanilla's `renderSelectedItemName` draws at **`height - 59`**, and **`+ 14`** in a gamemode that
  cannot hurt the player, because there is then no heart row to clear. It was `hotbarRect().y - 12`
  here, which is `height - 34` — straight through the hearts, which sit at `height - 39` and are
  nine pixels tall. Anchoring GUI text to another widget rather than to the screen is how a layout
  that looks right at one scale collides at another.

  ⚠ **And it fades on the TICK.** `toolHighlightTimer` is set to **40** when the held stack changes
  and counts down; the alpha is `timer * 256 / 10` clamped to 255, so the name is solid for thirty
  ticks and fades over ten. It is driven from `P.tick`, not from the frame, for D-270's reason: a
  better frame rate must not make it disappear sooner. A name that simply stays on screen is one of
  the commonest ways a clone's hotbar reads as not-Minecraft.
- **D-278** **the inventory draws the player, flat, out of the default skin — and the black
  window was never a bug**
  The rectangle in the middle of the player's screen is `inventory.png`'s **own pixels**: vanilla
  renders the player into it, so a clone that blits the sheet and stops has a black hole in the
  most-looked-at screen in the game. It read as a broken blit for most of a session; it was the
  artwork, and `guicheck` now asserts it is solid black precisely so the next person does not
  spend that hour.

  ⚠ **THE DEVIATION, DECLARED: the figure is flat and front-on.** Vanilla renders a lit 3D
  humanoid that turns its head and body toward the pointer. MC-Lite has no entity renderer until
  **G17**, which owns this. What ships is the skin's twelve front faces — head, body, two arms,
  two legs and their six overlay layers — drawn at vanilla's own anchor: `InventoryScreen` calls
  `renderEntityInInventory(x + 51, y + 75, 30)`, so the figure is centred on GUI `x + 51` with its
  **feet** on `y + 75`, at thirty pixels to the block, and a 32-unit model is sixteen units to the
  block — **1.875 GUI pixels per skin texel**, sixty pixels tall. No rotation, no lighting, and
  **no armour on the model**; the equipped pieces show in the four armour slots beside it, as they
  also do in the real game.

  `assets/minecraft/textures/entity/steve.png` is the eighth sheet in the GUI blob and costs
  **1.4 KB deflated**. ⚠ The parts table is asserted rather than trusted: the six base faces must
  **tile the 16×32 figure exactly** — 64 + 96 + 96 + 96 = 352 texels, no gap and no overlap — each
  overlay must land exactly on its own base part, and the artwork itself must be skin-toned at the
  face, cyan at the shirt and blue at the legs. A parts table that had two numbers swapped would
  otherwise draw a recognisable-but-wrong person.

- **D-279** **the survival HUD's layout is DATA, because an arithmetic slip put the hunger row on
  top of the hearts**
  Vanilla anchors the heart row to `width/2 - 91` and the hunger row to `width/2 + 91`, and the
  two grow in **opposite** directions — hearts rightward, hunger leftward, which is why their half
  icons are mirrored (D-274). The code held `left` (already `width/2 - 91`) and then wrote the
  hunger row as `left + (91 - 9 - i * 8)`: ten pixels **left** of centre, straight over hearts four
  through ten, and the experience level landed on them too.

  ⚠ **A screenshot did not give it away** — a red heart under a brown drumstick still reads as a
  row of hearts, and the two rows are the same height. What gives it away is arithmetic, so the
  layout is now `Gui.HUD`: one table of vanilla's own offsets, all of them relative to a **screen
  edge** rather than to another widget (D-277), with the two rows as functions of `i`. `guicheck`
  asserts the hearts end before the hunger begins, that the two mirror about the centre, that they
  run in opposite directions, that the held item's name clears the heart row and that the level
  sits in the gap between the rows — and its anti-vacuity section **replays the shipped slip** and
  requires it to be refused.
- **D-280** **one spelling for an atlas key, and a fallback that rescues a naming mistake keeps it
  alive**
  G10's ten `destroy_stage_N` tiles are reachable from no model (D-270), so `extract-blocks.mjs`
  forces them into the texture list by name — and forced them in as `minecraft:block/…` while all
  791 names the model walk produces are bare `block/…`. `tilecheck` has refused the redundant
  prefix project-wide since F-track and caught it the moment the atlas was rebuilt.

  ⚠ **The interesting part is what the runtime had done about it.** `crackTile` had grown a
  *second* lookup — try the prefixed name, then the bare one — so the picture was right and the
  bug was invisible from the game. That is the D-139 shape wearing different clothes: a fallback
  that silently rescues a mistake is a second implementation of the same thing, and it guarantees
  nobody ever fixes the first. The names are bare, the second lookup is deleted, and `handcheck`
  now asserts the ten tile names carry no prefix as well as that all ten are in the atlas.
- **D-281** **the browser stages run one at a time, because a starved harness accuses the engine**
  The container has **two cores**, and a browser stage is a whole Chromium driving a real render
  loop. Six launched together on 14 September 2026 produced **nine failures across four stages**:
  `cullcheck` — *"the occlusion flood culled 0 sections — it is not running"*; `soakcheck` — *"the
  backlog GREW while the player stood still: 251 → 1311"*, *"41 light seeds are still queued six
  seconds after the flight stopped"*; `palettecheck` — *"the world never settled at any of render
  distances 16, 8, 4"*; `smoke` — *"the 20 Hz simulation ran [6 ticks]"*. **Every one of them
  passed on a solo re-run against the same build.**

  ⚠ **The failure messages are worse than useless, because they name the engine.** Each of those
  sentences describes a real and serious bug, and reads as evidence for it. The stages take minutes
  each, so running them serially costs a few minutes and buys a result that means something.
  The tell, written down so the next session recognises it in one glance: **several stages failing
  at once with timing-shaped complaints** — "still arriving", "not draining", "never settled", a
  low tick count. One stage failing alone is a bug; four failing together on this box is the box.
- **D-282** **the whole of `en_us.json` ships, and Mojang's own test vectors grade the formatter**
  **PLAN G12.** Up to here the game named a diamond sword by taking its registry id and swapping
  underscores for spaces — "diamond sword", lower case, in a GUI that has said "Diamond Sword"
  since 2011. Every string a player reads is on the parity side of the charter.

  ⚠ **THE WHOLE FILE, AND THE ALTERNATIVE WAS MEASURED.** 5,163 keys, 285 KB of JSON, **57.8 KB
  deflated** — 77 KB once base64 takes its third, which is 0.5% of D-12's ceiling. Dropping the
  command, advancement, world-creation, multiplayer, statistics and options trees leaves 3,839
  keys and 37.6 KB: **25 KB saved for a curation list that has to be revisited at every stage that
  adds a screen and goes stale silently when it is not.** Not worth a maintenance decision.

  ⚠⚠ **`%s` AND `%N$s` INTERACT, AND NOT THE WAY YOU WOULD GUESS.** Vanilla's decomposer keeps ONE
  sequential counter: a bare `%s` takes the next argument and advances it; an indexed `%N$s` takes
  argument N−1 and **does not advance anything**. So in `"%s%2$s again %s"` with (a, b, c) the
  third placeholder is **b**, not c. Every naive implementation — one counter advanced by both
  forms — gets `c` there, and the two differ on exactly one word in the middle of a sentence.

  ⚠ **MOJANG SHIPS THE FIXTURES.** `translation.test.none`, `.complex`, `.escape`, `.invalid`,
  `.invalid2`, `.args` and `.world` are in `en_us.json` for one reason: Mojang's own unit tests use
  them. `textcheck` evaluates all seven, so the formatter is graded against the game's fixtures
  rather than this project's reading of the rule — D-263's referee discipline, for free. Its
  anti-vacuity section runs the naive implementation and requires it to give a different answer.

  ⚠ **18 BLOCKS ARE NAMED BY ANOTHER BLOCK'S KEY**, and it is vanilla's rule rather than a
  fallback: `WallBannerBlock.getDescriptionId()` returns the standing banner's — the wall form has
  no string of its own and never had — and `item_frame`/`glow_item_frame` are **entities**, named
  by their item. `pack-lang` derives the table by rule and asserts it is **exactly** the sixteen
  wall banners plus the two frames, so it is one lookup with a table beside it rather than three
  lookups in a row (D-280). Likewise a **block item is named by its block key**: `item.minecraft.
  stone` does not exist and never has. **900 of 900 blocks and 1,100 of 1,100 real items resolve.**
  ⚠ `real` is load-bearing on the item side: the registry carries 1,235 MODEL names and 135 of
  them (`bow_pulling_0`, `clock_01`, `broken_elytra`, `amethyst_bud`, `air`) are not items anyone
  can hold. Relaxing the check to make them pass would have hidden the 1,100 that must have a name.

  Components are a tree — literal or translatable, `extra` children, a style that **inherits** —
  and `Text.runs()` flattens one to the `[{text, style}]` list the HUD draws. ⚠ `undefined` is not
  `false`: a child that says nothing about `bold` inside a bold parent is bold, one that says
  `bold: false` is not, and collapsing the two makes a whole death message bold because one name
  in it was. The legacy `§` codes are a second, still-live style system, and ⚠ **a colour code
  clears the decorations** — `§lbold §ered` is not bold, because the colour reset it.

  Death messages come from the source: G5's ten damage ids are named exactly as `death.attack.<id>`
  names them, so the mapping is the identity rather than a table that can drift. `pack-lang`
  refuses to build without the ten keys and `textcheck` §6 reads **G5's own table out of the
  module** — not a copy — and refuses a source with no key. The death screen shows the line
  ("Dan tried to swim in lava") under the title; "You died" on its own is the one thing every
  clone shows and the real game never does.

- **D-283** **the chat is `ChatComponent`'s arithmetic, and the field swallows the keyboard whole**
  ⚠ **EVERY NUMBER IS VANILLA'S**: a message is visible for **200 ticks**; the box is **320** GUI
  pixels wide (`chatWidth` 1.0 is `value * 280 + 40`), **9** pixels a line, **10** lines closed and
  **20** open, bottom edge at `height − 40`, left edge at **4**, scrollback **100**, field **256**
  characters; the background is drawn at **half** the text's alpha. Each is a number a clone gets
  approximately right and that reads as not-Minecraft at a glance.

  ⚠⚠ **THE FADE IS `clamp((1 − t/200) × 10, 0, 1)` SQUARED.** Full opacity until tick 180, then
  away over twenty — and the square makes the last of those twenty far faster than the first. A
  linear ten-second fade is perfectly reasonable in a screenshot and a different game in motion,
  and no picture test can tell you which one you have. ⚠ 180 is the last opaque tick and the value
  there is **0.9999999999999996**, not 1: `180/200` is not exact in binary and vanilla computes the
  same expression in the same doubles. `chatcheck` asserts the boundary, not the bit pattern —
  asserting `=== 1` was that file's own first bug.

  ⚠ **THE SCROLLBACK AND THE DRAWN LINES ARE SEPARATE.** A re-wrap goes back to the scrollback,
  never to the already-wrapped lines: re-splitting split text compounds, and leaves the breaks from
  the narrowest the window ever was. ⚠ And the drawn list is **bottom-up** — `lines[0]` is drawn
  closest to the bottom — so a wrapped message's FIRST line must be LAST in the list. Reading it
  in list order gives the message backwards, which is correct; `chatcheck` asserting the
  un-reversed order was that file's own second bug, and it would have passed against a renderer
  that drew every multi-line message upside down. ⚠ Its fixture had to be numbered words, too:
  with forty copies of "word" every wrapped line is the same string, so "the first line is not the
  last line" compares a string to itself and passes whichever way round the renderer is.

  ⚠ **AN OPEN CHAT SUSPENDS THE FADE** — opening it is how you read what you missed — and ⚠ **the
  field swallows the keyboard whole**: while it is up, `w` types a `w` and does not walk, `e` does
  not open the inventory, `1` does not change slot, and the pointer lock is released so the mouse
  stops turning the player mid-sentence. That is not a special case; it is what a focused text
  field means, and the branch is first in the keydown handler so nothing else can see the key.
- **D-284** **the sound SET is complete and the BITRATE is the deviation, and the arithmetic says
  why**
  **PLAN G13.** ⚠ **The `.ogg` files are not in the jar** — they live in the launcher's
  content-addressed store, `assets/objects/<xx>/<sha1>`, indexed by `assets/indexes/1.18.json`, and
  `resources.download.minecraft.net` is outside this container's egress allowlist. So they cross
  the file bridge **fifty at a time**, which makes coverage a **measurement** rather than an
  assumption, and `pack-sounds` reports it: fully voiced, partly voiced, silent, and which.

  The numbers the choice rests on, all measured: the non-mob selection is **605 events / 1,214
  files / 22.2 MB** of Vorbis. D-12's ceiling is 15 MB for the whole file, ~4 MB was already
  built, and base64 adds a third. **Opus mono VBR measures 3.58× smaller** on 165 real files, so
  the full set lands at ~6.2 MB → **8.3 MB base64**, ~12.3 MB total.

  ⚠ **THE OTHER WAY ROUND WAS REJECTED ON THE EVIDENCE.** Keeping the original bitrate and cutting
  the set loses whole materials — deepslate, the nether blocks, amethyst — and **a missing
  footstep is far more audible than a lower bitrate on a 0.3-second footstep**. A variant cap of
  four was also measured (16.03 MB raw, 8.62 MB base64 at 48 kbps) and rejected for the same
  reason: footstep variety is heard constantly.

  Excluded by RULE, not by a hand-written list, so it re-runs when the budget changes: music and
  records (288 MB), mob sounds (**G18 owns them, 24 MB raw — and they will not fit alongside
  this, which is the next time this decision has to be made**), and 23 long ambient loops (4.5 MB).

  ⚠ **Opus-in-Ogg decodes natively through `decodeAudioData`, and that was verified in Chromium
  before anything was committed to it.** ⚠ **The header is deflated and the audio is not**: Opus is
  already entropy-coded, deflating the whole payload saved 9.89% on a 1.08 MB build and nearly all
  of that came from the JSON, so only the header is packed — the runtime does not inflate
  megabytes of incompressible audio at load, which is the part the 2200G would feel.

  `g13check` is a browser stage because **a headless check cannot tell a valid stream from a
  truncated one and the failure mode is silence** — no error, no console line, nothing in any
  counter. It hands every shipped clip to the browser's own decoder through an **OfflineAudioContext**,
  which needs no user gesture (a normal `AudioContext` in headless Chromium is created suspended
  and never starts, so anything built on one would have skipped rather than run). ⚠ It also asserts
  no clip decodes to **zero seconds** — a truncation decodes perfectly and plays nothing — and its
  anti-vacuity section proves a clip sliced **one byte late** is refused, so the offsets are doing
  work.

- **D-285** **every block's `SoundType` out of the bytecode, with the constructor's argument order
  DERIVED**
  PLAN said this one was "hand-tabled or taken from `minecraft-data`". Neither was needed: it is
  the **fifth** table D-263's referee technique has produced, after Material, EquipmentSlot, the
  furnace fuel map and DyeColor.

  - `SoundEvents` is the class with 1,000–1,400 static finals of one other type. ⚠ It has
    **exactly 1,203 fields and `sounds.json` has exactly 1,203 events** — an equality nobody could
    arrange by accident, and it is asserted.
  - `SoundType` is picked by **use**: the class of 50–90 own-type constants whose `<clinit>` reads
    SoundEvents **exactly five times per constant** — 76 constants, 380 reads. Nothing else in the
    jar has that shape.
  - ⚠⚠ **THE ARGUMENT ORDER IS DERIVED.** The five events are positional, and a clone that writes
    `break, place, step, hit, fall` from memory gets a game where **placing a block sounds like
    walking on it**. The registered names end in the role, so the order is read off the data: for
    every constant whose five events share a prefix, the suffix sequence must be the same
    sequence. It comes out **`break, step, place, hit, fall`, agreed by 66 sound types with none
    disagreeing**, and the extractor refuses to write if they disagree.
  - ⚠ **"0 unresolved" DOES NOT TRANSFER from `extract-materials`.** `BlockBehaviour$Properties`
    starts every block at `SoundType.STONE` and `.sound()` overrides it, so **280 of 898 blocks
    legitimately take the default**. That count is REPORTED; asserting zero would have been a lie
    dressed as rigour, and the default is identified by finding the type whose break event is
    `block.stone.break` rather than by position.

  The runtime holds **75 distinct types over 898 blocks, indexed by registry id, not by name** — a
  string lookup per footstep is the kind of cost that only shows up on the 2200G. ⚠ Three things
  a clone gets wrong and this does not: the variant is a **weighted** roll (`nextInt(totalWeight)`
  — a four-variant event weighted 1,1,1,4 plays the fourth **4/7** of the time, not 1/4); block
  sounds carry vanilla's own volume and a **`pitch * (1 + (rand − rand) * 0.1)` jitter**, without
  which a row of identical blocks sounds like a machine gun; and **the audio context cannot exist
  before a gesture** — every browser suspends one made at load, and a suspended context that is
  never resumed plays nothing, silently, for ever, so it is created on the pointer lock.

  ⚠ **Footsteps count DISTANCE, not time** (`Entity.moveDist`): a step plays each time the walked
  distance passes the next whole unit, so a sprint steps faster than a walk with no timer
  involved and crouching steps less often for free. The counter re-bases on the **actual**
  distance, so 21.5 blocks gives **20** steps, not 21 — `soundcheck` asserting 21 was that file's
  own first bug, and the same slip in the engine drifts footsteps out of phase with the walk.

- **D-286** **the transport is finished, so the floor that stood in for it is DELETED — a
  provisional assertion left beside the real one is a second, weaker truth** *(session 9, G13)*

  `soundcheck` fenced the sound coverage with `filesPresent >= 150` for as long as the `.ogg`
  files were still crossing fifty at a time. That was right while it was true: the clips live only
  on Dan's machine, a batch is a round trip, and a check asserting "all 1,214" would have been red
  for weeks for no engineering reason. All 1,214 are now across, verified file-by-file against the
  manifest's own sizes, so the fence is not softened or raised — it is **removed**, and
  `filesPresent === filesWanted && filesMissing === 0` stands in its place (D-139: a stage that
  replaces something is not done until the something is deleted, in the same commit). Keeping both
  would leave a check that passes at 150 clips sitting one line above a check that demands 1,214,
  and the next person to see red has two contradictory statements about what this project requires.

- **D-287** **the silence is Minecraft's, and a check that cannot tell "never recorded" from
  "never arrived" is not checking the transport** *(session 9, G13)*

  `pack-sounds` reported **5 silent events** of 605 selected. That number is exactly as consistent
  with five clips that failed to cross the bridge as with five sounds Mojang never shipped, and an
  unexplained residue in a coverage report is how a real gap survives a green suite. So it was
  settled at the source rather than shrugged at: all five — `block.fungus.fall`, `block.fungus.hit`,
  `block.roots.fall`, `block.roots.hit`, `block.roots.step` — carry `"sounds": []` in vanilla
  1.18.2's own `sounds.json`. ⚠ **Three of them carry a subtitle**, which is the tell: Mojang wrote
  the caption for a sound and then shipped the event empty, so the emptiness is deliberate and
  reproducing it is parity, not a hole.

  **Eleven** events are empty in 1.18.2. Six are mobs or music and the selection rule excludes
  them; five survive, and five is what the pack reports — the arithmetic closes. All eleven are
  recorded in `tools/golden/silent-events-1.18.2.tsv` (derived mechanically, like every other
  golden table here), and `soundcheck` asserts the set **in both directions**:
  - an unvoiced event **not** on the list is an unexplained silence — a clip that never arrived —
    and turns the check red;
  - an event **on** the list that has audio is invented audio, and turns it red too.

  ⚠ The second direction is the one worth having. Without it a fallback that quietly substituted
  some other clip for an empty event would read as *better* coverage — 605 of 605 voiced — while
  being a straight parity break that no ear-test would catch, because the wrong sound in a place
  that should be silent is indistinguishable from the right sound if you have never heard the
  original. Both directions are broken and caught in the anti-vacuity section (D-30): emptying
  `block.gravel.step` makes it the one unexplained silence, and giving `block.roots.step` a clip is
  caught as invention.

- **D-288** **the save was three stages behind the game it saved, and the check that guarded it
  was green the whole time** *(session 9, G14)*

  `Player.toJSON` wrote a position, a gamemode and **nine block states**. That was exactly right
  in session 2, when the hotbar WAS nine block states. G8 then gave the player a real 41-slot
  inventory of item stacks with counts, damage and NBT, `P.hotbar` became a derived VIEW of it,
  and `toJSON` went on reading the view. G5 gave the player health, food, saturation, exhaustion
  and experience, and nothing wrote any of it. The result was measured, not argued about:

  ```
   slot 0  diamond_pickaxe  count 1   damage 137  ->  saved as state 0, which is AIR
   slot 1  cobblestone      count 64              ->  saved as a state; the 64 is gone
   slot 20 golden_apple x2                        ->  no field existed
   slot 36 iron_boots  dmg 5                      ->  no field existed
   slot 40 stick x17  (the offhand)               ->  no field existed
  ```

  ⚠ An item that is not a placeable block has **no block state**: `Items.stateOf` returns −1 and
  the writer stored 0. So every tool, every piece of food and every ingredient a player owned
  vanished when they closed the tab — and the nine that survived came back as single blocks,
  because a state has no count.

  ⚠⚠ **`savecheck` PASSED ACROSS ALL OF IT, WITH 51 ASSERTIONS AND 3 BREAKS.** It is not a bad
  check; it is a check of a different question. It asks whether the format survives the block
  registry being shuffled — it does, and that is D-107's hard-won property — and it never asks
  whether the format CONTAINS THE GAME. This is D-276 a third time in one session: *a check that
  passes proves only what it touches, and the bugs live in the joins between stages.* The join
  here is a function in `14_player.js` reading a field in `14f_inventory.js` whose meaning changed
  a stage earlier, and nothing in either module was wrong on its own.

  **v4** writes the inventory and the survival state. Four rulings inside it:

  1. ⚠ **BY ITEM NAME, NEVER BY ITEM ID.** `NS.Items` is generated from the jar by the same kind
     of tool as `NS.Reg`; `s.i` is an index into a table the next build can reorder or grow. This
     is D-107's argument one registry over, and `savecheck` now shuffles BOTH between save and
     load. An item this build no longer has becomes an **empty slot**, never a substitute.
  2. ⚠ **EVERY SURVIVAL NUMBER IS CLAMPED ON THE WAY IN.** A save is a file on the player's disk:
     truncated, hand-edited, or written by another build. `health: 1e9` must not load as
     invulnerability. **NaN is the one that does not announce itself** — it fails every `<` and
     `>`, so a NaN food level neither starves nor regenerates and the player simply stops healing
     for ever, with nothing in the HUD to say why.
  3. ⚠ **A v3 SAVE IS MIGRATED; A v2 SAVE IS STILL REFUSED**, and the difference is not sentiment.
     v2 stored numbers into a table that no longer exists, so reading one means GUESSING which
     block it was. v3 stores NAMES, and a name still means what it meant. So each v3 entry becomes
     **one** of that block's item — the smallest number the old save actually implies — and a block
     with no item at all (water, fire, a wall torch) becomes an **empty slot rather than a guess**.
     Nothing is invented to fill a new field.
  4. ⚠ **THE MIGRATION LIVES IN `14f_inventory.js`, NOT IN `14_player.js`.** It was written in the
     player first, which is the one module too heavy to load in a check — a migration that runs
     exactly once per player, on the save they care about most, tested by nothing. It moved to the
     module that owns stacks, where `savecheck` reaches it in fifty milliseconds.

  ⚠ **`air` IS DELIBERATELY NOT A FIELD.** `15_hud.js` draws a bubble row from `P.air` and
  **nothing in the engine has ever set it** — the guard is `P.air !== undefined`, so the row has
  never been drawn once and drowning is not implemented, though `Sv.DAMAGE.drown` is defined and
  waiting. A save field for a value nothing produces always reads its default, which is worse than
  no field: it looks like the feature works.

- **D-288b** **two formats, two version numbers — sharing one constant would have deleted every
  world** *(session 9, G14)*

  Bumping `S.VERSION` from 3 to 4 for the inventory was nearly a catastrophe, and the only reason
  it was not is that the work was done with the file open rather than from a checklist. `S.encode`
  writes `S.VERSION` into the **binary block-edit blob's** header and `S.decode` requires an exact
  match. The blob format had not changed at all — the inventory lives in the JSON envelope — so
  the bump would have made `decode` reject **every existing v3 blob**: every block every player
  had ever placed, silently gone on next load, to record a field that has nothing to do with
  blocks.

  There are two formats, so there are now two numbers. `VERSION` (envelope, 4) and `DATA_VERSION`
  (blob, 3, untouched since session 2). ⚠ The rule: **bump `DATA_VERSION` only when the BYTES
  change; bump `VERSION` when the envelope gains, loses or reinterprets a field.** `savecheck`
  asserts they are DIFFERENT and carries a break that fails if they are ever merged again — the
  assertion is not "the number is 3", which would pass on the broken version too.

- **D-289** **a hook is a promise, and nobody ever asked who kept it — no furnace has ever
  smelted anything** *(session 9, G14/G9/G2)*

  `07c_blockentity.js` shipped `tickFurnace` calling two hooks, with a comment saying a later
  stage would fill them:

  ```
    BE.smeltResult(inputItem, type)  -> { item, count, time, xp } or null
    BE.fuelValue(item)               -> burn ticks, 0 for anything that is not fuel
  ```

  G9 then landed **1,058 recipes** including every smelting, blasting and smoking family, and
  `extract-fuel.mjs` produced the furnace fuel map straight out of compiled Java (D-269) — and
  **neither hook was ever assigned anywhere in the engine.** `BE.smeltResult` was `undefined` in
  every build ever produced, so `recipe` was always null, so no furnace has ever smelted anything.
  Two shipped tables, one block that wants them, and no line of code joining the two.

  ⚠ **`behavcheck` WAS GREEN, AND HONESTLY SO.** It supplied its own two-item stub —
  `raw_iron -> iron_ingot`, `coal -> 1600` — proved the counters against it to the tick, and set
  both hooks back to null afterwards. Its comment says it is testing "the part of it that IS G2",
  which is true. The gap is that **nothing anywhere asserted that the game fills the hooks**, and
  a stub that answers correctly is indistinguishable from a working feature from inside the module
  that offers it. The tell was available all along and nobody looked for it: the stub knows one
  item, the real table knows hundreds, so *asking about a third item* tells them apart. That is
  now an anti-vacuity break (`sand -> glass`).

  The hooks are **deleted** (D-139 — the replaced thing goes in the same commit). `tickFurnace`
  calls `Recipes.cookingFor` and `Recipes.fuelTime` directly, which is what G9 built them for, and
  `behavcheck` runs against the real tables: coal burns for the 1600 ticks the compiled Java says,
  raw iron smelts in the recipe's own 200 and blasts in its own 100.

  Two things fell out of doing it:
  - ⚠ **BLOCK-ENTITY SLOTS NOW HOLD `Inventory.stack`s.** They held `{item: name, count}` from G2
    while the player's 41 slots held `{i, n, d, t}` from G8, and **that mismatch was the actual
    blocker** — `cookingFor` and `fuelTime` take a stack and return a stack, and no amount of
    wiring reconciles two representations at the call site. One stack type in the codebase.
  - ⚠ **THE OUTPUT SLOT IS CAPPED AT THE ITEM'S STACK SIZE.** A furnace that merges past it makes
    items out of nothing. The check's first version asserted `input >= 62` after 400 ticks, which
    passes when the furnace never ran at all — precisely the state the hooks left it in. It now
    asserts `=== 62` and that the furnace is still lit, so a cap that holds because nothing
    happened cannot pass.

  ⚠ **AND IT IS STILL NOT REACHABLE BY A PLAYER**, which is said here so it cannot be mistaken for
  finished: nothing puts an item into a furnace, because the container screens are G11's named
  leftover waiting on G2's block-entity half. Block-entity CONTENTS are for the same reason not in
  the save — a field for a value nothing can produce is the `air` mistake in D-288, and this
  project does not make it twice in one session.

- **D-290** **a name read that nothing defines is the same class as a name defined twice, and
  JavaScript is just as quiet about it** *(session 9, G14)*

  `tools/dupcheck.mjs` exists because a duplicate definition let the stale copy win (D-276). The
  mirror image shipped alongside it for months and nothing looked: a property **read** that no code
  anywhere **assigns**. There is no error. The value is `undefined`, `!!undefined` is a
  serviceable `false`, and `undefined | 0` is a serviceable `0`, so the feature simply does
  nothing and every counter reads exactly as it would if the feature were off.

  Three shipped:

  | read | written | consequence |
  |---|---|---|
  | `P.eyesInWater` (`14_player.js`) | `e.eyeInWater` (`14b_physics.js`) | **the underwater mining penalty — vanilla's divide-by-five — never applied** |
  | `P.eyesInWater` (`15_hud.js`) | same | the air/bubble row has never been drawn |
  | `P.armour` (`15_hud.js`) | `e.armor` (`14d_survival.js`) | **the armour row has never been drawn** |

  ⚠ Neither is a typo you can see. Each file is internally consistent; the two spellings are
  hundreds of lines or a whole module apart — and `15_hud.js` line 509 spells `eyeInWater`
  CORRECTLY for the underwater screen tint, four hundred lines above the line that does not. The
  one that works is the one that was written first.

  ⚠ **THE PROJECT'S RULE, SETTLED HERE: a field that mirrors a vanilla identifier keeps vanilla's
  spelling.** `armor` is `LivingEntity.getArmorValue`'s spelling, so `armor` is right and the HUD's
  British `armour` was the error — the same reasoning as keeping `xpLevel` and `bypassArmor`. Prose
  in this project stays British; identifiers quoted from the game do not.

  `dupcheck` §5 now asks the question, **scoped on purpose**. An unscoped first pass over every
  `x.y` in the tree flagged 101 names of which almost all were fine — `e` is an event in the input
  module, a JSON entry in worldgen, a block-state object in the behaviour module — and a check that
  cries wolf a hundred times is a check nobody reads. So it asks one narrow question with a precise
  answer: on the PLAYER, is every property the engine reads a property the engine also writes?

  ⚠ **Its own first two versions were both wrong, and the mistakes are worth more than the check:**
  1. It reported `P.creative` as a dead read. `P.creative` appears exactly once in the tree — in
     the SENTENCE explaining that the field was deleted (D-139). Comments are stripped now.
  2. It counted object-literal keys as writes. `miningContext` **returns**
     `{ efficiency: P.efficiency | 0, … }`, so the very line that reads a dead property "defined"
     it and the check exonerated precisely the bug it was hunting. Only assignments count now,
     plus the keys of the single literal that constructs the player — found by its own opening
     line, and asserted to have been found, because otherwise §5 would flag every declared field.

  The five remaining read-only properties each sit on a **named allow-list with the stage that owes
  them** (`air` → drowning, `aquaAffinity`/`efficiency` → enchantments, `haste`/`fatigue` → status
  effects), and an assertion keeps that list from rotting: an entry for something the engine now
  writes is a stale promise, and a reader who trusts it will not look again.

- **D-291** **armour points out of the bytecode — the sixth referee table, and it corrected me
  twice while I wrote it** *(session 9, G14)*

  `Sv.afterArmor` is vanilla's `CombatRules.getDamageAfterAbsorb`, read out of the bytecode in G5.
  It sat in the codebase for four stages and **never once had a non-zero input.** G8 gave the
  player four armour slots; D-266 made shift-click put a helmet in the right one; nobody wrote the
  line that turns what is worn into a number. `15_hud.js` would have shown the zero, except that
  it asked for `P.armour`, which is not a field (D-290). Two independent silences over one missing
  function.

  `ArmorMaterials` is compiled Java — in no JSON file, no tag and no `minecraft-data` export — so
  `tools/extract-armor.mjs` is the **sixth** table D-263's referee has produced, after Material,
  EquipmentSlot, the furnace fuel map, DyeColor and SoundType.

  ⚠ **PICKED BY USE, NOT BY SHAPE**, which is the correction D-263 had to make. Shape offered two
  candidates. The decisive fact is that `Items.<clinit>` reads the enum **25 times: six constants
  four times each and one constant once** — and that 6×4+1 *is* the armour roster, six materials
  with a full set and one with only a helmet. Each constant is then identified TWICE and the two
  must agree: from the item names it is used beside, and from the enum's own `Enum(String, int)`
  name literal. Seven of seven. The array index is read from `EquipmentSlot`'s own constructor —
  each constant carries its own lowercase name and its index — and asserted to be a permutation of
  0..3, because an index that lands one slot over makes every piece worth somebody else's points.

  ⚠⚠ **IT CAUGHT ME TWICE, WHICH IS THE ENTIRE ARGUMENT FOR THE TECHNIQUE:**
  1. I expected TURTLE's protection array to hold a single non-zero value, because the turtle
     helmet is its only piece. It is `{2, 5, 6, 2}` — **iron's array**. A table written from
     memory ships the wrong helmet and no count of anything notices.
  2. My first parser took the int *after* the protection array as the durability multiplier. It is
     the **enchantment value**. That produced a leather helmet more durable than an iron one — 165
     against 99 — and it passed the file's own "every piece has a positive durability" assertion,
     because that is a threshold and not a comparison.

  So the parse is a phase machine over the constructor's fixed order, and two assertions were
  added, both DERIVED rather than remembered: a **positional** one — the two ints before the array
  boundary must be exactly `[multiplier, 4]`, so a drifting walk fails — and one that says
  **whichever material this table itself calls least protective must also be the least durable in
  every slot**, which is exactly what the bug broke. ⚠ An independent confirmation fell out for
  free: `extract-items` already had armour durability from another route, and all 25 values agree.

  `Sv.updateArmor(e, inv)` sums the four WORN slots — vanilla reads `EquipmentSlot.Type.ARMOR`, so
  a chestplate in the backpack and a pickaxe in the hand protect nothing — and runs **before** the
  damage in `P.tick`, because the tick a player lands is the tick they care whether the boots
  counted. ⚠ Knockback resistance **adds** across pieces and then clamps, which is why a full
  netherite set resists 0.4 and not 0.1; a `max()` would read 0.1 and look plausible.

  `survcheck` §5b wears every one of the 25 pieces in turn against the golden TSV, reads the
  expected values FROM that file rather than repeating them, and ends by hitting a bare player and
  an iron-clad one with the same 10 damage. Five breaks, including "sum every slot instead of the
  four worn ones", which gives 14 points where the right answer is 6.

- **D-292** **drowning, and the counter that has to be allowed to go negative** *(session 9, G14)*

  The last name on `dupcheck` §5's owed-list (D-290). `15_hud.js` drew a bubble row from `P.air`,
  a field nothing in the engine ever assigned, guarded by `P.air !== undefined` — so the row had
  never once been drawn and `Sv.DAMAGE.drown`, defined in G5, was unreachable. `14b_physics.js`
  had been setting `eyeInWater` correctly the whole time; nothing read it into a counter.

  Every number is out of the 1.18.2 bytecode, and the reading corrected me for the **third** time
  this session. Looking for drowning in the jar, the first method you find is
  `AbstractFish.handleAirSupply`, which sets the counter **straight back to 300** on the good
  branch. That is the FISH's override. `LivingEntity` is `min(air + 4, getMaxAirSupply())`, and
  taking the fish's for the player's would have refilled fifteen seconds of breath in one tick.
  - `Entity.getMaxAirSupply()` — a literal `sipush 300`
  - `LivingEntity.decreaseAirSupply(air)` — `air - 1`, once the Respiration branch is out
  - `LivingEntity.increaseAirSupply(air)` — `min(air + 4, max)`
  - `LivingEntity.baseTick` — at exactly **−20**, set the counter to 0 and `hurt(DROWN, 2.0F)`

  ⚠⚠ **THE COUNTER GOES NEGATIVE BY DESIGN, AND THAT IS THE WHOLE SHAPE OF IT.** 300 down at one
  a tick, then twenty more below zero; the hit lands at −20 and resets to 0. So the **first heart
  costs 320 ticks (16 s) and every heart after it costs 20 (1 s).** Clamping at zero — the obvious
  thing to write, and what almost anyone would write — gives a heart every tick and drowns the
  player in one second. "The player drowns" is true of both; only the timing tells them apart,
  which is why `survcheck` §5c asserts the first hit at tick 320, the gaps at exactly 20, and
  carries a break that replays the clamped version (hits at 300, and 21 times over).

  ⚠ It is saved, with the clamp `[-20, 300]` rather than `[0, 300]`: a save taken mid-drown holds
  a negative counter, and clamping it up on load would restart the sixteen seconds — or, worse
  with the other sign convention, drown the player again on the first tick back.

  ⚠ **BREATH TICKS BEFORE THE GAMEMODE GATE'S `return`.** A creative player does not drown but
  must still REFILL: swim down in survival, switch to creative, switch back, and a counter that
  stopped being topped up drowns you instantly.

- **D-292b** **the check measured the water overlay and called it bubbles — twice** *(session 9)*

  `g10check` §6 reads the HUD's own canvas for the row D-292 made real, and its first two versions
  measured the wrong thing in two different ways. Both are the same mistake in different clothes:
  **a comparison in which more than one thing changed.**

  1. It compared a DRY frame with a WET one and counted lit pixels. `drawFluidOverlay` paints the
     entire canvas blue while the eyes are under water, so the strip came back saturated at 6552
     lit pixels — its exact area — whether it held seven bubbles or one. "Lit pixels went from 0
     to 6552" was a perfectly true statement about the overlay.
  2. Moving to brightness and sampling the whole bar was no better: seven 9×9 icons in a 546×12
     strip move the average by about one percent, so 284 / 280 / 283 read as noise.

  It samples **one icon cell at a time** now — the bubbles are drawn from the right at
  `hungerX(i) = 173 − 8i`, so a window over cell 6 holds the seventh bubble or nothing at all —
  and every sample is taken UNDER WATER, varying only the air, so the overlay is common to all of
  them and cancels.

  ⚠ And the third correction: **the assertion asserted a direction, and the direction was wrong.**
  A bubble icon over the blue overlay is DARKER than the overlay, 263 against 284. The test is now
  that the cell **differs from an empty cell's baseline**, which is the thing actually being
  claimed; guessing which way the artwork goes is how a check ends up describing the wrong picture
  with confidence. Two breaks record why: the pixel count does not move at all, and the row is
  black out of the water.

- **D-293** **ask the question of every namespace, not only the one where the bug was found**
  *(session 9, G14)*
