  D-290 taught `dupcheck` to ask whether every property read on the PLAYER is one something
  writes. The player is where the bug happened; it is not where the class lives. Every `NS.Xxx` in
  this engine is a long-lived object several modules reach into, which is exactly the shape that
  grows a second spelling or a hook nobody keeps — so the same question was put to all **59** of
  them, in fifteen minutes, before starting the next stage.

  It found one: **`NS.Hud.onDeath`**, called by `14_player.js` twenty ticks after the player dies
  and **defined nowhere**. ⚠ The call was guarded — `if (... && NS.Hud.onDeath) NS.Hud.onDeath(P)`
  — so it never fired and never threw. The guard is the reason it survived: an unguarded call to
  an undefined function is a crash on the first death, and would have been fixed the same day.

  ⚠ **THE FEATURE IT LOOKED LIKE IT SERVED ALREADY WORKS BY ANOTHER ROUTE**, which is why nothing
  ever noticed: `H.drawSurvival` draws the death screen inline from `P.dead`, and `17_main.js`
  binds R to respawn. So the hook is not a missing feature, it is a **stale promise** — a line
  that tells the next reader a stage is owed when none is. Deleted, per D-139.

  ⚠ **AND IT REPORTED SEVEN FALSE POSITIVES BEFORE IT REPORTED THE REAL ONE**, both worth
  recording because both are the shape a structural check fails in:
  1. `NS.DATA.runtimeBytes`, `.itemTile` and five more came back as calls into nothing. They are
     defined in `19_data.gen.js`, which the scan EXCLUDES for being six megabytes of machine-
     written blob nobody reads. ⚠ A check that skips a file for being generated has to skip it
     for **reading**, not for **existing** — it is real code that runs.
  2. Including it then found only ten of its names, because the first attempt read a four-megabyte
     window from `NS.DATA` and the window ran out inside one of the base64 payloads. The keys all
     live on short lines and the payloads are single enormous ones, so the scan filters by line
     length — exact here, and it turns a 6.89 MB regex into a fast one. An assertion now fails if
     the blob yields fewer than twenty names, so "it was not read" cannot look like "it was clean".

  ⚠ **THIS HALF NEEDS NO ALLOW-LIST**, unlike the player's. A namespace METHOD is either defined
  or it is a lie; a player FIELD can legitimately be awaiting a stage that has not run, which is
  why `air`, `haste` and the enchantment fields sit on a named owed-list and a namespace member
  never can. Two questions of the same shape, two different standards of proof — and the check
  says which is which rather than splitting the difference.

- **D-294** **G15 is four stages, and the signal is the one that landed — with three bugs found by
  building circuits rather than by testing rules** *(session 9, G15a)*

  PLAN's G15 asks for wire, repeaters, comparators, pistons, observers and the update order, with
  "≥20 circuits asserted tick-by-tick" as its acceptance. Pistons alone are block-moving, a
  `moving_piston` block entity, push limits and sticky retraction — a stage's worth. So G15 is
  split, and the split is a RULING rather than a silent partial: **G15a the signal** (here),
  **G15b** repeaters and comparators, **G15c** pistons, **G15d** observers and the rest. Half a
  redstone stage that looks finished is worse than none.

  ⚠ **EVERY RULE IS OUT OF THE BYTECODE**, because redstone is pure code in vanilla — none of it
  is in a JSON file, a tag or `minecraft-data`. Each class was located BY USE: `Blocks.<clinit>`
  puts a block's own name literal immediately before its `new <class>`, giving `redstone_wire`,
  `redstone_torch`, `lever`, `redstone_block` and the rest with nothing guessed. The three rules a
  clone gets wrong, all read rather than remembered:
  - the decay is on the WIRE term only — `max(blockSignal, wireMax − 1)`, so a source beside a
    wire gives it 15 and not 14;
  - a wire **switches its own signal off** while asking its neighbours (`shouldSignal`), without
    which it reads its own power back through the block beside it and latches at 15 for ever;
  - the vertical rules are **asymmetric** — wire climbs a block only if the cell above the LOWER
    wire is open, and steps down past a block only if that block is NOT a conductor.

  **`isRedstoneConductor`** is a full collision cube minus seven exceptions, and the seven were
  identified by use, not by plausibility: three `StatePredicate` setters in `Blocks.<clinit>` take
  a similar-sized set each, and only one of them names `redstone_block` and `observer`. Both are
  full opaque cubes you suffocate in and cannot see through, so neither can belong to the
  suffocation or view-blocking predicate — an anchor that cannot be in doubt.

  ⚠⚠ **THREE BUGS, AND CIRCUITS FOUND ALL THREE WHERE RULE TESTS COULD NOT.** This is the whole
  argument for `redcheck` building things instead of asserting functions:

  1. **The direction convention was inverted.** `getBestNeighborSignal` asks the neighbour below
     with `DOWN` — the direction pointing FROM us TO it. The opposite reading ("the neighbour
     gives power in the direction pointing back at us") sounds airtight and is wrong. ⚠ **The
     wire-run test could not see it**: a redstone block answers 15 in every direction, and
     wire-to-wire propagation goes through the horizontal scan rather than through that function.
     It took a LEVER — the first direction-sensitive source — to expose it, and the same
     inversion had also broken the torch, which fed its own power into the block it stands on and
     read it straight back as its input.
  2. **`propName(state, 'powered') === true` is a comparison that can never hold.**
     `Behave.propName` returns the registry's VALUE NAME, so a boolean property reads back as the
     string `'true'`. Three places had it, and every lever, button and torch emitted nothing.
     ⚠ It is D-290's `!!undefined` in different clothes: a comparison that cannot be true reads as
     "this feature is off" rather than as an error, which is why neither the build nor any other
     check objected.
  3. **The consumer sweep was a fixed box around the changed cell**, so a lamp four blocks down a
     run never lit — the wire carried the signal perfectly and nothing looked at the far end. It
     follows the cells the update actually CHANGED now. A radius is a threshold; follow what
     moved.

  ⚠ **AND ONE BUG IN THE CHECK'S OWN FIXTURE**, recorded because it is the more dangerous shape:
  the "a redstone block powers all six neighbours" circuit laid a stone floor under every wire
  including the one on top, **quietly replacing the source with stone**. A fixture that destroys
  its subject outright fails honestly; one that half-destroys it is how a check ends up asserting
  nothing. There is now an assertion that the source survived the setup.

  ⚠ **THE WIRE PROPAGATES ITERATIVELY, NOT THROUGH `Behave.changed`'s RECURSION**, and the reason
  is `MAX_UPDATE_DEPTH`. Vanilla recurses and caps at 512; this engine caps at EIGHT, a number
  chosen for connection families like fences where nothing new happens after one hop. A run of
  fifteen needs fifteen, and raising the cap for everybody would let an oscillating rule take the
  frame with it — which is the reason the cap exists. So the wire gets its own work queue and the
  general recursion is left alone. ⚠ The order inside a queue pass cannot change the ANSWER (each
  target is a pure function of its neighbours, run to a fixpoint) but it does change vanilla's
  update ORDER, which matters for timing-sensitive contraptions built on the quirk. That is
  declared here and belongs to G15b, where repeaters make it observable.

  **Still not implemented and named so it cannot be mistaken for working:** torch burnout (the
  constants — a 60-tick window, 8 toggles — are read and recorded; the per-position history is
  not kept, and its only effect is on a torch driven by its own output, a G15b circuit).

- **D-295** **The two closed redstone sets came out of the jar, not out of a plausible-looking
  property test — and the seventh and eighth golden tables came from ONE scan** *(session 9, G15b)*

  G15b needed two sets that exist in no JSON file, no tag and no `minecraft-data` export: which
  blocks emit redstone at all (`isSignalSource`), and which blocks a comparator can read a NUMBER
  out of (`hasAnalogOutputSignal`). Both are one-line Java overrides.

  ⚠ **G15a HAD GUESSED THE FIRST ONE, AND THE GUESS WAS WRONG IN SEVEN FAMILIES.** Its test was
  "does this state have a `powered` property", which is true of doors, trapdoors, fence gates,
  note blocks, rails, tripwire and bells — none of which is a source, and every one of which
  redstone dust would therefore have connected to.

  `tools/extract-analog.mjs` is D-263's method for the seventh and eighth time, and the first
  time it has produced two tables from one pass:

  1. Disassemble all 6,352 classes and keep every `public boolean <name>(BlockState)` whose body
     is a bare `return true`. That is the shape of both overrides and of little else.
  2. Group by METHOD NAME. ⚠ **WHICH GROUP IS WHICH IS SETTLED BY ANCHORS THAT CANNOT BE IN
     DOUBT, NOT BY THE OBFUSCATED LETTER**: a LEVER is a redstone source and is not something a
     comparator reads a number out of; a CHEST is exactly the reverse. Four assertions, both
     directions, not one.
  3. Name every class through `Blocks.<clinit>`'s literal-immediately-before-`new`, and expand
     the abstract ones (button, pressure plate, diode, torch) through their subclasses.

  **38 signal sources, 61 analog blocks.** The hand-derived list in `07f_redstone.js` matched the
  mechanical one 38 of 38 — which is now *asserted* by `redcheck` §8 in both directions rather
  than hoped, so a future edit to either cannot drift.

  ⚠ **THE EXTRACTOR CORRECTED ITSELF FOUR TIMES, AND EACH ONE IS A DIFFERENT WAY A BYTECODE SCAN
  LIES TO YOU:**
  - It filed all **seventeen shulker boxes under the name `block`**. They are not built by a
    `new` in `Blocks.<clinit>` but by a static helper, so "the last `new` before the register
    call" picked up whatever literal happened to precede them. The rule is now "the last thing in
    this window whose TYPE is a Block subclass", which covers a helper's return type too.
  - It **lost `redstone_wire`** — the most important row in the table — because that one override
    returns the `shouldSignal` FIELD rather than a literal, so the "bare `return true`" filter
    dropped it. The assertion that names the wire explicitly is what caught it.
  - It put the **CHEST outside the Block hierarchy entirely**, because javap prints
    `class ceo extends cck<cmw>` and a parent pattern that stops at the `<` files it under a
    parent nothing else mentions.
  - It filed a **DETECTOR RAIL as a container**, because a detector rail's bytecode really does
    reach the container formula — via a minecart. Entity-shaped readings are now tested first.

  ⚠ **THE ANALOG TABLE'S THIRD COLUMN IS THE FORMULA, AND THE SET IS ASSERTED CLOSED.** Knowing a
  chest is readable is half an answer; `redcheck` asserts every row of the golden table is either
  implemented in the engine or on its own named OWED list (three command blocks, jukebox,
  lectern, sculk sensor, detector rail — five shapes that need entity or item state from stages
  that have not happened). A block that quietly reads 0 for ever is D-290's failure again.

- **D-296** **Two more G15a bugs, both in the half of the wire that a straight run cannot see —
  and one of them was being masked by a lie in the connection table** *(session 9, G15b)*

  Reading further into `RedStoneWireBlock` for G15b turned up two rules G15a did not have. Both
  are invisible to a straight run, because a straight run is wire at both ends and symmetric in
  exactly the two respects that were wrong.

  1. ⚠ **`getSignal` ASKS THE OPPOSITE SIDE.** Vanilla is
     `direction == UP || connected(direction.getOpposite()) ? power : 0`. `direction` points FROM
     THE ASKER TO THE WIRE, so the side that faces the asker is the opposite one. G15a asked
     `direction`, which means a wire powered the thing BEHIND it and not the thing in front.
  2. ⚠ **`getSignal` ASKS THE *COMPLETED* CONNECTION STATE, NOT THE RAW SIDES.**
     `getConnectionState` computes the four sides and then, for each horizontal AXIS that came
     out with nothing on it, sets BOTH of that axis's sides to SIDE. That is why a dust with a
     single neighbour to the west behaves as a straight LINE rather than a stub — and it is the
     rule that makes a run of dust light the lamp it ends at. The one exception is a wire with no
     raw connections at all: `getConnectionState` returns early for a dot, and a lone dot powers
     nothing horizontally.

  ⚠⚠ **AND G15a WAS HIDING THE SECOND ONE.** Its `canConnectRedstone` returned true for a
  REDSTONE LAMP, so a run of dust reached a lamp by claiming the lamp was a connection. Vanilla
  says flatly that a lamp is not a signal source and dust does not connect to it; the lamp lights
  because the wire grows its own axis back. **Deleting the mask and adding the real rule had to
  be one edit** — which is D-139's shape: a replacement is not done until the thing it replaces
  is gone. Doing either alone would have turned a green check red and looked like a regression.

  ⚠⚠ **AND A THIRD, WHICH IS THE WORST OF THE THREE: EVERY WALL TORCH IN THE ENGINE WAS
  OSCILLATING.** `RedstoneWallTorchBlock` overrides `getSignal` to
  `lit && state.getValue(FACING) != direction`, and FACING points AWAY from the block it hangs
  on — so `direction == FACING` is exactly the ask that arrives from its own support. G15a used
  the STANDING torch's `dir != UP` for both, so a wall torch powered the block it was stuck to,
  read that power back as its own input, and went out; then, unpowered, it relit; then out again.
  ⚠ **G15a's NOT gate and NOR truth table passed anyway**, because the torch was flipping every
  two ticks and happened to be lit on the tick the check read it. That is the most dangerous
  green there is: not a check that asserts nothing, but a check that asserts the right thing
  against a value that is only momentarily correct. Every torch in G15a's twenty circuits stood
  on the floor, which is why five sessions of green never touched it.

  ⚠ **THE CHECK'S OWN FIXTURE WAS LYING TOO, IN A WAY THAT MADE THE BUG SURVIVE THE FIX.** It
  wrote twenty cells straight into the array and then called one `Redstone.update` at one of
  them. In play every `setBlock` runs `Behave.changed`, and the redstone update is seeded from a
  ONE-BLOCK neighbourhood of the changed cell — deliberately, since G15a's own lesson was to
  follow what changed rather than to sweep a radius. So the far end of a circuit was never looked
  at, and the first correct wall torch made the NOT gate go dark. `scene()` now remembers every
  placement and notifies from all of them, which is what the game does.

- **D-297** **The repeater's FACING points at its INPUT, the comparator's number is not in its
  block state, and both of those are pinned by two methods each** *(session 9, G15b)*

  The two facts a diode implementation gets backwards, and the bytecode that settles each:

  ⚠ **FACING IS THE INPUT SIDE.** `DiodeBlock.getInputSignal` reads
  `pos.relative(state.getValue(FACING))` and `DiodeBlock.updateNeighborsInFront` writes to
  `pos.relative(FACING.getOpposite())`. Two methods, opposite ends, one conclusion. It follows
  that the output neighbour asks with `dir == FACING` — its own direction toward the repeater IS
  the repeater's facing — which agrees with the `d`-not-`OPP[d]` convention D-294 had to learn
  the hard way, so the two halves of the module are consistent rather than compensating.

  ⚠ **A COMPARATOR'S OUTPUT IS ANALOG AND ITS STATE IS BOOLEAN.** The state carries `powered`;
  the 0..15 lives in a `ComparatorBlockEntity`. G2 already registered the `comparator` type in
  the block-entity store and left it with no fields, so the number goes where vanilla puts it
  rather than into a second map that could drift. `redcheck` §14 zeroes the ENTITY alone and
  asserts the wire in front goes dark, which proves the state is not secretly carrying it.

  The rules, each read rather than recalled:
  - `RepeaterBlock.getDelay` = `DELAY * 2` (a literal `iconst_2; imul`) — so the four settings
    are 2, 4, 6 and 8 GAME ticks.
  - `RepeaterBlock.isLocked` = `getAlternateSignal(...) > 0`, and ⚠ **the two diodes disagree
    about what may reach a side**: `RepeaterBlock.isAlternateInput` is `isDiode(state)` — ONLY
    another repeater or comparator can lock a repeater, which is what makes the lock usable as
    memory rather than as a hazard — while the comparator inherits `state.isSignalSource()` and
    takes dust, a torch or a lever on its side.
  - `ComparatorBlock.calculateOutputSignal` = `input == 0 ? 0 : side > input ? 0 :
    SUBTRACT ? input - side : input`, and ⚠ `shouldTurnOn` is NOT `value > 0`: at EQUAL strengths
    COMPARE stays on and SUBTRACT goes dark, which is the mode difference a player relies on.
  - `ComparatorBlock.getInputSignal`'s override: an analog block behind the comparator REPLACES
    the redstone reading outright, and it is read **through one solid block** —
    `back = back.relative(facing)` and the same question again.
  - `AbstractContainerMenu.getRedstoneSignalFromContainer` = `floor(f * 14) + (i > 0 ? 1 : 0)`
    where `f` is the summed fill fraction divided by the SLOT COUNT. ⚠ Both halves are what a
    from-memory version gets wrong: the `+1` is why one item in a chest reads 1, and the divide
    by slots is why a full stack in one slot of twenty-seven reads 1 as well.
  - `DiodeBlock.tick`'s "turn on, and if the input has ALREADY GONE, schedule the turn-off
    `delay` ticks later" branch. ⚠ Leaving it out gives a repeater that swallows any pulse
    shorter than its delay; with it, a one-tick pulse comes out delay-length. `redcheck` §10
    asserts the drop happens on tick 8 of a delay-4 repeater and not immediately.
  - `TickPriority` is read from its own `<clinit>` (EXTREMELY_HIGH −3, VERY_HIGH −2, HIGH −1),
    and `checkTickOnNeighbor` picks EXTREMELY_HIGH when this diode faces into another diode,
    VERY_HIGH when it is turning OFF, HIGH otherwise. That is what makes two repeaters pointed
    at each other settle the same way every time instead of by array order.

  ⚠ **`Redstone.update` IS NOW RE-ENTRANT AND HAS ITS OWN DEPTH CAP.** `updateNeighborsInFront`
  calls back into it, so a repeater feeding a second repeater feeding the first would recurse for
  ever. Vanilla is saved by its scheduler — diodes only ever SCHEDULE from a neighbour change,
  they never settle inline — and this needs the same floor under it. ⚠ And `touched` is copied
  before the sweep, because a nested update clobbers it.

  **Still not implemented and named:** torch burnout (D-294's constants stand), vanilla's
  *ordering* quirks inside one tick beyond the priority classes above, and the item frame a
  comparator can read off the block in front of a container.

- **D-298** **Pistons are read out of the jar down to the push list's ORDER, and the ninth golden
  table is the one the stage cannot be written without** *(session 9, G15c)*

  `PushReaction` — NORMAL, DESTROY, BLOCK, IGNORE, PUSH_ONLY — is compiled Java from end to end:
  no JSON, no tag, nothing in `minecraft-data`. `tools/extract-push.mjs` derives it from **two**
  places, because one is not enough:

  1. **The material.** `BlockBehaviour.getPistonPushReaction` defaults to
     `this.material.getPushReaction()`, and each `Material` is built by a builder whose default
     is NORMAL with two protected calls that change it. ⚠ Which call is which is read from the
     `PushReaction` enum's own `<clinit>` name literals, not from the order they appear in.
  2. **The block.** Fourteen classes override it outright, and they are not a footnote: every
     door, every glazed terracotta (the only PUSH_ONLY blocks in the game), ice, end rods,
     lanterns, bells, amethyst, shulker boxes, pointed dripstone and the structure void. **A
     table built from materials alone is wrong for about sixty blocks.**

  The block → material join is NOT re-derived: `block-materials-1.18.2.tsv` already carries it
  for all 898, resolved through helpers and `Properties.copy` to a fixed point. A second
  implementation of the hardest part of that file would be free to disagree with it.

  ⚠ **THE EXTRACTOR'S FIRST TABLE WAS PLAUSIBLE AND WRONG IN TWO WAYS THAT CANCELLED.** javap
  prints a constructor with no return type, so a "TYPE NAME(" method pattern parses
  `public djb$a(djc);` as return type `public`, method `djb$a` — the constructor went onto the
  SETTER list and left the default `null`; and a `|| 'NORMAL'` fallback then turned all 584
  unresolved materials into NORMAL. The counts looked right. The fallback is gone: a material
  with no entry is a parse failure, and the assertion says so.

  ⚠ **AND THE FIRST SET OF ANCHORS WAS WRONG, CORRECTLY.** It asserted `obsidian: BLOCK` and
  `bedrock: BLOCK` and both failed. Obsidian's PushReaction really is NORMAL — a piston refuses
  it because **`PistonBaseBlock.isPushable` carries four rules the table does not**:
  - obsidian, crying obsidian and the respawn anchor, **by name**;
  - anything whose destroy speed is −1, which is bedrock, the barrier and the portals;
  - an already-**EXTENDED** piston (⚠ and the bytecode's `else` branch SKIPS the reaction switch
    for a piston entirely, so a RETRACTED piston is perfectly pushable even though the table
    calls pistons BLOCK — which is what every piston-shoves-a-piston contraption relies on);
  - **anything with a block entity**, which is why a chest and a stone with the same NORMAL
    reaction give opposite answers.
  Writing those into the table would have made the table wrong AND hidden the fact that the
  piston has to carry them.

  ⚠ **AIR IS PUSHABLE.** `isPushable` returns **true** for air, and it matters: `addBlockLine`
  relies on a pushable-but-empty cell to END a line rather than to fail it.

  **`PistonStructureResolver`, faithfully, including the parts that look like accidents:**
  - ⚠ **The limit is twelve BLOCKS, not twelve cells of length.** A slime blob that branches
    sideways spends the same budget as a straight column. `pistoncheck` §9 measures the
    threshold by pushing 1..14 and reporting the largest that moves, rather than asserting 12.
  - ⚠ **The backward walk.** While the block is sticky, `addBlockLine` walks BACKWARDS along the
    push axis dragging the chain behind it, and only then scans forward. Leaving it out gives
    slime blocks that push what is in front and abandon what is stuck behind.
  - ⚠ **Slime and honey do not stick to each other** — two lines in front of the general "either
    of them is sticky" rule, written out in BOTH orders in the bytecode, which is why this
    implementation does not have to know which obfuscated field is which.
  - ⚠ **`reorderListAtCollision`.** When a branch meets the trunk the push list is rewritten so
    the newly added run sits ahead of everything from the collision point on. The ORDER is what
    decides which cell is written first, and writing them in the wrong order overwrites a block
    that has not moved yet.

  ⚠⚠ **QUASI-CONNECTIVITY IS NOT A BUG TO BE TIDIED AWAY.** `getNeighborSignal` asks the
  piston's five non-facing sides, then its OWN cell from below, then **all six sides of the cell
  one block up**. Every BUD switch and half the door designs in the game are built on it.
  ⚠ And the edge of that region is not where it looks: a strongly-powered block **two** above
  still reaches the piston through the cell above's UP side. Three above does not. `pistoncheck`
  §6 asserts both, after its first version asserted "two above does not fire" and failed —
  against the real rule.

  **Two ticks, not one.** `PistonMovingBlockEntity` advances `progress` by a literal `0.5F` per
  tick, so the cells change in the firing tick and the block LANDS two ticks later. A clone that
  teleports the block in one step passes every "did it move" test and gets every tick-sensitive
  contraption wrong.

  ⚠ **THE PISTON SETTLES THROUGH `Redstone.update` AND NOT THROUGH `Behave.changed`.** There has
  to be exactly one door marked "something near this cell changed": a second entry point fires
  every piston twice per change, and a piston that fires twice retracts into its own push.
  ⚠ And `moveBlocks` writes a dozen cells, every write runs `Behave.changed`, and that comes
  straight back — so there is an explicit re-entrancy flag, where vanilla is protected by its
  block-event queue.

  ⚠ **ONE BYTE PER BLOCK IN `block-runtime.bin`, AND THE PRE-PASS IS PART OF THE RECORD.** The
  decoder walks the block records TWICE — once to count states before allocating, once to read —
  and adding the byte to one and not the other made the pre-pass walk off into the payload and
  report **fifteen million** real states for a registry of twenty thousand. `regcheck` caught it
  on the first run; the skip arithmetic now carries the same comment as the read.

  ⚠ **TWO BLOCKS IN THIS ENGINE'S REGISTRY ARE NOT BLOCKS IN VANILLA.** `item_frame` and
  `glow_item_frame` are entities there, so the golden table has no row for them and should not.
  They are named in `pack-runtime` with their vanilla answer (DESTROY — a piston collides with
  the entity and breaks it) rather than falling through a default; anything else missing is a
  packing error and throws.

  **Still not implemented and named so it cannot be mistaken for working:** the moving block is
  not DRAWN part-way between its two cells — the entity, its progress and the two-tick timing
  are all real and asserted, but the mesher has no sub-cell offset for a block in flight, which
  is a renderer change and rendering is the half of this project allowed to be cheap. Entities
  riding a piston are G17's. Observers, target blocks, the daylight detector and the rest are
  G15d.

- **D-299** **The observer is a one-shot, and closing the SOURCE set found a third silent
  family** *(session 9, G15d)*

  `ObserverBlock` looks like a sensor and is not one. Its `updateShape` fires **only** when the
  block it FACES changes state, **only** when the observer is not already powered, and what it
  does is SCHEDULE: two game ticks later it goes high, and two ticks after that it goes low.
  ⚠ **The output is a fixed two-tick pulse no matter how long the thing it watched stayed
  changed.** A "while the neighbour differs" implementation is a different block, and it passes
  every "does the observer notice" test ever written.

  ⚠ **THE `!powered` GUARD IS THE WHOLE BLOCK.** Without it a stream of changes re-arms the pulse
  every tick and the observer never drops — a one-shot turned into a level detector.

  Its `FACING` is the **eye**: it watches the cell one step along `facing` and its output comes
  out of the cell BEHIND it, which is why the block at the back asks with `dir == FACING` — the
  same convention the diodes use (D-297), so the two halves agree rather than compensate.
  ⚠ And `observer` is on `NEVER_CONDUCTS` for the reason `redstone_block` is: a source that
  also carried power through itself would feed its own output back into its input.

  ⚠ **CLOSING THE SOURCE SET IS WHAT MADE THIS STAGE WORTH THE TIME.** `redcheck` §8 now walks
  every row of `signal-sources-1.18.2.tsv`, drives each state to its powered form, and asks
  whether it emits ANYTHING in ANY direction. Two rows came back silent:

  - ⚠⚠ **BOTH WEIGHTED PRESSURE PLATES.** They have no `powered` property — they have `power`,
    0..15 — so the generic boolean branch read `powered` on a state that has none, got `null`,
    and emitted nothing. **This is the third member of the family D-290 names**, after
    `!!undefined` and `propName(…) === true`: a test that cannot come out true reads as "this
    feature is off" rather than as an error. Nothing in five sessions had ever asked a weighted
    plate for a number.
  - The **comparator**, correctly — its strength is not in its block state at all, and §12
    asserts it where it lives. It is skipped by name with that reason rather than by a threshold.

  The remaining eight sources are named in `Rs.OWED_SOURCES` **with the stage each waits for**:
  daylight detector (sky light and a time of day, G16), detector rail and tripwire hook and
  target (entities, G17), lightning rod (weather, G16), lectern (item stacks in a block entity,
  G8), sculk sensor (vibrations, G17/G18), trapped chest (container screens, G11). "The list is
  short" is not a reason to leave it uncounted.

  ⚠ **AND A PRESSURE PLATE'S STRONG POWER IS NOW EXPLICIT RATHER THAN A FALL-THROUGH.**
  `BasePressurePlateBlock.getDirectSignal` is `dir == UP ? signal : 0` — it strongly powers only
  the block BENEATH it. The generic lever rule happened to give the same answer, because
  `attachedDir` returns UP for a state with neither `face` nor `facing`. A right answer reached
  by a default is the same shape as a wrong one; the plate says so itself now, and the check
  asserts all six directions.

  ⚠ **The observer is notified from `Behave.changed` and not from `Redstone.update`'s settle**,
  which is the opposite of where the piston hooks (D-298) and for a reason: the question is "did
  THIS EXACT CELL change", which `Behave.changed` knows and a settle sweep does not. Sweeping a
  radius would fire an observer on a change it never watched.

- **D-300** **The sky is a rendering stage with a parity CORE, and the core is where the bytecode
  lives** *(session 9, G16a)*

  The CHARTER lets rendering be cheap and demands everything else be exact, and the sky is the
  first stage where one thing is both. Its *picture* — a dome, two quads and 1,500 star quads —
  may be drawn however is convenient. Its *numbers* may not: the time of day, the sun's angle,
  the moon's phase, the colour of the sky at this minute in this biome, how dark it goes when it
  rains, how far you can see and when the rain starts are all rules a player can see being wrong,
  and every one of them is compiled Java in vanilla with no JSON behind it. So `src/09b_sky.js`
  holds the numbers, `skycheck` asserts them without a canvas, and the drawing is G16b's.

  ⚠ **IT IS NUMBERED 09b AND NOT 16.** The three renderer modules all read it and the build
  concatenates in list order, so a module named for its PLAN stage would have loaded after its
  own consumers. The number is the load order, not the stage.

  ⚠⚠ **THE SKY WAS A HARD-CODED `[0.62, 0.76, 0.98]`** — one blue, at every hour, in every biome,
  used as the clear colour AND the fog colour. So the world never got dark, the fog never took a
  biome's tint, and neither the time of day nor the weather could be seen at all.

  **What the bytecode corrected, and it was most of what I wrote from memory:**
  - ⚠⚠ **NOON IS `timeOfDay` ZERO, NOT 0.25.** It is the SUN'S ANGLE as a fraction of a turn, and
    the sun is overhead at dayTime 6000; the `- 0.25` in the formula is what moves it there. The
    check's first anchors said "the day starts at dawn, so dawn is 0" and all four were wrong.
  - ⚠⚠ **THE WEATHER LEVELS MOVE BY `0.01` A TICK, NOT `1/12000`.** A storm fades in over a
    hundred ticks — five seconds — not ten minutes. Every other weather constant was wrong too:
    the four ranges are `Mth.randomBetweenInclusive(min, max)` pairs (thunder 3600..15600, rain
    12000..24000, clear 12000..180000 for both flags), not `min + nextInt(span)`.
  - ⚠ **`clearWeatherTime` DOES MORE THAN COUNT DOWN.** While it runs it forces both flags off
    and sets each timer from the flag *as it was*, so `/weather clear` suppresses a storm rather
    than pausing it. A version that only decrements is identical until someone uses the command.
  - ⚠ **`CubicSampler`'s kernel is SEVEN entries, `{0,1,4,6,4,1,0}`, and the weight for tap `i`
    is `lerp(delta, k[i+1], k[i])` — the later entry first.** The six-entry mirrored version I
    wrote first is a different kernel that looks plausible and puts the biome blend out
    everywhere.
  - ⚠ **THE FOG'S BRIGHTNESS RAMP IS THE SKY'S CLAMPED COSINE, NOT `skyDarken`.** `skyDarken`
    bottoms out at 0.2 and already carries the rain term, so using it would leave the fog lit at
    midnight and dim it by rain twice.
  - ⚠ **THE FOG'S BLUE CHANNEL IS NOT THE OTHER TWO.**
    `color.multiply(b*0.94+0.06, b*0.94+0.06, b*0.91+0.09)` — which is what keeps a trace of
    blue in the fog at midnight instead of letting it go grey. And **rain scales red and green
    by 0.5 but blue by only 0.4**, while thunder scales all three by 0.5.
  - ⚠ **`isRainingAt` IS NOT REIMPLEMENTED.** `Biomes.warmEnoughToRain` and `Biomes.snowsAt`
    already carry vanilla's height-adjusted temperature rule — W5 built them for the snow cap —
    and a second copy of a rule is two truths (D-139). This module asks them.

  ⚠ **THE STAR FIELD REPRODUCES THE REJECTED CANDIDATES.** `LevelRenderer.drawStars` runs 1,500
  times and keeps a candidate only when its squared length is inside the unit ball and outside a
  small core, and **a rejected candidate still consumes its four `nextFloat` draws** — so the
  yield is the unit ball's fraction of its cube — about 785 of 1,500, not 1,500 — and
  skipping or re-drawing moves every star after the first.
  `skycheck` asserts the count against π/6 and asserts two engines build a bit-identical array,
  which is the only way to know both the LCG and the rejection loop match.

  ⚠ **THE ENVELOPE IS v5** (D-288b's rule: the block bytes did not change, so `DATA_VERSION`
  stays 3). A v4 world has no time at all and the right default is not 0 — a world that loads at
  tick 0 opens at dusk — so `Sky.fromJSON` puts it at `NEW_WORLD_TIME`, mid-morning, which is
  where vanilla starts a new world.

  **G16b is declared, not forgotten:** the sun, the moon, the stars and the sunrise tint band all
  need a second draw pass and are the picture half.

- **D-301** **`Behave.tick()` WAS NEVER CALLED BY THE GAME, AND EVERY CHECK WAS GREEN ACROSS IT**
  *(session 9, the largest finding in this project so far)*

  The main loop ran `Player.tick()` and nothing else. `grep -c "Behave.tick()" dist/mclite.html`
  → **0**. So in every build that has ever shipped:

  - **no scheduled tick ever ran.** `Behave.schedule` puts water, lava and fire on a queue that
    was never drained, so **fluids never spread past their first update** and fire never burnt
    out;
  - **no block entity ever ticked.** D-289 said "no furnace has ever smelted anything" and fixed
    the *hooks* — the furnace still never smelted, because nothing called the loop the hooks
    live in;
  - and as of this session, **redstone torches would never flip, repeaters never fire, observers
    never pulse, and a piston would start moving and freeze mid-flight for ever**.
  - ⚠ `Piston.init` was never called either, found in the same reading. A module that is never
    initialised reports `ready: false` for ever and every entry point returns early — silently,
    because "not ready" is a legitimate state during boot.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE REASON NOTHING CAUGHT IT IS THE POINT.** Every check drives the tick ITSELF —
  `redcheck.runTicks`, `pistoncheck.ticks`, `behavcheck`'s own loop — because a check that owns
  its clock is deterministic, which is *good practice*. Each honestly proves the RULE. **Not one
  of them proves the GAME runs it.** That is D-276 — *a check that passes proves only what it
  touches* — at the largest join in the project: the join between the whole behaviour layer and
  the game loop. Five sessions of green, 1.17 million assertions, and the world was not ticking.

  **The missing assertion is not about any rule.** `tools/tickcheck.mjs` asks a structural
  question of the **SHIPPED BUNDLE**: *is every function whose name says it happens once per tick
  reachable from the loop?* It walks out from `Main.loop` and `Main.worldTick`, and every
  `*.tick*` in `src/` must be either reached or on a named OWED list **with its reason** — the
  same closed-set habit as D-295 and D-299. It asks `dist/mclite.html` and not `src/`, because a
  module that is written, correct and simply absent from `build.mjs`'s list is exactly this
  failure and looks identical in the source.

  ⚠ **AND THE RUNTIME PROOF IS IN `smoke`**, which now measures `Behave.gameTime` in a real
  browser. `Main.ticks` counts the loop's fixed steps and has always been in the hundreds;
  `Behave.gameTime` counts the queue being drained and was **zero for ever**. Two numbers, one
  of which was a lie by omission.

  ⚠ **THE FIRST VERSION OF `tickcheck` HAD A BUG OF ITS OWN, AND IT IS THE SAME SHAPE**: it
  mapped short names to namespaces with a hand-written table, but `P` is `Player` in
  `14_player.js` and `Piston` in `07g_piston.js`, and `H` is `Hud` in one module and `Hand` in
  another. Four of `Hand`'s functions were filed under `Hud` and reported missing. The namespace
  is read from each file's own `NS.X =` line now — derived, not tabulated (D-263, in its
  JavaScript-shaped form).

- **D-302** **`NS.World.get` takes CHUNK coordinates, so every redstone circuit in the game read
  chunks as block states — and `redcheck`'s own fixture hid it with one line** *(session 9)*

  `World.get(cx, cz)` returns a CHUNK; the block accessors are `getBlock`/`setBlock`.
  `Redstone.init(NS.World)` and `Piston.init(NS.World)` stored that object, so every
  `w.get(x, y, z)` inside the redstone engine answered with a chunk object or `undefined`.
  **In the game, every wire read 0, every torch saw nothing, and no circuit ever did anything.**
  `Behave` has always wrapped the world in exactly the right adapter and published it as `B.w`;
  taking that is the whole fix, and both modules now refuse to be `ready` without it.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE CHECK HID IT WITH ONE LINE OF ITS OWN FIXTURE.** `redcheck`'s `scene()` did
  `M.Behave.init(w); M.Behave.w = w;` — it OVERWROTE Behave's adapter with its own object, whose
  `get` is the block getter. So 330 assertions across twenty circuits exercised **an interface
  the game does not have**. The line is gone; both fixtures hand their world to `Behave` and
  everything downstream reads it through the same adapter the game uses, and both checks assert
  `worldIsBehaveAdapter()`.

  ⚠ **A FIXTURE THAT MAKES THE INTERFACE EASIER THAN THE GAME'S CANNOT SEE AN INTERFACE BUG.**
  That is D-276 for the third time in one session, and the three instances are worth listing
  together because they are the same failure at three scales:
  - D-289: a hook that nothing filled (the value never arrived);
  - D-301: a function that nothing called (the code never ran);
  - D-302: an object that meant something different at the call site (the code ran on nonsense).
  Each was behind hundreds of honest green assertions, and each needed the GAME to show it.

  ⚠ **IT WAS FOUND BY `tools/worldcheck.mjs`, ON ITS FIRST RUN, WRITTEN TO PROVE A DIFFERENT
  FIX.** That is the argument for browser stages in one sentence: the check written to
  demonstrate D-301's repair found D-302 within a minute of existing. In a real browser, in a
  real world, it now shows water spreading 1 → 14 cells, fire burning out on bare stone, a torch
  staying lit in the tick its input arrives and being flipped by the GAME two seconds later, a
  piston holding `moving_piston` mid-flight and landing its block, and **a furnace putting an
  iron ingot in its output slot — the first this project has ever produced.**
  ⚠ Its decisive assertion is an EXPERIMENT rather than an outcome: it removes `Main.worldTick`
  from the running page, shows the same water sitting still for five seconds, puts it back, and
  shows it spread. The difference is one call.

  ⚠ **AND ONE MORE CHECK-SHAPED BUG IN THE SAME HOUR**: `g14check` asserted the save envelope was
  literally `4` and failed on a correct v5 save. A check that hard-codes a number the code owns
  has to be edited every time the code is right, which is the same mistake as asserting a
  remembered constant (D-263). It reads `Save.VERSION` now.

- **D-303** **The sky is a DRAW PASS, and it goes down first with depth writes off** *(session 9)*

  G16b. `src/09b_sky.js` grew the geometry — `buildSkyDisc(y)`, `celestialMatrix`,
  `celestialQuad`, `moonUV` — and `src/12_gfx_webgl2.js` a fifth program, `progSky`, with the
  smallest shader pair in the project: `uViewProj * (uModel * pos)`, and a colour that is either
  a uniform or a uniform times one texture sample. The order is vanilla's: **sky disc → stars
  (additive) → sun → moon → dark disc**, called from `beginFrame` straight after the clear, with
  `depthMask(false)` throughout so the world draws over all of it and nothing ever occludes the
  world. `Gfx.frameState.skyFrame` carries the whole of `Sky.frame()` — colours, `skyDarken`,
  `starBrightness`, `moonPhase`, rain — so the backend asks `Sky` for nothing and computes
  nothing.

  ⚠ **The two celestial textures are GUI SHEETS, not atlas tiles.** `environment/sun.png` (32×32)
  and `environment/moon_phases.png` (128×64, a 4×2 grid) are packed by `tools/build-gui.mjs`
  alongside `widgets` and `ascii`, because they are flat 2D images sampled with their own UVs and
  the block atlas is a `TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY` of 16×16 layers. About five kilobytes deflated between
  them.

  ⚠ **The sun and moon fade with RAIN, not with the hour.** Vanilla's alpha here is
  `1 - rainLevel`: they are always up there and a storm is what hides them. Fading them by time
  of day would double-count `skyDarken`, which the sky colour has already applied.

  ⚠ **`buildSkyDisc`'s X term carries the sign of `y` and its Z term does not** — so the dark
  disc at y = −16 is a MIRRORED fan, which flips its winding to face down. Writing `512 * cos`
  for both gives two discs facing the same way and the one under your feet is back-face culled: a
  hole in the sky that only appears when you look down.

- **D-304** **The sky pass needs its OWN far plane, because the world's is the fog wall and the
  sun is further away than that** *(session 9)*

  `Gfx.render` sets `cam.far = max(64, rd * 16 * fogEnd + 16)` so nothing is drawn past the fog
  wall — that is D-90, and it is a good rendering economy. But `Sky.CELESTIAL_DIST` is **100**,
  and at the CELERON preset `cam.far` comes out at **76.8**. Projecting the sky with
  `state.viewProj` therefore clipped the sun and the moon away **entirely, at every hour of every
  day, on the bottom rung of the hardware ladder** — while the sky pass dutifully issued its four
  draws a frame and `skycheck`'s 141 numbers stayed green.

  `NS.Cam.skyViewProj(cam, out, near, far)` builds the same eye-relative, translation-free view
  (D-179) against a perspective at `Sky.SKY_FAR` = 1024; `Gfx` writes it into
  `frameState.skyViewProj` each frame and `drawSky` uses that and nothing else. 1024 also
  contains the 512-radius disc, so the horizon is sky rather than a far-plane cut — which is what
  vanilla draws, and vanilla has no such problem because its sky projection is built at
  `renderDistance * 4` BLOCKS and never at the fog wall. It costs nothing: the pass is ten
  triangles, two quads and ~785 star quads with depth writes off, so a wider frustum draws
  exactly the same geometry.

  ⚠⚠ **THE BUG UNDERNEATH IT WAS WORSE, AND IT WAS A STALE GENERATED FILE.** `build-gui.mjs` had
  been taught to pack `sun` and `moon_phases` and `assets/gui.bin` really did contain them — but
  `tools/gen-data.mjs` had not been re-run, so `src/19_data.gen.js` still held the EIGHT-sheet
  blob. `texFromSheet` returned null for both, `initSky` skipped them without a word, and the sky
  pass issued **two** draws a frame instead of four. **`node build.mjs` alone does not rebuild the
  data module from a changed asset**: the suite runs `build-gui` → `pack-runtime` → `gen-data` →
  `build` in that order and would have caught it, and a bare rebuild after editing an asset
  generator will not. After touching anything under `tools/build-*.mjs`, run the pipeline and not
  its last stage.

  ⚠ **BOTH WERE FOUND BY `tools/skyviewcheck.mjs` ON THE DAY IT WAS WRITTEN**, and neither is
  visible from any number the engine holds. This is the fourth instance in one session of the
  same failure at a different scale, and the list from D-302 now reads:
  - D-289: a hook that nothing filled (the value never arrived);
  - D-301: a function that nothing called (the code never ran);
  - D-302: an object that meant something different at the call site (the code ran on nonsense);
  - D-304: a generated file that was never regenerated, and a matrix with the wrong far plane
    (the code ran, on the right objects, and drew nothing you could see).

  ⚠ **The check had to learn two things about its own instrument before it could be trusted.**
  Its first run measured the **CROSSHAIR** and reported it as the sun — `#ui` is its own canvas
  stacked over the GL one and `Page.captureScreenshot` composites the two, so the overlay is
  hidden before anything is measured. Its second version passed at the Celeron preset and failed
  at Dan's medium, because at render distance 12 the spawn's **trees** are generated and meshed
  and the camera was looking up through a canopy (D-196, again). It flies to y = 220 first, so the
  same picture is under test at every preset.

  ⚠ **Its decisive break FORCES the fault rather than borrowing it.** Reusing the world's real
  matrix only reproduces the bug on a preset whose far plane happens to be nearer than 100, so at
  medium the break would quietly skip — and the one break covering the bug the file was written
  to catch would never run in Dan's own setup. It installs an 80-block sky far plane instead, and
  asserts both halves: the sun goes, and **the disc stays**, which is exactly how the bug
  presented. A break that cannot fire is not a break (D-30).

- **D-305** **Drawing the sky changed a measurement nobody had touched: `cullcheck`'s pinned
  occlusion gap doubled, and the flood was not the thing that changed** *(session 9)*

  The morning G16b landed, `cullcheck` §2 went red at Dan's medium preset: **6,351** of 434,880
  pixels differ with the occlusion flood on and off, against D-173's pinned limit of ~3,000. It
  reproduced to the pixel across independent runs, and it passed at HIGH.

  It is not a culling regression. Instrumented, the differing pixels sit entirely in a band at
  the top of the frame, and **with the sky pass switched off in the same running page, the two
  pictures are identical — zero pixels differ.**

  D-173 is the explanation, and the thing it was measured through is the point. A
  section-granular visibility graph cannot express a sight line that clips the CORNER of a
  section it never enters, so the flood drops a thin band of sections at the render-distance
  edge. Terrain at that edge is fogged to **exactly** the clear colour (D-90: the fog reaches
  full strength precisely at the render-distance edge, and the clear colour is the fog), and
  until G16b the background behind it was that same clear colour. So the gap differed from its
  background by **zero** and could not be counted. ~3,000 was what remained visible of it, not
  its size. With a sky disc behind the horizon the same sections differ by up to 634 of 765 and
  the count roughly doubled.

  ⚠ **A NUMBER MEASURED THROUGH A WINDOW MEASURES THE WINDOW TOO.** The response is not a bigger
  constant. §2's count is re-pinned at ~6,400 with the reason written, and **§2f now makes the
  claim that does not drift**: remove the sky pass, and the flood-on and flood-off pictures must
  be IDENTICAL. That states exactly what the gap is — the flood only ever drops geometry that
  renders as the clear colour — and it goes red the moment the flood drops something a player
  could tell apart from fog, whatever the pixel count happens to be that day. Its anti-vacuity
  break shows that removing the sky pass really does change the frame by thousands of pixels, so
  §2f cannot pass by comparing two identical skies.

  ⚠ **AND THIS IS THE THIRD TIME IN ONE SESSION THAT A CHECK OWNED A NUMBER THE CODE OWNS**:
  `g14check`'s literal save envelope `4` (D-302), `guicheck`'s `sheets.length === 8` (D-304), and
  this. The first two had a mechanical fix — read `Save.VERSION`, parse `build-gui.mjs`'s own
  table. This one did not, because the quantity is genuinely empirical; so the repair was to
  assert a **relationship** instead of a magnitude. When a constant in a check cannot be derived,
  look for the experiment that makes it unnecessary.

- **D-306** **The entity table is the TENTH bytecode table, and a builder method is its name AND
  its descriptor** *(session 9)*

  PLAN G17a. Every entity type's hitbox, fire immunity and two networking numbers, read out of
  the 1.18.2 bytecode into `tools/golden/entity-types-1.18.2.tsv`, packed by
  `tools/pack-entities.mjs`, read by `src/07h_entities.js`, asserted by `tools/entitycheck.mjs`
  — **113 types, 42 assertions, 6 breaks.**

  ⚠ **THERE IS NO JSON FOR AN ENTITY'S HITBOX, IN ANY VERSION OF THE GAME.** Not in a data pack,
  not in a tag, not in the registry dump, and what `minecraft-data` carries is somebody's
  transcription of the wiki. A zombie's 0.6 × 1.95 exists in exactly one place:
  `EntityType.<clinit>`, as one long
  `register("zombie", Builder.of(Zombie::new, MobCategory.MONSTER).sized(0.6F, 1.95F)...)` chain.
  That is the whole argument for the referee (D-263) rather than a table typed in from memory.

  ⚠⚠ **A BUILDER METHOD IS ITS NAME **AND** ITS DESCRIPTOR, NEVER ITS NAME.** Obfuscation renames
  every overload to the same letter: on `EntityType.Builder`, `a` is `of`, `sized`, `immuneTo`
  AND `clientTrackingRange` — four different methods, one letter. Keying the parse by name alone
  made `calls.find(c => c.m === 'a')` return `immuneTo` for every entity that happens to be
  immune to a block, so **polar_bear, wither, wither_skeleton and snow_golem came out with no
  dimensions while the other 109 looked perfect.** Four wrong rows in 113 is exactly the size of
  mistake that ships. This is the same family as D-298's constructor-parsed-as-a-setter: in
  obfuscated bytecode, a NAME is not an identity.

  ⚠ **AND JAVAP OMITS THE CLASS PREFIX FOR A METHOD ON THE CLASS BEING DISASSEMBLED.** The
  registration calls print as `// Method a:(Ljava/lang/String;Laxo$a;)Laxo;` with no `axo.` in
  front, so a pattern that demands the prefix found ZERO register calls in a method that makes
  113 of them. The prefix is optional for the class's own methods and mandatory for the
  builder's, which are on another class.

  ⚠ **ZERO IS A SIZE.** `marker` and `lightning_bolt` really are `sized(0.0F, 0.0F)` — a marker
  is a position with no body, a lightning bolt is an effect — so a `w > 0` sanity guard rejects
  two correct rows and reports the parse as broken. The guard is that the two floats were
  THERE, which is a fact about the parse; the value is a fact about the game. Both are now
  asserted, and the set of bodiless types is CLOSED at exactly those two.

  ⚠ **THE SET IS CLOSED AGAINST A SOURCE THE EXTRACTOR DID NOT PRODUCE.**
  `.mcdata/1.18.2/_registries.json` is the game's own registry dump, fetched by
  `fetch-vanilla-data.mjs` and touched by nothing here. It lists 113 entity types; the table has
  113; both directions check out. A parse that silently dropped four rows — which an earlier
  version of this file did — cannot survive that, and a count the extractor checks against
  itself would never have caught it.

  ⚠ **THE BOX IS FEET-AT-THE-POSITION WITH THE FOOTPRINT CENTRED ON IT** —
  `[x − w/2, y, z − w/2] .. [x + w/2, y + h, z + w/2]`. Centring vertically too is the other
  obvious reading, it is self-consistent, no rule test distinguishes them, and it puts every mob
  half-buried in the floor. `entitycheck` §7 breaks it both ways to prove the check can tell.

  ⚠ **`07h_entities.js` HOLDS NO BEHAVIOUR, AND THAT IS THE RULING.** PLAN splits G17 three ways
  — the table, the movement core, the concrete entities and their picture — because they have
  different referees and different acceptance tests, and because `src/14b_physics.js` turns out
  to have been written ENTITY-shaped rather than player-shaped all along (`Ph.move(e, …)`,
  `Ph.tick(e, cmd)`), so G17b is much smaller than it looks. Writing behaviour stubs here is how
  a half-built stage gets mistaken for a finished one (D-294).

- **D-307** **A table that gets every anchor right can still be wrong everywhere else — the
  eleventh referee table, and the bug its own anchors could not see** *(session 9)*

  Ahead of G17b, `tools/extract-entity-motion.mjs` reads the constant downward push each entity
  class adds to its own delta movement — vanilla's
  `setDeltaMovement(getDeltaMovement().add(0.0D, -0.04D, 0.0D))` — into
  `tools/golden/entity-motion-1.18.2.tsv`. It is possible at all only because D-306's class
  column exists: every entity's constructor reference sits in the lambda bootstrap table, so the
  obfuscated class behind `item` or `falling_block` is KNOWN rather than guessed.

  ⚠⚠ **ITS FIRST VERSION MATCHED THE ARITHMETIC INSTEAD OF THE STATEMENT, AND ALL FOUR ANCHORS
  WERE GREEN.** The pattern it looked for was a negative double between two `dconst_0`s before a
  `(DDD)` call — which is also how you offset a POSITION. So it read a boat's gravity as **0.7**,
  an ender dragon's as **2**, and gave a shulker bullet one at all — while `item`,
  `falling_block`, `tnt` and `experience_orb` all came out exactly right, because those four
  classes happen to contain no position offsets in that shape. **Twelve rows, four anchors, four
  green, and half the table wrong.**

  ⚠ **WHAT FIXED IT WAS NOT A BETTER ANCHOR BUT A NARROWER PATTERN.** The Vec3 must be READ from
  a no-argument getter and WRITTEN BACK through a one-argument void setter — which a position
  offset never is. Adding more anchors would have caught this one eventually and would not have
  caught the next; tightening the pattern to the whole statement made the false positives
  impossible rather than detected. **When a measurement is wrong, ask what it is matching, not
  what else you could compare it against.**

  ⚠ **AND THE NEGATIVE ANCHORS ARE NOW ASSERTIONS.** `arrow` must NOT resolve (it inherits its
  tick, so a value for it is by definition a false positive), `ender_dragon` must not, and every
  resolved gravity must be ≤ 0.1 because a per-tick acceleration cannot be 2. Those three are the
  ones that would have failed.

  ⚠ **THE TABLE IS NOT WIRED INTO THE RUNTIME, ON PURPOSE.** Ten types resolve and 102 inherit
  their tick from a superclass and are listed by name as OWED rather than defaulted. Nothing in
  `dist/mclite.html` reads any of it, because there is no entity list for it to act on yet — and
  **a constant the runtime carries but nothing consumes is exactly D-289's shape**. G17b is the
  stage that consumes it; the measurement is simply ready before the stage that needs it.

  ⚠ **Vertical drag comes in two shapes and BOTH are now read, structurally.** `scale(0.98)` is
  unambiguous. `multiply(f, 0.98D, f)` is not, and the middle argument is found **without
  simulating the operand stack**, by using the one thing that is true of this call and nothing
  else: the horizontal factors are the SAME COMPUTED VALUE pushed twice, so the instructions
  before the literal and after it must be IDENTICAL sequences, neither pushing a constant.
  ⚠⚠ **THAT LAST CLAUSE IS THE WHOLE THING.** `ItemEntity` also contains
  `multiply(1.0D, -0.5D, 1.0D)` — the bounce when it lands — whose flanks are `dconst_1` on both
  sides and are therefore ALSO identical. Matching on symmetry alone reads an item's drag as
  **−0.5**. Requiring the flanks to be non-literal is what separates "the two horizontal factors
  are a variable" from "they are the number one", and the anchor that says so is asserted:
  `item` and `experience_orb` must read 0.98, and every drag in the table must lie in (0, 1].
  Eight types now carry both constants, and `EntityList` will simulate exactly those eight.

- **D-308** **`Physics.move` was entity-shaped in its signature and PLAYER-shaped in its body, and
  a check that only ever moved the player could not see it** *(session 9)*

  PLAN G17b. `src/14b_physics.js` takes an entity everywhere — `Ph.move(e, dx, dy, dz)`,
  `Ph.tick(e, cmd)`, `Ph.frictionOf(e)` — and NEXT has said for two sessions that this makes G17
  smaller than it looks. Writing the first entity that is not the player found two places where
  the shape was a promise the body did not keep:

  1. ⚠⚠ **THE COLLIDER'S WIDTH WAS `Ph.W` — the player's 0.6 — while its HEIGHT came from the
     entity.** So `move` was half parameterised. A falling block is **0.98** wide and would have
     fitted through a 0.7 gap it cannot fit through in the real game, and nothing would have
     looked wrong: it falls, it lands, it is simply in a place it could not be. It is now
     `(e.width !== undefined ? e.width : Ph.W)`, and the fallback leaves every existing caller
     exactly where it was because the player sets no `e.width`.
  2. ⚠ **LANDING RAN THE PLAYER'S `Ph.landed` FOR ANYTHING THAT TOUCHED THE GROUND** — fall
     damage, the slime bounce, the bed bounce. Vanilla puts all of that in
     `LivingEntity.checkFallDamage`; base `Entity.checkFallDamage` only resets the counter. It is
     gated on `e.living !== false` now. This one announced itself loudly — `Ph.landed` reads the
     block below through `NS.World`, which a headless fixture does not have, so the first falling
     block crashed instead of quietly taking fall damage. **The loud failure was luck**, not
     design: had `landed` been pure arithmetic, a stick of TNT would have been taking fall damage
     for ever with every check green.

  **`src/07i_entitylist.js`** is the list: spawn, remove, and one tick of the motion every entity
  shares. **`tools/entlistcheck.mjs` — 31 assertions, 5 breaks.**

  ⚠ **THE ORDER IS GRAVITY, THEN MOVE, THEN DRAG**, which is `FallingBlockEntity.tick` verbatim
  and not what intuition suggests. The check reproduces the recurrence by hand from the two
  measured constants and compares it to the engine for a hundred ticks; §6 then runs the wrong
  orders and shows they diverge. ⚠ **And one "wrong order" in the first draft was not wrong at
  all**: damping at the TOP of the tick and at the BOTTOM are the same multiplication, so with
  `vy` starting at zero the two loops agree for ever. The order that actually differs is damping
  BETWEEN the gravity and the move, and that is the one asserted. *An anti-vacuity break that
  cannot fail is the same error as a check that cannot fail.*

  ⚠ **WHAT THE ENGINE WILL SIMULATE IS A CLOSED SET.** `EntityList.spawn` REFUSES any type whose
  gravity and drag were not both measured (D-307): six types today, 107 named by `EL.owed()`. A
  default would be invisible — a wrongly-defaulted entity still falls, still lands, still looks
  fine, and is wrong for ever. `item` is the case that proves the rule: its gravity is known,
  its drag is not, and it is refused rather than lent the 0.98 that every other entity uses.

  ⚠ **AND TWO OF THE FIXTURE'S OWN BUGS ARE WORTH THE LINE.** Its first run compared a hundred
  ticks of "free fall" for an entity that reached the floor on tick 35, and it stubbed
  `Ph.solidAt` — which `clip` never calls. `clip` asks `Ph.shapeAt` and nothing else. A fixture
  that stubs the wrong function tests the real one against a world that does not exist.

- **D-309** **Walking the superclass chain to shorten the owed list was built, measured and
  REJECTED: in an obfuscated jar there is nothing to detect an override with** *(session 9)*

  D-307's motion table resolves ten entity types and leaves 102 owed, because most entities apply
  gravity in a superclass. Walking the chain is the obvious repair, it is fifteen lines, and it
  takes the owed list down to a handful. It is also **wrong**, and the extractor's own negative
  anchor is what said so.

  `ender_dragon` must not resolve — nothing in EnderDragon adds a constant downward push to its
  delta movement; it overrides `travel` outright. The chain walk handed it the superclass's
  number without hesitation, **because the walk had no way to tell an override from an
  inheritance**. So the walk is not in the file and the 102 stay named in the table's header.

  ⚠⚠ **THE FIRST VERSION OF THIS ENTRY GAVE THE WRONG REASON, AND THE SECOND ATTEMPT FOUND THE
  RIGHT ONE.** It said detecting the override was impossible — that obfuscation "gives an
  override a different letter from the method it overrides as readily as the same one, so there
  is nothing to compare." **That is false, and for a reason that is not a matter of opinion: the
  JVM dispatches a virtual call on name AND descriptor, so an obfuscator MUST rename an override
  and the method it overrides together or the program stops working.** An override always shares
  its parent's signature, so the test exists: attribute the literal to a `name(descriptor)` —
  `javap -c` prints each member's signature above its code — and refuse when any class between
  it and the entity declares that same signature. **That test was then built, and it works.**

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE WALK IS STILL REJECTED, FOR A SECOND AND BETTER REASON: THE METHOD HOLDING THE
  LITERAL NEED NOT BE ON THE TICK PATH AT ALL.** With the override test in place, the walk gave
  `ender_dragon` a gravity of **0.04** out of a method two classes up that neither class below
  overrides. That is not a wrong answer to "is it overridden"; it is the right answer to the
  wrong question. A class can hold a gravity-shaped statement in a helper that runs only in
  water, only in lava, or only while ridden, and nothing short of control-flow analysis can say
  which. **An entity's own class is the one place where "adds a constant downward push to its
  delta movement" and "falls at this rate" reliably coincide** — a `FallingBlockEntity` has one
  such statement and it is its tick — which is exactly why the table's header defines its column
  as the former and not the latter, and why the file stops at the own class.

  So G17c does not get to walk the chain either. It shortens the owed list by reading the
  superclasses it actually needs, **one at a time, checking that the statement it found is on the
  unconditional path**, and asserting each result against something independent. That is slow,
  and it is the only version that can be right.

  ⚠ **AND THE ATTEMPT CORRECTED SOMETHING ELSE, WHICH IS WHY IT WAS WORTH MAKING.** While the
  chain was in, an assertion read "arrow should resolve once the chain is walked". That was
  written from memory of how vanilla *ought* to be shaped, and it is wrong: `AbstractArrow` does
  `setDeltaMovement(vec3.x, vec3.y - 0.05F, vec3.z)` — the three-argument form, a FLOAT literal,
  no `.add()` at all. The extractor refused to write a table it could not vouch for, and said so.
  **That is the whole argument for asserting in both directions**: the negative anchors are the
  ones that fail when you are wrong about the shape of the thing you are reading (D-263).

  ⚠ **A rejected fix is recorded, not silently dropped** — the same rule as D-137 — **and so is a
  rejection whose reasoning turned out to be wrong.** The failure mode a decisions file has is
  not being incomplete; it is being confidently wrong and never revisited. This entry has now
  been wrong once and rewritten twice, and the conclusion did not move: the walk is out, and the
  reason it is out is better than the one first given. **A right answer for a wrong reason is a
  bug with a delay on it.**

- **D-310** **THE GAME DID NOT START ON DAN'S MACHINE, AND 1,174,964 ASSERTIONS WERE GREEN**
  *(session 9, reported by Dan)*

  He opened `dist/mclite.html` and got the fatal screen: *"No usable GPU backend."* Two faults,
  and **neither was reachable by any check this project owned.**

  **1. WebGPU asked for a device with no `requiredLimits`, so it got the SPEC DEFAULTS.**
  `maxTextureArrayLayers` defaults to **256**; the block atlas has **778**. `createTexture` for
  the atlas failed validation, on every real GPU this project has ever run on. His adapter would
  have allowed 2048 and the error said so outright. ⚠⚠ **This is the whole of the "WebGPU renders
  the world black on real hardware" constraint the CHARTER has carried since 6 Sept** — the atlas
  texture was never created, so every block sampled nothing. It was never a shader bug. The limit
  is now requested against `adapter.limits`, and an adapter that genuinely cannot do it is refused
  **in a sentence** — "this adapter allows 256 layers and the block atlas needs 778" — rather than
  through a validation stack trace.

  **2. The boot fallback asked the SAME canvas for WebGL2, which is impossible.** A canvas that
  has handed out a `webgpu` context can never hand out a `webgl2` one. `Main.applyBackend` has
  known that since F9 existed and replaces the element for the manual swap; **the boot path did
  not.** So WebGPU failed, the fallback that exists to rescue exactly that got `null`, and the
  game died showing him a message blaming his graphics driver. `Gfx.replaceCanvas` is now a hook
  `Main` installs, `Main.swapCanvas` is the one copy both callers use, and **`Input.el` moves with
  the element** — a replaced canvas with the input layer on the removed node is a game that draws
  and cannot be played.

  ⚠⚠ **THE REASON NOTHING CAUGHT IT IS THE FINDING, NOT THE BUGS.** Headless Chromium has
  `navigator.gpu` and **no adapter**, so `GfxGPU.init` bails at "no WebGPU adapter" *before it
  ever touches the canvas*. The only environment that has ever attempted WebGPU failed so early
  that neither fault could occur. Worse: **no check ever forced the WebGPU backend at all**, so
  the path was not merely untestable, it was untested. Every browser stage booted the default way
  and measured a picture that a working WebGL2 renderer had already drawn. *A green suite was a
  statement about this container, and I reported it as a statement about the game.*

  **`tools/backendcheck.mjs` — 22 assertions, 3 breaks.** It does not wait for a WebGPU adapter
  it will never get. It **sabotages the boot** through a new `initScript` hook in `cdp.mjs` that
  runs before the page's own scripts: WebGPU takes the canvas and then fails, which is his
  sequence exactly, and the game must still start, draw, and keep its input attached. Its
  decisive break removes the replacement canvas and the boot fails **precisely as his did**.
  ⚠ §2 asserts the MECHANISM rather than assuming it — `getContext('webgpu')` succeeds here even
  with no adapter, and the canvas then refuses `webgl2` — because the entire second fault rests
  on that being true. ⚠ §5 asserts the other direction: a WebGPU that fails *before* touching the
  canvas must NOT swap it, or the swap count in §3 means nothing.

  ⚠ **AND THE CHECK'S OWN FIRST BREAK DID NOT FIRE.** It nulled `Gfx.replaceCanvas` from the init
  script, and `Main.play()` re-assigns that hook during boot — so the sabotage was undone by the
  very code it was testing, and the break passed a build where the fix did nothing. It works
  through the `swapCanvas` wrapper now. **An anti-vacuity break that the code under test can
  overwrite is not a break** (D-305, D-308: this is the third time in one session).

  ⚠ The rule that follows: **a check that has only ever exercised the default path has measured a
  default, not a program.** Every configuration the shipped file can boot in — each backend, each
  preset, each fallback between them — is a path, and an untaken path is an untested one.

- **D-311** **"THERE IS NO HAND MODEL, THE ITEM IN BLOCK MODEL IS NOT EVEN CLOSE, AND MANY BLOCKS
  HAVE WRONG TEXTURES IN HOTBAR AND IN WORLD."** — Dan, playing, 14 September 2026. Three
  complaints, and they were one finding wearing three faces: **the hotbar was drawing the ITEM
  SHEET's flat sprite for every block.** That sprite is not a block icon and never was. Vanilla
  renders the block's REAL MODEL at its `gui` display transform — `rotation [30, 225, 0]`,
  `scale 0.625` — and the flat sprite is its fallback for a block that has no model at all.

  **`src/15d_blockicon.js`** is the software rasteriser that does it: the baked geometry the
  mesher reads, z-buffered (not painter-sorted — a stair, a fence post and a cauldron all have
  quads that interpenetrate in screen space from this angle), back-face culled BY WINDING rather
  than by face id (a model element rotated 45 degrees has a face id that no longer says which way
  it points), with the per-face shade and the biome tint. The same rasteriser at
  `firstperson_righthand` draws the HELD block, and `BI.renderArm` draws the arm out of the
  64×64 skin's own faces — so the hand exists.

  ⚠ **THE "WRONG TEXTURES" HALF WAS THE ENGINE BEING RIGHT.** `tools/texaudit.mjs` walks 318 cube
  blocks face by face (1,908 faces) and 471 model blocks by layer-set containment: **0 wrong, 0
  missing from the atlas.** It produced three FALSE POSITIVES before it produced that number, and
  each is a lesson worth more than the audit: the atlas dedupes tiles by **SHA-1**, so a furnace
  legitimately shares a layer with a piston and a reverse name map reports a bug that is not
  there; **a clean permutation of faces is the signature of a missing x/y rotation**, not of wrong
  textures; and `placementsFor(bs, {})` matches only UNCONDITIONAL variants, which is why 640 of
  900 blocks looked unresolved until the properties came from the registry.

  ⚠ The hand then "did not draw" — it was drawing, at 52 device pixels, a thumbnail in the
  corner. It was found by cropping and magnifying rather than by looking harder at a number.

- **D-312** **THE SIXTY-FOUR-BLOCK STARTER KIT IS DELETED, NOT FLAGGED OFF.** A new world used to
  begin with nine pre-filled hotbar slots — 64 each of grass, dirt, stone, cobblestone, planks,
  log, sand and glass, plus a torch. Minecraft does not do that, in any gamemode, and the charter
  says everything that is not worldgen or rendering is absolute full parity. It was scaffolding
  from before there was an inventory, and D-139's rule is that the stage which replaces something
  deletes the something **in the same commit**.

  ⚠ **AND THE REPLACEMENT HAS TO EXIST, WHICH IS D-139 READ FROM THE OTHER SIDE.** In survival the
  replacement is the world: you punch a tree. In CREATIVE there is exactly one way to obtain a
  block and it is the creative inventory, so this deletion is only correct alongside D-313. A
  creative world with neither is a game with no blocks in it — strictly worse than the
  placeholder. The two went in together.

- **D-313** **THE CREATIVE INVENTORY'S TABS ARE THE TWELFTH BYTECODE TABLE, AND THE FIRST DRAFT OF
  THIS FILE IS THE ARGUMENT FOR WHY.** That draft classified all 1,100 items into tabs with eight
  ordered regular expressions typed from memory, in a file whose own header said *"the contents
  come from the item table, not from a list typed here"*. It had **eleven tabs in an invented
  order, no `hotbar` tab at all, `search` first instead of sixth, and `materials` missing.** Every
  part of it was plausible: the names were real, the order looked like the game's, the regexes
  matched. **A hand-written classification is its own authority — nothing in the engine can
  disagree with it**, which is the same class of fault as D-304's hard-coded sheet count.

  `tools/extract-creative.mjs` reads it out of the obfuscated 1.18.2 jar by D-263's procedure:
  **thirteen `CreativeModeTab` constants in TWELVE columns** (`TAB_MATERIALS` is the same OBJECT
  as `TAB_MISC`, stored into a second field — thirteen lang keys, twelve constructions), the tab
  of every one of the 1,101 items, and each tab's icon read out of its own anonymous subclass.
  Closed against two sources the tool did not generate: the jar's own `lang/en_us.json` (thirteen
  `itemGroup.*` keys, both directions) and `_registries.json` (1,101 items, both directions).
  **1,083 placed, 18 in no tab at all** — the command blocks, the barrier, the jigsaw, the debug
  stick, the spawner, the dragon egg.

  ⚠⚠ **THE `int` IN THE CONSTRUCTOR IS THE COLUMN, NOT AN ORDINAL.** Vanilla's strip is six wide
  and two deep and that argument is the CELL. Misc is declared fifth and sits in cell 6; Search is
  declared sixth and sits in cell 5; Hotbar is declared twelfth and sits in cell 4. Reading it as
  a declaration index gives a strip whose tabs are in the right order and the wrong PLACES.

  ⚠ **AND "THE LAST int BEFORE THE `putstatic`" IS NOT THE COLUMN EITHER.** Four of the twelve
  constructions go on to build an array of enchantment categories — `bipush 12; anewarray;
  iconst_0; … aastore` — so a looser rule read the array's length or its final index instead. It
  gave tools column 3 (it is 8) and combat column 11 (it is 9), and it was right about the first
  five. The column is the int **immediately before the lang string**, because the constructor
  takes them adjacent.

  ⚠ The referee corrected a belief twice during the build: **bedrock IS in Building Blocks** (the
  extractor's own anchor list said it was in no tab, and the bytecode said otherwise), and
  `materials` is a dead alias rather than a thirteenth tab. Both were caught because the
  assertions run in BOTH directions against a file the tool did not write.

  The tab is **one byte per item in `items.bin`**, beside the item it describes, with the
  twelve-entry strip in the same header — a column number in a row means nothing without the strip
  that says what column 6 is, and shipping them apart is how a runtime ends up with an item in
  tab 7 and no tab 7. `src/15e_creative.js` owns the geometry and classifies NOTHING.

  ⚠ **OWED, NAMED:** the HOTBAR tab's nine saved toolbars need an options file MC-Lite does not
  have. The tab draws and is empty, and `Creative.OWED` says so rather than the tab quietly
  going missing from a twelve-tab strip.

- **D-314** **TWO FACE-NUMBERING CONVENTIONS WERE BEING INDEXED BY ONE FIELD, AND EVERY MODEL
  BLOCK IN THE WORLD WAS LIT AS IF IT WERE LYING ON ITS SIDE.** Found while chasing D-311's icon,
  which is the only reason it was found at all.

  The greedy path — full cubes, stone and dirt and planks — packs **ARCH §3 face numbering**
  (`0 +X, 1 -X, 2 +Y, 3 -Y, 4 +Z, 5 -Z`), which is what `Gfx.SHADE.FACE = [0.6, 0.6, 1.0, 0.5,
  0.8, 0.8]` and the shaders' `shadeExpr` are indexed by. The MODEL path — anything with a real
  model: grass blocks, stairs, slabs, fences, walls, torches, doors — packed the baked quad's
  `dir` **straight through**, and that is **vanilla's `Direction` order** (`0 down, 1 up, 2 north,
  3 south, 4 west, 5 east`). Emitting a grass block through the real mesher and reading the packed
  vertices back:

  ```
  emitted face 0  plane y=0     the BOTTOM,  shaded as +X = 0.6   (should be 0.5)
  emitted face 1  plane y=256   the TOP,     shaded as -X = 0.6   (should be 1.0)
  emitted face 2  plane z=0     NORTH,       shaded as +Y = 1.0   (should be 0.8)
  emitted face 3  plane z=256   SOUTH,       shaded as -Y = 0.5   (should be 0.8)
  ```

  A grass block's top was lit like a side wall and its north face was lit like the sky.
  `MESH_OF_DIR = [3, 2, 5, 4, 1, 0]` already existed three lines above, already converted this
  exact number for the quad's CULLING and its LIGHTING, and was simply never applied to the thing
  the shader colours by.

  ⚠⚠ **WHY 119,989 ASSERTIONS DID NOT SEE IT.** `emitcheck` asserted `emitted.face === source.d`
  — that the mesher faithfully copies the baked number. It does. **"Did it copy the number" and
  "does the number mean the same thing as the one the greedy path packs" are different questions,
  and only the first was ever asked.** D-276's rule, again and at its sharpest: *a check that
  passes proves only what it touches, and the bugs live in the joins between stages.* This is a
  join between two numbering conventions inside one 3-bit field.

  Two further faults in the icon rasteriser came out of the same pull:

  ⚠ **`matrix()` COMPUTED `Rx·Ry` WHILE ITS OWN COMMENT SAID `Ry·Rx`.** The arithmetic and the
  sentence above it disagreed, and at vanilla's own 225 degrees the wrong product is
  **degenerate**: `cos 225` and `sin 225` are both −0.707, so +X and +Z land on the SAME screen x,
  the two side faces collapse onto one another and the top face slides off to the left. The icon
  still looked like a solid shaded lump of the right block, which is why nothing noticed.

  ⚠⚠ **AND 45 DEGREES IS NOT 225 DEGREES.** Both give a clean symmetric hexagon. They show
  **different faces**: 45 shows top, east and south; 225 shows top, **north** and west. A sign
  flip made to "fix the skew" would have produced a perfectly plausible cube of the wrong three
  faces — with a furnace showing its back. Vanilla shows the north face, and the proof is in the
  game: a furnace's front opening and a carved pumpkin's face are both visible in the inventory.
  `iconcheck` renders each quad alone, asserts exactly three survive the cull, that the furnace's
  FRONT is one of them and is on the LEFT half — and breaks it by setting 45 degrees and watching
  the front disappear.

  ⚠ The icon also read its corners FORWARDS while `Mesher.emitModelBlock` reads them REVERSED
  (D-133: the bakery keeps Mojang's own corner order, which is the opposite winding from the one
  the renderer culls by). So the winding test kept the BACK faces, and the icon drew a furnace's
  bottom and its two far sides — a perfectly good furnace with its front hidden. Six blocks moved
  out of the flat-fallback set when it was fixed, from 115 to 109.

  ⚠ The rule that follows, and it is the session's third of this shape: **when one number is
  written by two producers, assert that they agree — not that each copied its own source.**

- **D-315** **THE SETTINGS SCREEN WAS DRAWN IN THE BROWSER'S FONT, AND THE CHARTER FORBIDS THAT IN
  AS MANY WORDS.** Dan: *"remove the old settings menu and wire it into the gui of the real
  game."* `Hud.drawPause` painted twenty-odd rows of filled rectangles at `'13px "Segoe UI"'`,
  reflowing into two columns when the window got short. It worked. It looked nothing like
  Minecraft, and the GUI is on the "absolute full parity" side of the charter's line explicitly.

  `src/15f_options.js` is vanilla's tree — Game Menu → Options → Video Settings / Controls /
  Music & Sounds / Language — on **`widgets.png`'s own three button sprites**: y=46 disabled,
  y=66 normal, y=86 hovered, each 200×20, measured off the texture and asserted against it in
  both directions. A slider is the disabled sprite with a live 8-wide knob, and it FOLLOWS THE
  POINTER, because a slider that jumps to where you pressed and stops is a stepper wearing a
  slider's art. Escape and Done both walk back ONE screen.

  ⚠ **THE LAYOUT NUMBERS ARE CONSTANTS, NOT RATIOS, BECAUSE THEY ARE CONSTANTS THERE.** 150×20 at
  `width/2 - 155`, columns 160 apart, rows 24 apart, title at y=15, Done at `height/6 + 168`.
  Vanilla's options screen does not reflow at any window size; a version that did would stop
  being the screen a player recognises. `optionscheck` asserts the pair spans −155..+155 — 
  symmetric about the centre with a ten-pixel gutter — which is where a one-pixel slip in either
  constant shows up and nowhere else.
