  ⚠ **TEN BUTTONS VANILLA HAS AND THIS DOES NOT ARE DRAWN DISABLED RATHER THAN LEFT OUT.** A
  player reads a menu by SHAPE, and a grid with two entries missing is a different grid.
  "Resource Packs..." greyed out is the truth; `Options.OWED` names all ten and the check closes
  the set both ways.

  ⚠ **TEN SOUND SOURCES, AS A REAL GAIN GRAPH.** Vanilla's `SoundSource` is chosen by the CALLER
  at play time and is not in `sounds.json`, so the source travels in `play`'s options and each one
  gets its own `GainNode` feeding the master. Multiplying two numbers at each `play` would sound
  identical today and would stop being vanilla's graph the moment anything wants to duck the
  music. Six of the ten have nothing routed into them yet and `Sound.OWED_SOURCES` names what
  each waits on.

  ⚠ **D-139, ENFORCED BY A CHECK THAT READS THE SOURCE.** `pauseRows()` is deleted, not flagged
  off, and `optionscheck` §5 greps `15_hud.js` and fails if it comes back. A settings screen kept
  behind a flag is two settings screens, and the one nobody looks at is the one that rots.

  ⚠ Also fixed in passing: the modal background is vanilla's GRADIENT — `fillGradient(0, 0, w, h,
  -1072689136, -804253680)`, which is `0xC0101010` to `0xD0101010` — and not a flat
  `rgba(0,0,0,0.6)`. Near-black at 75% at the top and 82% at the bottom, and not pure black. It
  is the single most common way a clone's menus read as *nearly* right.

- **D-316** **BRIGADIER, AND THE COMMAND ROSTER IS THE THIRTEENTH BYTECODE TABLE.** Dan asked
  *"when are commands coming?"* and then chose how: **"real parser, player commands first."** A
  clone that splits on spaces gets `/give @p stone 64` right and then gets
  `/give @e[type=item,limit=3] ...` wrong, with no error position, no completion and no
  `<--[HERE]`.

  `tools/extract-commands.mjs` reads all **74** commands out of the 1.18.2 jar with their
  **operator levels** and their **aliases**. Identification by use, throughout: a COMMAND CLASS is
  one with a static method whose first parameter is `com.mojang.brigadier.CommandDispatcher` (78
  of them); `Commands.literal` is found **by descriptor** — `(Ljava/lang/String;)L…/
  LiteralArgumentBuilder;` — never by name; a command NAME is the first `ldc String` *immediately*
  followed by a call to it, because a register method is full of other strings; an ALIAS is a
  literal whose builder goes on to call `redirect`, which is exactly how `/tp`, `/w`, `/tell` and
  `/xp` are declared; and a LEVEL is the int in the source class's only `(int)boolean` method.
  Closed against `Commands`' own constructor in both directions.

  ⚠ **THE REFEREE CORRECTED ME AGAIN: THE COMMAND IS `/experience` AND `/xp` IS ITS REDIRECT.**
  The anchor list said `xp` and the bytecode said otherwise. Third time in one session.

  ⚠⚠ **BRIGADIER IS NOT IN THE JAR, AND ITS ERROR MESSAGES STILL DID NOT HAVE TO BE TYPED.**
  There was no bytecode referee for the library's text — but **Mojang TRANSLATE those messages**,
  so every one is a key in the `en_us.json` this game already ships whole: `parsing.int.expected`,
  `parsing.quote.expected.end`, `command.unknown.argument`, `command.expected.separator`,
  `command.context.here` = `<--[HERE]`. So "Expected integer" is the game's wording rather than
  mine, and a typo is impossible. `commandcheck` §5 **tokenises both modules** and fails on any
  hard-coded English phrase.

  ⚠ **THAT SCAN'S FIRST VERSION WAS MEASURING ITS OWN REGEX.** It stripped lines that BEGIN with
  `//` and then matched quotes with a regular expression, so a trailing comment survived, an
  apostrophe inside one opened a "string", and it reported eight hard-coded phrases in a file
  that had none. It is a real tokeniser now — strings, line comments, block comments and regex
  literals — and its anti-vacuity break feeds it a comment containing quotes.

  ⚠ **AND TWO OF THE CHECK'S OTHER ASSERTIONS WERE ASSERTING THINGS BRIGADIER DOES NOT DO.** With
  TWO failing children, brigadier reports the GENERIC `command.unknown.argument`, not the
  specific error — `execute` throws the single exception only when there is exactly one. The
  check demanded `argument.integer.big` from a two-child node and demanded
  `command.unknown.command` from a dispatcher with ONE root, where brigadier correctly propagates
  that root's own failure. Both are now asserted as the rule actually is, in both of its halves.

  The nine implemented: **/gamemode /give /time /weather /teleport (/tp) /kill /seed /help
  /summon**, with `game_mode`, `entity` selectors (`@p @a @r @s @e` and `[type=,limit=,
  distance=]`), `item_stack`, `entity_summon`, `time` (`d` = 24000, `s` = 20, `t` = 1) and
  `vec3`/`block_pos` with `~` and `^`. `/time set day` is tick **1000**, not 0 — `day` meaning 0
  is the commonest way a clone's `/time set day` comes out looking like dawn. **The other 65 are
  OWED and `commandcheck` names them against the golden table on every run.**

  ⚠ `readUnquoted` STOPS AT A COLON, which is correct and load-bearing for selector options like
  `type=cow` — and it meant `minecraft:stone` came back as `minecraft` and a perfectly valid line
  failed. `ResourceLocationArgument`'s character set is a SEPARATE reader that also takes `:` and
  `/`, because vanilla accepts the namespaced and bare forms interchangeably everywhere.

  ⚠ Permission levels are ENFORCED rather than decorative, even with one player. `/help` is level
  0 and lists only what the source may run; `/gamemode` is level 2 and a level-0 source cannot
  see it in `/help` or in tab completion. That is the one place the gate is visible without a
  second player, and it is what `commandcheck` uses to prove the plumbing is real.

- **D-317** **SIXTY ITEMS DREW NOTHING, AND FIXING IT NEEDED THE FOURTEENTH BYTECODE TABLE.**
  G11b's creative inventory made the gap visible: every chest, all 17 shulker boxes, all 16 beds,
  all 16 banners, the six heads, the conduit and the shield are `builtin/entity` in vanilla — no
  item sprite, no block model — and the game draws each by running a BLOCK-ENTITY RENDERER into
  the slot. MC-Lite had neither the boxes nor the textures, so sixty slots were blank, including
  the Survival Inventory tab's own chest icon.

  ⚠⚠ **THE BOXES EXIST ONLY AS COMPILED JAVA.** There is no JSON for a chest's lid anywhere in any
  version of the jar. `ChestRenderer.createSingleBodyLayer()` is
  `CubeListBuilder.create().texOffs(0, 19).addBox(1, 0, 1, 14, 10, 14)` and that is the whole
  source of truth. `tools/extract-models.mjs` reads **70 layers, 310 boxes** out of it and serves
  G17c's entity rendering as well, which is why it extracts every layer rather than the ten the
  icons need (a hand-picked subset is the second roster D-313 spent a session learning not to
  write).

  Five classes identified by shape and none by name: `CubeListBuilder` is the only class in the
  jar with both `(int, int) -> itself` and `(float x6) -> itself`; `PartDefinition` is whatever
  takes `(String, CubeListBuilder, X)`; `LayerDefinition` is `(MeshDefinition, int, int) -> self`.

  ⚠ **`LayerDefinitions` AND `ModelLayers` CANNOT BE FOUND ALONE BY COUNTING FIELDS, AND THE FIRST
  VERSION TRIED.** "The class with 100+ static finals of one type" is `SoundEvents`, which has
  1,203. What is unique is the PAIR — one class that reads another's static fields and hands each
  straight to a method returning a LayerDefinition. That happens in exactly one place, 155 times,
  and names both classes at once.

  ⚠⚠ **`PartPose` HAS TWO THREE-FLOAT FACTORIES WITH THE SAME DESCRIPTOR AND OPPOSITE MEANINGS.**
  `offset(x, y, z)` and `rotation(rx, ry, rz)` are indistinguishable by signature, and reading
  either as the other gives a bed whose legs are translated instead of turned. They are told apart
  BY USE: both delegate to the six-float constructor, and `offset` pushes its arguments first then
  three zeroes while `rotation` pushes three zeroes first. Four lines of bytecode, and not
  something an obfuscator can disguise.

  ⚠ **THE UV LAYOUT'S REFEREE IS THE PLAYER SKIN.** A box at `texOffs(u, v)` sized `w x h x d`
  lays its faces out as up `(u+d, v)`, down `(u+d+w, v)`, west `(u, v+d)`, north `(u+d, v+d)`,
  east `(u+d+w, v+d)`, south `(u+d+w+d, v+d)`. That is not read off a wiki: it is the rule that
  reproduces the right arm's documented coordinates — `texOffs(40, 16)`, `4 x 12 x 4`, outer side
  at (40, 20), front at (44, 20), inner at (48, 20), back at (52, 20), top cap at (44, 16), bottom
  at (48, 16) — which `15d_blockicon.js`'s arm table already uses and the hand is already drawn
  with. `bemodelcheck` asserts the formula against that table and that the six rectangles do not
  overlap.

  ⚠ **AND THE ROSTER IS THE JAR'S TOO.** `BE.gui` is built from the `builtin/entity` PARENT CHAINS
  of every item model, which is precisely what "nothing else can draw this" means — so the
  blank-icon set is not a list anybody typed. It comes out at exactly the sixty that were measured
  blank, and `bemodelcheck` asserts `Creative.NO_ICON` against it in both directions.

  ⚠ **EVERY ONE OF THESE ITEMS HAS ITS OWN `gui` ROTATION AND THEY ARE NOT THE SAME.** A chest is
  `[30, 45, 0]`, a shulker box the same, a bed `[30, 160, 0]`, a banner `[30, 20, 0]` — nearly
  front-on, because a flag seen at 45 degrees is a line. The first build drew all of them at the
  block icon's `[30, 225, 0]` and the banner's flag came out FOUR PIXELS WIDE.

  ⚠ **AND A BANNER IS ONE TEXTURE TINTED SIXTEEN WAYS while a bed is sixteen textures.** Beds and
  shulker boxes each ship their own coloured PNG; banners do not — `BannerRenderer` draws
  `banner_base.png` through `DyeColor.getTextureDiffuseColors()`. Asking the ITEM table for
  `red_dye`'s tint returns nothing (a dye's icon is a coloured sprite, not a tinted one), so the
  first build had sixteen white banners. The colours are the bytecode's own, and the column is
  anchored: white is `0xF9FFFE`, and `0xF0F0F0` — which the check refuses — is `fireworkColor`,
  the neighbouring column of sixteen plausible wrong numbers.

  ⚠ **A DECLARED DEVIATION, stated rather than hidden.** Vanilla positions each of these by its
  renderer's own `translate` and then applies the item's gui translation and scale on top. MC-Lite
  reproduces the ROTATION exactly and then CENTRES the model on its PROJECTED extent instead of
  reproducing five renderers' preambles. The first version fitted the model's longest AXIS times a
  1.42 fudge, which is right for a cube and wrong for everything else — a banner is 70 units tall
  and 20 wide, so the flag got a third of the width it had room for. Projecting the corners once at
  unit scale costs one extra pass over eight corners per part, is exact at every angle, and
  deletes the fudge factor.

  ⚠ **A FLIP REVERSES WINDING.** `BannerRenderer` scales Y by −1 and `ChestRenderer` does not, so
  the families need a flip table — and flipping without also flipping the back-face cull renders a
  shulker box INSIDE OUT: hollow, and lit from within. `g11bcheck` §9 measures it as coverage,
  because a hollow box covers a fraction of what a solid one does.

  ⚠ **OWED, NAMED: seven.** The six heads and the conduit. Vanilla registers the head layers in a
  loop over `SkullBlock.Types`, so there is no per-head static field to pair with a builder, and
  the conduit's renderer never registers a layer. `g11bcheck` §9 fails if a blank icon is not on
  `BE.OWED`.

- **D-318** **`build.mjs` DOES NOT REBUILD THE DATA MODULE, AND THAT HAS NOW COST FOUR SESSIONS.**
  `src/19_data.gen.js` is generated from `assets/*.bin` by `tools/gen-data.mjs`; `build.mjs` only
  CONCATENATES. So a session that repacks an asset and then runs `node build.mjs` gets a build
  that is green, idempotent and STALE — and the symptom is never "the asset is missing", it is a
  feature that silently does nothing. The sun and moon never drew (D-303). The creative tab strip
  came back empty. A block-entity icon rendered at the wrong angle because its display transform
  was not in the blob yet, and half an hour went into the renderer before the payload was the
  suspect.

  The fix is not another line in a document, because the document already said it. `build.mjs`
  now compares mtimes: if any `assets/*.bin` is newer than `src/19_data.gen.js`, the build STOPS
  and names the file. Four sessions of "why is nothing happening" against one comparison.

  ⚠ The general rule: **when a build step's output can be silently stale, the build that consumes
  it must refuse to run, not warn.** A warning in a 40-line build report is a warning nobody
  reads on the one run where it matters.

- **D-319** **THIRTEEN MORE COMMANDS, AND THE GAME RULES ARE THE FIFTEENTH BYTECODE TABLE.**
  D-316 landed the nine Dan asked for first; this is the batch that could be built on what the
  game already has — the world, the inventory, the XP curve, the chat formats, the sound graph and
  the sky's clock. **/setblock /fill /clear /experience (+/xp) /defaultgamemode /say /me /msg
  (+/tell /w) /playsound /stopsound /spawnpoint /setworldspawn /gamerule.** Twenty-two of
  vanilla's seventy-four; the other fifty-two are named against the golden table on every run.

  `tools/extract-gamerules.mjs` reads all **35** rules with their type and default out of
  `GameRules.<clinit>`.

  ⚠ **THE TYPE IS THE DESCRIPTOR OF THE FACTORY, NOT THE CONSTANT.** `randomTickSpeed` defaults
  to 3 and `doFireTick` to 1; deciding "boolean or integer" by looking at the value calls one of
  them the other. `create(Z)` is a boolean rule and `create(I)` an integer one.

  ⚠ **AND THE FACTORY HAS TWO OVERLOADS.** `create(boolean)` and `create(boolean, BiConsumer)`
  both exist — `reducedDebugInfo` and `doImmediateRespawn` take the second, because changing them
  has to tell the client — so a regex demanding exactly `(Z)` read **33 of 35** and reported a
  complete-looking roster. The type is the FIRST parameter; what follows is a callback, not a
  different kind of rule.

  ⚠⚠ **`minecraft:block_state` DISTINGUISHES TWO VANILLA ERRORS AND THE FIRST DRAFT COLLAPSED
  THEM.** `argument.block.property.unknown` means "this BLOCK has no such property";
  `argument.block.property.invalid` means "that property does not take that value". `facing` is a
  real property name — dozens of blocks have it — so checking only the global `Reg.PROP` table
  reported `stone[facing=east]` as a bad VALUE when the truth is that stone has no facing at all.
  The block's own property slots are `Reg.propFirst[b]..propFirst[b+1]`, and asking those is the
  difference between a message that explains and one that misleads.

  ⚠ `States.withProp` RETURNS THE SAME STATE when the block does not accept a property or a value,
  so `/setblock ~ ~ ~ stone[facing=east]` would have placed plain stone and reported success. The
  parser now treats "the state did not change and it was not already that value" as a refusal, and
  `commandcheck`'s break asserts that a bracketed stair really is a different state from a bare
  one.

  ⚠ **LEVELS ARE NOT POINTS.** `Survival.xpNeeded` is not linear — level 16 costs 42 points and
  level 31 costs 112 — so `/xp set @s 30 levels` and `/xp set @s 30 points` differ by more than a
  hundredfold. The check asserts the level AND that the total is over a thousand, because the two
  paths are easy to wire to one another and impossible to tell apart from the message.

  ⚠ **`/spawnpoint` AND `/setworldspawn` ARE DIFFERENT FIELDS.** Vanilla keeps one world spawn and
  a personal spawn per player; a command that wrote the same field for both would make
  `/spawnpoint` move everybody, and nothing in a single-player world would ever show it.

  ⚠ **THREE CHAT FORMATS, THREE LANG KEYS.** `chat.type.announcement` is `[%s] %s`,
  `chat.type.emote` is `* %s %s`, and a whisper has one wording for the sender
  (`commands.message.display.outgoing`) and another for the receiver. The check asserts all three
  reach chat as DIFFERENT translatable components, which is the only way to catch a `/me` that
  quietly says what `/say` says.

  ⚠ **VANILLA CAPS A FILL AT 32,768 BLOCKS** and has its own message for it. Without the cap a
  mistyped coordinate locks the tab for a minute and reads as a crash.

  ⚠ Only **two** of the 35 rules do anything yet — the day/night and weather clocks —
  and `Commands.RULES_LIVE` names exactly which. A rule that is stored and ignored says so,
  rather than looking like it worked.

- **D-320** **THE FIRST-PERSON ARM WAS UPSIDE DOWN, AND A FREE ROTATION IN THE DRAWING LAYER IS
  WHAT LET IT LOOK PLAUSIBLE.** Dan, 14 Sept 2026, three times: *"the hand I can see is reversed:
  the sleeve is where the arm should be and vice versa."* He was right. The arm rendered with the
  shoulder at the top of the screen and the fist at the bottom, and the whole suite was green.

  ⚠⚠ **THE CAUSE IS A COORDINATE SPACE, NOT A MINUS SIGN.** `BI.ARM`'s UV table is
  `PlayerModel`'s own — `texOffs(40, 16).addBox(-3, -2, -2, 4, 12, 4)` — and Mojang writes that
  table in a space whose **+Y points DOWN**, because the humanoid model is built upside down and
  turned over at render time. The rasteriser read the same table in a **+Y-UP** space. Two
  consequences, and both were visible: the shoulder cap `(u+d, v)` went on the bottom of the box,
  and the four side faces ran their texture from hand to shoulder. This is D-314 again in a
  different file — one table, two readers, different conventions, and nothing asserting they
  agree.

  ⚠⚠ **WHY IT SURVIVED A SESSION OF TESTING.** `Hud.drawHand` drew the arm through a hand-picked
  `ctx.rotate(-0.55)`. **Given a free rotation in the drawing layer, almost any orientation can
  be talked into the corner of the screen.** The fudge did not cause the bug; it hid it. Every
  hand-tuned constant between a renderer and the screen is somewhere a real error can sit and
  look like a style choice.

  ⚠ **AND `iconcheck` HAD PINNED THE NUMBERS RATHER THAN THE PICTURE.** §1 asserted
  `HAND_ROT_X === 0 && HAND_ROT_Y === 45` against `block/block.json` and passed for months.
  Not one assertion had ever asked *which end of the arm was the hand*. A constant that matches
  the jar is not a rendering that matches the game (D-310's rule, restated).

  The fix is `ItemInHandRenderer.renderPlayerArm`, ported whole from 1.18.2 — obfuscated class
  `eqo`, method `a(dtm, eqs, int, float, float, axt)` — with the axis constants identified by
  their **values** in `k`'s static block (`k.c = (1,0,0) = XP`, `k.e = (0,1,0) = YP`,
  `k.g = (0,0,1) = ZP`) rather than by any name (D-263):

      translate(f2 + 0.64, f3 - 0.6 + e*-0.6, f4 - 0.72);   rotateY(45);
      rotateY(f6 * 70);   rotateZ(f5 * -20);                  // the swing
      translate(-1, 3.6, 3.5);
      rotateZ(120);   rotateX(200);   rotateY(-135);
      translate(5.6, 0, 0);                                   // then rightArm.setPos(-5, 2, 0)

  ⚠ **`rotateX(200)` IS THE TURN-OVER** — it stands in for the entity renderer's
  `scale(-1, -1, 1)`, which the hand path does not apply. Drop it and the arm hangs the wrong way
  up; round it to 180 and it is upside down by twenty degrees, which reads as bad art rather than
  as a bug. `iconcheck` asserts the arm box's model +Y — the shoulder-to-hand axis — points **up**
  in view space, and its break sets the rotation to zero and watches that flip to −0.50.

  ⚠⚠ **THE TRANSLATIONS ARE LOAD-BEARING AND ORTHOGRAPHIC RENDERING CANNOT FAKE THEM.** In three
  dimensions vanilla's right arm points up, away, and slightly to the **RIGHT**; on screen it
  leans up and to the **LEFT**, because it sits right of centre and recedes, so perspective walks
  its far end toward the vanishing point. The first repair of this bug got the arm the right way
  up and still leaned it the wrong way, because the rasteriser was orthographic and centred on
  the box. `BlockIcon.armSprite` now runs the full chain and vanilla's own projection (the FOV
  from settings, which is the *base* FOV — `getFov(camera, partial, false)` — not the effects-
  scaled one) and returns the sprite **and the place it goes**. `Hud.drawHand` blits it and is
  not allowed to rotate, scale or position it; the old `armCanvas(size, rotX, rotY)` is deleted
  rather than left beside it (D-139).

  ⚠ **PERSPECTIVE MEANS PERSPECTIVE-CORRECT TEXTURING.** The arm's near end is about half the
  distance of its far end, and UVs interpolated straight across the screen over a 2:1 depth range
  slide by several texels — enough to bend the cuff and put a seam through the knuckles. `u/w`,
  `v/w` and `1/w` interpolate linearly; `u` and `v` do not.

  ⚠ **SHADE FOLLOWS THE ROTATED NORMAL, NOT THE FACE'S NAME.** After a 200-degree turn-over the
  box's model-space "up" face points at the floor. A shade table indexed by the model-space name
  lights the underside of the arm like the sky.

  ⚠ **THE SLEEVE IS A SECOND BOX.** `PlayerRenderer.renderHand` draws `rightArm` *and*
  `rightSleeve` — `texOffs(40, 32)`, inflated by `CubeDeformation(0.25)`. Steve's overlay is
  empty, so the omission was invisible on the default skin and would have been obvious on
  every other one.

  ⚠ **AND THE CHECK THAT CATCHES IT IS ABOUT PIXELS.** `iconcheck` §6 renders through the real
  `armSprite` with a synthetic skin whose arm rect is a shoulder-to-hand colour ramp, and asserts
  the hand-ward quarter of the drawn pixels sits **above** the shoulder-ward quarter, that the arm
  runs off the bottom edge, that it is in the right-hand half, that it leans left, that the sleeve
  covers the bare arm, and that the near end is wider than the far end. §7 breaks each one.

  ⚠ The first draft of that check looked for the shoulder DECILE, found none — vanilla's shoulder
  is legitimately off the bottom of the screen — and passed on a `NaN` comparison. **A check whose
  subject can be absent must assert that it is present before it compares.**

  ⚠ `bemodelcheck` §2 used to regex `BI.ARM` out of the source text, which made it a reader of one
  file's spelling rather than a referee between two producers (D-313). It now compares the two
  LIVE unwraps — `BEModel.faceRects`, which draws the chest and the bed, and `BlockIcon.boxFaces`,
  which draws the arm — and its break swaps the arm's two caps and watches the agreement fail.

- **D-321** **AN ENTITY IS A BLOCK MODEL AT A PLACE THE WORLD HAS NO SECTION FOR.** G17a read the
  entity table and G17b built the motion; both were behind green checks, and **nothing in the game
  had ever drawn an entity.** `NEXT.md` said so in as many words — *"no entity is spawned during
  play, so there is no play-test item for G17b"* — which is PLAN §23's shape exactly: a stage
  whose output is a moving picture, tested only by numbers.

  ⚠⚠ **IT REUSES THE MODEL STREAM RATHER THAN ADDING A RENDERER.** A falling sand block *is* a
  block: the same baked quads, the same atlas layer, the same shade table, the same fog. The §8
  mesh format already carries a model stream and both backends already draw it, so an entity is a
  §8 buffer with no greedy quads in it and an origin that is not a section's. **No shader changed,
  no vertex format changed, and not one backend method was added.** A separate entity pass is how
  the seam between a falling sand block and the sand it fell out of appears.

  ⚠ **THE BUFFER IS REBUILT EVERY FRAME, AND THAT IS THE CHEAP OPTION.** Entities move every
  frame, so a kept mesh would be re-uploaded every frame anyway; the only real choice is whether
  the transform runs on the CPU or as a per-entity uniform. A uniform means one draw call per
  entity **and a second geometry path in both backends**. One buffer means one draw call for all
  of them and no backend change at all. `createSectionMesh` takes a slot from the arena that
  already exists, so the per-frame cost is one `bufferSubData` of a few kilobytes — less than one
  section of terrain costs when it is remeshed.

  ⚠ **THE ORIGIN IS THE CAMERA'S BLOCK, AND THAT IS A FORMAT CONSTRAINT, NOT A TASTE.** A model
  position is signed 16-bit in 1/256 of a block, so it reaches 128 blocks: an entity drawn past
  that **wraps to the other side of the camera** rather than disappearing, which looks like a
  teleport and reads like a physics bug. `ER.RANGE` is 64 — half the limit, so a model that
  reaches outside its own cell still cannot get there — and `g17ccheck` asserts the arithmetic
  rather than trusting the number. Anchoring at the camera also means the float `uOrigin` carries
  the sub-block part exactly, which is D-179's argument one level down.

  ⚠⚠ **`EntityRender.emit` IS A SECOND WRITER OF THE MODEL VERTEX STREAM, AND THAT IS WHAT
  ALMOST ALL OF `g17ccheck` IS ABOUT.** D-314 cost a session over precisely this: the mesher
  packed the face in one convention, the icon rasteriser read it in another, every model block in
  the world was lit as if lying on its side, and `emitcheck` stayed green because it asserted
  each writer copied its OWN source and never that the two agreed. So §1 asserts that for a
  whole-block offset the entity writer produces **byte for byte** what `Mesher.emitModelBlock`
  produces — **twenty states, at four cells each** — and §2 re-creates D-314 by un-mapping
  `MESH_OF_DIR` and watches 24 words diverge.

  ⚠ **A DEFAULT BELONGS TO THE ENTITY, NOT TO THE RENDERER.** `EntityRender` refuses to draw a
  falling block whose state it cannot resolve, and that refusal is only *correct* because there is
  no such thing as a stateless falling block: vanilla's `FallingBlockEntity` — obfuscated class
  `blh`, the only one in the jar carrying both the `TileEntityData` and `DropItem` NBT keys —
  opens its constructor with `this.blockState = cdr.C.defaultBlockState()`, `dropItem = true`,
  `fallDamageMax = 40`. `cdr` is `Blocks`, whose static fields are declared in vanilla registry
  order, so `C` is its 29th (`a`..`z`, then `A`, `B`, `C`) — index 28, which in 1.18.2 is `sand`.
  Putting that fallback in the RENDERER instead would have turned "nobody said what fell" into a
  plausible grey cube for ever. `PrimedTnt` is `blj`: `setFuse(80)` and a constructor kick of
  `(-sin(r·2π)·0.02, 0.2, -cos(r·2π)·0.02)`, which is why lit TNT hops.

  ⚠ **THIS ENGINE'S REGISTRY IS ALPHABETICAL, SO THE INDEX PROVES NOTHING HERE** — index 28 is
  `azalea`. The check says so out loud and pins the VALUE instead, ruling out air, stone and
  gravel: dressing a coincidence of ordering up as a proof is worse than admitting there is none.

  ⚠ **ROUNDED, NOT TRUNCATED.** `| 0` truncates toward zero, so the same sub-block offset
  quantises one way at x = +0.002 and the other at x = −0.002, and a falling block twitches by a
  256th as it crosses the origin. The check measures it the only way that tells the two apart:
  six tenths of a unit **below** a boundary must move the cube down a unit, which truncation
  would not do. The positive case alone proves nothing.

  ⚠ **WHAT IS NOT DRAWN IS NAMED.** `ER.SHAPE` holds the two types that are (falling_block, tnt)
  and `ER.OWED` the six that are not, and `g17ccheck` §3 fails three ways: a spawnable type on
  neither list, a drawn type still on the owed list, and an owed type that cannot be spawned at
  all. A renderer that silently draws nothing for a type it does not know is how G17b passed.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE LAST OF THE FIVE WAS THE SKY.** Every claim in that file is "the frame changed more
  than doing nothing changes it", and over the three minutes the check runs, the **day/night cycle
  moves ten thousand pixels between two frames 700 ms apart** — several times what a block four
  metres from the eye is worth. The noise floor climbed as the run went on, so §3 passed at the
  start and §4 and §5 failed at the end: the signature of a **drifting baseline**, not of a broken
  renderer. `Sky.daylightCycle` and `Sky.weatherCycle` are off for the run, and the controls fell
  from ten thousand pixels to nought. **A check that measures pixels must hold still everything it
  is not asking about**, and the world's clock is the easiest one to forget.

  ⚠ **AND `g17cbcheck` IS MANDATORY, NOT OPTIONAL.** It boots the shipped file, spawns a falling
  block three metres from the eye and asserts the PIXELS changed, that they kept changing as it
  fell, and that **tnt and sand are different pictures** — the last one because a renderer that
  ignored the state and drew one shape for everything would pass every other assertion. Every
  claim is made against a CONTROL pair of frames rather than a bare threshold (D-234).

- **D-322** **A LEAKED BROWSER DOES NOT FAIL THE CHECK THAT LEAKED IT.** `climcheck` went red with
  *"Climate.init took 175 ms"* against a 120 ms budget, on a build that had not touched Climate.
  The two-core container was at **load average ten**, and `ps` found **forty stray Chromium
  processes**, one of them holding 71% of a core. Every browser stage that threw, timed out, or
  called `process.exit` before reaching its `close()` had left a whole headless Chromium behind,
  each with a SwiftShader renderer still spinning.

  ⚠⚠ **THE FAILURE LANDS SOMEWHERE ELSE, AND LOOKS LIKE A REGRESSION THAT IS NOT THERE.** In the
  same run `structcheck` took **404 s against 191 s** in the clean one, `surfcheck` 115 s against
  27 s, and `featcheck` 129 s against 33 s — three stages slow and one red for a reason belonging
  to none of them. Killing the strays took the load from ten to 1.5 and `climcheck` back to
  **19 ms**. A resource leak in the test harness is not a tidiness problem; it is a source of
  false failures in unrelated files, and the harder it is to attribute the more expensive it is.

  `cdp.mjs` now reaps its child on `exit`, `SIGINT`, `SIGTERM` and `uncaughtException`, not only
  on a clean `close()`.

  ⚠ **AND THE BUDGET ITSELF WAS THE OTHER HALF OF THE BUG.** `< 120` is 120 ms *on a quiet machine
  of a particular speed*, and the check had no way to know it was not on one. It is now scaled by
  a speed the run measures itself: `treeUs`, the per-lookup cost of the R-tree timed over 200,000
  queries in the same process, against a `TREE_REF` of 2.0 µs. The budget keeps its meaning on a
  reference-speed host and stretches on a slow one. **A flat wall-clock threshold in a check is a
  measurement of the host, not of the program** — the same rule that D-321 found five times in one
  browser check and that fixed `worldcheck`'s furnace and `cullcheck`'s render-distance sweep.

- **D-323** **AN ITEM ENTITY IS THE SAME BLOCK MODEL THROUGH A DIFFERENT DISPLAY TRANSFORM.**
  D-321 drew falling blocks and TNT — the two entities that are a block model with no transform at
  all. An item on the ground is the third, and it needs only a matrix: `block/block.json`'s own
  `display.ground` (`rotation [0,0,0]`, `translation [0, 3, 0]`, `scale [0.25, 0.25, 0.25]`, read
  out of the jar rather than recalled), plus the bob and the spin from `ItemEntityRenderer.render`
  (obfuscated class `ewf`) and `ItemEntity.getSpin` (class `bli`, the only one carrying both the
  `PickupDelay` and `Thrower` NBT keys):

      bob  = sin((age + partial) / 10 + bobOffs) * 0.1 + 0.1
      spin = (age + partial) / 20 + bobOffs
      translate(0, bob + 0.25 * groundScale.y, 0);  rotateY(spin)
      [ground] translate(0, 3/16, 0);  scale(0.25);  translate(-0.5, -0.5, -0.5)

  ⚠⚠ **THE TWO DIVISORS ARE DIFFERENT AND IT IS NOT A TYPO.** The bob runs on a ten-tick period
  and the spin on a twenty-tick one, so an item turns once for every two bobs. Make them equal —
  which is exactly what a reading from memory would do — and the motion reads as one mechanical
  wobble instead of two independent ones. `bobOffs` is `random.nextFloat() * PI * 2`, per entity,
  and it is why two items dropped together do not move in lockstep.

  ⚠ **THE COLLAPSED FORM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE UNCOLLAPSED CHAIN.** Because a Y rotation fixes
  the Y axis, the five PoseStack operations reduce to
  `local = 0.25 * Ry(spin) * (p - 0.5) + (0, 3/16 + 0.0625 + bob, 0)`. **An algebraic
  simplification is precisely the kind of thing that is nearly right**, so `g17ccheck` §9 runs the
  chain as vanilla writes it, over sixty samples of position, age and bob offset, and asserts the
  two land on the same point to 1e-12. The saving is real — one matrix per entity instead of five
  transforms per vertex — and so is the risk.

  ⚠ **SHADE FOLLOWS THE ROTATED NORMAL, FOR THE THIRD TIME** (D-314, D-320). A spinning item whose
  faces keep their model-space shade has a bright side that turns with it, which reads as a
  flickering lamp rather than as a block catching the light.

  ⚠ **HALF OF `item` IS STILL OWED AND IS NAMED SEPARATELY.** An item entity holding a BLOCK is
  that block's model; one holding a SPRITE item — a stick, an ingot — is a flat billboard of the
  ITEM atlas, which the model shader does not sample at all. `ER.OWED_ITEM` carries that and the
  2-to-5-copy stack pile (`ItemEntityRenderer.getRenderAmount`, whose offsets need
  `java.util.Random` reproduced exactly). A dropped stick being invisible is a written-down
  deviation, not a silence — which is the whole point of the second list.

- **D-324** **A GAP EXPLAINED BY A MECHANISM NOBODY CHECKED STAYS A GAP FOR AS LONG AS THE
  EXPLANATION IS BELIEVED.** `extract-models` read **82 of the game's 155 model layers** and both
  the tool and `NEXT.md` said why: the rest were *"registered by LOOPS — `for (SkullBlock.Types t
  : values()) put(byType(t), …)` — so there is no `getstatic` anywhere to pair"*. The six blank
  heads in the creative inventory were owed to that sentence, and G17c's "next extractor job" was
  written against it.

  ⚠⚠ **THERE IS NO LOOP IN `createRoots` AT ALL.** 157 puts: **89 take their LayerDefinition from
  a direct call and 68 take it from a LOCAL VARIABLE**, because one definition serves many layers.
  The humanoid 64x64 body is one local and it covers player, zombie, husk, drowned, stray,
  skeleton, piglin and giant; the quadruped is another and covers cow, pig and mooshroom; one more
  is every skull. The walk needed **a two-slot memory** — what each `astore` stored, resolved at
  the `aload` — and that alone took 82 layers to **147**.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE SECOND HALF WAS NOT A SHAPE EITHER.** The report then said 50 layers were "built by
  a shape this walk cannot read". They were not: the walk accepted only methods whose **RETURN
  TYPE** is `LayerDefinition`, and half the game's models put their boxes in a `createMesh()` that
  returns a `MeshDefinition`, with the layer method doing nothing but
  `LayerDefinition.create(createMesh(), 64, 32)`. Reading mesh factories and following one hop of
  delegation — **keeping the caller's sheet size, because the boxes are in the callee and the
  64x32 is in the caller** — took it from 97 layers of boxes to **138, and from 310 boxes to 699**.

  ⚠ **THE ASSERTION THAT CAUGHT IT WAS WRITTEN TO FAIL.** `extract-models` asserted that the head
  layers were EMPTY — *"the `player_head` layer IS readable now — the loop note in this file is out
  of date"* — so the day somebody read them, the tool said so instead of silently shipping a table
  whose comment lied. **A documented limitation should carry an assertion that fires when the
  limitation ends.** It fired on the first run of the fixed walk.

  Five of the seven blank creative-inventory icons are now drawn: **58 of 60 `builtin/entity`
  items**, up from 53. Each head is one 8x8x8 cube at `texOffs(0, 0)` starting at (-4, -8, -4);
  the only difference between them is the sheet — a mob skull is 64x32 and a player or zombie head
  64x64, which is why vanilla has two factories. The player's head reuses the `steve` sheet the
  inventory preview and the first-person arm already ship, so five heads cost four textures.

  ⚠ **THE TWO THAT ARE LEFT ARE HONEST.** The DRAGON HEAD's layer is among the nine
  `extract-models` still cannot build, and the CONDUIT's renderer assembles its parts without
  registering a layer at all, so there is nothing in `ModelLayers` to find. The 699-box table is
  also most of what G18 will need, which was never the point of this and is the best part of it.

- **D-325** **`/clone`, `/locatebiome` AND `/list` — AND A RULING ABOUT WHAT A COMMAND MAY COST
  ON THE THREAD THAT DRAWS.** Three more of vanilla's 74, chosen because this engine already has
  what they need: `/clone` is `/fill`'s machinery, `/locatebiome` is `Climate.biomeNameAt`, and
  `/list` is one line whose absence is louder than its presence. **25 of 74.**

  ⚠⚠ **A CLONE READS EVERY SOURCE BLOCK BEFORE IT WRITES ANY, AND THAT IS NOT AN OPTIMISATION.**
  With `force` the boxes are allowed to overlap, and a loop that writes as it reads copies its own
  output — shift a column up by one and the bottom block is smeared the whole way. `move` clears
  the source **after** the copy and only where the destination did not land on it. `commandcheck`
  has a smear test: a column with a hole in it, moved up one with `force`, and the hole has to
  move with it.

  ⚠ **`findBiomeHorizontal` IS A RING WALK IN QUART COORDINATES, NOT A FILLED SQUARE.** Biomes are
  constant inside each 4x4x4 cell, so vanilla searches the quart grid, and it samples only the
  BOUNDARY of each ring because everything inside was covered by a smaller one. A filled search of
  the same radius asks roughly the square of the questions for the same answer.

  ⚠ **`readUnquoted` STOPS AT `:` — FOR THE SECOND TIME** (D-316 was the first). `M.oneOf` read
  `minecraft:plains` as `minecraft` and rejected every namespaced value. An id is not a word, and
  the parser has two readers for that reason.

  ⚠⚠ **THE RULING (the deviation, with the measurement that chose it).** Vanilla's radius (6,400)
  and step (8) are kept exactly; running them to exhaustion is not. `Climate.biomeAt` costs
  **58 microseconds** — six noise samples and an R-tree query — and a miss walks all **160,801**
  cells, so asking for a biome that is not nearby would lock the tab for **nine and a third
  seconds**. Vanilla pays that on a server thread; this game would pay it on the one that draws
  the frame. **The search gives up after half a second and reports
  `commands.locatebiome.notFound`** — whose own wording, *"within reasonable distance"*, is
  already the honest answer.

  ⚠ **IT IS A REAL DEVIATION AND IT IS NOT SILENT**: on a slow machine a findable biome can come
  back as "not found". The alternative — quietly shrinking the radius — fails the same way and
  lies about why. `C.LOCATE_MS = 0` disables the budget; `commandcheck` turns it off to test the
  search and then sets it to 20 ms with a deliberately slow lookup to prove the budget bites.

  ⚠ **AND THE CLOCK IS READ ONCE EVERY 256 SAMPLES.** `Date.now()` costs more than a fifth of what
  a biome lookup does, and a budget that spends a quarter of itself on measuring is not a budget.

- **D-326** **`/tellraw` AND `/title` — A JSON COMPONENT PARSER AND A REAL TITLE OVERLAY.**
  **27 of vanilla's 74 commands.** Both needed something the engine did not have, and both of
  those are worth having on their own: `Text.fromJson` is how any command or sign or book will
  ever carry formatted text, and the title overlay is a piece of HUD parity a player sees every
  time anything important happens.

  ⚠⚠ **AN ARRAY IS NOT A LIST OF SIBLINGS: ITS FIRST ELEMENT IS THE PARENT.** Vanilla folds
  `["a", "b", "c"]` into `"a"` with `b` and `c` as its `extra`, which means the FIRST element's
  style is inherited by all the rest. Building a bare container instead gives a line whose first
  word is coloured and whose remainder mysteriously is not — and it looks close enough to right
  that nobody files it. `commandcheck` asserts the inheritance, not just the concatenation.

  ⚠ **VANILLA PUTS STYLE KEYS AT THE TOP LEVEL OF A NODE** — `{"text":"hi","color":"red"}` —
  while this engine keeps them under `.style`, so `fromJson` lifts them. `false` is kept and is
  not the same as absent: a child that says `bold: false` inside a bold parent is not bold, and a
  child that says nothing is.

  ⚠ **THE COMPONENT KINDS THIS ENGINE CANNOT DO ARE REFUSED BY NAME, NOT RENDERED AS NOTHING.**
  `score` and `nbt` need stores that do not exist, `selector` needs entity names, `keybind` needs
  a queryable key map, and the two events need a clickable chat line. `Text.JSON_OWED` names all
  six and `/tellraw` raises `argument.component.invalid` with the reason in it, because a
  `/tellraw` that silently prints nothing is indistinguishable from a broken command.

  ⚠⚠ **A SUBTITLE ALONE SHOWS NOTHING, AND THAT IS VANILLA.** `Gui.render` opens with
  `if (this.title != null && this.titleTime > 0)` and draws the subtitle INSIDE that, so
  `/title @s subtitle` with no title is invisible. It is the commonest confusion about the
  command and reproducing it is the point.

  ⚠⚠ **THE FADE RAMP'S TWO TESTS MUST NOT BE `else if`.** `time` counts DOWN, fading in while
  `time > fadeOut + stay` and out while `time <= fadeOut` — and with `stay` at **zero both are
  true at once**, where only the fade-out answer is right. Written as an if/else-if, a title snaps
  off instead of fading the moment somebody sets `stay 0`. `H.titleAlpha` is a pure function for
  exactly this reason: the ramp is the part that can be wrong in a way nobody sees until they are
  looking for it, and `commandcheck` walks it tick by tick including the `stay 0` case.

  ⚠ **THE CLOCK TICKS AT 20 Hz, NOT ON THE FRAME.** A fade driven by the frame rate runs at a
  different speed on every machine, which is why vanilla counts these in ticks. `H.tickTitles`
  rides with `Chat.tickChat`.

  ⚠ **THE TWO LANG KEYS ARE PASSED WHOLE, NOT BUILT BY CONCATENATION.** `commandcheck` §6 scans
  these files for the translation keys they use and asserts every one is in the shipped table; a
  key assembled at runtime is invisible to that scan — and `commands.title.times`, the base it
  would have seen, is not a real key at all. **A string the check cannot see is a string nobody
  notices is missing until it renders as its own key on screen.**

  ⚠ `/difficulty` was in this batch and Dan pulled it: *"dont worry about /difficulty until all
  its wirings are implemented fully."* Storing a difficulty that changed nothing would have been
  the command as theatre, which is the right call.

- **D-327** **`/execute`, AND THE THREE THINGS IT BROKE ON THE WAY IN.** **28 of vanilla's 74
  commands**, and this is the one every other one is worth more because of. Almost all of it is
  the parser: each clause is a node that REDIRECTS back to `execute` carrying a modifier from
  "the context parsed here" to "the source the rest of the line runs against", and the chain is
  walked at EXECUTE time. Supported: `as`, `at`, `positioned` (and `positioned as`), `rotated`
  (and `rotated as`), `align`, `anchored`, `if`/`unless` with `block`, `blocks` and `entity`, and
  `run`. `C.EXECUTE_OWED` names the six that are not: `store`, `facing`, `in`, and the
  `if score|predicate|data` forms, each waiting on a system that does not exist.

  ⚠⚠ **THE MODIFIER RUNS AT EXECUTE TIME, NOT PARSE TIME.** Applying it while parsing would fix
  the source before the selector had anything to select, and `as @e` would mean "the first one"
  for ever.

  ⚠⚠ **THE FIRST BUG: A CHAIN, NOT A MERGE.** The redirect used to fold the parent's arguments
  into the child's single namespace. That is fine until one line uses the same argument NAME
  twice — and `/execute positioned 1 2 3 positioned 4 5 6 run …` is legal, common, and had its
  two `pos` arguments collapse into one. Vanilla keeps a `CommandContext` per redirect level;
  so does this now.

  ⚠⚠ **THE SECOND BUG, AND IT IS THE INSTRUCTIVE ONE: `parseNodes` RETURNS THE DEEPEST CONTEXT,
  NOT THE ONE IT JUST MADE.** Writing `sub.context.parent = ctx` as the recursion unwound set the
  *same field* at every level, and the last write won — so a four-level
  `/execute positioned … positioned … run …` collapsed to **two levels** and silently dropped
  every clause but the first. It parsed, it ran, it reported success, and it ignored most of what
  you typed. The fix is to walk to the top of what came back and link there. **A field that every
  level of a recursion writes is a field only the last level owns.**

  ⚠⚠ **THE THIRD BUG: VANILLA'S ROTATION ARGUMENT IS DEGREES AND THIS ENGINE STORES RADIANS.**
  `Player.yaw` goes straight into `Math.cos`. `rotated 90 0` must be a quarter turn; ninety
  RADIANS is fourteen and a bit turns and lands the block somewhere that merely looks random —
  and a check asserting only "somewhere different" would have accepted it. `commandcheck` asserts
  the landing cell is on an AXIS, which ninety radians is not. The two conventions agree
  otherwise: yaw 0 is +Z and pitch −90 is up, in both.

  ⚠ **`@s` IS THE SOURCE'S ENTITY, NOT THE PLAYER**, and `^` uses the SOURCE's rotation and
  anchor. Before `/execute` the two were always the same; afterwards, reading the player directly
  makes `execute as … run … @s` and `execute rotated … run … ^ ^ ^1` silent no-ops that look like
  the clause was ignored. Every one of those was a one-line change and none of them would have
  been noticed by a check that only asked whether the command parsed.

  ⚠ **A FORK RETURNS THE COUNT OF SOURCES; ONE SOURCE RETURNS THE COMMAND'S OWN RESULT.** So
  `/execute as @e run …` with three entities returns 3, and `/execute run seed` still reports the
  seed rather than 1. And a selector that matches nothing runs nothing and **is not an error**.

  ⚠⚠ **AND IMPLEMENTING IT EXPOSED A WRONG ROW IN THE REFEREE.** `extract-commands` decided an
  alias was "a literal other than the first, followed by a redirect" — true of `/teleport`'s `tp`
  and **also true of every clause of `/execute`, which redirects to its own node**. The golden
  table therefore listed `run`, `positioned`, `rotated`, `entity`, `align`, `anchored`, `in`,
  `score`, `value` and `max` as ALIASES of `/execute`, and nothing noticed for two sessions
  because nothing had implemented `/execute`. The rule is now vanilla's actual shape: an alias
  registration is **tiny** — a second `dispatcher.register` whose builder holds one literal and a
  redirect. That removed ten false aliases **and found a real one nobody had**: `teammsg → tm`.
  **A referee table is only checked where something reads it.**

- **D-328** **A CACHE KEYED ON THE THING THAT IS CHANGING IS NOT A CACHE.** Dan, session 11:
  *"the hand punching animation when looking at a block is low fps"*. `BlockIcon.armSprite` is a
  software rasterisation of a twelve-quad model with a z-buffer and perspective-correct texturing,
  and it was measured at **2.71 ms at 854x480, 3.35 at 720p, 7.69 at 1080p, 13.19 at 1440p and
  28.30 at 4K** — one arm, per frame, on a fast machine. The cache held ONE sprite keyed on the
  quantised swing, so it hit whenever the arm was still and **missed every single frame of every
  swing**, which is the only time the arm moves.

  ⚠⚠ **THE REQUIREMENT WAS WRITTEN DOWN FOUR LINES ABOVE THE CODE THAT BROKE IT.** The comment
  over the two caches says, correctly, *"Re-rasterising a 3D model every frame at 60 Hz would cost
  more than the rest of the HUD put together."* That is exactly what it did. A comment stating an
  invariant is not an assertion, and nothing in `iconcheck` had ever counted a rasterisation.

  ⚠ **THE FIX IS THAT A FIXED-LENGTH ANIMATION HAS A FIXED NUMBER OF PICTURES.** Vanilla's swing
  is six ticks — 0.3 s — so a 60 Hz display shows 18 distinct frames of it and a 144 Hz one 43.
  `Hud` now keeps a SET of up to 32, keyed on viewport, device ratio and FOV, and the steady-state
  cost of a swing is zero. ⚠ The frame count is bounded by MEMORY and the deviation is named: a 4K
  arm sprite is 1221x331 and 32 of them is 52 MB, so `ARM_CACHE_BYTES` caps the set at 24 MB and
  the count falls out of it — 32 at and below 1440p, 14 at 4K. `armCacheStats().n` reports it.

  ⚠ **AND THE WARM-UP RUNS WHILE THE HAND IS STILL, WHICH IS THE ONLY MOMENT THE WORK IS FREE.**
  Without it the first swing after a resize still pays one rasterisation a frame. One picture per
  idle frame fills the set in about half a second of standing still.

  ⚠ **THE SAME CLASS OF BUG, IN THE SAME FILE, FOR THE ICONS.** Dan: *"most hotbar/inventory icons
  are incredibly pixelated, some like campfires arent for some reason"*. The reason is that a
  campfire has no block model, so its icon falls through to `Hud.beCanvas`, which renders **at the
  size it is asked for**; everything with a model came off a sheet of 16x16 tiles blown up by the
  GUI scale AND by the device ratio — up to twelve times on a 4K display at scale 4. **One of the
  two producers of the same picture was resolution-aware and the other was not**, which is D-314's
  rule in a third costume. `Hud.iconCanvas` renders a block's own model at the device size it will
  occupy, cached per (block, size); `beCanvas` gained the device ratio it was missing; and the
  held-item raster was capped at 160 px while being drawn at up to 450, which is now 512.
  ⚠ A 16x16 SPRITE item magnified with nearest-neighbour is NOT this bug: vanilla's item sprites
  are 16x16 textures and they are meant to be chunky.

- **D-329** **THE HOTBAR'S DRAW ORDER AND ITS SELECTOR RECT — AND A CHECK THAT ASSERTED THE BUG.**
  Dan, session 11: *"blocks in selected slot of hotbar do not look cortrect at all"*. Two faults,
  neither reachable by reading this engine's own code.

  ⚠⚠ **THE SELECTION FRAME WAS DRAWN AFTER THE NINE SLOTS.** It is one pixel proud of the slot on
  every side and its texture is not transparent inside that margin, so it was composited over the
  selected slot's icon and over nothing else — which is precisely the shape of Dan's report.
  Vanilla's `Gui.renderHotbar` blits the bar, then the frame, then loops the slots: in the
  bytecode the selector blit is at offset 136 and the nine-slot loop at 231. **A draw order is
  part of what a picture IS, and nothing here had ever asserted one.**

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE FRAME IS 24 WIDE BY 22 TALL, NOT 24 BY 24.** `widgets.png`'s selection sprite is 24
  rows and the game draws 22 of them, clipping its own bottom border so the frame ends flush with
  the bar. Drawing 24 puts it two pixels below the bar's bottom edge.

  ⚠⚠ **`guicheck` PINNED `sel[3] === 24` AND HAD BEEN GREEN FOR THREE SESSIONS.** That is D-305's
  rule — never let a check own a number the code owns — and the consequence is worse than a missing
  check: **the correct value FAILED the suite**. A wrong check converts a bug into a requirement.

  ⚠⚠ **A SUB-AGENT WAS ASKED WHAT VANILLA DOES HERE AND ANSWERED 24x24 FROM MEMORY**, in a report
  that read as a source reading throughout. `docs/AGENTS.md` rule 2's bright line — never delegate
  the last word on what vanilla does — is why that answer was checked rather than believed.

  ⚠ **THE FIX IS A REFEREE, NOT A CORRECTED LITERAL.** `tools/extract-guigeom.mjs` is the
  SIXTEENTH bytecode table: every blit in `Gui.renderHotbar` with its source rect AND its bytecode
  offset, plus the nine-slot loop's offset and the five constants its body pushes. `guicheck` §3
  reads it, so the rectangles and the ORDER are both assertions about the jar.
  ⚠ Identification cost three attempts and each failure is a rule: "the class that pushes 182" is
  ambiguous because the spectator menu is also 182 wide — **a constant is not a use**; "the method
  that blits (0,0,182,22)" is ambiguous because the spectator bar draws the same bar — **a rect
  shared by two drawings is not an identifier**; what separates them is the OFFHAND, which only
  the real hotbar has. ⚠ And the spectator bar is kept as a SECOND WITNESS rather than discarded:
  it blits the same selection sprite from its own call site and must agree. **Two independent
  drawings in the same jar saying 24x22 is a fact, where one is a reading.**
  ⚠ The offhand frames themselves are in the table and are NOT drawn by this engine; `guicheck`
  carries an assertion that fires when they are added, so the gap cannot go quiet.

- **D-330** **A GATE WHOSE TWO HALVES LIVE IN TWO FILES IS A GATE NOTHING IS TESTING.** Dan,
  session 11: *"sliders dont work as sliders"*. Every part of the drag was written and correct —
  `Options.dragging`, `O.drag`, `O.release`, the `uidrag`/`uirelease` events and their routing in
  `17_main.js` — and **`uidrag` had never fired once in the life of the program**.

  ⚠⚠ `13_input.js`'s `mousedown` fired `uiclick` and RETURNED three lines before
  `I.mouse[e.button] = true`, and `mousemove`'s drag gate is `if (I.uiOpen && I.mouse[0])`. The one
  flag that could open the gate was set on the one path that could never run while a screen was
  open. A slider set its value on the press and then ignored the pointer: a stepper wearing a
  slider's art.

  ⚠ **`optionscheck` DROVE `O.drag` DIRECTLY, SO IT WAS GREEN.** THE RULE: **a check that calls the
  function under test has not tested the thing that is supposed to call it.** §4b now asserts the
  handler's own shape — that the `uiOpen` branch records the button before returning — and the
  anti-vacuity section feeds it the handler that shipped and requires a rejection.

  ⚠ **THE ASSIGNMENT IS INSIDE THE UI BRANCH, NOT HOISTED ABOVE ALL THREE.** Hoisting it also
  records the click that merely RECAPTURES the pointer, which would start mining the block under
  the crosshair whenever the window is clicked back into focus. `optionscheck` asserts that too.

  ⚠ **AND THE VALUE MATH WAS WRONG IN A WAY THE DRAG WOULD HAVE EXPOSED.** Vanilla's
  `AbstractSliderButton.setValueFromMouse` is `(mouseX - (x + 4)) / (width - 8)` — subtract half
  the 8-wide knob, divide by the TRAVEL — and this divided by the full width with no offset. Since
  `drawSlider` already lays the knob out across `width - 8`, **the drawn position and the value
  disagreed**: two expressions for one geometry, only one of them right. The knob position also
  rounded where vanilla's `d2i` truncates. Both are read off the bytecode and both are asserted
  against the formula recomputed over the whole track.

  ⚠ **KEYBOARD OPERATION IS NAMED AS OWED RATHER THAN HALF-BUILT.** Vanilla's arrows step a
  FOCUSED slider, and focus is a screen-wide concept — Tab traversal, the focused widget drawn in
  its hover sprite, Enter to activate. Wiring arrows to a slider without that is arrow keys that
  act on whichever slider a hidden variable happens to point at. `O.OWED_INPUT` names all four
  parts and `optionscheck` holds the list closed and fails if arrow handling appears beside it.

- **D-331** **A RENDERING FACT WAS STANDING IN FOR A GAMEPLAY FACT, AND 224 ITEMS COULD NOT BE
  PLACED.** Dan, session 11: *"some items like zombie eggs and candles dont work and place"*. It is
  not two items.

  ⚠⚠ The engine decided "is this placeable, and as what" from one precomputed number,
  `Items.state[i]`, and `pack-items.mjs` wrote it only when `kind === 'block'` — where `kind` is
  set in `extract-items.mjs` by whether the item's INVENTORY MODEL inherits from a `block/...`
  parent. Vanilla's set of BlockItems and vanilla's set of items DRAWN as 3D blocks are different
  sets, and every BlockItem whose icon is a flat sprite or a `builtin/entity` model falls into the
  gap: every candle, torch, door, sign, rail, lever, repeater, sapling, flower, ladder, lantern,
  chain, glass pane, iron bar, cake, hopper, sea pickle and turtle egg, plus every bed, banner,
  chest, shulker box and skull. All of them got the sentinel `0xFFFF`, `syncHotbar` left the hotbar
  slot at 0, and `placeBlock` refused on its second line **with no swing, no sound and no message**.

  ⚠⚠ **THE CANDLE RULE WAS ALREADY IMPLEMENTED, TWICE, CORRECTLY, AND WAS UNREACHABLE.**
  `States.canBeReplacedBy` and `Player.stackOnto` both carry vanilla's `candles < 4` increment and
  `placecheck` §3 and §4 assert it — by driving them with raw block STATES. **A check that enters
  the system below the broken layer cannot see the broken layer.**

  ⚠⚠ **AND `itemcheck` ASKED THE SAME QUESTION THE PACKER USED TO DECIDE.** Its §7 loop guarded on
  `src.kind === 'block'` and then asserted every such item had a state, so it could only ever
  confirm the packer's opinion of itself. **A check that asks the same question the code asked
  cannot see a wrong question.** It now reads the golden table and asserts the count in both
  directions; the anti-vacuity section reproduces the shipped rule and requires the two sets to
  DISAGREE, which they do by 223 items.

  ⚠ **AND THE BUILD REPORTED SUCCESS.** `pack-items` printed *"block items ........ 558 (default
  state resolved)"* and warned only when its `noState` list was non-empty — which it never was,
  because an item never classified as a block is never asked for a state. **A report of what worked
  is not a report of what was attempted.** It now prints the attempted count and FAILS the build if
  any BlockItem in the golden table did not resolve.

  ⚠ **THE FIX IS THE SEVENTEENTH BYTECODE TABLE.** `tools/extract-blockitems.mjs` walks
  `Items.<clinit>` field by field: **1101 items, 782 BlockItems, 67 spawn eggs**, closed in both
  directions against the registry. The two registration shapes — `registerBlock(Block, ...)`, where
  the item takes the BLOCK's name, and `registerItem("name", new SomeBlockItem(Blocks.X, ...))`,
  where it does not — differ exactly by whether the segment carries a string of its own, which is
  what makes the **twelve name-mismatched items** fall out rather than having to be typed:
  `redstone -> redstone_wire`, `string -> tripwire`, `wheat_seeds -> wheat`,
  `powder_snow_bucket -> powder_snow`, `cocoa_beans -> cocoa`, `pumpkin_seeds -> pumpkin_stem`,
  `melon_seeds -> melon_stem`, `carrot -> carrots`, `potato -> potatoes`,
  `beetroot_seeds -> beetroots`, `sweet_berries -> sweet_berry_bush`, `glow_berries -> cave_vines`.
  **No rule over names or models could have found any of them.**

- **D-332** **A DOOR IS TWO BLOCKS AND SO IS A BED.** D-331 made 223 more items placeable and 33 of
  them do not fit in one cell: **17 carry `half=upper/lower`** (eight doors and nine tall plants)
  and **16 carry `part=head/foot`**. Placing only the half the player clicked gives a door with no
  top and a bed with no pillow, and Dan's rule the same night was *"do not half do a feature"*.

  ⚠ **THE SET IS DERIVED FROM THE STATE DATA, NOT FROM A LIST OF NAMES**: a block is two-cell if
  its default state carries `half=lower` or `part=foot`, which is what vanilla's `DoubleBlockHalf`
  and `BedPart` mean. ⚠ The second cell is checked BEFORE anything is written — vanilla's
  `DoorBlock.getStateForPlacement` returns null when the cell above cannot be replaced, and
  checking afterwards would leave half a door standing in a world already told about it.

  ⚠⚠ **THE HINGE IS A VOTE, NOT A SIDE.** `DoorBlock.getHinge` counts full collision blocks on
  both sides of the door at both heights — counter-clockwise as −1, clockwise as +1 — and only a
  level vote falls through to which quarter of the block face was clicked. A lower door half on the
  CLOCKWISE side hinges this one LEFT, which is how a double door is made. ⚠ **My first assertion
  about it was backwards and the implementation was not**: the bytecode returns `cpq.b` on
  `(bl && !bl2) || i > 0` and `cpq.a` otherwise, and that enum declares "left" then "right". The
  assertion had been written from the same memory that told a sub-agent the selector was 24x24 an
  hour earlier (D-329). `placecheck` §5c now walks all four facings against all four click
  quadrants and both neighbour cases.

  ⚠ **AND THE VOTE NEEDS A TABLE NEITHER `solid` NOR `opaqueBase` COULD PROVIDE.** Vanilla counts
  `isCollisionShapeFullBlock`: a glass block is one and a fence is not. `solid` is "has any
  collision at all", which is true of a fence post and a slab; `opaqueBase` is a RENDERING fact,
  which is false of glass. `States.fullCollision` reads the collision boxes that are already in the
  registry — one box, exactly 0..1024 on all three axes — so nothing new is stored and nothing is
  approximated. `placecheck` asserts that all three tables answer differently for the cases that
  separate them.

- **D-333** **A BROKEN BLOCK DID NOT DROP ANYTHING — IT TELEPORTED INTO YOUR POCKET.** Dan, session
  11: *"items dont drop as block entities"*. `breakBlock` computed the real 1.18.2 loot and handed
  it straight to `Inventory.add`, so the whole middle of Minecraft's loop — the thing falls, it
  bobs, you walk over it — did not exist.

  ⚠⚠ **IT IS ALSO G17c's OWN NAMED GAP CLOSING.** `NEXT.md` had said it plainly: *"nothing spawns
  into the entity list during play"*. The renderer built in session 10 drew an empty list in every
  real game, and no amount of green assertions could have said so.

  ⚠ **EVERY CONSTANT IS OUT OF `ItemEntity`'s BYTECODE**, not remembered: the four-argument
  constructor is `(random()*0.2 − 0.1, 0.2, random()*0.2 − 0.1)`, the pickup delay is 10, the
  despawn is the `sipush 6000` that discards it, and `mergeWithNeighbours` inflates by 0.5
  horizontally and runs on every other tick. `Block.popResource` jitters ±0.25 inside the broken
  cell on all three axes and subtracts half the item's height, which is why a dropped block rests
  ON the floor rather than in it.

  ⚠ **MERGING IS NOT A NICETY.** Without it a sixty-four-block dig is sixty-four entities, each
  with its own quads, its own collision sweep and its own bob — which is both wrong and the
  cheapest way to make the frame time depend on how fast the player is mining.

  ⚠ **THE PICKUP BOX IS INFLATED BY DIFFERENT AMOUNTS ON DIFFERENT AXES** — `Player.aiStep`
  collects `getBoundingBox().inflate(1.0, 0.5, 1.0)` — and it takes only what FITS: when
  `Inventory.add` cannot take the whole stack the entity keeps the remainder and stays on the floor.

  ⚠ **D-139 APPLIES AND THE OLD PATH IS DELETED.** There is no fallback that quietly fills the
  inventory when the entity list is missing; drops are counted on `Player.lostDrops` instead,
  loudly, because a fallback would hide exactly the failure this replaces.

  ⚠ **Q THROWS THE HELD ITEM AND CTRL+Q THE STACK**, at `Player.drop`'s own velocity — the look
  direction at 0.3 plus 0.1 of lift and a small random spin — with a pickup delay of 40 rather than
  10, because an item that merely fell at your feet would be picked straight back up.

- **D-334** **THE HAND SWINGS ON THE CLICK, NOT ON THE BREAK.** Dan, session 11: *"there is no
  combat and no mid air punching without looking at anything"*. `Hand.swing` was complete and
  vanilla-correct — six ticks, the halfway-restart rule, all of it behind `handcheck` — and its
  only two callers were `breakBlock` and `placeBlock`, **both of which fire when a world EDIT
  SUCCEEDS**. A click at the sky did nothing, and in survival a click on stone did nothing until
  the stone finally gave way.

  ⚠ **THE MODEL WAS FINISHED AND THE INPUT EDGE THAT DRIVES IT WAS NEVER WRITTEN**, which is
  D-330's shape exactly, in a different subsystem, found the same night. ⚠ `handcheck` calls
  `H.swing()` itself, so it would pass unchanged with the swing wired to nothing — D-330's rule
  again: **a check that calls the function under test has not tested the thing that calls it.**

  ⚠ `missTime` IS VANILLA'S OWN RATE LIMIT: `Minecraft.startAttack` returns immediately while it is
  positive and sets it to 10 on a miss, and `hasMissTime()` is false in creative. Without it,
  holding the button at the sky restarts the swing every frame and the arm never finishes a stroke.

  ⚠ **AND IT KEEPS SWINGING WHILE A BLOCK IS BEING MINED, ONCE PER TICK.** A frame is not a tick,
  so the attack is stepped on its own 20 Hz accumulator; swinging per FRAME would restart the
  stroke three times as often at 180 fps as at 60 and look like a different game.

- **D-335** **D-271 IS PAID: EVERY ITEM IN THE GAME HAD BEEN SWINGING AT 4.0.** `Hand.attackSpeed
  Table` was declared null in G10 with an honest note, and it stayed null for fourteen sessions, so
  a diamond sword and a feather were the same weapon and `handcheck` printed "NOT BOUND" on every
  run while SKIPPING its own diamond-sword assertion.

  ⚠ **THE NUMBERS ARE IN NO JSON FILE.** `Attributes.ATTACK_DAMAGE` and `ATTACK_SPEED` are applied
  by `SwordItem` and `DiggerItem` as attribute MODIFIERS built in their constructors from arguments
  passed at each item's registration. `tools/extract-itemattrs.mjs` is the EIGHTEENTH bytecode
  table: five tool classes found BY DESCRIPTOR `(Tier, int|float, float, Item$Properties)`, each
  constructed exactly six times, and the `Tiers` enum found BY USE — the enum whose constants are
  handed to those thirty constructors — because an enum declares its own constants as ITSELF, not
  as the interface it implements, so looking for fields of the `Tier` type finds nothing at all.

  ⚠⚠ **A ROUNDING ASSUMPTION WAS WRONG AND AN ANCHOR CAUGHT IT.** The first version rounded to a
  sixteenth on the reasoning that vanilla's modifiers are all multiples of 1/16. A sword's is −2.4,
  so its speed is 1.6, and 1.6 × 16 is 25.6 — the assertion that a diamond sword swings at exactly
  1.6 failed on 1.625. **That is what an anchor on a case that cannot be in doubt is for**, and it
  is the second assumption of mine this table has corrected.

  ⚠ **THE SWORD IS TOLD FROM THE OTHER FOUR TOOL CLASSES BY ITS SUPERCLASS** — four extend
  `DiggerItem` and `SwordItem` does not — because only a sword sweeps, which is a real branch in
  the damage formula rather than a label.

  ⚠ **THE TABLE HOLDS FINAL VALUES AND THE MODIFIER FIELD IS DELETED (D-139)**, so there is no
  second place for a second answer to live; and it is an EXCEPTION table — most of the 1,100 items
  carry no modifier at all, and asserting its SIZE is what stops a missing payload from reading as
  "no item has a modifier".

- **D-336** **"HAS A MAX HEALTH" IS VANILLA'S OWN DEFINITION OF A LIVING ENTITY, AND NO ENTITY HERE
  HAD ONE.** `EntityList.spawn` built a position, a velocity and a hitbox and nothing that could be
  reduced. `tools/extract-entityattrs.mjs` is the NINETEENTH bytecode table: max health, movement
  speed, attack damage, follow range and knockback resistance for every type, resolved through the
  SUPERCLASS CHAIN — which is how a cow gets its speed from `Animal` and a zombie its follow range
  from `Monster`. **74 of the 113 types resolve a max health and 39 do not**, and that split is a
  fact about the jar rather than a list somebody keeps up to date.

  ⚠⚠ **IT MIS-READ EVERY PASSIVE MOB UNTIL THE RETURN TYPE WAS CHECKED.**
  `AttributeSupplier.Builder.add(Attribute)` and `LivingEntity.getAttributeValue(Attribute)` take
  the same single Attribute parameter and in the obfuscated jar share a letter; they differ only in
  what they RETURN. Matching the parameter alone read `getAttributeValue(ATTACK_DAMAGE)` inside
  `LivingEntity` as a bare add, and **every cow, sheep and bat came out carrying an attack damage
  of 2** — a wrong number that looked entirely reasonable on every row. That is D-306's rule for
  the third time: **a method is its name AND its descriptor, and the descriptor includes what comes
  back.**

  ⚠⚠ **A MOB THAT ADDS AN ATTRIBUTE WITH NO VALUE TAKES THE ATTRIBUTE'S OWN DEFAULT**, and that is
  where a zombie's twenty hearts actually live: nothing in `Zombie` says 20.
  `LivingEntity.createLivingAttributes()` adds `MAX_HEALTH` bare and
  `new RangedAttribute("attribute.name.generic.max_health", 20.0, 1.0, 1024.0)` supplies it.
  Reading only the VALUED adds found 57 of 112 types and silently dropped every monster in the
  game.

  ⚠ **`Entities.isLiving` IS NOT `e.living` ON A SPAWNED ENTITY.** That flag is the PHYSICS one —
  it says whether `Physics.move` runs `LivingEntity.checkFallDamage`'s landing path — and the two
  questions only look the same. Keeping them apart is why D-308 was findable at all, and
  `combatcheck` asserts that a spawned turtle has health and `living === false`.

- **D-338** **MELEE COMBAT — THE SUBSTRATE, COMPLETE AND ASSERTED; THE PICTURE IS G18's.** Dan,
  session 11: *"there is no combat and no mid air punching without looking at anything (its fine if
  this is allocated for later, if not, do it fully now)"*. It was allocated nowhere, so it was
  built. `src/14j_combat.js` carries entity picking, `LivingEntity.hurt`, `LivingEntity.knockback`
  and `Player.attack`; `combatcheck` is 81 assertions and 8 breaks.

  ⚠⚠ **A SECOND HIT INSIDE THE GRACE PERIOD IS DOCKED, NOT IGNORED.** While `invulnerableTime > 10`
  a new hit does nothing UNLESS it is bigger than the one that bought the grace, in which case only
  the DIFFERENCE lands. Reading the grace as a plain "ignore" is the obvious reading and it makes
  every weapon in the game feel identical; it is also why hitting a mob with a stone sword and then
  a diamond one does more than the stone alone.

  ⚠ **KNOCKBACK HALVES THE EXISTING MOTION AND SUBTRACTS THE IMPULSE; IT DOES NOT ADD.** The
  halving is what stops a knockback chain from launching anything out of the world, and the upward
  part — clamped at 0.4 — applies only when the target is on the ground.

  ⚠ **THE DAMAGE ORDER IS VANILLA'S AND IT MATTERS**: the cooldown ramp `0.2 + h²·0.8` FIRST, then
  whether the blow was full strength (`h > 0.9`), then the 1.5× crit, then the sweep. Doing the
  ramp last would make a crit on a half-charged swing worth more than a full one. ⚠ A crit and a
  sprint-knockback are mutually exclusive, which is the rule every player knows as a habit — *stop
  sprinting to crit* — without knowing it is one boolean. ⚠ And a swing immediately after a swing
  is not at zero charge: `Player.attack` asks for `getAttackStrengthScale(0.5)`, half a tick of
  interpolation, which the first version of `combatcheck` got wrong and the engine got right.

  ⚠ **AN ENTITY ONLY WINS THE CROSSHAIR WHEN IT IS NEARER THAN THE BLOCK**, which is
  `GameRenderer.pick`'s whole job. Preferring the entity makes it impossible to mine a block with a
  chicken behind it; preferring the block makes it impossible to hit anything in a doorway. Each
  candidate's box is inflated by vanilla's own 0.3 first.

  ⚠⚠ **AND THE STAGE IS ◐, NOT ✅, WHICH IS THE HONEST HALF.** Eight entity types can be simulated
  and three can be DRAWN, none of them a mob, so the whole of this can be pointed only at a turtle,
  a dolphin or a guardian that nothing renders. Dan's rule the same night was *"do not half do a
  feature"*, and a zombie you cannot see is exactly that. `Cb.OWED` names the eight parts that need
  systems this engine has not built, and **`combatcheck` §6 carries an assertion that FAILS the day
  a mob shape is added** — so the "substrate only" note cannot outlive the limitation it describes.
  That is D-324's rule: a documented limitation carries an assertion that fires when it ends.

- **D-339** **A CHECK THAT CALLS THE FUNCTION UNDER TEST HAS NOT TESTED THE THING THAT IS SUPPOSED
  TO CALL IT** — and `tools/inputcheck.mjs` is the answer to it. Four of the seven faults Dan
  reported in session 11 were a **complete, correct model with no input edge**, and every check
  over every one of them was green:

  | fault | the model | why the check could not see it |
  |---|---|---|
  | the slider never dragged (D-330) | `Options.drag` was perfect | `optionscheck` called `O.drag` itself |
  | no swing on a miss (D-334) | `Hand.swing` was perfect | `handcheck` calls `H.swing()` itself |
  | candles could not stack (D-331) | the rule was implemented **twice** | `placecheck` drives it with raw block states |
  | every item swung at 4.0 (D-335) | the cooldown model was whole | the table it reads was null |

  ⚠⚠ **EVERY OTHER CHECK IN THIS PROJECT ENTERS THE SYSTEM AT A MODEL.** That is what makes them
  cheap and precise, and it is exactly why a missing wire is invisible to all of them at once.
  `inputcheck` enters at a `MouseEvent` and a `KeyboardEvent` dispatched on `window` — which is
  where `Input.attach` binds — and asserts what a player would see: a slider dragged end to end, a
  click at the sky counted as a swing, a broken block dropped and then picked up by walking onto
  it, Q and Ctrl+Q throwing one item and a stack, a door placing BOTH halves, two candles stacking,
  and the selected hotbar slot's pixels compared against an unselected slot holding the same block.
  **Every one of those assertions fails against last night's build.**

  ⚠ **ONE THING IS REACHED INTO AND IT IS NAMED.** `Input.locked` is set by hand, because pointer
  lock cannot be granted to a headless browser without a real user gesture and `mousedown` refuses
  to record a press while unlocked *by design* — it requests the lock instead. Naming the single
  exception is what keeps the rest of the file honest.

  ⚠⚠ **THE SWING IS COUNTED, NOT WATCHED** (`Hand.swings`). A swing is six ticks; this browser
  draws about four frames a second with the loop catching up twenty ticks a frame, so by the time
  anything outside the page can look, a correct swing is over. Waiting for a momentary state here
  is D-321's mistake in a new costume — **a check outside the loop cannot see a momentary state,
  but it can see a counter.**

  ⚠ **AND THE WORLD IS BUILT, NOT FOUND.** The sections that break and place stand the player on a
  five-by-five platform of dirt they lay down themselves. Stone drops NOTHING to a bare hand, which
  is correct vanilla and would have failed §3 for a reason that has nothing to do with item
  entities; a slope changes which face the ray hits; and a door aimed straight down is refused by
  the self-collision veto, correctly. **A check that depends on where the player happened to spawn
  is measuring the world, not the code.**

  ⚠ **IT ALSO CAUGHT ONE OF MINE.** `g17cbcheck` failed with *"it is drawn (0 triangles)"* on a
  dropped item: an item entity spawned with no explicit count carried `undefined`, and the moment
  pickup existed `count - taken` went NEGATIVE and removed the entity on its first tick — a dropped
  block that vanished the instant anything looked at it. Vanilla's `ItemStack` can never hold zero.
  The default is 1 now and `entlistcheck` asserts it, along with `PICKUP_NEVER = 32767`, which is
  `ItemEntity.setNeverPickUp()`'s own sentinel and not a large number.
  ⚠ **A PICTURE CHECK NAMED A SYMPTOM TWO LAYERS FROM ITS CAUSE, WHICH IS WHAT PICTURE CHECKS ARE
  FOR.** No counter in the project could have said "an item entity's count is undefined".

  ⚠ **AND A FALSE ALARM WORTH RECORDING.** Before that, `g10check` reported 126 stray pixels in the
  armour row and the cause was **a Chromium I had leaked by killing a run mid-flight** — two
  browsers on two cores, D-322 to the letter, and *a leaked browser never fails the check that
  leaked it*. The band now reports WHERE its ink is by twentieths, not only how much, because a
  failure that says "126 pixels are lit" costs an hour and one that says "in the left fifth" costs
  a minute. ⚠ `pkill -f chrome` also matches the shell that runs it; `pkill -f "[c]hrome-linux"`
  does not.

- **D-340** **A SLIDER THAT MOVED ONCE AND THEN STUCK — FOUND BY MOVING THE POINTER TWICE.**
  `inputcheck` (D-339) found this on its first run, against the fix that had just landed for D-330.

  ⚠⚠ `Options.drag` finds the row it is dragging by **object identity** — `O.hit[i].row !==
  O.dragging` — and `O.videoRows()`, `O.soundRows()` and the rest return **fresh object literals
  every time they are called**. `O.draw` called them on every frame, and `17_main`'s `uidrag`
  handler is `Options.drag(I.mx); Hud.draw();`. So the first pointer move dragged correctly and
  rebuilt the row set; the second found nothing matching `O.dragging` and did nothing at all.

  ⚠ **D-330's FIX WOULD HAVE SHIPPED WITH IT**, and it would have read as the same bug: a slider
  that does not follow the pointer. The only thing that separates the two is a second `mousemove`,
  which no model-level check had ever performed — `optionscheck` called `O.drag` directly, twice if
  it liked, and the row objects it passed were its own.

  ⚠ **THE FIX IS WHAT VANILLA DOES.** A `Screen` builds its widgets in `init()`, not in `render()`.
  `Options.rowsFor()` builds the rows once per screen and `Options.invalidate()` drops them on any
  navigation — **and nothing is lost by caching, because every value on a row is a function.** That
  was the point of the row contract from the beginning; the cache makes it pay.
  ⚠ `invalidate()` also clears `O.dragging`: a drag whose row no longer exists is a drag on
  nothing, and leaving it set is how a pointer keeps dragging a dead widget.

  ⚠ **THE GENERAL LESSON, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT SLIDERS.** Identity-based lookup into a table that
  is rebuilt every frame is correct for exactly one frame. **Anything that survives longer than a
  frame must be keyed by something that also survives longer than a frame.** The same shape is
  waiting wherever a check holds a reference across a redraw.

  ⚠ AND THREE FAULTS IN THE CHECK ITSELF, each worth keeping:
  1. **Render distance CLAMPS to the preset's maximum**, so dragging its slider to the far right
     lands at 24 of 32 and reads 0.733. The drag was perfect and the assertion was measuring a
     clamp. The question is "did the drag run out of track", not "did the value reach one".
  2. **`Inventory.getItem` hands back the LIVE stack** and `removeItem` mutates it in place, so
     reading `.n` after the keypress read the value after the throw — the check reported "holding
     four" for a stack it had just set to five. **A reference is not a snapshot.**
  3. **POSITIVE PITCH IS UP IN THIS ENGINE.** The ray is `(sin(yaw)cos(pitch), sin(pitch),
     -cos(yaw)cos(pitch))`, so `-PI/2` points at the FLOOR — which is what every other check uses
     it for. Aiming "at the sky" with a negative pitch aimed at the ground, and the swing counter
     went up anyway **because mining swings too**: the section passed its real assertion while its
     precondition told the truth. ⚠ **A precondition that fails while the assertion passes is the
     check telling you it measured the wrong thing.**

  ⚠ **AND A BACKTICK INSIDE A TEMPLATE LITERAL BROKE A CHECK FOR THE SIXTH AND SEVENTH TIME.**
  These files are full of code-in-strings evaluated in the page, and the house comment style puts
  identifiers in backticks. `gatecheck` §3b now runs `node --check` over every file in `tools/`,
  which costs under a second — and **caught the seventh on its very first run**, in a file edited
  an hour earlier. The failure it replaces costs a three-minute browser run and reports
  "Unexpected identifier" a hundred lines from the cause.

- **D-341** **THE ITEM SPRITES SHIP AS TEXTURE-ARRAY LAYERS, NOT AS A SECOND PNG.** A dropped
  item is drawn in the WORLD, and the world's model stream carries a `tile` field that is an
  array LAYER index — so item sprites living in their own 2D sheet could not be sampled by that
  shader at all. `extract-items.mjs` writes `item-tiles.bin` in exactly the form `build-atlas.mjs`
  writes the block tiles; `06_atlas.js` appends them after the block layers and publishes
  `A.itemTile0`/`A.itemTiles`; `15_hud.js` cuts its own 2D sheet out of `A.mips[0]`. **One source
  of item pixels in the file** (D-139), and it is SMALLER than the PNG it replaces — 58,722 bytes
  deflated against 101,631.
  ⚠ Item sprites are 16x16, which IS the block array's layer size, so they append with no
  resampling, no padding and no seams. **A mob texture cannot come this way**: a zombie sheet is
