  64x64 and a texture array's layers are all one size. That is G18's problem and a different one.
  ⚠ **AND IT BROKE THE GAME AT 14% IN A WAY THAT NAMED NOTHING.** `NS.DATA` ended up with
  `itemTiles` declared TWICE — the new base64 blob and, ninety lines later in the same object
  literal, a pre-existing lazy name->index function. **A duplicate key in an object literal is not
  an error, not even in strict mode**; the later one wins, in silence. `A.build` called `atob` on
  a function and the page died with `InvalidCharacterError: the string is not correctly encoded`,
  which names neither key nor file. The function is now `itemTileMap`, and `tools/gen-data.mjs`
  has a **§DUP** scan that brace-walks the emitted `NS.DATA` literal and refuses to write the file
  if any top-level key appears twice (3 anti-vacuity breaks: one dup, two dups, and a NESTED key
  that must not be reported).
  ⚠ **AND THE CHECK THAT FOUND IT LIED ABOUT IT.** `smoke.mjs` reported *"the page has no MCL
  global"* about a page whose MCL global was right there, because `Runtime.evaluate` answers a
  THROW with `exceptionDetails` and a `result` that IS the error object, whose `.value` is
  undefined — indistinguishable from a probe that returned null. Its diagnostic also truncated the
  key list at 40, which made module loading look like it stopped at `Mining`. **A harness must
  never turn its own exception into a claim about the program under test.** Fixed in `smoke.mjs`
  AND in `tools/cdp.mjs`, which every browser stage is built on.
  ⚠ And `H.buildItemIcons` was called from the boot chain ABOVE `Atlas.build`, so it read a null
  `A.mips`, returned early, and — being build-once — never ran again: every sprite item in the HUD
  was blank, in silence. `iconcheck` could not see it, because **a check that CALLS the function
  under test has not tested the thing that is supposed to call it**. `smoke` now asserts the
  running game's `Hud.itemSheetReady`, its size, and that it has real pixels in it.

- **D-342** **A DROPPED STICK IS VANILLA'S EXTRUDED SPRITE, BAKED THROUGH THE BLOCK BAKER.**
  `ER.OWED_ITEM` named "sprite items (no block model)" as a written-down deviation and every
  headless check stayed green while a dropped stick, apple, ingot and diamond were INVISIBLE.
  Vanilla has no billboard either: `ItemModelGenerator` extrudes the sprite into a real model one
  sixteenth of a block deep, with a ring of side quads around every alpha boundary, merged into
  runs. That geometry is compiled Java — not in any data pack, not in the assets, and not
  readable off a screenshot — so it comes out of the jar.
  ⚠ **THE 20th REFEREE TABLE**, `tools/golden/itemmodel-1.18.2.tsv`. THREE classes carry the
  string `layer0`, so that identifies nothing (**a constant is not a use** — the same trap
  `extract-guigeom` fell into with the hotbar's 182). Two independent discriminators must pick the
  same class: the one that assembles the whole `layer0..layer4` list, and the one declaring two
  `private static final float` ConstantValues 7.5 and 8.5. The Direction enum is read from its own
  `<clinit>` so `go.c` is NORTH because the jar puts that string next to that putstatic. The span
  enum's ordinal switch map is read from the synthetic `eru$1` class, so the four geometry cases
  are attached by the COMPILER's table rather than by source order.
  ⚠ **LEFT CARRIES EAST AND RIGHT CARRIES WEST.** The pairing looks backwards and it is what the
  jar says, because the sprite is seen from +Z. Written down so nobody "fixes" it from intuition.
  ⚠ **IT STOPS AT `elements` AND GOES THROUGH `bakelib.bakeModel`** — the same baker, the same
  winding rule, the same UV rotation as every block in the game. A second copy of `faceCorners` is
  D-314 waiting to happen, and D-314 has already cost two sessions. 14,405 quads over 534 sprites,
  avg 27, max 66; the parts are APPENDED to the block parts so no block part index moves and the
  runtime reaches item tile `t` at `spritePart0 + t` with no new decoder and no new emit loop.
  ⚠ **THE MODEL DECIDES WHICH PICTURE AN ITEM GETS, NOT `isBlock`.** `rail`, `torch`, `ladder`,
  every sapling, every flower and every candle place a real block state AND are drawn flat,
  because their item model's parent is `item/generated`. ⚠ `IT.isBlock` does NOT mean "places a
  block" — it is `kind === 'block'`, i.e. "its item model IS a block model" — and I wrote a check
  section asserting the opposite on the strength of the name. The engine already knew the right
  partition: an item with sprite LAYERS is a generated model.
  ⚠ **A DROPPED SPRITE IS NOT A DROPPED BLOCK'S SIZE.** `block/block.json` puts a dropped block at
  translation (0,3,0) scale 0.25; `item/generated.json` puts a dropped sprite at (0,2,0) **scale
  0.5**. The renderer carried only the block pair, and **half-size is a perfectly plausible
  picture — nothing would have reported it**. The two happen to give the same vertical lift
  (0.25*0.25 + 3/16 and 0.25*0.5 + 2/16 are both 0.25) and that coincidence is not relied on.
  ⚠ **THE 2-5 COPY STACK PILE IS DRAWN EXACTLY**, so the second `OWED_ITEM` entry is gone too.
  `java.util.Random` is a 48-bit LCG and `ER.JRand` reproduces it in two 24-bit halves; the
  referee generates the expected sequences **from a real JVM** (a JDK is already required for
  `javap`), so "exactly" is an assertion and not a claim — 6 seeds x 8 draws. The flat and the 3D
  cases differ and both are implemented: a block-model item jitters in all three axes by +-0.15; a
  flat sprite jitters in X and Y only by half that, and its copies are STACKED along Z by
  0.09375 * the ground scale, centred by an initial -0.09375*(n-1)*0.5*scaleZ. Copy 0 takes NO
  random draw, so the sequence must not be advanced for it.
  ⚠ `ER.OWED_ITEM` is down to ONE entry — the 67 `builtin/entity` items (chests, beds, banners,
  skulls, shulker boxes), which need a block-entity renderer. Both removed entries are DELETED,
  not commented (D-139).
  ⚠ **AND WEBGL2 NEVER ASKED THE DRIVER HOW MANY ARRAY LAYERS IT HAS.** WebGPU has negotiated
  `maxTextureArrayLayers` since D-310 and refuses in a sentence; this path called `texStorage3D`
  blind. Past the limit that raises INVALID_VALUE, the texture stays unallocated, every
  `texSubImage3D` after it raises INVALID_OPERATION, and the world draws BLACK with nothing in the
  console naming a layer count — the exact failure that cost this project the WebGPU backend for a
  week. It matters more now: the atlas went from 778 layers to 1,435. GL guarantees 256.

- **D-343** **THREE COPIES OF THE LOOK VECTOR, AND ONE HAD THE WRONG SIGN.** Found while chasing
  D-342's invisible stick. `14_player.js` wrote the forward vector out by hand in three places:
  `retarget` (the crosshair) and the entity pick used `(sin y*cos p, **+sin p**, -cos y*cos p)`,
  agreeing with `Cam.forward` and with `10_camera.js`'s own comment — *"yaw 0 looks -Z, +yaw turns
  right, +pitch looks up"*. `dropHeld` used **`-sin p`**. **So a player looking UP and pressing Q
  threw the item at the FLOOR**, and looking down threw it over their head. Nothing reported it,
  because a dropped item goes SOMEWHERE either way and "somewhere" looks like physics.
  All three now call `P.lookVec`, which delegates to `Cam.forward` — **the camera decides which
  way the screen is pointing, so it owns the convention and everything else asks it.** The
  fallback formula in `lookVec` exists only for a headless check that loads the player alone, and
  says so. `spritecheck` §2b pins `P.lookVec` against `Cam.forward` at four poses and asserts that
  an item thrown while looking up has a positive `vy`.
  ⚠ **THE CHECK CARRIED A FOURTH COPY, ALSO REVERSED.** `spritecheck` spawned its test item at
  `dx = -sin(yaw), dz = cos(yaw)`, which at yaw 0 points at +Z while the camera looks -Z — so the
  item was BEHIND the camera every time. The renderer dutifully built it, submitted a hundred
  triangles for it and reported them, and the frame was empty: **the numbers and the pixels were
  both telling the truth, about different things.** An hour went into the renderer before the
  convention was questioned. **A check must never carry its own copy of a convention the engine
  owns** (D-305, one level up: it is not only numbers).

- **D-344** **AN ITEM'S TINT IS BAKED INTO ITS OWN ATLAS LAYER.** Vanilla multiplies a sprite
  layer by a colour from `ItemColors` at render time — that is how one white egg sprite becomes
  sixty coloured ones, how a leather cap becomes sixteen dyed ones and how a potion gets its tint.
  The HUD did that compositing on a 2D canvas; the WORLD could not, because the model shader's
  only per-vertex tint field is two bits wide and already carries the grass/foliage/water map. So
  the inventory showed a coloured zombie egg and **the dropped one was white** — the same item,
  two pictures, which is D-314's warning in its most literal form.
  ⚠ **BAKE, DO NOT ADD A SHADER PATH.** Every one of these colours is STATIC in this engine —
  there is no NBT, so `tint0`/`tint1` are constants per item — and a multiply done at build time
  is bit-for-bit the multiply the shader would do. Each distinct (sprite, colour) pair becomes its
  own atlas layer: **123 pairs, not 78 items x 2 layers**, because every spawn egg shares the same
  two source sprites. From then on there is exactly ONE set of pixels for an item, the HUD blits
  it and the world samples it, and they cannot disagree. Alpha is untouched — it is the cutout
  mask, and scaling it by a colour channel would eat the silhouette and change the render pass.
  ⚠ **AND THE OLD HUD PATH WAS WRONG, NOT MERELY DUPLICATED.** It composited with `source-in` and
  a `fillRect`, which **REPLACES** every pixel's RGB with one flat colour; vanilla **MULTIPLIES**.
  So a spawn egg in the inventory was a solid silhouette with its spots and shading erased, and
  every dyed leather piece was a flat blob. **Two bugs, one cause: a rule written twice and right
  neither time.** The composite path and its scratch canvas are deleted (D-139), and
  `spritecheck` §5b asserts the PIXELS — that a tinted layer equals base x colour to within a
  rounding step, not merely that its tile index differs, which would pass on a tile full of
  anything.

- **D-345** **THE PICTURE CHECKS WERE ALL WAITING ON THE WRONG CLOCK, AND ONE OF THEM STARTED
  FAILING ON WORKING CODE.** `g17cbcheck` went green for two sessions and then reported a control
  of **1,050 changed pixels against a falling block worth 1,129** — the day the shipped file grew
  by 240 KB and the boot timing shifted. Nothing about the renderer had changed. Three separate
  faults, and every one of them is a wait:
  1. **A nine-second `sleep` standing in for "the world has finished arriving".** The chunk stream
     is FINITE — about 545 columns at medium — so it reaches a cap, and until it does two frames
     differ by thousands of pixels. `session.settleWorld()` in `tools/cdp.mjs` now waits for that
     cap, and both this file and `spritecheck` call it. ⚠ It deliberately does NOT wait on the
     MESH count as well: meshes churn as sections are rebuilt and never settle, and requiring them
     timed out for sixty seconds on a world that was visually finished. **A proxy one inference
     away from the thing that matters is one inference away from being wrong.**
  2. **`frames(4)` used as a unit of TIME.** On a two-core box with SwiftShader and a
     ten-megabyte page, one frame is about seventeen ticks — so between spawning a falling block
     and photographing it, **the block covered twenty-four metres** and ended 81 degrees off the
     view axis. The check was photographing an empty shaft and blaming the renderer. §3's claim is
     "a falling block reaches the screen", not "while falling at a given rate", so the entity's
     own `gravity` field is zeroed for that measurement and put back — from the value read off the
     entity, never a literal — before §4, which owns the falling.
  3. **A pixel count with no cause in it.** "34 px vs a control of 5" is unactionable, and twice
     this file reported a small diff for a working renderer and a camera pointed elsewhere. It now
     prints **how far away the entity is, how many degrees off the view axis, and how far it has
     fallen since it spawned** — which named the cause on the first run after it was added.
  4. **AND THE MIRROR IMAGE, found on the next run.** §4 reported *"the picture changed as it
     fell: **0 px**"* for a block whose own sampled `y` and `vy` showed it accelerating through
     38 ticks — because its two screenshots were **the same frame**. At four frames a second a
     260 ms gap can contain no new frame at all, and `captureScreenshot` hands back the identical
     picture twice. **Four frames were seventeen ticks; 260 milliseconds were zero frames.** Same
     root, opposite direction. The gap is a number of FRAMES now, with the millisecond value kept
     only as a floor, and it is in the shared `control()` helper so every claim in the file gets
     it.
  5. **AND THE CONTROL FOR IT WAS TAKEN DURING A REMESH.** With the frames fixed, the fall
     measured 1,361 px against a control of **3,200** — because the control was taken after the
     block LANDED, while the column it landed in was being re-meshed. It is taken before the
     lift now, with the block at rest and the world settled: 34 px against a fall of 3,233.
     **A control has to be measured where nothing is happening, not merely at a different time.**
  ⚠ **THE GENERAL RULE, AND IT IS THE THIRD TIME THIS PROJECT HAS PAID FOR IT (D-321, D-296):
  wait for the STATE, never for a duration — and a frame, a round-trip and a tick are three
  different clocks.** A check that waits on the wrong one is not flaky; it is measuring something
  else, and it will go green or red according to how fast the machine happens to be.
  ⚠ And the backtick-in-a-template-literal broke a check for the **eighth** time while writing
  this, in a file whose own comment says not to. `gatecheck` §3b caught it in a second.

  built for and cannot express any of those: a rail needs a RIGID face below, a cactus needs no
  solid neighbour on any side, a lever asks the face it is attached to.

  LevelReader, BlockPos) returning boolean. **There are TWO such descriptors and the other one is
  the trap** — it takes a `BlockGetter`, the WIDER interface, and is `propagatesSkylightDown` with
  46 overriders of its own. They are told apart by asking which level interface EXTENDS the other;
  picking by count alone is a coin flip between two real methods. **56 overriders; 267 of the 898
  blocks have a rule, across 55 owner classes.** A block's rule is whichever ancestor overrides
  the method, so two blocks share a rule exactly when they share an owner — exact, not a grouping.
  ⚠ **THE THREE SUPPORT TYPES, and this is the part worth carrying away.**
  **FULL** is the whole face — a door needs it below. **CENTER** is a 2x2-pixel patch at the
  middle — a torch or a lever needs it. **RIGID** is the outer two-pixel RIM — a rail or a
  repeater needs it. A fence passes CENTER and fails the other two, which is why a torch goes on a
  fence post and a rail does not; a **HOPPER is the reverse**, a rim with a hole in the middle, so
  it takes a rail and refuses a torch. **Neither is a special case in the engine** — one
  `faceCovers` primitive over the collision boxes answers all three, and the rectangles come out
  of the enum's own three subclasses (CENTER box(7,0,7..9,10,9), RIGID a whole block MINUS
  box(2,0,2..14,16,14)) rather than being typed into the code.

  From collision boxes I concluded soul sand is not sturdy, and I guessed that cauldrons,
  composters, hoppers and scaffolding override `getBlockSupportShape`. Following the support
  types' own call chain says **exactly two blocks override it: snow and soul_sand**. Soul sand
  returns a WHOLE BLOCK though it is 14/16 tall and you sink into it — which is why redstone,
  rails and repeaters sit on it. Reading the collision shape alone refuses all three on a block
  players build on constantly. ⚠ The standing warning for this whole area — **a rule that refuses
  a LEGAL build is worse than one that allows an illegal one** — is why `supportcheck` asserts

  ⚠ **212 BLOCKS STILL HAVE AN OVERRIDE THIS ENGINE DOES NOT IMPLEMENT**, counted in

- **D-347** **A CLAIM ABOUT A SMALL OBJECT IN A BUSY FRAME IS MADE IN THE OBJECT'S OWN RECTANGLE,
  AND THE RECTANGLE COMES FROM THE ENGINE'S CAMERA.** 15 Sept 2026, session 12.
  `g17cbcheck` §4's *"the picture changed as it fell"* failed four times in a row, each time on a
  renderer that was working. The diagnosis only arrived when the check started printing where the
  block was: **gravity is per TICK and a picture is per FRAME, and on this two-core box with
  SwiftShader one frame is about seventeen ticks.** A falling block released with vanilla's 0.04
  leaves a 70-degree field of view in roughly ten ticks — so both screenshots taken across a free
  fall are photographs of a shaft the block has already left, and the check reported **0 px** of a
  block its own 38 samples proved was falling. ⚠ **Waiting cannot fix a measurement that is faster
  than the shutter**, and the noise argument runs the other way too: this world is a forest, whose
  canopy churns **11,341 px between two frames**, against a falling block worth 3,400. No
  whole-frame threshold separates those, at any settling time — the check sat in its `quiet()`
  loop twenty times and the world never went still enough.
  ⚠ The first fix was *"measure the middle half of the frame — the shaft is carved straight
  ahead"*, and it was a guess dressed as a region of interest: it measured **0 px** for the same
  reason, and a rectangle chosen by eye **cannot tell "the block is not there" from "the block was
  never drawn"**. That is the same mistake as a check owning a number the code owns (D-305), one
  level up: it is a check owning a LAYOUT the camera owns.
  **So the rectangle is asked of the shipped camera.** `boxOf` projects the eight corners of the
  entity type's own box — `Entities.boxAt`, the table vanilla's `EntityDimensions` gave us, so
  this file owns no width — through `Gfx.cam.viewProj` exactly as the vertex shader does, and
  returns the bounding rectangle as FRACTIONS of the viewport, so the screenshot's resolution is
  nobody's business. Measured that way the block's own 114x101 rectangle changes **0 px by
  itself** and **8,434 px when the block leaves it**: a signal-to-noise ratio that no amount of
  forest can touch.
  ⚠ **AND THE PROJECTION IS NOT TAKEN ON TRUST.** A rectangle nobody has checked is a rectangle
  that can be anywhere, and a wrong one fails silently in exactly the direction that reads as
  "the renderer is broken". So §3 pins it against the one claim in the file that is known true
  for independent reasons — the block demonstrably arrived, the whole frame says so — and asserts
  three things of the projected box: the arrival is visible INSIDE it, the box is a PART of the
  frame and not most of it, and MOST of the arrival is inside it. A transposed matrix layout, a
  flipped Y, a camera-relative offset applied the wrong way (D-179) or a canvas that does not
  fill the screenshot each fail there, loudly, on a claim whose answer is already known.
  ⚠ **AND THE CLAIM IS MADE IN BOTH DIRECTIONS** (D-346's rule again): the block falling out of
  the rectangle empties it, and putting it back FILLS it again — which is what makes the
  measurement a statement about the block rather than about the passage of time.
  ⚠ The physics and the picture are now measured separately and both fully: the free fall is
  sampled inside the page from the engine's own `tickOne` (38 airborne ticks, `vy` growing on
  every one of 37 intervals), and the drawn picture is measured where the camera says the entity
  is. **Bundling them into one pair of screenshots required the renderer to be faster than the
  simulation, which was never a property of the program under test.**
  `g17cbcheck` went from 39 assertions and 4 breaks to **50 and 5**, and the browser board to
  **17 of 17**.

  constructor copies that field from ONE field of the Properties object, which identifies both the
  Properties class and the field; and the Properties methods that write that field with a zero are
  the setters. **Two of them**, which is vanilla exactly: `noCollission()` turns occlusion off as a
  side effect, `noOcclusion()` is the one that only does that.

  `Blocks` has a dozen static methods called `a` and the first one javap prints is the two-argument
  REGISTER method, whose body mentions no Properties at all. The number it produced — 317

- **D-354** **A TORCH BURNS OUT BY BEING SWITCHED OFF TOO OFTEN, AND THE TWO EDGES ARE NOT
  SYMMETRICAL.** 15 Sept 2026, session 12. G15a recorded vanilla's two constants — a 60-tick
  window and 8 toggles — and named burnout as NOT implemented, because what was missing was the
  per-position history, *"state this stage does not otherwise need"*. Its only effect is on a
  torch driven by its own output, which is G15b's clock: **the clock that used to run for ever
  now burns out the way vanilla's does.**
  ⚠⚠ **THE ASYMMETRY IS THE BEHAVIOUR.** Vanilla's `isToggledTooFrequently(level, pos, logToggle)`
  takes that boolean for one reason: the torch LOGS a toggle when it goes OUT, and COUNTS without
  logging when it wants to come back on. Logging on both edges fills the window twice as fast and
  burns a torch out in half the time; logging on neither never burns one out at all. Both call
  sites are distinct here for the same reason.
  ⚠ The list is per LEVEL and the count is per POSITION, and it is trimmed by TIME, not by length
  — so a hundred torches toggling elsewhere share the list and do not burn this one out.
  `redcheck` asserts exactly that, because a count that forgot to compare positions would pass
  every other assertion in the section and burn out the whole world at once.
  ⚠ **AND THE RECOVERY IS THE OTHER HALF.** A torch that never relit would pass *"it did not come
  back on"* and be a worse bug than no burnout at all. The window is run out and the torch lights
  again — the direction a one-sided check misses (D-346's rule, a fourth time).
  ⚠ The anti-vacuity break raises the budget out of reach and runs the SAME clock, which changes
  nothing else: without it, "the torch is dark" could have been any bug at all.
  `redcheck`: **330 assertions -> 341, 14 breaks -> 17.**

- **D-355** **`/locate` IS NOT `/locatebiome` WITH A DIFFERENT PREDICATE.** 15 Sept 2026, session
  12. The 29th command. A biome is a field to be sampled, so `locatebiome` walks a ring of QUART
  CELLS outward and asks each one. A structure is not: its placement is a GRID — one candidate
  chunk per `spacing x spacing` REGION — and vanilla's `findNearestMapFeature` walks rings of
  REGIONS, asks each for its single candidate chunk, and tests only that. Sampling the world for
  a structure would be thousands of times the work for a worse answer.
  ⚠⚠ **AND THE PRIMITIVE MATTERS MORE THAN THE LOOP.** The first draft asked `startsNear(cx, cz)`
  — *"what starts touch this chunk"* — which scans all seventeen sets and builds a 16x16-region
  BLOCK of the start cache per call. Consecutive candidates on a ring land in different blocks, so
  every single call was a cache miss that generated 256 regions: **seven `/locate` calls did not
  finish in two minutes.** `ST.startsOfRegion(si, rx, rz)` is the one region of the one set the
  search is actually about, and the same seven calls now take 16-700 ms. *A primitive that answers
  a wider question is not a free substitute for the narrow one.*
  ⚠ **THE STRONGHOLD IS A DIFFERENT PLACEMENT AND A DIFFERENT SEARCH.** `concentric_rings` has no
  spacing grid at all: its positions are computed outright from the world seed, and vanilla
  branches to them rather than searching. Folding it into the ring walk would look tidier and
  answer wrongly at every distance where no region contains one. `commandcheck` makes
  `startsOfRegion` **throw** in that test, so a fall-through does not merely fail — it explodes.
  ⚠ **VANILLA'S QUIRK IS REPRODUCED, NOT IMPROVED:** the loop returns from INSIDE the ring scan,
  so a structure on the far side of a ring can win over a nearer one on the same ring. A `/locate`
  that answered "nearer" would disagree with the real game on a seed a player could compare, and
  the assertion that plants two on one ring is what would fail the day somebody tidied it.
  ⚠ **THE ARGUMENT SET IS DERIVED FROM THE REGISTRY**, as the distinct types of the live sets —
  the same argument `C.IMPLEMENTED` makes about the command list itself. The eighteen that come
  out are exactly vanilla's `/locate` keys, `endcity`'s odd spelling included.
  ⚠ And `structcheck` §10b holds the half a stub cannot: with the REAL generator,
  `startsOfRegion` and `startsNear` must agree about every start's own chunk. They are different
  questions and the second is built out of the first, which holds until somebody optimises one of
  them — and if they ever disagreed, `/locate` would send a player to an empty field.
  ⚠⚠ **AND IT NEEDED ITS OWN TIME BUDGET, WHICH IS NOT THE BIOME ONE.** D-325 gave `findBiome`
  500 ms because vanilla pays this cost on a server thread and this game pays it on the one that
  DRAWS. A full hundred-ring structure walk is forty thousand regions, and a region that has to
  build a start costs **a third of a millisecond** — thirteen seconds of frozen tab. But at 500 ms
  the nearest **mansion** to the origin on seed 1337 is REFUSED: it is 28 km out and costs 712 ms
  over 2,143 regions, and **refusing a legal query is worse than the pause** (D-346's rule, in a
  fourth place). So the structure budget is 3,000 ms — four mansions' headroom, the pathological
  case capped at three seconds — and `commandcheck` asserts it is LARGER than the biome budget,
  with the reason, so the two cannot be quietly collapsed into one number.
  ⚠ The expansion cannot be skipped: for a jigsaw structure the biome test needs the y the pieces
  choose (D-184), which is vanilla's own coupling and why `/locate` takes seconds there too.
  **29 of vanilla's 74 commands; `commandcheck` 415 assertions -> 437.**

  - flood on vs off with the sky pass removed: **4,043 px**.

  their ordered literal sequence. `handposecheck` then holds `14k_hand3d.js` against that file:
  32 constants, the composition against a SECOND matrix implementation written row-major (they
  agree to 6.1e-8), and the three motions as differences rather than absolutes.

  ⚠ **AND THE ITEM'S OWN DISPLAY TRANSFORM, WHICH IS MOST OF "NOT EVEN CLOSE".** The engine had
  ONE — `block/block`'s `[0,45,0]` at 0.40, hard-coded in the icon rasteriser — and used it for

- **D-362** **FOOTSTEPS HAVE BEEN 67% TOO FREQUENT SINCE G13, AND THE CHECK HAD REASONED ITS WAY
  INTO AGREEING.** 15 Sept 2026, session 13. Found while porting `walkDist` for the hand's view
  bob (D-359): `Entity.move` accumulates **`sqrt(dx²+dy²+dz²) * 0.6`** into `moveDist`, and
  `Entity.nextStep()` is **`(int)moveDist + 1`** — `f2i; iconst_1; iadd` in the bytecode, an
  INTEGER truncation — with the gate `moveDist > nextStep`, strictly greater.
  This engine added the **raw horizontal** distance and re-based on `moveDist + 1`, carrying the
  overshoot. A step therefore landed every 1.0 blocks walked instead of every ~1.67: a 21.5-block
  walk gave 20 steps where vanilla gives 12.
  ⚠⚠ **AND `soundcheck` §5 RE-IMPLEMENTED THE RULE RATHER THAN DRIVING THE ENGINE'S**, got it
  wrong, and wrote the wrong reasoning down as a warning to future readers: *"asserting 21 was
  this file's own first bug"*. It was defending the overshoot-carrying variant, which is not
  vanilla's. **A check that restates the rule cannot disagree with the code about it** — it can
  only disagree with the game, which is the one comparison nobody was making. The section now
  reads the two lines out of `14_player.js` and fails if the engine's formula changes under it.
  ⚠ The irony is exact: §5's own header warns that a row of identical blocks must not *"sound
  like a machine gun"*, and the cadence was 67% too fast the whole time.

- **D-363** **"IS THE BRIDGE UP?" HAS NO SINGLE-READ ANSWER ON THIS MOUNT.** 16 Sept 2026.
  MineHTML's `CLAUDE.md` §4 states, correctly, that `ai-jobs/runner-status.json` is a real
  heartbeat rewritten every five seconds even mid-job, so a stale `updatedAt` means dead rather
  than busy. That is true of the file and not true of the READ. Session 14 read it through the
  connected-folder mount and got a copy dated **9 September — seven days stale** — published "the
  bridge is dead", and was wrong: re-read six seconds later the same file was ticking (pid 20924,
  +5 s per read). A cached or mid-sync first read is **indistinguishable** from a dead runner if
  you only read once, and the stale copy even said `"alive": true`.
  ⚠ So the honest form of the question is **did the number move**, which needs two reads and a
  wait. `tools/bridgecheck.mjs` is that, so no session has to remember it: MOVING / RESTARTED /
  FROZEN / UNREADABLE, five breaks, and the comparator is required to ignore the `alive` field in
  **both** directions because that field is what made the stale copy convincing.
  ▶ It deliberately **cannot fail the suite**. Dan's PC being switched off is not a defect in
  MC-Lite, and a check that goes red when he closes a window teaches sessions to ignore red.
  `--require` exists for the one caller that cannot proceed without a lane; the suite stage runs
  `--selftest`, which grades the comparator and never touches his machine.
  ⚠ The general rule, which is bigger than the bridge: **any tool that decides something from a
  file's timestamp on this mount needs two reads.**

- **D-364** **157 TOOLS AND NO INDEX, SO SESSIONS WROTE THE 158th.** 16 Sept 2026. `tools/` held
  157 `.mjs` files and nothing listed them. A session could not answer *"what do I already have?"*
  in one command, so it answered by reading — expensive — or by writing a second tool that did
  what one of the 157 already did, which is cheaper and worse. MineHTML pays for the same problem
  with `tool_index.js` and prints the relevant slice per route "so a session sees what already
  exists before it builds a duplicate".
  `tools/toolscheck.mjs` generates `docs/TOOLS.md` and `docs/tool-index.json` **from the files
  themselves** and then asserts the whole render still matches, so the catalogue cannot go stale:
  159 tools, 132 of them run by the suite. ⚠ **The count of 27 that the suite does not run is
  itself a finding** and is not a defect — probes and generators belong outside it — but until
  now nobody could see the number.
  ⚠ The purpose line comes from each tool's own header and **nowhere else**. A tool with no header
  is reported by name rather than given an invented description: a catalogue that makes up
  summaries is the referee problem in miniature. Five headerless scratch probes (`_vg*.mjs`) were
  given one-line headers describing what they actually do, rather than being hidden by an
  exemption.
  ▶ It sits beside `doccheck` in the suite because both enforce D-6: a fact in a document must be
  reproducible by running the suite. **If it is red, run `--write`. Never edit `docs/TOOLS.md`.**

- **D-365** **THE READING CHAIN WAS OVER A MEGABYTE, SO SESSIONS EITHER UNDER-READ OR
  OVER-READ — AND BOTH LOOK LIKE DILIGENCE.** 16 Sept 2026. `CLAUDE.md` named
  `CHARTER` → `NEXT` and called `PLAN.md` and `DECISIONS.md` "references", which is the right
  instruction and is not enforceable: the stated chain totals over a megabyte, of which
  `DECISIONS.md` is two thirds and `PLAN.md` most of the rest. A pass that read it spent Dan's

  already settled. **This is the mechanism behind "sessions aren't rigorous": the rigour was
  written down in a form too expensive to consult.**
  `tools/brief.mjs` is a **router, not a summary** — a summary goes stale and hides exactly the
  disagreement a session needs to see. It prints live figures derived from the tree and then
  names, by path and byte size, the two or three FULL documents *this* route must read.
  `docs/brief-routes.json` is the one home for the routes; `docs/STATE.md` is a template and
  **wins over every other document in the repo, this file included**.
  ⚠ Three failure modes, all graded by `briefcheck` because all three look fine from inside:
  a route that orders a 700 KB document has not routed anything; a brief that grows one useful
  line per session becomes the chain again (hence its own byte budget); and **a live number
  typed by a human is wrong by the next session with no way for a reader to tell which.** Any
  bare four-digit number in `STATE.md` is a failure — cite the state key and let the tool supply
  the value (D-6). Years and `D-` numbers are excluded, and that exclusion is itself a break.
  ▶ **`brief` reports the decision COUNT as `doccheck`'s to give, not its own.** The two
  disagreed by five the first time both printed it, because `doccheck` expands multi-number
  entries. One number, one owner; duplicating the parser would have been the two-homes bug.

- **D-366** **A MESSAGE SENT MID-TURN DOES NOT START A TURN, SO NOTHING WAS FORCING A REPLY.**

  It measures the **software-rendering floor**, which is a useful floor, and it says **nothing**
  about the black-WebGPU bug (KW-1); that needs real hardware. ⚠ A graphics measurement taken
  over SSH is wrong whatever the hardware — session 0 has no desktop and reports software
  rendering every time.
  ⚠ `vmcheck` runs `--selftest` in the suite, like `bridgecheck`: Dan's VM being switched off is
  not a defect in MC-Lite, and a check that reddens when he shuts something down teaches sessions
  to ignore red.

- **D-369** **THIRTEEN SESSIONS WORKED AROUND A PERMISSION NOBODY HAD ASKED FOR.** 16 Sept 2026.
  `rm` is blocked on the Cowork device mount **by default**, and a session can request that it be
  unblocked — one prompt, granted for the folder's whole subtree for the rest of the session.
  Nobody asked. Instead the project evolved a six-step commit recipe that moves both lock files
  aside, adds, moves the fresh lock aside again and then commits, all in one shell call because
  two calls never converge; session 13 spent six attempts deriving it and it has been in
  `CLAUDE.md` ever since.
  ▶ **What the workaround cost, measured:** every interrupted object write left a `tmp_obj_*`
  file that git could not unlink. `mclite/.git/objects` held **902 of them**, plus seven stale
  `.lock.aside*` files, and `git gc` refused to run at all — so the pile could only grow. With
  the permission granted, the garbage was removed and **the first `git gc` in this repository's
  history** took `.git` from **29 MB to 9.5 MB**, `garbage: 0`, working tree clean.
  ⚠ **The general lesson is bigger than git.** A constraint that is *configurable* looks exactly
  like a constraint that is *fixed* from inside a session, and the difference is one question.
  This project has now been bitten by both shapes in one night: an instruction that was true for
  a day and kept for a week (AGENTS.md §8), and a restriction that was never fixed at all.
  **Before building a workaround, ask whether the thing being worked around is a setting.**
  ⚠ Deleting on this mount is permanent — no Trash, and on a synced folder it is a delete on
  every machine. Ask for the permission, use it narrowly, and move anything uncertain to
  `.trash/` rather than removing it.

- **D-370** **A BACKUP CHECK THAT ASKS "IS THIS COMMIT IN IT", NOT "HOW OLD IS IT".** 16 Sept
  2026. The audit found this project with 97 commits, no git remote, and absent from Syncthing's
  two folders — **one disk**, with the gitignored `.tgz` archives as the only off-machine copies,
  and those are the symptom of a different bug entirely.
  ▶ `tools/backupcheck.mjs` writes and grades a `git bundle` in `C:\claudeisthegoat\_backups\`,
  which **is** a synced folder, so a bundle reaches the second PC within seconds of being
  written — an off-machine backup that needs no account and no network.
  ⚠ **It fails on "HEAD is not in the newest bundle", never on age**, and that is the whole
  design. A bundle from three weeks ago is perfectly good if nothing has been committed since; a
  bundle from an hour ago is worthless if four commits landed after it. Age is the wrong question
  and it is the one everybody asks — which is why one of the five breaks is a bundle whose
  filename date is newer than its contents.
  ⚠ **A MIRROR IS NOT A BACKUP** and this file says so rather than implying it: a delete
  propagates in seconds and `.stversions` keeps 30 days. MineHTML is safe because it has both a
  mirror and a remote. A bundle is the second protection, not a substitute for the first.
  ▶ Still owed and deliberately not pretended away: **neither MC-Lite nor the VM tooling has a
  remote.** A bundle and a mirror both live on hardware in one house (KW-13).

- **D-371** **A SESSION CAN READ ITS OWN SPEND NOW, AND THE HEADLINE IS THE QUADRATIC.** 16 Sept
  2026. MineHTML's `usage_meter.js` opens by stating that a session cannot read its token spend
  and that nothing in the repo can — honest when written, and no longer true: **the transcript is
  a `.jsonl` on disk and every model request in it carries its own `usage` block.**
  `tools/passcost.mjs` sums the four fields that decide cost — uncached input, cache writes,
  cache reads and output — and prices them.
  ▶ **This session, measured on itself: 375 requests, $0.232 each, 111.7 M cache-read tokens,
  median context 299,460, 98.4% cache hit rate, 511,759 output tokens.** ~$87 at Opus list price;
  ~$35 on Sonnet, ~$17 on Haiku.
  ⚠⚠ **THE NUMBER THAT MATTERS IS NOT THE TOTAL.** Split into four equal request-count quarters:
  **Q1 $16.07, Q4 $32.80 — 2.04× for the SAME number of requests.** Nothing got harder; the
  conversation got longer and every request re-sends all of it. **So a new session for unrelated
  work is cheaper than continuing a long one, which is the opposite of the instinct**, and the
  quarters are printed first for that reason.
  ⚠ The caching is not the problem — 98.4% of input tokens were served from cache. Cost is
  `requests × context size`, and the only two levers are **fewer requests** and **smaller
  context**. A shell call is at least one request, so batching two commands into one call is a
  measurable saving, not a style preference.
  ⚠ Thinking is billed as **output**, which is what makes effort level a cost lever rather than a
  quality dial.
  ⚠ List prices, an estimate, never an invoice — the same caveat `usage_meter.js` states about
  its own figures. `EFFICIENCY-AUDIT.md` in the project root has the full research.

- **D-372** **THE MIDDLE GROUND BETWEEN OPUS AND SONNET IS NOT A MODEL. IT IS THE EFFORT DIAL.**
  16 Sept 2026. Dan asked whether to move to Sonnet, having heard *"Sonnet high was
  inefficient"*, and wished for something between the two tiers.
  ▶ **He is right, and `docs/AGENTS.md` §2 already says it** — *"Sonnet at `low` and `medium`
  only — never `high` or above; effort scaling is the real cost driver."* That rule was
  transposed from MineHTML before anyone had measured it here.
  ▶ **Anthropic's own benchmark says the same with numbers.** On SWE-bench Pro, **Sonnet 5 at
  default effort solves 77.4% at $0.84 per solved task; the frontier model at `low` effort solves
  88.6% at $0.54** — eleven points better for 35% less per solved task, at five times the
  per-token price. And *"Opus 5 at `low` effort beats Opus 4.8's default for about 30% of its
  cost per solved task."* **A stronger model at reduced effort beats a weaker model at raised
  effort**, and the metric is **cost per completed task, never cost per token.**
  ⚠ The effort curve is flat for knowledge work and real for coding: `medium` gives up ~2 points
  for **50%** of the cost, `low` gives up ~8 for **25%**. For knowledge work `medium` matched
  default accuracy at 70–87% of the cost and default bought *"nothing measurable"*.
  ⚠⚠ **AND THE SIZE OF THIS LEVER, MEASURED ON THIS SESSION RATHER THAN ASSUMED:** it ran at
  **Opus 5 High** for a night of file edits, greps and doc trims, and **81% of its output tokens
  (~475,000) were thinking**. But output is only **13.9%** of the bill; **cache reads are 67.9%**.
  So effort is worth having and **it is not the main lever — the quadratic is** (D-371).
  ⚠ A naive "Sonnet is 40% of Opus" assumes an identical token shape. It is exactly the
  assumption the benchmark refutes: a weaker model takes more turns, and more turns means more
  cache reads, which is the 67.9%.
  ▶ **The ruling: match the dial to the task, not the model to the budget.** Mechanical passes —
  doc edits, renames, transcription, anything a check grades afterwards — run at low or medium.
  `high` is for a decision about what vanilla does, and those are rare.

- **D-373** **THE OPERATING CONFIGURATION, CONSOLIDATED — WHICH MODEL, WHICH EFFORT, WHICH
  SURFACE.** 16 Sept 2026. Three questions Dan asked together, answered together because the
  answers interact.
  ▶ **ORCHESTRATOR: Opus 5 at `medium`.** The orchestrator is the decider, and `AGENTS.md` §2's
  bright line already reserves every interpretation and every last word for it. The benchmark
  agrees with the tier and **disagrees with the dial**: a stronger model at reduced effort beats
  a weaker model at raised effort, on cost per solved task (D-372). So the saving comes from the
  dial, not from demoting the orchestrator. `low` for a mechanical night; `high` only for a
  decision about what vanilla does, and those are rare.
  ⚠⚠ ~~**IF THE WINDOW IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT, orchestrate on Sonnet 5 at `medium` and
  escalate to Opus for the decision moments only.**~~ **STRUCK THE SAME DAY — SEE D-374. Dan:
  *"'decision moments' is incoherent, because switching models resets cache so it has to be all
  thru."* He is right, and it is worse than he said: changing the EFFORT does it too.**
  ▶ **WORKERS:** Haiku 4.5 for enumeration, transcription and counting; Sonnet 5 at `low`/
  `medium` where more care or more context is needed. ⚠ Unchanged and not negotiable: **only
  where a MACHINE verifies the output afterwards** (`AGENTS.md` §2).
  ⚠⚠ **NEVER SONNET AT `high`.** `AGENTS.md` §2 banned it before anyone here had measured it, and
  the measurement now backs it: raising a weaker model's effort is the one move that costs more
  AND scores worse than the alternative.
  ▶ **`SONNET 4.6 high` vs `SONNET 5 medium` IS NOT CLOSE — take Sonnet 5 at `medium`**, on three
  independent grounds: 4.6 is **not on the current recommended-models list at all**, Sonnet 5
  supersedes it; Sonnet 5 costs **$2/$10 against 4.6's $3/$15**, a third less; and it is the
  newer-at-lower-effort side of the rule above. There is no reading on which 4.6 at `high` wins.
  ▶ **SURFACE: Claude Code on the PC for the long passes, Cowork for the phone and the inbox.**
  Claude Code is where the +25% of 14 Sept landed, where Remote Control keeps execution and
  files local while being steered from a phone, and where **every mount bug of 16 Sept stops
  existing** — the 180-second cap, blocked `rm`, 902 orphaned git objects, `gc` refusing, the
  seven-day-stale read, the two-lock commit dance.
  ⚠ **The saving is not per token.** Same model, same prices, same quadratic. What changes is the
  allowance, the levers (`/usage` attribution, `/context`, hooks that filter tool output before
  it reaches the conversation, per-subagent `model:`), and the removal of a class of waste that
  was roughly a third of the 16 Sept bill.


- **D-374** **MODEL AND EFFORT ARE SESSION-LEVEL DECISIONS. NEITHER CAN BE CHANGED MID-SESSION
  WITHOUT RE-PROCESSING THE WHOLE CONVERSATION.** 16 Sept 2026, correcting D-373 the same day.
  Dan: *"'decision moments' is incoherent, because switching models resets cache so it has to be
  all thru."* Correct, and the documentation makes it worse than the objection claimed.
  ▶ **CHANGING THE EFFORT SETTING DOES IT AS WELL AS CHANGING THE MODEL.** The caching docs are
  explicit: *"Changing the `output_config.effort` value **always invalidates message blocks**,
  with the same model-specific effect on tool and system caches as thinking parameters"*, and the
  same is said of the thinking configuration — *"changing it always invalidates message blocks"*.
  Message blocks are the conversation. So both dials are **all-the-way-through choices**.
  ⚠ **WHAT THAT COSTS AT THIS PROJECT'S CONTEXT SIZE**, on the 16 Sept measurement of ~300,000
  tokens per request (D-371): re-writing that prefix costs **~$1.20 on Sonnet** (1h writes at
  $4/MTok) or **~$3.00 on Opus** ($10/MTok) — *per switch*. Switching up and back is ~$4.20 of
  pure re-processing, about **eighteen Sonnet requests' worth, for one question.**
  ⚠ Whether a cache entry is shared between models is **not stated in the documentation**. It is
  a model's own processed prefix, so treat a model switch as a cold start; that is the safe
  assumption and it is the one the arithmetic above uses.
  ▶ **THE RULING: choose the model AND the effort at the START of a session, from what the
  session IS, and do not touch either afterwards.**
  * a mechanical night — doc edits, renames, transcription, sweeps → **Sonnet 5, `low`**
  * ordinary building work with judgement in it → **Sonnet 5, `medium`** (Pro's default anyway)
  * a session whose whole purpose is deciding what vanilla does → **Opus 5**, effort to taste
  ▶ **AND ESCALATION IS A SEPARATE SESSION, NOT A SWITCH.** Open a fresh Opus session carrying
  only the question and the one file it needs — a few thousand tokens, cents — settle it, write
  it up as a **DECISION with a number**, and carry that one line back. The hand-off artefact this
  project already requires *is* the escalation mechanism. **That is what "decision moments" should
  have said.**
  ⚠ This makes D-371's "start a new session for unrelated work" stronger, not weaker: you cannot
  re-dial inside a session, so the session boundary is the only place the dials exist.

- **D-376** **A CROP DOES NOT GET ITS OWN ATLAS LAYER — IT GETS A SHARE OF ONE.** 17 Sept 2026,
  PASS 15 JOB 3. `pack-blockentity.mjs`'s first version gave each of a block-entity item's sliced
  ≤16x16 texture crops its own atlas layer — 1718 crops, 1718 layers — stacked on the 778 block +
  657 item layers already there (D-341/D-342). Total: 3153, and the test machine's real
  `MAX_ARRAY_TEXTURE_LAYERS` (`12_gfx_webgl2.js`'s `uploadAtlas` guard) is 2048: the game would
  not boot at all — `webgl2: this GPU allows 2048 texture array layers and the atlas needs
  3153 ... — WebGL2 cannot run here`. Almost every crop is far smaller than the 16x16 layer it
  was given (a chest hinge is 2x2; the largest face crop is 14x14), so one-crop-per-layer was
  spending a whole layer's area on a handful of pixels — measured, the 1718 crops' total area is
  118272px², an ideal-packing floor of 462 layers (118272 ÷ 256), against the 1718 actually used.
  ▶ **`packTiles` BIN-PACKS MANY CROPS INTO EACH SHARED LAYER** — a first-fit-decreasing-height
  shelf packer, same family as any sprite-sheet/font-atlas tool — and each quad's `uv`, instead of
  assuming its tile is one whole sprite, is that crop's own local `(0,0)..(w,h)` rectangle PLUS
  the placement offset `packTiles` gave it inside its shared layer. This needed no format change:
  a quad's `uv` was always allowed to be a sub-rectangle of the tile it names — a thin block model
  already draws a partial rectangle of its own single-content tile; this is the same mechanism
  aimed at a tile more than one item shares. Result: 1718 crops pack into 472 layers (778+657+472
  = 1907, comfortably under 2048), 25 layers off the theoretical floor.
  ⚠ **THE ACCEPTED TRADE-OFF:** the atlas array's mip chain (`NEAREST_MIPMAP_LINEAR`,
  `12_gfx_webgl2.js`) is built per LAYER, not per crop — layers never bleed into each other
  (`uploadAtlas`'s own comment), but at mip level ≥1, a shared layer's box-filter downsampling can
  blend one packed crop's edge pixels into an unrelated neighbour's, the same way any atlas page
  holding more than one sprite can. This is rendering, not behaviour (the worldgen/rendering
  "cheap and clever" half of the charter split), it only ever touches small decorative sub-details
  of a dropped block-entity item's own texture, and it only shows up exactly where minification
  blur is already expected. Not fixing this (e.g. by downsampling each packed region in isolation)
  was a deliberate scope call, not an oversight — the alternative was hundreds of hours cheaper.

  ▶ **THE FALLBACK LOCK DANCE STILL WORKS UNATTENDED** — this session committed with it, no

- **D-378** **A CACHED OPUS ENCODE IS VALID WITHOUT ITS RAW SOURCE SITTING NEXT TO IT — AND
  `pack-sounds.mjs` DID NOT CHECK THE CACHE UNLESS THE SOURCE WAS ALSO PRESENT.** 17 Sept 2026,
  PASS 16 JOB 4.2's own session, found by accident: a `--from pack-blockentity --to gen-data`
  suite range re-ran `pack-sounds` in an environment where `.mcsnd/objects` (the raw `.ogg`
  cache) had zero files staged, and the tool silently wrote a 0.01 MB `sounds.bin` — 600 of 605
  events reporting "silent" — in place of the real 4.17 MB payload, because its cache lookup
  (`present.get(n)` -> encode-or-reuse) only ever ran for names it had already matched to a
  RAW `.ogg`, never falling back to `.mcsnd/opus32/<hash>.opus` on its own when the raw file was
  missing but a prior session's real encode of the exact same content hash was sitting right
  there (1,205 of 1,214 files, 7.3 MB, present and unused). This would have committed a silently
  near-mute game if `git diff` on `src/19_data.gen.js`'s `sounds` field size (5.8 MB base64 ->
  13 KB) had not been checked before committing — the suite's own green run does not catch this,
  because `soundcheck.mjs` reads the SAME meta file `pack-sounds.mjs` writes about itself; a tool
  that measures its own bad output as good is not caught by a check that trusts that measurement.
  ▶ **THE FIX:** `pack-sounds.mjs` now checks `.mcsnd/opus<bitrate>/<hash>.opus` directly, by the
  hash `index-1.18.json` already gives every wanted file, for any name with no raw source staged
  — used as-is, never re-encoded (nothing to re-encode from), and reported separately
  (`filesFromRawSource` vs `filesFromCacheOnly` in `sounds.meta.json`) so a future session can
  see which kind of coverage it actually has rather than one merged number. `soundcheck.mjs`'s
  compression-ratio assertion, which divides by a raw-byte total that is genuinely unmeasurable
  when zero raw sources were read this run, now skips itself (and says why) rather than either
  faking a number or false-failing a correct, complete rebuild.
  ▶ **THE LESSON THAT COST THE MOST:** `assets/` is gitignored and regenerated every session
  (D-6) — but a session's SOURCE MATERIAL for that regeneration (which raw jars, caches and
  staged objects happen to be sitting in this particular mount right now) is not guaranteed
  identical across sessions or across the machines this project runs on, and a stage that
  degrades gracefully instead of failing loud on missing source is exactly how a real regression
  reaches `git commit` looking like a clean, green, "idempotent: output changed" build. Compare
  a rebuilt asset's OWN reported numbers against the last-committed `19_data.gen.js`'s, not just
  against the suite's pass/fail, before trusting a full-pipeline regeneration enough to commit it.

- **D-379** **THE ATLAS'S 2048-LAYER PROBLEM IS NOT A HEADLESS-TESTING ARTIFACT — IT REPRODUCED
  WITH A REAL GPU AND A REAL INTERACTIVE DESKTOP.** 17-18 Sept 2026, chasing G18c's pixel check
  (session 23/24). `MAX_ARRAY_TEXTURE_LAYERS` read 2048 against the atlas's 2475 in FOUR
  separate environments: the host's headless Chromium/Edge session, that same session with
  `cdp.mjs`'s forced SwiftShader flags removed, a fresh Ubuntu VM with no GPU passthrough at
  all, AND — after attaching a real AMD Radeon iGPU partition to a Windows 11 VM guest and
  running the check through its own logged-on desktop session (not SSH/session 0, which
  the VM tooling's own agent notes already warn always report software
  rendering) — still 2048, same masked "WebKit WebGL" renderer string ANGLE always returns.
  ▶ **THE LIKELY REAL CAUSE, NOT YET CONFIRMED AGAINST DAN'S OWN ORDINARY BROWSER:** Direct3D 11
  hard-limits `Texture2DArray` to 2048 array slices (`D3D11_REQ_TEXTURE2D_ARRAY_AXIS_DIMENSION`).
  Chrome and Edge on Windows use ANGLE's D3D11 backend by default. If that is what is happening
  here, **every Windows Chrome/Edge player is capped at 2048, not just this VM** — this stopped
  being a testing-infra problem and became a possible real-parity bug the moment the real-GPU
  run also came back 2048. Not yet checked: what `MAX_ARRAY_TEXTURE_LAYERS` reads in Dan's own
  everyday desktop Chrome (not a VM, not automated) — if that also reads 2048, the atlas itself
  needs to fit under it, or the game needs to steer players off ANGLE's D3D11 path (D3D12/Vulkan
  backends do not carry this limit). ⚠ Owed before PASS 16's pixel check can mean anything: that
  one manual check, then a ruling on which side moves.

- **D-380** **THE 2048-LAYER CEILING (D-379) IS ROUTED AROUND, NOT WAITED OUT: THE ATLAS SHARDS
  ACROSS TWO `TEXTURE_2D_ARRAY`S ON WEBGL2.** 18 Sept 2026, session 24, following PASS-16-CURRENT's
  own ranked list of fixes (option 5, "shard the atlas") rather than continuing to chase whether
  some ANGLE flag or backend avoids D3D11's real 2048-slice limit — the fallback the pass docs
  said needed no more GPU luck at all, and Dan asked for it directly rather than more environment
  chasing. `uploadAtlas()` in `src/12_gfx_webgl2.js` now asks the driver for its real
  `MAX_ARRAY_TEXTURE_LAYERS`, puts the first `cap` layers in `uAtlas`/`atlasTex` and the rest in a
  second array, `uAtlas2`/`atlasTex2` (a harmless 1-layer stand-in when no split is needed, so the
  sampler is never incomplete). `L.atlasSplit` is the one real number both the CPU-side split and
  the GPU-side `uAtlasSplit` uniform are built from — never a literal baked into either shader —
  and the fragment shader (`FS`, shared by the cube and model programs, and `FS_HAND`) reads
  `vLayer < uAtlasSplit` to pick which array to sample. Two arrays cover up to 2x the driver's
  real cap; past that `uploadAtlas` throws by name (a third shard is a decision, not a threshold
  someone quietly moves).
  ▶ **VERIFIED FOR REAL, NOT JUST BUILT:** `shadercheck.mjs` (230/0) got a new anti-vacuity block
  that forces a driver cap smaller than the test atlas and asserts the exact split arithmetic —
  two `texStorage3D` calls, the right layer count in each, `L.atlasSplit` and the `uAtlasSplit`
  uniform agreeing, both arrays' full mip chains uploaded. Then the real proof: `g18ccheck.mjs`,
  queued through the ai-jobs lane onto Dan's own Windows box (`root: mclite`, job
  `2026-09-18-g18c-d380`), which for every prior run since D-379 could not get past `Hud.fatal`
  before frame 0 — this run exits 0, 17/17 assertions: a guardian spawns, draws, visibly changes
  the picture (3960 px), and disappears cleanly when removed. **This is the first real-browser
  pixel proof of a drawn mob in this project's history** — the bar JOB 4 (PASS 15/16) has named
  since session 15.
  ▶ **WHAT THIS DOES NOT SETTLE:** WebGPU (`src/11_gfx_webgpu.js`) still refuses cleanly and
  falls back to WebGL2 when the adapter's own `maxTextureArrayLayers` is under what the atlas
  needs (D-310) — untouched by this decision, since D-3's fallback already handles it correctly
  and WebGPU is independently black on real hardware for unrelated reasons (CLAUDE.md). Sharding
  WebGPU's own texture array is a separate, owed piece of work if the WebGPU path is ever fixed
  and needs more than 2048 layers itself.
  ▶ **THE OTHER RANKED EXPERIMENTS IN PASS-16-HISTORY.md (bare-metal browser console check,
  `--use-angle=gl`/`vulkan`, WebGPU adapter limits) are now moot for shipping** — they were ways
  to find a driver that does not need this fix; this fix works unconditionally on every backend,
  which is exactly why the pass docs called it out as the fallback that "needs no more GPU luck
  at all."

- **D-381** **G18D CLOSES THE MOB-LOOT ROW OF `Cb.OWED`: `pack-loot.mjs` NOW PACKS THE 91 ENTITY

- **D-405** **THE CRAFTING TABLE SCREEN — PASS 17 JOB 1's fourth unit — AND THE BUG BUILDING IT
  FOUND: the crafting result slot had never consumed the grid, for EITHER grid, since G9
  shipped.** 19 Sept 2026, session 44. Reading `Menu.playerMenu` and the old
  `Hud.refreshCraftResult` to model the table's own 3x3 screen after the player's existing 2x2
  turned up that `m.grid` was set on the menu object and read by the result recompute, and never
  read anywhere else — `Menu.playerMenu`'s result slot had `mayPlace`/`noDrag`/`cap` and no
  `onTake` at all. So taking a crafted item from the player's own inventory screen removed
  nothing from the four grid cells: every survival recipe crafted that way, in this build, since
  G9, was free. Not on `Use.OWED`, not in `docs/PLAN.md`'s known-gaps table, not caught by
  `craftcheck.mjs` (which calls `Recipes.craft(grid, w, h)` directly and never touches a menu or
  a click) or by `invcheck.mjs` (which exercises `Menu.doClick` at length but never crafts
  through it) — exactly the shape D-276 and the lessons in `NEXT.md` warn about: a check proves
  only what it touches, and the join between "the grid matches a recipe" and "taking the result
  spends the grid" had no check standing in it at all.
  · **The fix** is one shared helper, `craftingTaken(gridContainer, n)` in `14g_menu.js`: on
  `onTake`, remove ONE item from every occupied cell of `n` grid slots. Wired as the `result`
  slot's `onTake` in BOTH `Menu.playerMenu` (the pre-existing 2x2, now actually correct) and the
  new `Menu.craftingMenu` (the table's 3x3, built this session) — one function, two callers, so
  they cannot drift into two different rules the way two hand-written copies eventually would.
  · **The one gap this fix knowingly leaves, named rather than silent:** vanilla's own
  `ResultSlot.onTake` does not just decrement — an ingredient with a "crafting remainder"
  (`Item.getCraftingRemainingItem`: a water/lava/milk bucket becomes an empty bucket, most
  potions become a glass bottle) has that remainder placed back rather than simply vanishing.
  This engine has no such table yet, so a bucket or a potion used as a crafting ingredient is
  just consumed like any other item until one is built. Moved from the old crafting-table-screen
  row on `Use.OWED` (`14l_use.js`) to a row of its own, naming exactly this.
  · **`Menu.craftingMenu`** (`14g_menu.js`) is vanilla's own `CraftingMenu` layout: slot 0 the
  result, 1..9 the 3x3 grid (row-major, matching `Recipes.craft`'s own `w*h` convention), 10..36
  the 27-slot backpack, 37..45 the hotbar — NO armour band and NO offhand slot, unlike
  `Menu.playerMenu`; `CraftingScreen`'s own image has neither. Its `quickMove` mirrors
  `Menu.chestMenu`'s own two-region shift-click rule (D-397).
  · **`Hud.openCraftingTable`/`drawCrafting`/`craftingClick`** (`15_hud.js`) follow `Hud.openChest`'s
  own shape, with one deliberate difference named in both: a crafting table carries no block
  entity and no per-position state at all (`CraftingTableBlock.use` builds a FRESH `CraftingMenu`
  every time), so opening it only confirms a real `crafting_table` state is still at (x,y,z) and
  otherwise looks up nothing. `Hud.close` gained a crafting-specific branch: since the 3x3 grid
  lives only in this ephemeral menu (unlike a chest's own persistent block entity), whatever is
  still sitting in it when the screen closes is returned to the player's inventory — through
  `Menu.drop` (newly exported alongside `craftingTaken` for exactly this caller) if it does not
  fit — rather than silently discarded, matching vanilla's own `CraftingMenu.removed`/
  `clearContainer`.
  · **`G.CRAFTING`** (`15b_gui.js`) is vanilla's own `CraftingScreen` geometry — 176x166,
  transcribed from public decompiles the same not-yet-bytecode-walked way `G.CHEST` (D-397) is —
  plus `G.craftSlotXY`/`G.craftSlotAt`, the same shape as `G.chestSlotXY`/`chestSlotAt`. The
  `crafting_table` GUI sheet already shipped (`tools/build-gui.mjs`, listed since before this
  screen existed) and needed no change.
  · **Proof:** a new headless check, `tools/craftingtablecheck.mjs` (21/0), loading the real
  `15_hud.js`/`14g_menu.js` — opening only succeeds over a real `crafting_table` state and builds
  a fresh menu every time (§1); a hand-filled 3x3 grid produces the real matcher's result (§2);
  taking the result through a REAL `Menu.doClick` removes exactly one item from every occupied
  grid cell, proven both for a single item per cell and for a cell stacked past one (§3/§3b); an
  unmatched grid is left untouched because there was never a result to take (§4's anti-vacuity);
  closing with unfinished ingredients still in the grid returns them to the player rather than
  discarding them (§5); and — the regression proof that matters most — the SAME fix closes the
  bug on `Menu.playerMenu`'s own pre-existing 2x2 grid, driven through the identical click path

- **D-411** **KW-22 WAS A FALSE POSITIVE: `lumacheck`'S SUSTAINED RULE MEASURED THE FLIGHT'S TERRAIN, NOT
  A FLASH.** 20 Sept 2026, session 48. Reproduced three times on Dan's GPU (Edge, medium) through the
  runner: one run of ~110 frames ending f1671, always the same place (1000400, −599400). A per-frame
  dump and a back-buffer photograph of it: sky fraction drifts 0.42 → 0.50 → 0.43 over the run, the
  camera climbs 108 → 118 as the ground rises, 0 unmeshed near sections, ~2,500 meshes resident, and
  the picture is a savanna river valley whose far terrain has faded into fog. Fog colour is what the
  check calls "sky". The global median (0.18) simply was not the right baseline for a flight that, at
  ~22 fps on a real GPU, covers ~800 blocks in 75 s where SwiftShader covers ~170 and never leaves
  its starting biome — the D-236 lesson again (never set a bound from a different sample than the one
  it runs at). D-247 is untouched.
  · **The rule.** A sustained run is now a frame ≥ 0.25 above the median of the 60 frames either side
    (`RUNWIN`), OR ≥ 0.85 sky outright (`RUNABS`), over a resident world with a complete near disc.
    Numbers from the real flight: worst healthy excess over the local median 0.103 (W=60; 0.142 at
    W=120, 0.385 at W=200 — a window as wide as the run absorbs it); healthy maximum sky 0.507; the
    single-frame spike statistic is unchanged (worst 0.034 against a 0.15 fence).
  · **Three new anti-vacuity cases**, each run through the real scorer: a slow 110-frame drift to 0.50
    is not flagged; a 40-frame 0.60 run over a calm 0.18 flight is; a 200-frame 0.97 run (longer than
    the window, so its own median) is caught by `RUNABS`. Passing on the real GPU: 25 assertions.
  · **Tooling kept:** `lumacheck --dump` prints the frames around every run, photographs the first
    frame that jumps 0.25 over the last 30, a first frame at ≥ 0.4 and frame 600, and saves the frames

    neither ≥ 0.85 sky nor 0.25 over a window it does not fill escapes the sustained rule; that is

- **D-413** **THE DOUBLE CHEST — AND IT HAD NO PLACEMENT AT ALL, SO TWO CHESTS NEVER JOINED.** 20 Sept 2026,
  session 49 (G19b, PASS 17 JOB 1). The QUEUE said the hard part was "the merge, not the screen"; the
  hard part was that nothing in the game ever wrote `type=left/right` — a player who put two chests
  side by side got two single chests. Three pieces, each with its vanilla source named:
  · **Placement — `Player.withChestType`** (`ChestBlock.getStateForPlacement`): sneaking on a side face
  pairs with the lone chest on THE CLICKED side and takes its facing (only if at right angles to the click);
  otherwise a lone same-block chest on the clockwise side makes this `left`, on the counter-clockwise
  side `right`. Only a `single` chest is a candidate, so a third chest beside a pair stays single.
  · **Neighbour update — `Behave.chestShape`** (`ChestBlock.updateShape`): the FIRST chest flips to the
  opposite half when the second lands, and a half whose partner cell no longer holds that block goes back
  to `single` — which is all "breaking one half leaves a 27-slot chest" is. Threaded in vanilla's own
  `UPDATE_SHAPE_ORDER` (west, east, north, south). A chest never pairs with a trapped chest.
  · **The container — `Menu.chestMenu(..., be2)` and `Hud.chestPair`:** ONE 54-slot menu whose slots 0..26
  read and write `first.items` and 27..53 `second.items` — the LIVE arrays, never a merged copy. Opening
  from either half gives the same pair the same way round. `be.open` counts both halves.
  ⚠ **THE ONE UNREFEREED FACT: `type=right` is FIRST (the top three rows).** Transcribed from the public
  1.18.2 source (`getBlockType`: RIGHT→FIRST, LEFT→SECOND; `CompoundContainer(first, second)`), NOT read
  from the jar — there is no javap on the machines this runs on. `chestcheck` §8 and `chestpaircheck`
  pin it so changing it is a decision, but they do not prove it vanilla. If a JDK is ever installed,
  `extract-guigeom.mjs`'s method reads `ChestBlock.getBlockType` in a minute (KW candidate).
  · **Checks:** `chestcheck` §8 (the merge, close-and-reopen, shift-click both ways, swapped halves and a
  no-second-half menu as anti-vacuity) and the NEW `chestpaircheck` (27 assertions, 4 deliberate breaks:
  neighbour update off, halves swapped, sneak flag ignored, un-pairing off) — headless, the real
  `14_player.js`/`15_hud.js`/`07b` against a flat world. In `suite.mjs`.
  · **`titlecheck` red fixed (found first):** "the tint seam is being measured at render distance 10 (preset
  medium)". Medium is 12; the ADAPTIVE governor (D-46) walked it to 10 on a software renderer while the
  check waited. The check measures the seam, not the governor, so it now pins `adaptive = false` and the
  preset's own distance (`cullcheck` already did the same). ⚠ Browser stage: not run here — the full
  suite on Dan's PC at close is its proof.
  · **Found, NOT done (on QUEUE):** a chest with a solid block above or a cat on it must refuse to open

  the script being run" with `import.meta.url === \`file://${process.argv[1]}\``, which never matches a
